- `system/scripts/migrate_claude_auth.py` is deleted. It was a manual, one-time move of Claude keys out of the mngr host env file, from when auth moved into accounts. Without it, `workspace-scripts` no longer depends on the chat app or mngr, so chat's tests can depend on it without a dependency cycle.

- The gcp and azure create templates no longer forward `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and `GH_TOKEN` into the workspace's host env. Every other template stopped in July (Claude auth moved into accounts, and GitHub sync became an opt-in skill); these two were added on a parallel branch and kept the old line.

- `system/scripts/stdlib_only_scripts_test.py` checks every module of `workspace_bare_scripts` instead of a hand-kept list of scripts, so the modules that list left out -- the four guard checks, the rewrite hook's `agent_rewrite_bash_command` and `with_secrets` -- are now held to the stdlib-only rule on their own.

- `system/test_no_type_errors.py` type-checks the root project with ty: the skills and their shared scripts, `system/scripts`, the root-level tests and `conftest.py`. A skill listed in `.agents/third-party-skills.toml` is excluded from it and from the bare checks. It also checks the bare tier (what the system `python3` runs) a second time, against an environment with no third-party packages. There, an import the system `python3` could not make at runtime shows up as `unresolved-import`, at Python 3.12. The bare check covers the bare packages, the stdlib-only modules of other packages that run under `python3` (such as `notify_user.py`), and every bare skill's script, and it searches exactly the directories a bare file may put on `sys.path`. A bare skill's test, which imports its script by name, is left out of the root check and checked against the root venv with that skill's `scripts/` on the search path. This replaces `stdlib_only_scripts_test.py`, and fixes the errors the new check found.

- The workspace's Python floor is 3.12: `requires-python = ">=3.12"` in the root and every project, and ruff targets 3.12. The build no longer installs a uv-managed 3.12 itself: with no project allowing 3.11, uv can no longer settle on a system 3.11 that the lock rejects, and the build's `UV_PYTHON=3.12` pin has uv download a managed 3.12 when the system has none.

- Local workspaces from before 2026-09-14 (Debian 12, system Python 3.11) can no longer be updated in place (see the update-self change).

- The root launch rules read supervisord program lines the way supervisord does (`command = ...`, `bash -lc "..."`), and a bare-tier file that imports venv-tier first-party code (such as `workspace_scripts`) now fails a root test.

- The workspace-app contract (`contracts.md` section 14) now says a pre-manifest app and the background services run from `.venv/bin/<name>`, not under `uv run`, matching the launch rule.

- `AGENTS.md`'s lockfile rule now says a `uv.lock` change that follows from a `pyproject.toml` change (a dependency or a new skill `python/` project) is committed, not dropped as churn.

- Every `.venv` (the checkout's and each worktree's) is now a symlink to a target beside the uv cache (`/var/cache/user/venvs` on docker), so uv hardlinks packages from its cache instead of copying them onto the workspace volume: the root venv was a 512M copy. `system/scripts/workspace_bare_scripts/venv_links.py` keeps the links. The boot window, worker provisioning, the session-start sync, the build and the dependency install run its `ensure` before they sync. `ensure` recreates a target a rebuilt root filesystem lost, turns a real `.venv` directory into a link (putting the directory back if the sync fails), and deletes every target whose link is gone, so removed worktrees leave nothing behind. A target on a different filesystem from the cache gets a warning in the boot log.

- An image build bakes the root venv's target into the image layer, and the first-boot seed copies only the `.venv` link, not a 512M venv.

- New blueprint `docs/system/blueprint/app-environments/plan-app-environments.md`: one shared environment for the built-in packages, and a standalone project for each user package.

Built-in apps share the workspace venv, and every user-built package is its own uv project (`docs/system/blueprint/app-environments/plan-app-environments.md`).

- **One install per built-in app.** Each built-in app's supervisord program execs its entry point from `.venv/bin` instead of a bare name, and the build no longer installs each app as its own uv tool (a second copy only an agent's PATH and the update pre-flight reached; a stale one rolled back a good update). The build removes any such tool an older image still carries (`tool_env.py drop-app-tools`). The built-in apps are root dependencies, and `system/config/mngr_plugins.toml` assigns plugins only to the mngr tool.

- **Explicit root members.** The root `pyproject.toml` names every built-in library, service and app instead of globbing `system/*/*`. A package under `system/apps`, `system/services` or `system/libs` that it does not name is a user package, and `system/test_user_packages_are_standalone.py` holds each to the standalone layout: its own `uv.lock` (checked with `uv lock --check`), no workspace sources, and a program line that syncs its own project `--locked` before it execs from its own `.venv/bin`. `system/test_app_manifests.py` reads the built-ins from `members` and fails on a package that is neither listed nor standalone; the launch rules flag a root-venv one-off of a user package's command.

- **User packages at boot, build and worker setup.** The bootstrap window links every user package's venv without syncing it; `build_workspace.sh` and worker provisioning sync each from its own lock, a failure stopping only that package (`system/scripts/workspace_bare_scripts/user_packages.py`). The root test run leaves user packages out; each runs from its own directory.

- `contracts.md` section 14, the workspace-app-model plan, `workspace-internals.md`, the stop-when-no-windows spec, the critical-app-editing test plan and the app READMEs describe the layout.

- The Style Guide app's drop-in execs `.venv/bin/style-guide-app` from the workspace venv like every other built-in app's, tagged into the app's own `style-guide` band.

Multiplayer, part one (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, sections 4 and 5): the workspace knows who is here, and chats know who said what.

- `AGENTS.md` tells the agent, under "Communication", that a message prefixed `[from: <name>]` came from someone other than the workspace's owner, and that the prefix is not part of what they said.

- The desktop interface contract (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/contracts.md`) gains the participant key (section 4.3), the heartbeat's input age (`input_age_seconds`, stamped by the shell; an older page's `last_input_at` accepted and clamped) and the roster route (5.1), the refusal of a present `X-Imbue-Identity` header that does not parse (5.5, with the client inventory's participants), the `roster_updated` push (6; on a person's input time moving too, a burst of file events announced once, never an unchanged document) beside the new `clients_updated` push (a registered window's disconnect, a pruned client), and the handshake's third trigger, the page's `shell:capabilities` (7).

- `system/scripts/workspace_bare_scripts/message_chat.py` says a chat room is answered with `mngr message --start <room>`, never through the script: a send no proxy vouched for is nobody's speech, raising no bubble and acting on no mention.

- The grants parsers the share gateway and the shell both need now live in one library, `system/libs/share_grants`.

Chat rooms (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 7):

- The new `room` agent type (`[agent_types.room]` in `.mngr/settings.toml`): a chat room's agent, whose process, `system/scripts/workspace_bare_scripts/room_agent.py`, appends what `mngr message <room>` types into its pane to the room's common transcript, so `mngr transcript <room>` reads a room and `mngr message <room>` posts into one as the workspace's agent. It reads its pane unbuffered, so a pasted paragraph longer than a terminal line arrives whole, and launches through the OOM band wrapper like every chat.

- `system/scripts/workspace_bare_scripts/require_create_account.py` lets a create through on no account when `MINDS_CREATE_WITHOUT_ACCOUNT=1` is set, which the chat app sets for a room's create.

- `AGENTS.md` tells the agent what a `[from: <name> in #<room>]` prefix means and how to read and answer the room with `mngr transcript` and `mngr message`.

`system/scripts/workspace_bare_scripts/forward_port.py` copies a launch path's `mention_param` onto the registry row beside its `text_param` and `draft_param` (the multiplayer spec, section 7.5).

`workspace_layout`'s `EntryPresentation` gains `is_window_shown` (default true): whether a client lists a pinned window in its taskbar, false after that client closed it.

The desktop interface's contract table (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/contracts.md`, section 2) lists the chat app's `lounge` launch path beside its other intake paths, and `system/test_app_manifests.py` holds the manifest to it.

The post-launch-paths plan (`docs/system/blueprint/post-launch-paths/plan-post-launch-paths.md`) lists the `lounge` intake target and launch path beside the others, and its launcher section (4) names the rows the chords run now that `main` is first: `main` is Enter, `new` is Ctrl+Enter, and a Getting Started tile's text goes to the main chat; the launcher plan (`docs/system/blueprint/launcher-and-getting-started/plan-launcher-and-getting-started.md`, sections 3.1, 3.5, 4.4, and 4.5) names the same rows in its stock-machine examples.

The desktop-interface blueprint (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/`) records the desktops phase of the multiplayer spec (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 8): the desktop record's `owner` and the display order the `POST /api/desktops/order` route rewrites in `contracts.md` (sections 4.1 and 5.2, and the overview's, chip's, and backdrop menu's selectors in section 12, beside the tray's, which replace the retired Presence widget's), the overview and viewing another person's desktop in `concepts.md` (sections 2.1 and 2.8), and the plan's view list naming the overview and the wallpaper chooser in place of the desktops widget and the settings dialog.

Viewing somebody else's desktop with a fullscreen window on it draws that window over the whole letterbox (the owner's backdrop alone), never over the viewer's taskbar, which keeps "Stop viewing"; Fullscreen is refused while viewing like every other window verb, and the overview's thumbnails draw a fullscreen window as a maximized one.

`system/test_app_manifests.py` also holds the terminal and files launch paths to declaring no `mention_param` and no `app_params`, as it already did for their `text_param` and `draft_param`.

The contract table's chat row (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/contracts.md`, section 2) lists the `main` launch path ("Send to main chat", `target = "main_chat"`) the manifest declares and the manifest test asserts, which the row had left out since the path was added.

The app-chat phase of the multiplayer spec (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 9): `system/scripts/workspace_bare_scripts/forward_port.py` copies a launch path's `app_params` pair onto the registry row; the new `system/scripts/rename_chat.py` renames the chat under one title to another through the chat app's rename route, for an app whose display name changed; the desktop-interface blueprint (`contracts.md` sections 2, 5.3, 5.5, and 12; `concepts.md` section 2.7) and the post-launch-paths plan (the `show` launch target, the `app_chat` intake target) record the title bar, the launch target, and the launch path field; `system/test_app_manifests.py` holds the chat manifest to its seventh launch path.

The Screen spec's visibility section (8.2) now names the fourth input the viewer reads, the stage's size as the 1.5 s belt sees it, and says the stream owns the connect-info fetch, ignoring a superseded one and retrying a failed one; its keyboard section says keys are read from a hidden editable input inside the stage so command-binding browser extensions stand down.

The routines spec (section 12) says how the cron migration converts a command with shell syntax, what it does with `%`, and that it also reads job state from `system/data/.state/jobs/`, where releases before minds-v0.8.7 kept it.

Upgrade Fortress (the Screen's stealth Chromium) from v151.0.7908.0 to v156.0.8078.47 in the Screen's env.d unit (`system/scripts/env.d/2000-screen.sh`), resolving imbue-ai/default-workspace-template#896.

- Both architectures now install from the official tiliondev/fortress release (the minhtrinh-imbue fork build that supplied arm64 at v151 is retired), checked against the pinned SHA-256 sums; the tarballs unpack to `fortress-v156/` and the stable symlink `/opt/fortress/tilion-fortress/tilion` is repointed as before.

- The CDP click hang that blocked the v153 upgrade is fixed upstream and verified with the issue's repro against the v156 linux-x64 binary: a Playwright click that moves the pointer returns (in up to about a second, the motion animation's cost) instead of hanging, over a direct launch and over `connect_over_cdp` alike, including on a page that re-renders on click.

- No license key is provisioned: unlicensed, Fortress prints one notice and runs the public first-generation engine, matching the fleet's v151 behavior (and this repository is public, so a shipped key would be too).

- v156 replays a recorded human cursor trajectory for every pointer move it is sent (v151 teleported the pointer): a click on a target away from the pointer's last position returns in up to about a second, and after the press the cursor glides across whatever lies between the two points, so a hover-sensitive control can change under a test that reads it right after such a click, and a control that follows the press from pointerdown to pointerup can read the glide as a drag. `AGENTS.md` says so beside the Playwright instructions, and the two workspace tests this caught sidestep it: the chat's auto-compact e2e test drives its submenu with the keyboard, and its phone-drawer e2e test hovers the chat row before tapping it, which plays the glide out before the tap.

- The Chrome extensions are fetched for Chrome 156, and the pre-2026-10-18 legacy-layout satisfied check (a CLEANUP for images that unpacked v151 straight into the stable path) is dropped -- those images exist only on this branch's history and a layout that old now simply reinstalls.

- The unit keeps writing the eMudhra CA distrust policy (the `CADistrustedCertificates` machine policy distrusting the eight compromised intermediates): v156 is still below the 158.0.8115.0 threshold at which Chromium's own root store and SPKI blocklist make the policy removable.

User-profile-state phase 3B groundwork, workspace side:

- The bug-report diagnostics collector now carries the two new per-workspace update records beside the schedule, `skipped-target.json` and `dismissals.json` (the skipped update target and update-row dismissals the Imbue Studio app moves into the workspace).

- `system/scripts/fetch_mngr_assets.sh` vendors one more asset: the desktop's `workspace_profile_contract.json`, which pins the workspace profile snapshot's format and keys for `workspace-profile`'s cross-repo contract test.

- `data/.state/README.md`, `data/system/README.md`, and the blueprint contracts docs document the new paths: the profile snapshot at `data/.state/profile/account.json`, the workspace's own settings layer under `data/system/profile/`, the `verification_disabled` key in `backup.toml`, and the previously undocumented `data/.state/update-apply/` records.

- The manage-routines skill's prose reflects that the container timezone now comes from `data/.state/user_timezone` (written once at create) rather than a boot-time fetch.

Phase 3C of the user-profile-state spec (rebindable keyboard shortcuts) wires `workspace-profile` into the uv workspace sources and the shell's, chat's, and files' dependencies (lockfile regenerated), has `forward_port.py` copy a manifest's `[[keybindings]]` onto its registry row, checks that every built-in manifest spells its default chords in the grammar (`system/test_app_manifests.py`), and adds the shared browser-side chord utilities to `system/libs/workspace_ui`: the canonical chord spelling of a keydown (`keybindings.ts`), and the `shell:keybindings-changed` app-contract message every framed page re-fetches its resolved chords on. The desktop-interface contract (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/contracts.md`, sections 5.1, 6, and 7) and the workspace app model's browser-side contract (section 10) record the manifest's and the registry's `keybindings` field, the shell's keybindings routes, the `keybindings_changed` event, and that message.

The new `latchkey-access` library joins the uv workspace (members, sources, and the lockfile) and the `system/libs/` index: the shared spelling of the agent-to-gateway environment and header contract, replacing the chat app's and the shell's identical copies.

The Screen spec (`docs/system/specs/screen/spec.md`) designs a neko-streamed Linux desktop as one workspace window, with the browser as a launch path of it and the browser app deleted: packaging, the Screen service, the viewer, the control lease over neko's `locked_controls`, sizing through added RANDR modes, three video profiles, visibility and audio policy, a never-stop-for-emptiness lifecycle whose group ends together, occupancy-aware OOM bands, clipboard and files, mobile, the three fullscreen layers (a `FULLSCREEN` placement state, Studio's immersive mode, and the X session's own), the share gateway's brokering, the browser migration, the `screen` command, tests and the implementation order.

The Screen's first two implementation steps land the infrastructure around the new `system/apps/screen` package:

- The env.d unit `system/scripts/env.d/2000-screen.sh` replaces `1000-playwright-fortress.sh`: it installs the Screen's apt packages (Xorg with the dummy driver, XFCE, PulseAudio, GStreamer with x264, xdotool, wmctrl, xclip) from the pinned snapshot and the pinned neko v3.2.0 binary at `/opt/neko/bin/neko` (taken from the `ghcr.io/m1k1o/neko/base` image's one layer through the registry API, checked against pinned digests), and carries Fortress and the Chrome extensions over unchanged, `DWT_SKIP_BROWSER_UNIT` included. The offload configs and `offload_sandbox_init.sh` point at the new unit.

- `system/supervisord.conf.d/xvfb.conf` is gone: display `:99` is the Screen's Xorg from now on (the browser program keeps `DISPLAY=:99` and renders onto the Screen until its migration). New drop-ins: `screen.conf` (the service and the `screen-stack` group), `screen-xorg.conf`, `screen-pulse.conf`, `screen-session.conf`, `screen-neko.conf` (the group's members, started by the service on demand) and `screen-watch.conf` (the event listener that ends the group together).

- `system/test_app_manifests.py` pins the Screen's manifest, accepts an event listener as a declared wiring program, and treats programs an app's manifest wires as that app's rather than standalone. The Dockerfile's npm manifest layer and `system/package.json` carry the viewer's frontend; its build output is gitignored like the other frontends'.

- The Screen's launch path for its own page is `screen` rather than the spec's `open`, which the manifest schema reserves for the launch path the shell synthesizes.

The desktop interface's documents take the Screen spec's `FULLSCREEN` placement state: `contracts.md` adds the `screen` manifest row (the browser row stays until its migration), the state in the placements file and the `place` op, the viewport as the fullscreen frame under the geometry rules, and the strip's selectors; `concepts.md` lists the state, the strip and the Fullscreen and Immersive menu rows, and marks decision 17 superseded; `plan-desktop-interface.md` 9.4 describes the browser as a launch path of the Screen. `geometry_vectors.json` gains the `fullscreen` cases and `snap_frames.FULLSCREEN` (`"viewport"`).

Step 8, the browser's migration and the deletions (the Screen spec, sections 16.2 and 18):

- `system/apps/browser` is deleted (its changelog entries with it; the browser's history continues in `system/apps/screen`'s), with `system/supervisord.conf.d/browser.conf`, the `pixelflux` and `pcmflux` dependencies (`uv.lock` regenerated), and what the image baked only for the browser: `xvfb`, `xclip`, the libva and pixman runtime libraries, `x11-utils` and the baked PulseAudio (`system/scripts/setup_system.sh`); the Screen's env.d unit installs xclip and PulseAudio with the rest of the stack on first boot. `system/test_app_manifests.py` and `docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/contracts.md` section 2 lose the browser's rows.

- `system/scripts/env.d/2000-screen.sh` keeps Fortress at v151.0.7908.0 (x64 from the official release, arm64 from the fork build the previous unit pinned), checked against the pinned SHA-256 sums; the tree is installed under a versioned directory and `/opt/fortress/tilion-fortress/tilion`, the path AGENTS.md, the root conftest and the Screen service use, is a symlink the unit repoints at the pinned release, so a pin bump reinstalls (an install the previous unit made of the same release is accepted as it is). Fortress v153 (Fortress v3) was tried and dropped: its license now charges organizations of our size for production use, and its recorded-human mouse motion makes CDP mouse clicks hang under Playwright, which would stall agents driving the browser fleet. The Chrome extensions are fetched for Chrome 151.

- `2000-screen.sh` also carries the eMudhra CA distrust policy the replaced unit wrote (the `CADistrustedCertificates` machine policy distrusting the eight compromised intermediates, written whether or not Fortress is installed yet), and `system/scripts/fortress_distrust_policy_test.py` checks the new unit's policy the way it checked the old one's. Fortress v151 is below the 158.0.8115.0 threshold at which Chromium's own root store and SPKI blocklist make the policy removable.

- The workspace shell's `open https://...` opens the page through the Screen's `browser` launch path (`system/libs/workspace_layout`), and the shell's layout pipeline test expects the Screen app to be named when it is not registered.

- `docs/system/blueprint/workspace-app-model/contracts.md` loses the browser app too: the Screen takes its row in the built-in manifest table and the `wiring` and `launcher_rank` examples, and the instances API's browser-specific notes and row are gone with the app.

Step 9, the document sweep of the Screen spec's section 19: `concepts.md` decisions 16 and 18 follow the Screen's rule (the browser is no longer window-bound; an agent opens the Screen's window), the services README names the Screen's stack sidecars where it names the rule they follow, and the Screen spec's status line says implemented, with an "Implementation notes" subsection at the end of section 22 recording the deviations the implementers verified (the `screen` launch path id, the `screen-stack` group, the admin-password event session, the REST clipboard route for HTML, the file drop that does not land, mouse events for taps, the hidden pointer lock, the gateway's `/connect-info` route, no audio null-device fallback, Chromium's renderers shed before programs on the Screen, `GET /json/version` on the CDP proxy, and Chromium starting maximized so its window fills the Screen).

- `system/scripts/env.d/2000-screen.sh` also installs neko's Xorg input driver, `/usr/lib/xorg/modules/input/neko_drv.so`, from the pinned `ghcr.io/m1k1o/neko/base:3.2.0` image (one layer per architecture, pinned by digest and by the module's SHA-256, through the same registry fetch as the binary; the image builds it on Debian trixie against xorg-server 21.1, XInput ABI 24.4, which is what the pinned snapshot installs), so a phone's taps reach the Screen as real touches.

- Every create template that runs a workspace declares the Screen's published ports, `publish__extend = ["59000/udp", "59000/tcp"]` (`.mngr/settings.toml`); the `modal` template declares `["59000/tcp"]` alone, because Modal tunnels carry TCP only and mngr refuses a UDP declaration before the sandbox exists.

- `system/scripts/env.d/2000-screen.sh` also installs the Screen's browser command, `system/apps/screen/scripts/screen-browser-open`, at `/usr/local/bin/screen-browser-open` (re-installed whenever the tree's copy differs) and registers it as the `x-www-browser` alternative, so XFCE's "Web Browser" launcher, an `http(s)` link opened by a program on the Screen, and `sensible-browser` all open the page in the fleet's Chromium through the Screen's browser launch path.

- The five Screen stack drop-ins (`screen-xorg`, `screen-session`, `screen-pulse`, `screen-neko`, `screen-watch`) tag themselves by their own program name, landing in the stack's band (`SCREEN_STACK`, 850) rather than the Screen service's (72).

### system/apps/browser

The `telemetry_watch` usage line runs it with `uv run --no-sync`.

The preview test imports update-app's preview tool from the `update_app_skill` package instead of loading `preview_app.py` by path, which is now a thin entry file.

The wake-up the fleet sends a queued agent's chat goes through `message_chat.send()` in-process instead of running `message_chat.py` as a subprocess, on threads of its own so a slow send never holds up a browser's start or stop, and the app depends on `workspace-scripts`. A send that is not delivered is still logged as a warning.

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

The CDP proxy's refusals and the fleet CLI's no-agent error now tell an agent to run `uv run --no-sync agentic-browser-fleet ...`. The bare `agentic-browser-fleet` reached an agent's shell only through the browser app's own uv tool, which the workspace no longer installs; the CLI now runs from the workspace venv, as the `agentic-browser-fleet` skill already said.

### system/apps/chat

An idle compaction in a Claude chat no longer shows the `/compact` the idle sweep sent as a user bubble: the command shows on the "Compacting while idle…" chip instead, which opens on why it ran and then that `/compact`. That `/compact` no longer counts as a new turn either, so the last turn's "Done" mark stays once the compaction lands, and it does not use up one of auto fast mode's turns. The "Compacted" chip opens on why it ran and then the summary; the start chip of every compaction no longer repeats the summary.

Hardened the chat file watcher against OS thread exhaustion: when the OS refuses a new thread midway through starting a directory watch (watchdog starts the inotify helper thread and only then the emitter thread), the watcher now reaps the orphaned helper thread and keeps running so it retries, instead of leaking the thread and dropping the watch. Also fixed an intermittent failure in the auto-compact-notice end-to-end test by waiting for the chat transcript to load before triggering the compaction, so the streamed compaction event is no longer dropped before the page has subscribed.

Switching between chats no longer leaves the transcript blank and scrolled to the top. When a chat's frame is hidden and shown again (what happens whenever you click between chats), the browser resets its scroll position to the top; the transcript now re-pins to the newest message instead of getting stranded at the top until you scroll by hand.

- Chats watch their files through one filesystem observer the app shares, and chats on one account share one watch of its projects tree, so viewing a chat no longer starts an observer and a projects-tree watch of its own. Viewing a chat used to cost about five threads, each holding up to ~1.9 MB of stack in a sandboxed workspace.

- The app answers as soon as it starts instead of after its first read of the agent list (about 40 s for 31 agents on a loaded workspace); a page connecting meanwhile gets the chat list when that read finishes.

- The idle-compaction sweep tells mngr which providers its chats are on, so mngr stops replaying its whole discovery event log every minute.

When the chat cannot tell whether a message reached the agent, it sends it again once and says so under the message, and a message still unconfirmed after that gets a notice of its own; a message sent to a Claude chat while it is still starting is no longer reported as possibly unsent, or lost when its process exits.

- A message mngr could not confirm reaching the agent (`submission_unconfirmed`), or whose send failed in a way mngr could not classify (`unknown`), is sent again once, automatically, where the agent is. When that lands, the message shows as sent, with a small "Sent again" line under it and a "?" explaining that the chat could not confirm the first copy arrived, so the agent may see it twice; if the first copy did arrive too, its second copy folds into that line rather than showing as a second bubble. The message route answers such a send `{"status": "resent"}`. Only when the second send cannot be confirmed either does the chat stop and show "Couldn't confirm your message arrived": the agent may already have it, Cancel and Send again are offered without Force or mngr's diagnostic text, a pressed Send again or Retry goes out once rather than being repeated automatically, the message goes back in the composer, and it comes back out once the agent's turn for it shows up. A message whose send mngr reports typed nothing (`agent_not_found`) is looked up again and sent once more.

- A message sent to an agent not accepting messages yet (`not_ready`), or on a host too loaded to read (`state_unknown`), is tried again after 1, 2 and 4 seconds before it shows a failure, and one for an agent that was down and would not start (`agent_unreachable`) is tried once more. Nothing was typed, so these tries cannot double it. Each `not_ready` try includes mngr's 30-second wait for the input box, so those can take about two minutes. Stop ends these tries, and the automatic resends above: it hands the message back to the composer, so nothing more is sent.

- A message sent to a Claude chat while it is still starting is no longer reported as possibly unsent. Claude takes a message at once but writes it down only after its startup hooks finish; mngr now reads Claude's screen when it has waited out its window, so a message Claude holds counts as sent, and one Claude never took is cleared from its input box and sent again automatically, once, where the agent is (`not_submitted`). An unconfirmed send now remains only where the screen cannot settle one: the rare Claude screen that shows neither.

- A message a Claude chat showed but had not written down yet (while its startup hooks run) is no longer lost when the agent's process exits before it does, from a crash or a kill. The chat reads the agent's final transcript and sends again, once, each delivered message sent after the last message it wrote down, restarting the agent to do so. Nothing is sent again after a deliberate stop, after Stop takes the turn back, to a chat that is switching or has moved on, for a message older than half an hour, or for a message that was itself such a resend.

The tool-call reader treats `uv run --no-sync` / `--frozen` / `--quiet` in front of `tk` the same as a bare `uv run`, so a tk step command run that way is still recognised (the option set is shared with the secrets guard through `tk_command_parsing`); the README runs the backend from `.venv/bin` and the tests with `uv run --no-sync`, and the editor format command uses `uv run --no-sync`.

The venv sync a failed chat create runs before its retry is `uv sync --all-packages --frozen`, so it never rewrites a `uv.lock` another agent has left out of date with `pyproject.toml`.

The tests that pin `message_chat.py` and `run_in_background.py` constants import them from the `workspace_bare_scripts` package, now a chat dev dependency, instead of loading the files by path, and the one that pins update-self's resume note imports `update_self_skill.update_resume_note` (`update-self-skill` is a chat dev dependency too).

The README and the account index lock's docstring no longer mention `migrate_claude_auth.py`, which this release deletes. The README and the background-task docs name `run_in_background.py` by its module path, `system/scripts/workspace_bare_scripts/run_in_background.py`, and the secret-request and background-task end-to-end tests run `request_secret.py` and `run_in_background.py` from their modules.

The README's development section starts the backend from `.venv/bin/chat-app` rather than under `uv run`, following the rule that a long-running process never runs under `uv run`.

The README now says the app runs from the workspace venv (its one install), not from its own uv tool.

Chats know who said what (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 5):

- A message from anyone but the workspace's owner (a person the workspace is shared with, or a visiting agent) reaches the agent as `[from: <name>] <text>`, so the agent knows who is asking, on every route that delivers a person's words: the message route, a new chat's first message (the create's and the new-chat intake's, the prefix riding `--message` or following the create, inside the seed context of a seeded chat), and the message that confirms a switch. Slash commands and bash-mode input are delivered as typed. The owner's messages are unchanged. Whether a text is prefixed is decided for the harness it is for (the switch's target while a handoff is in flight, the room being created for a chat with no agent yet, else the active agent's), so a send held while a chat converges into a room lands unprefixed, and a room step that still carries one is shown without it.

- Each chat keeps an `authors.jsonl` beside its transcript, and every `user_message` event the app serves carries `author` (the sender's participant key) and `author_name` when the sender was not the owner. The prefix never shows in the transcript, nor in a send held while the chat switches harness. A send is attributed only once its chat is known (a listed agent, or a chat still being created); a send to an id the app does not know answers 404 with nothing written. A request whose `X-Imbue-Identity` header is present but does not parse is refused with 400 rather than read as the owner's. A prefix typed by hand whose name holds what a participant key may not (a slash, a control character) is still stamped, under a synthetic key with those characters read as spaces, and shown as typed.

- The page draws your own messages on the right as before, and another person's on the left under their name and picture; a turn under either of the owner's keys (`owner`, or the account the roster marks as the owner) is the owner's. The agent's replies are drawn as bubbles, one per reply, under the workspace's picture and name. The page re-reads its own key and the roster when it comes back into view or focus and when anyone's mentions change (a few seconds' cache between), so a page opened before the workspace was shared learns the owner's new key, and anyone who joins later gets their name and colour.

- New routes: `GET /api/me` (the page's own participant key), `GET /api/participants` (the shell's roster, every picture the shell serves -- a person's profile picture, the workspace agent's avatar icon -- pointed at this app's `GET /api/participants/<key>/picture`, which relays it with the shell's caching, since the roster names those pictures on the shell's origin, which the page cannot reach).

- The chat list's rows show a kebab beside the rename pencil on hover, opening the row's context menu.

Chat rooms and mentions (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 7):

- A room is a chat among the people in the workspace with no AI agent. A chat waiting for its first send becomes one from its provider chooser ("Chat room (no provider)"), which its provider chip opens (and its first send does, while nothing is signed in), and any chat (the main chat included) becomes a room, or a room becomes an agent chat, from the composer's provider menu: the switch keeps the conversation so far as the chat's earlier segments, and a chat leaving a room hands its new agent the room's transcript. Rooms sit in the chat list with the other chats, wearing a people glyph, and take every chat verb (rename, delete, stop, start). A message sent into a stopped room is appended to its transcript without reviving its reader, so the room keeps reading as stopped until `mngr message --start <room>` (the send `AGENTS.md` has the agent make; a bare `mngr message` refuses a stopped agent), the row's Restart, or boot starts the reader again.

- A room is an mngr agent of the template's new `room` type: its process reads what `mngr message <room>` types into its pane into the room's transcript, which `mngr transcript <room>` renders and the chat app tails. The chat app appends people's messages to the same transcript, so every message in a room is drawn as its author's turn under their name and picture, the owner's unmarked.

- Typing `@` in a room's composer opens a list of handles: the people here, `@agent` for the workspace's agent, and every chat by its title (`@Main-chat`). Mentioning `@agent` or a chat from a room (a room's first message included, once the room is up) sends that chat the message, marked as said in the room, and the room's row shows a working dot until the agent answers into the room (a chat that refuses the message, as one whose account was signed out does, is not waited on; the wait is also let go when either chat is destroyed, and once five minutes have passed since the newest ask it is dropped the next time the chat list is computed, whether or not a page had the room open). A mention in a send no proxy vouched for (an in-workspace script's) acts on nothing. Mentioning a person marks the room's row with an `@` for them until they look at it (the owner's pending mentions are read and cleared under both of the owner's keys; a destroyed chat's mentions are dropped from everyone's file, which is named by the key itself), and tells the workspace's owner through the Imbue Studio app's feed as the room itself, so the notification opens the room. In an agent chat a handle is a word the agent reads, and the composer offers no popover.

- The chat snapshot carries `kind` (`agent` or `room`) and `awaiting_chat_ids`; `POST /api/chats/create` and `POST /api/chats/<id>/handoff` take `kind` (a room is refused beside an account or a model, before anything is written); `GET /api/mentions` and `GET /api/mentions/pending` are new, with the `mentions_updated` push on `/api/ws`. There are no room-only routes, no room store, and no second chat id shape.

The chat app feeds the desktop's tray and makes the Lounge (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, sections 6 and 7.5):

- Every message a person or a visiting agent sends through a route a proxy vouched for (a new chat's first message included; an in-workspace script's send, such as a background task's report, is nobody's speech and raises none), and every turn the workspace agent closes with text in a chat some page is reading (its post into a room included; the turns reach the feed through the session watcher a page's stream builds, so a chat nobody has open raises none), is posted to the shell as a speech bubble (`POST /api/bubbles`, with the people a room message mentions), and every chat-list change is posted as what each chat is doing (`POST /api/chats-activity`), both best-effort and off the request thread; the last chats-activity report is posted again once a minute, so a shell restarted since paints the agent's card. A secondary chat posts neither.

- The Lounge is the chat titled "Lounge", of either kind, found by title alone, by the rule a create refuses a taken name by (canonical forms compared case-insensitively, so "lounge" and "Lounge " are the Lounge too; a Lounge converted into an agent chat, or a chat so named, is the Lounge). A room under that title is made the first time the roster holds anyone besides the owner (a person, an invited email, or a visiting agent), from the roster the shell answers (read once a minute), and again when a click on a person needs the Lounge after it was deleted or renamed, only while no chat of any kind carries the title. The new `lounge` intake target resolves to it, making the room when there is no such chat, and the manifest's `lounge` launch path (`mention_param = "message"`) drafts `@<handle> ` into it when a person's tray entry is clicked.

- The README's intake paragraph names the `lounge` target and every launch path the manifest declares, and the manifest's comments on the `main`, `new`, and `send` paths name the key each answers (`main` is the launcher's Enter, `new` its Ctrl+Enter, `send` is bound to none, as `draft` is).

The chat app's browser test of a desktop switch drives the shell's overview (the taskbar's "Manage Desktops" button and its thumbnails) rather than the desktop switcher the shell no longer draws (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 8.2); nothing in the chat app itself changes.

The chat about an app (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 9.2):

- The manifest declares `app-chat` ("Chat about this app", `POST /api/chats/intake`, params `app` and `app_display_name`, preset `target = "app_chat"`, `app_params = {name = "app", display_name = "app_display_name"}`), which a window's title bar balloon runs; never a launcher row.

- The new `app_chat` intake target answers the chat labelled `app_chat` with the `app`'s registered name (so a renamed app keeps its chat), else the one titled "<app_display_name> Chat" by the rule a create refuses a taken name by (canonical forms compared case-insensitively, so a chat titled "docs chat" by hand is found rather than the create refused beside it), of either kind or still being made, else creates one with that title and label on the default account (never auto-named), else, with nothing signed in, mints one awaiting its first send under them (`mint_awaiting_chat` takes a name and labels). The intake is always held, even with nothing sent, as a draft that prefills the composer with "Change something about the <app> app: " (the lead-in that tells the agent which app the message is about, prepended over anything already typed, never sent by itself), with a `hint` ("How do you want to change <app>?") on the pending intake's view and its apply answer, which the chat root puts on the chat's composer as its placeholder and focuses (`setComposerHint`, the page's embed API's `hintComposer`). An applied intake with nothing to draft or launch now answers `null` for `composer_text` and `first_message` rather than an empty string. The chat app's own windows open "Chat Chat".

- The chat's pinned entry defaults to the bar (the manifest drops `default_mode = "floating"`): the avatar sits in the tray among the people, and a client floats it from the entry's menu.

- A room never answers to an account label: the workspace's create defaults (`.mngr/settings.local.toml`) stamp the default account's label and `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` onto every create, so a room's create clears both for its own invocation (`-S commands.create.label=` and `-S commands.create.env=`, with mngr's `MNGR__ALLOW_SETTINGS_KEY_ASSIGNMENT_NARROWING` opt-in in that create's environment, since mngr otherwise refuses an assignment that narrows a list), and every reader of the label answers no account for a room regardless, so a room's snapshot names none, a sign-out of that account never refuses the room's sends, and a sign-in's restart sweep never bounces it. A seeded chat launched as a room appends its first words alone, with no seed context.

- Chat bubbles take the prototype's look: the agent's turns sit in the same 24px-gutter column as another person's (the workspace name over the run's first bubble, the face beside it, a spacer holding the gutter under continuation groups), a bubble that is not yours (a person's or the agent's) wears one 5% grey, the viewer's own a green tint, and every bubble an 18px round with a 4px corner squared toward the sender. The chat list's selected row wears the same grey as a not-yours bubble, its rows' hover a fainter 3%.

- Every delivering route annotates every sender a proxy vouched for -- the owner's page sends included, while a request with no identity header (a script's, the terminal's) still writes nothing -- and each chat's snapshot gains `participants`, the distinct annotated senders in order of first message (never the workspace agent). The chat list's rows show their pictures when two or more have written, stepping aside under the pointer where the pencil and the kebab come out.

- The chat root's relay forwards its nested pages' `shell:input` activity reports up to the shell, like their focus.

- A monogram (a person with no picture, or one whose picture would not load) sits on the person's roster colour, as the desktop's tray draws it.

- The terminal behind a chat attaches as a viewer (read-only, never sizing the owner's window) while the shell's handshake says the chat's window is being looked at on somebody else's desktop: the back face's pty URL carries the viewer argument after the agent name, which is always sent (empty for the ambient session).

- `system/scripts/message_chat.py` says a room is answered with `mngr message --start <room>`, never through the script, since a script's words are nobody's.

Two e2e tests sidestep the cursor glide of Fortress v156, which the workspace's browser tests run on: it replays a recorded human cursor trajectory around a click that moved the pointer. The auto-compact test picks the chat's Off option and the new-chats default with the keyboard rather than a click, since the glide from the Auto-compact row to the option crossed the menu's other rows, which took the hover and changed the submenu the test was still reading. The phone-drawer test hovers a chat row before tapping it, since a glide whose points land between the press and its release starts back at the list button, which the drawer read as a leftward drag that dismissed it without picking the row.

The chat's send shortcut becomes rebindable (user-profile-state spec, phase 3C): the app's `app.toml` declares the one `send-message` action under `[[keybindings]]` (default Enter, with Ctrl/Cmd+Enter also sending), a new `/api/keybindings/me` route answers its resolved chords, and the composer matches the resolved chords instead of a hard-coded Enter, re-fetched when the shell announces a change (`shell:keybindings-changed`, forwarded to the inner chat pages).

The gateway access the chat app's backend reads from its environment (`latchkey_gateway.py`) moves into the new `latchkey-access` library, shared with the shell; the call sites import `GatewayAccess` from there and the module is gone.

### system/apps/datalib

The README runs the tests with `uv run --no-sync`.

### system/apps/files

The file browser's shortcuts become rebindable (user-profile-state spec, phase 3C): the app's `app.toml` declares the browser actions under `[[keybindings]]` (select-all, go-up, back/forward, new-folder, open, rename, delete, clear-selection, save-file) with their existing chords as the defaults, so the Keyboard shortcuts dialog lists them even while Files is stopped, a new `/__files/api/keybindings/me` route answers their resolved chords, and `keyboard.ts` and the file page's save match the resolved chords instead of hard-coded ones, re-fetched when the shell announces a change. The selection arrows and the type-ahead jump stay built in. The project also gains the `[tool.ty]` table its siblings carry, so its type-check ratchet stays inside the repo in a nested checkout.

The relay client takes the gateway's environment and header names from the new `latchkey-access` library instead of spelling them itself.

### system/apps/getting_started

The README runs the backend from `.venv/bin` and the tests with `uv run --no-sync`, and the editor format command uses `uv run --no-sync`.

The README starts the backend from `.venv/bin/getting-started` rather than under `uv run`, following the rule that a long-running process never runs under `uv run`.

The README now says the app runs from the workspace venv (its one install), not from its own uv tool.

### system/apps/routines

A preview of the Routines app (update-app's, or update-self's check of a customized app) now boots the app's own `routines-app` entry point. Its `[preview]` table named no command, so the preview ran the program's name, `routines`, which in the workspace venv is the routines library's command line rather than the app, and no preview of it ever came up.

### system/apps/screen

The Screen viewer no longer sticks on "Connecting to the screen" after it hid its own stream. Its 1.5 s belt used to clear the viewer's intersection flag whenever the stage momentarily had no size, with nothing but a later IntersectionObserver change able to set it back, so a transient relayout left the viewer hidden for good; the belt now owns a separate laid-out input that it both clears and restores. The stream now fetches connect-info itself, ignores the answer of a fetch a later request or a release superseded, and tries a failed fetch again after a moment, where a failed fetch used to leave the viewer believing it held media until hidden and shown once more; and the viewer now knows when its neko socket closed, so a request made during a reconnect is no longer counted as delivered.

Keys typed at the Screen now land in a hidden text input inside the stage, which takes the focus the stage is given. A browser extension that binds letters as commands (Vimium and its kin) stands down for an editable element and for nothing else, so a visitor with one installed used to see "n" open its find bar instead of reaching the Screen.

The Screen app (`docs/system/specs/screen/spec.md`, implementation steps 1 and 2): the workspace's one streamed Linux desktop as a window.

- The `screen-service` daemon on `127.0.0.1:8090` renders `xorg.conf`, `neko.yaml` (mode 600, with that start's passwords and API token) and the PulseAudio script under `data/.state/screen/`, starts the `screen-stack` group on demand (a page load, the Start button, the `browser` launch path, `screen run`, an agent's `acquire`) and answers `starting` until neko's health route does; `GET /api/state` carries the lifecycle (`installing` while env-converge has not installed the stack), the lease, the frontmost window's title and the display mode; `/api/ws` pushes `state`, `stopped` and `handoff_request`.

- Sessions and identity: `POST /api/session` logs the requester in to neko with the user password and a name from `X-Imbue-Identity` (the name, else the email's local part, else Owner or Guest); the viewer logs out on `pagehide` and the service deletes sessions disconnected for ten minutes.

- The control lease (`ScreenControl`), the browser fleet's state machine with `acquire`, `release`, `take_control`, `handoff` and `return_to_agents`, a FIFO wait queue and a resume queue, the 60-second idle TTL and the 12-second claim window, checkpointed to `control.json` and projected onto neko (`locked_controls` while an agent holds it, the human made host otherwise, a human taking an uncontrolled Screen learned from `control/host`). Human routes `POST /api/control/take` and `/return`; agent routes `/acquire`, `/release`, `/handoff` with `X-Mngr-Agent-Id`.

- `GET /api/screenshot` (PNG by default, from neko's admin screenshot), `GET /api/windows` and `POST /api/windows/<id>/activate` through `wmctrl`, `POST /api/run` launching a command with `DISPLAY=:99` in the `AGENT_SUBPROCESS` band, the `/neko/` reverse proxy (HTTP and WebSocket, with a rate limit on the login route), and `GET /api/connect-info` answering no endpoints yet.

- The `screen` command: `run`, `windows`, `activate`, `shot`, `size`, `control acquire|release|handoff`, `open`, with the fleet CLI's exit codes. The `screen-watch` event listener stops the rest of the group when a member exits, appends a `screen_stopped` event and tells the service.

- The viewer (`frontend/`, built into `src/screen/static/`): the video over neko's signaling with the server's candidate used as given, the strip (who has control, Take control, Give control back), the installing, starting and stopped overlays, the agent dim, mouse and keyboard input while this session controls, and the shell connection with `closeChord` sending Ctrl+W to the remote.

- Pointer lock (spec section 12): the viewer carries the plumbing (`frontend/src/pointer_lock.ts`: a strip control that locks the pointer on the stage, the relative motion it yields while locked, Escape releasing it in the browser itself), but the control is hidden, since neko v3 has no relative-motion event (`control/move` is absolute only); the README says so, and `IS_RELATIVE_MOTION_SUPPORTED` turns the control on once neko gains one.

Implementation step 3 (sizing, profiles, visibility, audio):

- `POST /api/screen-size` resizes the Screen from the controller's stage size: rounded down to 16 px (the cap itself at or past 1920 or 1080), clamped to 640x480 through 1920x1080, the RANDR mode `<w>x<h>_60` added with `xrandr --newmode`/`--addmode` from the package's own CVT modeline when the dummy output lacks it, then selected through neko. A non-controller's report is ignored; added modes are recorded in `data/.state/screen/modes.json` for the stack's life. `screen size WxH` sets it through the same route.

- The profile chooser: `control` while a human holds control and sent input in the last ten seconds, `idle` after a minute without input while no agent holds the lease, `watch` otherwise, fed by `POST /api/input-seen` from the controller's viewer and by every agent command; announced as `profile` on `/api/ws` and in `GET /api/state`, and selected by every viewer with `signal/video`.

- The viewer releases its media (`signal/close`) after five seconds hidden, judged from `document.hidden`, the shell's `shown`/`hidden` messages and an IntersectionObserver on a 1.5-second belt, and requests it again when visible; input goes only while visible and controlling. A phone never reports a size. A large mute control in the strip enables audio for this session alone (`signal/audio`); every session starts with audio disabled.

Implementation step 7 (clipboard, files, mobile):

- Clipboard both ways while this viewer controls: text and HTML through neko's clipboard route on `clipboard/updated` and on focus or paste; images remote-to-local through neko's `clipboard/image.png` when the service's X clipboard watcher (`xclipboard.py`, the browser app's bridge carried over) announces one on `/api/ws`, and local-to-remote through `POST /api/clipboard/image`, which places the image on `:99` with `xclip`. A paste chord sets the remote clipboard first and then taps V there. `keyboard/map` from `navigator.language`.

- Dropping files on the viewer uploads them through neko's `upload/drop` route at the pointer's Screen coordinates; neko receives them, but its own drag emulation does not complete on this stack yet (the strip reports the failed drop), which is a follow-up.

- Under the phone layout: pan and pinch-zoom of the drawn video, tap as click and long press as right click mapped into Screen coordinates, two-finger scroll, a modifier bar (Ctrl, Alt, Shift latching for the next key, Esc, Tab) and a Keyboard button raising the soft keyboard; the Screen is never resized from a phone.

Step 4, connectivity (spec section 5):

- `GET /api/connect-info` asks the desktop through the latchkey gateway's `minds-api-proxy` (`media-endpoints`, and `ice-servers` only with `?relay=1`) and the share gateway's loopback `GET /connect-info` in parallel with a two-second bound each, and answers the union: candidates filtered to guest port 59000, de-duplicated, protocol lower-case; `ice_servers` from every broker; the earliest `expires_at`. A slow, unreachable or refusing broker is absent; both absent is empty lists. The answer is held in memory only and the route forbids caching.

- The viewer rewrites every server candidate to the endpoints `connect-info` named (one copy per matching endpoint, address and port replaced, a distinct foundation, the original dropped unless no endpoint is known), builds its peer connection with the ICE servers and `iceTransportPolicy: "all"`, and escalates a connection that is not up within four seconds or fails later: `connect-info?relay=1`, the servers handed to the peer and neko asked for an ICE restart, with `screen:needs-relay` remembered in `localStorage` so the next load fetches with `relay=1` first. A relay attempt that fails the same way shows neko's JPEG screencast (10 fps, quality 60) with input still over the WebSocket, and the strip says so.

Step 8, the browser's migration (spec section 16): the browser app's history continues here.

- The browser is a launch path of the Screen: `POST /launch/browser` (body `url` optional) starts the stack when it is down, starts one Fortress Chromium when it is not running (or registers it to start with the stack), opens the start page as a new tab in front, raises Chromium's window and answers the Screen's one page. Chromium's windows are ordinary X windows the window manager places; nothing pins or closes them, and the browser is never stopped when its windows close. `GET /api/state` carries `chromium` (`state`, `name`, `pending_url`) and its `title` reads "Browser" for a Chromium window.

- The fleet API moved into the service under its old paths (`GET`/`POST /browsers`, `DELETE /browsers/<name>`, `.../stop`, `.../start`, `.../close-tab`, `.../attach`, `.../acquire`, `.../release`, `.../handoff`, `.../pending-url/cancel`), with the Screen's `ScreenControl` as the one lease behind the agent verbs; browsers keep their names (`browser-1`), the profile stays under `$MNGR_HOST_DIR/browser-profiles/` and the tab manifest at `data/.apps/browser/instances.json`, checkpointed every ten seconds, on every stop, start and close, and before the service stops the stack. A stack that ends takes Chromium with it; the next start relaunches the browser on its saved tabs unless the user stopped it on purpose, and a lost manifest brings the profiles on disk back stopped.

- The CDP proxy on `127.0.0.1:8083` is ported to synchronous websockets with its gate now over the Screen's lease: the token's agent drives while it holds the lease, a free Screen is taken on the first frame, a human in control refuses the frame without closing the socket. `Browser.setWindowBounds` leaves the block list; `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride`, `Browser.close`, the incognito verbs and the download redirects stay blocked, and so does closing the last page.

- `POST /api/open-url` (the `open:url` handler) opens a local link as a tab in Chromium, raised, and shows the Screen's page to the client that clicked; while an agent drives, the page is held and the viewer's agent overlay names it with "Take control and open it" and "Cancel", opening it when the agent lets go.

- `agentic-browser-fleet` is a console script of this package now (`fleet_cli.py`), with its verbs and exit codes unchanged, opening the Screen's window minimized on `new` and `acquire` and shown on `handoff`; `ls` says "human (driving the Screen)" for an unpinned human in control.

- The service runs a raise-only band sweep every ten seconds (`band_sweep.py`, spec section 9.4): programs started from the Screen are raised to `AGENT_SUBPROCESS`, Chromium's processes are remapped into the shared-browser band as the browser app's `oom_retag` did, with a burst after each launch or new tab.

- The `open_popups_as_tabs` extension, `chrome_args`, `chrome_launcher` (Fortress's launcher waits up to 45 seconds for the debug port), the CDP client (synchronous) and the manifest and name modules moved here with their tests; the viewer-sizing, capture-backend and videopipe tests of the browser app are gone with the code they covered.

Step 9, the tests that need the whole (spec section 20):

- `test_screen_integration.py` sets its own timeout (the root config's ten seconds would end a stack start), marks the Fortress case `browser`, wires the browser fleet before the stack as the service does, and gains the Quit case: the service's shutdown ends every member and frees the display, and a fresh service's first page load starts a new stack.

- `test_screen_acceptance.py`, marked `acceptance`: Imbue Studio's Electron app creates a local Docker workspace from this tree and Playwright drives the whole journey of the spec's acceptance row (a frame, control, a terminal typed into, the browser launch path with a URL, close with the stack running, Quit with everything gone). It runs on a developer's machine with `MNGR_WORKTREE` naming the mngr checkout and skips at collection without it; the README has the recipe.

- The acceptance run passes end to end (2026-10-17, a local Docker workspace built from this branch, about seven minutes with the image's layers cached): the Electron app's create form to a booted workspace, the Screen opened from the launcher, a frame with a desktop's spread of grey levels, control taken by a click, `xfce4-terminal` typed into through the viewer (the typed command created its marker file), `workspace-layout open https://example.com` putting Chromium with "Example Domain" on the Screen with the title "Browser" and the tab listed by the fleet once env-converge had installed Fortress, the window closed with the stack still running, and Quit from the window menu ending the service and every member with the display gone. Electron exposes neither the Screen's nested frame nor a new page to Playwright, so the run shows the viewer in a Chromium of the operator's machine (`SCREEN_ACCEPTANCE_CHROMIUM`, else this venv's Playwright build, else the newest build under `~/.cache/ms-playwright`) at the same address with the desktop session's cookies; every mngr the app spawns reads the clone's settings, opted into pytest, through `MNGR_PROJECT_CONFIG_DIR` with the Docker provider enabled, and `MNGR_INTERNAL_GIT_TOKEN` is required only while the tree pins the private mngr repo.


The owner gate:

- A workspace visitor (an `X-Imbue-Identity` whose `owner` is false, admitted to the Screen's origin by a share) is refused with 403 on every route that acts on the Screen outside the lease: `POST /api/run`, the agent verbs `/api/control/acquire`, `/release` and `/handoff`, `GET /api/screenshot`, the window routes, `POST /api/clipboard/image`, a session-less `POST /api/screen-size`, `POST /launch/browser`, `POST /api/open-url` and the whole `/browsers` fleet API. The viewer's routes (the page, state, start, connect-info, the events socket, sessions, the human verbs, input-seen, a session's own size report and the neko proxy) still answer a visitor, who gets control through the lease as before, but only for a visitor's session: the human verbs, input-seen and a size report that name the owner's session (its id is in the state document while the owner controls) answer a visitor 403; a header-less request still reads as the owner, so agents and the shell over loopback are unaffected.

- The viewer offers the held page's Cancel (an owner-only verb) to the owner's session alone; a paste that the Screen refused, such as a visitor's image, says so in the strip instead of failing quietly.

- Programs started on the Screen (`screen run` commands, Chromium) no longer inherit the service's `LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PASSWORD` and `LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PERMISSIONS_OVERRIDE`; nothing launched there needs them, and an agent that does holds them in its own shell.

- `test_screen_integration.py` no longer depends on the order its tests run in: every test takes a `running` fixture that starts the stack over the module's service life on demand (and builds a fresh life after a test quit the service), so each passes alone in its own CI sandbox.

File drop lands on the desktop:

- Dropping files on the viewer now posts them to the service's own `POST /api/drop` (multipart `session_id` and `files`, the controlling session alone, a visitor in control included) instead of neko's `upload/drop`, whose drag emulation never completes on this stack. The service writes them into the Screen's desktop folder, the XDG desktop directory `xfdesktop` shows as icons (`XDG_DESKTOP_DIR` from `~/.config/user-dirs.dirs`, else `~/Desktop`), creating it when missing, keeping each file's name, suffixing a clash (`report-1.pdf`), refusing names with path separators or a leading dot, and answering 413 past 64 MiB for one drop. The strip says where the files landed (`Saved to /home/user/Desktop: report.pdf`).

- `test_screen_integration.py` drops a file through the route in the workspace image and finds it in the desktop folder.

Lease arbitration for the paste and the held page's Cancel:

- `POST /api/clipboard/image` takes multipart `session_id` and `image` and the service accepts it from the session in control alone, so a visitor in control pastes images again; `POST /browsers/<name>/pending-url/cancel` takes `session_id` in its body or query and answers the session in control or the owner (a header-less caller over loopback, an agent or the shell, still works with no session). Both left the owner gate; a visitor's session that does not control gets the lease refusal (403, `only the session in control of the Screen may do this`), and naming the owner's session the owner-gate refusal as before.

- The viewer sends its session id on both calls and offers the held page's Cancel to the sessions the service lets drop it (the session in control, or the owner's); a page is held only while an agent drives, so in practice that is the owner's viewer.

Touch through neko's input driver (spec section 14):

- `xorg.conf` declares neko's `xf86-input-neko` touchscreen (`screen_touchscreen`, `Driver "neko"`, `SocketName /tmp/screen-runtime/xf86-input-neko.sock`, the layout's `CorePointer`) and `neko.yaml` enables `desktop.input` on that socket; the stack waits for the display socket and the driver's socket before starting the other members, removes a stale driver socket before Xorg starts, and reports `installing` until the env.d unit has put `/usr/lib/xorg/modules/input/neko_drv.so` in place.

- The viewer sends a phone's tap as `control/touchbegin` and `control/touchend` at the mapped point with the finger's pressure (a byte, never zero) and a fresh sixteen-bit touch id, when neko's `system/init` says `touch_events`; otherwise, and for a long press (a right click), the mouse path stays.

- `test_screen_integration.py` asserts in the workspace image that Xorg loaded the `neko` driver for the device and accepted neko's connection, that `system/init` carries `touch_events`, and that a touch over neko's WebSocket moves the core pointer to the touched point (read back with `xdotool getmouselocation`).

The pointer (spec section 12):

- The controller's own pointer takes the remote cursor's shape. neko sends the X cursor's image (size, hotspot, PNG) over the peer's WebRTC data channel when the channel opens and on every change, and the viewer sets it as the stage's CSS cursor with its hotspot (a data URI), shrunk with the drawn video when the stage shows the desktop smaller than 1:1 and capped at 128 px a side, with the browser's own pointer as the fallback when the image cannot be drawn. The stage no longer hides the pointer (`cursor: none`), so a viewer that is watching sees the default pointer, and the screencast fallback its painted-in pointer; `show_pointer` stays off in neko's WebRTC pipelines.

Sizing from a small desktop window (spec sections 7.2 and 14):

- A phone is now a phone-sized viewport with a finger as the primary pointer (the shared `PHONE_MEDIA_QUERY` and `TOUCH_MEDIA_QUERY` both), so a Screen window that is merely small on a desktop reports its stage size and the Screen resizes to fit it instead of being scaled down to a tiny 1920x1080; real phones keep the mobile controls and never resize the Screen.

- The controller's latest stage size goes out as soon as its session controls with the stack running, whether or not it matches the last report (the Screen may have been sized by someone else meanwhile).

The screencast fallback, after the first test on Imbue Cloud (spec sections 5.4 and 12):

- No pointer is painted into the screencast any more: neko's global `capture.video.show_pointer`, the flag its screencast pipeline takes (the per-pipeline flag covers the WebRTC pipelines alone), is off in `neko.yaml`, so the browser's own pointer is the one pointer there instead of two, one of them lagging. The screencast runs at 5 fps rather than 10 (each frame is a full JPEG of the display, and the fallback is for seeing the Screen, not for motion), and the viewer polls it at that rate.

- The rate lives in two places (neko's `capture.screencast.rate` in `neko_config.py`, the viewer's `SCREENCAST_FPS` in `frontend/src/screencast.ts`); a `frontend`-marked test now reads the viewer's and fails when the two drift apart.

- The viewer tries WebRTC again from the screencast instead of staying there until a reload: 15 s after the fall, then 30 s, then every 60 s, and at once on the strip's new "Retry now" button, each time with fresh `connect-info?relay=1`; the screencast keeps showing the Screen until a retry's peer connects. The strip's row carries a loud alert while the picture is the screencast ("Low-quality picture: no direct or relay path connected. Retrying.") in place of the quiet "Slow picture" line.

- A screencast retry still pending when the stream asks for a fresh peer on its own (the server dropped a retry's peer) is dropped by the new attempt, rather than firing later and restarting ICE on the peer that connected. A peer that connects late, after its deadline had already fallen the viewer back to the screencast, drops the pending retry the same way.

- While the screencast shows the Screen, a peer that fails or is set up again leaves it showing whatever the policy's phase (a late peer that fails, or one failing while a retry's relay servers are fetched, no longer flips the viewer to a blank "Connecting" until the next retry); the stream keeps that rule in one place.

- The strip gains a "Details" toggle: a panel over the stage naming the media path in use (direct or through a relay, udp or tcp, the remote address, from the peer's `getStats()`), the endpoints `connect-info` offered, the relay server count, the Screen's size and profile, and the picture's size, rate, bitrate and round trip; the viewer also logs one "media path" line to the console per connection.

- `GET /api/connect-info` waits up to eight seconds for relay servers (candidates keep their two): the desktop's first `ice-servers` answer mints a credential through the connector and Cloudflare, which took longer than two seconds on the dev tier and left the first relay attempt with no servers, which is how the whole first test ran in the screencast.

The browser shortcut on the Screen's desktop (spec section 16):

- XFCE's "Web Browser" launcher failed on a fresh Screen (`exo-open --launch WebBrowser` found no helper and `sensible-browser` no `x-www-browser`). The service now renders the session's browser entries into the home at each stack start (`xfce_helpers.py`): `~/.config/xfce4/helpers.rc` naming a `WebBrowser` helper, the helper's `.desktop` under `~/.local/share/xfce4/helpers/`, an application `.desktop` under `~/.local/share/applications/`, and `~/.config/mimeapps.list` pointing the `http` and `https` scheme handlers at it, each merged with what the file already holds (a repeated key keeps its last value, and a file the service cannot read, parse or write is logged and left alone without failing the start). All of them run `screen-browser-open`, a one-line script of the package that calls the new `screen browser open [URL]` verb, which posts to `/launch/browser`: the page opens in the fleet's one Chromium (its profile, its CDP proxy, the lease, the held-URL rule while an agent drives) rather than in a second browser. The integration suite runs the verb against a real listener and sees the tab.

The mouse wheel (spec section 11):

- Scrolling was inverted on a conventional mouse: neko's `XScroll` sends X button 4 (wheel up) for a positive `delta_y` and button 6 for a positive `delta_x`, the opposite of the DOM's sign (neko's own client flips it by default). The viewer now flips the sign once, where it sends `control/scroll` (`input.ts`), for the wheel and the phone's two-finger scroll alike; the gesture classifier reports wheel steps in the DOM's sign as before.

- Chromium starts maximized (`--start-maximized`) instead of at a fixed 1280x800: the Screen is sized to the controller's window and is often smaller than that, xfwm4 never shrinks a window larger than the display, and a maximized window follows the Screen's later size changes.

Scrolling on a phone (spec section 14):

- A one-finger drag on the video is now a touch held and moved on the Screen through neko's input driver (`control/touchbegin`, `control/touchupdate`, `control/touchend` at the mapped points), so a page in the browser scrolls under the finger with the browser's own momentum, as on any phone. Once the video is pinch-zoomed the drag pans the view as before, and without the driver it always does. The two-finger wheel scroll stays.

- The mobile bar gains Scroll Up and Scroll Down buttons, three wheel steps each, for programs on the Screen that ignore touch.

Files and the desktop's icons (spec section 4.3):

- The desktop shows no icons any more: a desktop icon wants a double click, which a phone cannot give, and anything an icon would do belongs in the panel. The service sets the `xfce4-desktop` channel's `desktop-icons/style` to none in `~/.config/xfce4/xfconf/xfce-perchannel-xml/xfce4-desktop.xml` before each stack start (`xfdesktop_config.py`, keeping the channel's other properties, and leaving alone a file it cannot read, parse or write).

- A dropped file still lands in the desktop folder, and the service now opens that folder in a Thunar window on the Screen right after the drop (started as `screen run` starts a command), so the file is reachable from a phone and the strip's "Saved to ..." line has a window to point at.

- A one-finger drag that starts in the letterbox band around the video, where no touch can begin, now begins its touch where the finger first reaches the video instead of retrying the start point forever; the next drag starts afresh at its own start.

- The manifest declares a `description`, so the visiting-agent primer describes the Screen rather than listing it with none; the OpenAPI document (`api_schema_path`) stays a follow-up, since the route table it needs covers forty routes.

- Stale text: the spec body now says what the implementation notes said (the 5 fps screencast with no pointer painted into it, the retries from the screencast, the one-finger drag as a touch), `data/.state/README.md` describes `screen/` in place of the browser's screenshots, and `window-bound-resources.md` names the Screen where it named the deleted browser app.

- A drop whose Thunar window cannot be opened (the launch fails) still answers the folder and the saved names: the failure is logged at warning and the files are on disk either way, where before the route answered 500 after saving them.

- `desktop_files.py` and the drop tests describe the desktop folder as the XDG desktop directory a drop shows in a file manager window, no longer as the folder `xfdesktop` shows as icons.

- `routes_test.py` opens a session that holds control through one helper (`_controlling_session`) in the drop and paste tests, in place of the same take-control preamble repeated in each.

- The `browser` launch path's start page is held while an agent drives the browser, as the README said and as `open:url` already did: `workspace-layout open https://...` (or the launcher's "Browser" row with a start page) no longer opens a tab over the agent's work; the viewer's agent overlay offers to take control and open it, or to cancel, and the page opens when the agent lets go.

- The service logs every lease transition at debug (controller, agent, human, pinned, the queue), so a lease that moved while nobody was watching can be reconstructed from the service log.

- A service restart ends the stack (spec section 9.3), and the viewer then said "The screen was stopped" with no reason: the stack now records why it ended in `data/.state/screen/stop_reason`, the next service life shows that reason until the next start, and a start wipes it.

- Only the human's asks are held while an agent drives (the launch path's start page and `open:url`): an agent's own `agentic-browser-fleet new --url` (a nameless `POST /browsers`) opens its page at once, as it did before the launch path's page was held, instead of waiting as a page offered to the human. The launch path also no longer raises Chromium over the agent's work when its page was held.

- A start that fails records its reason in `data/.state/screen/stop_reason` as a stop does, so a service restart after a failed start shows why the stack did not start rather than the reason of an earlier stop.

- `stack_test.py` builds the second service life's stack through one helper (`_second_service_life`) in the adoption and stop-reason tests, in place of the same construction repeated in each.

- An agent's `handoff` gives the Screen to the human pinned, as the browser app's lease did, rather than freeing it with the agent queued: no other agent's `acquire` is granted until the human gives it back (`busy_human`), the human's first input or Take control claims the handoff with the pin kept, and the owner may give an unclaimed handoff back from the strip (`POST /api/control/return` accepts the owner's session for it). The strip reads "Control: Handed to you" meanwhile and input flows so the first click claims it.

- The stack's programs sit at `SCREEN_STACK` (850) rather than the service's band: under memory pressure the desktop is shed after the programs on it and before any agent, and the service (still at 72) starts it again on the next open. The README's band section and spec section 9.4 say so.

- The Screen's desktop folder is `data/Desktop` under the workspace, where the Files app shows it, and Chromium downloads to `data/Downloads` beside it: the service renders the session's `~/.config/user-dirs.dirs` before each stack start with `XDG_DESKTOP_DIR` and `XDG_DOWNLOAD_DIR` naming the two (`user_dirs.py`, the file's other entries kept, `xdg-user-dirs-update` turned off), so a dropped file and a download both land under `data/` (Chromium resets a download directory that equals the desktop directory to its own default, so they are not one folder). A drop raises the Thunar window already showing the folder instead of opening one more.
