- A page asked for while Chromium is still launching (an agent's own `new --url`, or a launch path's start page) is queued for the launch and opened in front once Chromium is up, rather than parked as a page held from the human: the viewer no longer offers "Take control and open it" for a page nobody is holding back. A launch that does not finish (the stack ended under it, a relaunch failed, the user stopped the browser) drops the queued pages as it drops a held page. Whether a page is opened at once or queued is decided under the browser's own lock (`Browser.open_tab_or_queue_for_launch`), so a page asked for in the instant the launch finishes is opened rather than left queued behind a drain that will not come again.

- The Screen service registers the saved browsers from the tab manifest (or, with no manifest, the profiles on disk) when it starts, before any stack runs. Previously the fleet learned of them only when the stack came up, so a `browser` launch or an agent's `new` arriving while the stack was still down minted a fresh name beside the saved browser; that browser's first checkpoint dropped the saved entry from the manifest, and the next restore swept the saved profile -- deleting an upgraded (or merely restarted) workspace's tabs and logins. What relaunches when the stack comes up stays the restore's decision. Found by the pre-Screen -> Screen upgrade end-to-end test, where the first browser launch after the update destroyed the migrated `browser-1`.

- The Screen is a built-in app the way the Python packaging stack lays them out: a root dependency and workspace member run from the workspace venv (`.venv/bin/screen-service` and `.venv/bin/screen-watch` in its supervisord drop-ins) rather than its own uv tool; its manifest declares `[theming] mode = "none"` as the browser app did; the fleet CLI and the CDP proxy tell an agent to run `uv run --no-sync agentic-browser-fleet ...`; and the wake a queued agent's chat gets goes through `message_chat.send` in-process (the app depends on `workspace-scripts`) instead of running the messenger script as a subprocess.

- The Screen describes its API the way every other app does (the workspace app model's contracts section 2): the manifest declares `api_schema_path = "/api/schema"`, the service serves the OpenAPI document there from a route table (`api_models.py` names what every one of its routes takes and answers; a page, a file, a socket or an image is declared schemaless), every view carries a docstring the document uses as its summary, and `app_schema` checks every parse and answer against the table at request time. A refusal on any route is the one `{"detail": ...}` shape; the fleet CLI reads it through one `refusal_reason`, which takes `detail` first and `error` from a service not yet restarted on the typed routes.

### system/apps/style_guide

The Style Guide app is a built-in like every other app the template ships: a root dependency and workspace member, run from the workspace venv (`.venv/bin/style-guide-app`) rather than installed as its own uv tool. It takes a band of its own (`style-guide`, right before System Monitor's) instead of the user band, which the built-in rules reserve for user-built apps, and its preview boots `style-guide-app`, the entry point its program runs, rather than the program's name.

### system/apps/system_interface

Stabilized two multiplayer end-to-end tests (viewing another person's desktop, and the independent pinned window shared by two clients): each now waits for a window's restore to be durable server-side before asserting on it, so a concurrent layout refetch can no longer transiently drop the window and fail the check.

The README runs the backend from `.venv/bin`; the editor format command and the avatar registration usage line use `uv run --no-sync`.

The update-staleness test reads the update apply contract at its new path inside the `update_self_skill` package.

The README's update-apply section points at that package, rather than at update-self's `scripts/`, as the apply's reference.

The README's update-apply section points at update-self's `update_self_skill` package in `.agents/skills/update-self/python/` as the reference code, where the scripts-as-packages change moved it.

The README starts the backend from `.venv/bin/system-interface` rather than under `uv run`, following the rule that a long-running process never runs under `uv run`.

The README now says the app runs from the workspace venv (its one install), not from its own uv tool.

The shell knows who is here (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 4):

- `GET /api/roster` lists the workspace's participants: the owner first, then everyone the workspace is shared with (by account, by invited email, and visiting agents), and the workspace's own agent last, each with a display name, picture, a mention handle, a colour, and whether they are connected and when they were last seen and last active. A `roster_updated` push on `/api/ws` follows every change (someone coming or going, a person's newest input time moving, a grants file or the gateway's last-seen record changing, a burst of file events announced once a second later), only when the document differs from the one last pushed, and the roster is sent on connect. A `share_grants.toml` entry the participant key refuses (a hand-edited user id or email) costs that one entry, warned about once per version of the file, leaving the rest of the roster, the heartbeat, and the Lounge keeper standing.

- Every request's identity resolves to a participant key (`owner`, `user:<id>`, `agent:<id>`); the heartbeat answers the page its own key and records when the person last typed or clicked, and the owner of an unshared workspace is now counted as present under the `owner` key. A present `X-Imbue-Identity` header that does not parse is refused with 400 on every route; only a missing or blank header reads as the anonymous owner.

- The heartbeat reports how long ago the page last saw keyboard or pointer input (`input_age_seconds`) rather than a moment by the page's own clock; the shell stamps the moment itself, never later than its own now, keeps the newest, and announces the roster whenever a person's newest input time moves, so every window's "Active" and "Idle · 4m" follow real typing. A page from before the age may still send `last_input_at`, accepted and clamped; an age beyond a century is refused with 400, like any malformed body.

- A `clients_updated` push follows a window's socket registering its client, a registered window's disconnect, and the prune of a stale client, so a page re-reads the clients listing and the tray's ring follows a window that reconnects.

- A visiting agent's presence comes from the share gateway's last-seen record (which it now refreshes every 10 seconds), so an agent with a grant shows as connected while it is calling in.

- The client inventory (`/api/clients`) names each client's participant.

- The grants parsers moved to the shared `share_grants` library; `shell/identity.py` moved to `workspace_layout.identity`.

The taskbar's tray becomes where the people and the agent live (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 6):

- The tray is the share button (a dashed circle with a plus, drawn only under an Imbue Studio chrome, which it asks to open the share panel on the whole workspace), one picture per person in the roster (faded while they are away, a dashed envelope for an invited email, a monogram tile for a visiting agent, a neutral silhouette for the owner of a workspace that has not shared, stacked from four on and spread while the pointer is over them), your own picture, and the agent's avatar -- the one avatar creature's docked home, and its default: a client may float it over the windows instead (the pinned entry's Float row), which draws it there and not in the tray. An entry hops when it arrives and when a bubble of its appears. The desktop switcher moved to the left of the window entries, where the desktops phase puts the overview button.

- The chat's pinned window wears a plain taskbar entry like every other window's, whatever the avatar's mode, and its Close closes it for that client alone: the window is minimized and its entry leaves that client's bar until something shows the window again (a launch, the floating avatar's or the launcher's click).

- Hovering a person opens their card: the name, whether they are active, idle, offline, or invited, what they are looking at (the window at the top of the stack on their newest client), and their desktops, with "New desktop" on your own. Hovering the agent opens its card: the workspace name with a pencil to the avatar chooser, whether it is working, and the chats it is working on and the ones waiting on you, which open on a click. Clicking a person drafts a mention of them into the Lounge through the first launch path of the machine that declares a `mention_param` (a launch path a desktop is never seeded with a shortcut of, as with one taking text); clicking the agent opens the main chat.

- Speech bubbles: the chat app posts every message somebody sends and every turn the agent closes with text to `POST /api/bubbles`, and the shell broadcasts each as `bubble` to every window but the speaker's own clients (the owner's under either of their keys). A page already looking at the bubble's chat does not raise it (a mention of the viewer still rises). A bubble hangs over the speaker's entry for five seconds after its last change; a person's new message replaces theirs, the agent's new message within its bubble's lifetime is appended ("and N more" past three lines), bubbles of different speakers stack, and a mention of the viewer wears an accent border and stays until dismissed or its chat is opened. A click opens the chat it was said in.

- `POST /api/chats-activity` takes what every chat is doing from the chat app, kept and broadcast as `chats_activity` (sent on connect once reported); `roster_updated` is read by the page now, so the tray draws the roster rather than the connected users alone.

Desktops belong to people by convention, and the desktop switcher becomes an overview (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 8):

- A desktop carries an `owner`: the key of the visitor it was seeded for on their first arrival, or created by (`POST /api/desktops` writes the requester's key; the workspace owner's desktops, and every desktop from before, carry none). "Mine" is a keyless desktop for the owner, or one carrying your key. A desktop whose owner has left the roster is left behind: the owner's overview lists it under "Left behind", to view or delete. There is no access control.

- The taskbar's desktop switcher is replaced by the overview button (four squares, "Manage Desktops") between the launcher field and the window entries. The overview tiles the active desktop's windows as live, inert, scaled tiles (a click raises one) over thumbnails of the viewer's own desktops drawn from their wallpapers and this client's placements: a click switches, a double-click on the name renames, a drag sideways reorders (the new `POST /api/desktops/order`, which lists the requester's own desktops in a new order and leaves the others in place), a right-click offers "Delete desktop..." confirmed in place (the menu ends with the element reference rows, as the backdrop's does), and the plus makes "Desktop N". Escape or a click on the bare backdrop closes it. The backdrop's context menu offers "New desktop", "Show all desktops", and "Change wallpaper...", which opens the wallpaper chooser (the settings dialog pared down to it); a desktop's colour and glyph are no longer shown or edited, though the record keeps them. The launcher's window rows name the owner of a desktop that is not the viewer's.

- A person's tray card lists the desktops they own, and a click on one of somebody else's views it: the client switches there with the viewing chrome on (an outline in the owner's colour around the whole desktop, and a chip in that colour with their picture, "<Name> · <Desktop name>", and "Stop viewing" in place of the tray, the overview button hidden and the backdrop menu's "Show all desktops" disabled); Stop viewing goes back to the desktop the window came from, else the viewer's first, else (a visitor with no desktop left) the desktop the shell seeds when they arrive again; when the viewed desktop is deleted the window lands the same way, the letterbox and the way back cleared. Nothing is viewed until the page's first heartbeat has said who the viewer is, so a visitor's own desktop never wears the chrome while it is on its way; an overview open when that answer lands on somebody else's desktop closes, and the overview never opens while viewing. The phone layout never views: a phone-width window whose active desktop is somebody else's lands on one of the viewer's own. On other clients the owner of a desktop somebody else is on wears a ring in their colour in the tray, which follows a viewing window that closes while its person stays connected elsewhere.

- `POST /api/desktops` and `POST /api/desktops/<id>/settings` take `color` and `glyph` as optional (absent: the shell picks the next free glyph and its colour for a create, and a settings post keeps them as written); the frontend sends the name alone. The desktop object and `desktops.json` carry `owner`.

Every window gets "Chat about this app" (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 9):

- A focused window's title bar is now the window menu, Refresh, and a speech balloon, "Chat about this app", on the left, the app's icon and title centred over the bar, and minimize, maximize, and close on the right as before (`data-window-control="app-chat"`; the menu and Refresh swap places). The balloon is drawn on every window of an app that is not internal, the chat app's included, when some app declares a launch path with `app_params`.

- The balloon runs the first such launch path (the chat app's `app-chat`), naming the window's app and its display name in the params it declares, through the launch route's new `show` target: the page lands where the `show` op would put it (a window already there raised, else the app's pinned window pointed at it for this client, else a new window) and, since the target names the window, the two are snapped side by side for this client, the chat on the half of the backdrop its frame's centre was already on (the right when it is minimized or was never placed) and the app's window on the other, the chat on top; nothing is laid out when the window shown is the one the balloon is on (the pinned window's own, which the show navigates) or when either window is pulled out into a window of the chrome's own, which the show leaves where it is. The launch target `{"kind": "show", "beside"?}` is open to any caller; the shell names no app in any of this.

- `POST /api/desktops/<id>/launch` takes the `show` kind; the `app` object's launch paths carry `app_params`.

- Viewing somebody else's desktop shows it as they have it, live and read-only: the placements read gains `?of=owner` (the desktop as its owner last arranged it, from their most recently seen client with a written layout), which a viewing window reads in place of its own layout, refreshed on every `placements_updated` push for the desktop, by a slow backstop poll, and the moment the first heartbeat says who the viewer is; the whole desktop stage (the wallpaper, the shortcut grid, the windows, the ghosts, the pages host) is `inert`, so nothing on it takes a press, a key, or focus and Tab reaches nothing inside it; the taskbar's entries mirror theirs without acting; the backdrop menu keeps "New desktop" and disables "Change wallpaper...", "Change theme...", and "Show all desktops"; the launcher's launch, window, and free-text rows stand down with "Stop viewing to open things here"; every change the store could still make (shortcuts, wallpaper, theme, launches, the app chat, closing, raising, minimizing, restoring, resizing, navigating, a bubble's chat) is refused with one "Stop viewing first" note per gesture, a viewed page's focus report raises nothing, and the owner's layout is reloaded whole on every read, so nothing that slipped through outlives the next poll; and nothing a viewing window holds is saved as the viewer's layout. A presentation mode, not access control: the records stay shared and every route still answers the viewer.

- The overview's rename works and is discoverable: the rename input keeps what you type through the shell's constant redraws (it was a controlled value that every redraw reset, so typing appeared dead), the thumbnail's right-click menu offers "Rename" beside "Delete desktop...", and the delete confirmation hangs above the thumbnail rather than clipping past the bottom of the screen, the tiles' live pages stepping aside while it is up, since they lie above everything drawn inside the overview.

- The agent's hover card trades its pencil for action rows -- "Change avatar..." and "Float" -- and the tray's agent entry takes a right-click menu with the same two, the way the floating creature offers its own.

- Presence reads real activity: the app pages' `shell:input` reports feed the heartbeat's input age beside the shell window's own pointer and key events, so a person typing in an app's frame reads as active.

- A person's card marks the desktop they are on ("There now", with a dot in their colour) beside the "Viewing" mark of the one you are on, read off their newest connected client as the card opens.

- A viewed desktop is drawn as its owner sees it: every desktop layout reports its backdrop size to the shell (`POST /api/clients/<id>/viewport`, on boot once the backdrop is measured and after each resize settles; never from the phone layout or a pulled-out window), the clients listing and the inventory carry each client's `viewport`, and the `?of=owner` placements read answers the chosen client's beside the layout. A window viewing a desktop whose owner's size is known lays the wallpaper, the shortcut grid, the windows, and their pages out in a box of that size, scaled down to fit this backdrop (never up) and centred, with a band in the owner's colour around it; the taskbar and the floating entries stay the viewer's own. With no size on record the desktop is drawn at this backdrop's size, as before.

- A person's profile picture is served from the shell's own origin: the roster points at `GET /api/roster/<key>/picture?v=<version>`, which answers bytes the shell fetches once from the profile's URL and keeps beside the profile cache (versioned by that URL, so a newer picture is a newer address, cached by the page for good; a failed fetch is remembered for five minutes, as a failed profile fetch is). The pages' content security policy admits no outside image.

- The handshake to a page carries `isViewing`, whether its window is being looked at on somebody else's desktop, and is sent again when that changes and when the page's `shell:capabilities` arrives (so a page learns it before its frame's load, which a nested frame can hold back); a terminal attaches to its session as a viewer by it from the first moment.

Keyboard shortcuts become rebindable, per account or per workspace (user-profile-state spec, phase 3C).

- New keybindings routes: the shell's own resolved chords (`/api/keybindings/me`, its action declared under `[[keybindings]]` in its `app.toml`), the whole-workspace catalog the Keyboard settings lists (`/catalog`, every app's declared actions read from its registry row, so an app that is stopped is listed too and a save for its actions is accepted), and the save / reset / discard / deliver flows (`/api/keybindings`, `/reset`, `/discard`, `/deliver`).

- The owner's "everywhere" save lands in `data/system/profile/unsent.json` plus the owner's override file, so the workspace behaves as asked at once, and is delivered to the account through the latchkey gateway's `minds-workspaces-account-settings` verb; the first delivery 403s and files one `workspace` permission request, retried when the chrome announces the verdict (`minds:permission-resolutions`) or from the Keyboard settings, until it lands or is discarded there. A visitor's (or a "this workspace only") save is the requester's own override file.

- The backdrop's context menu gains "Keyboard shortcuts...", a dialog listing every app's declared actions, with a chord recorder, per-app conflict checks, and the save-scope choice (with why "everywhere" is unavailable without an Imbue Studio connection).

- A `keybindings_changed` WebSocket broadcast and a `shell:keybindings-changed` push to every framed page make apps re-fetch their resolved chords; a watch on the profile snapshot announces changes other computers deliver. The launcher's secondary-send chord is the shell's first rebindable action.

- `workspace_profile` joins the update-staleness dependency lists.

- The viewing e2e test (`test_a_persons_card_lists_their_desktops_and_a_click_views_one_with_the_chrome_on`) presses Enter right after the refused focus on the viewed window's Close instead of after its twelve Tabs: the Tab cycle's end depends on how many launcher rows render, and in CI it landed on a control whose Enter ended the viewing.

- The keybindings delivery reaches the gateway through the new `latchkey-access` library instead of a shell-local copy of the chat app's `GatewayAccess`; `latchkey-access` joins the update-staleness dependency lists.

The shell gains the Screen spec's `FULLSCREEN` placement state and immersive mode (`docs/system/specs/screen/spec.md`, section 12; mngr's `specs/screen-studio-integration/spec.md`, section 5):

- A fullscreen window fills the whole viewport, the taskbar's band included, with no title bar, resize handles, corners or shadow. Both geometry editors answer its frame as the viewport (`Viewport` / `"viewport"` beside the frames; `fit_state_frame` / `fitStateFrame`, `viewport_rect` / `viewportRect`, `backdrop_frame_of` / `backdropFrameOf`), the fit metrics gain the taskbar height, and the shared geometry vectors gain the `fullscreen` cases and `snap_frames.FULLSCREEN`. While a fullscreen window is on the active desktop's screen the layout root carries `data-fullscreen-window`, under which the backdrop stops clipping and paints over the taskbar.

- The title bar of a maximized window offers Fullscreen beside Restore; the window menu gains Fullscreen (Exit fullscreen) and, where the Imbue Studio chrome announced `immersive: true`, Immersive (Leave immersive); the taskbar entry's Restore size covers a fullscreen window too. A fullscreen window shows a strip at its top edge on hover (`data-fullscreen-strip`) with Exit fullscreen, Immersive where the chrome can, and a word on the keys ("Press Immersive to send every key").

- Immersive mode goes through the embed contract (v12): `minds:immersive-request {windowId, on}` is sent straight from the click of the strip's or the menu's Immersive, only to a chrome whose capabilities carried `immersive: true`; `minds:immersive-changed {on, keyboardLocked, error?}` lands in the store, an `error` as a toast. The mode is never persisted. The store's `toggleFullscreen`, `isFullscreenShown`, `requestImmersive`, `leaveImmersive` and `onImmersiveChanged` carry it, and `store/embedderBridge.ts` wires the chrome's capabilities and changes to the store.

- The page iframes gain `fullscreen` in their `allow` list and `allow-pointer-lock` in their sandbox list, so the Screen's viewer can lock the pointer and the chrome's fullscreen request is delegated down every frame. A fullscreen page drops its rounded bottom corners.

- `place --state FULLSCREEN` round-trips through the op route and the placements files like every other state.

The layout pipeline test for `workspace-layout open https://...` expects the Screen app to be named when it is not registered, since a bare URL opens through the Screen's `browser` launch path now.

- The launcher's rows for a one-window app (an unpinned app whose default shortcut focuses: the Screen, Getting Started, Memory & disk) launch with the `focus` target, so a second client pressing "Screen" or "Browser" lands in the Screen window the desktop already holds (raised in that client's layout) instead of opening another; before, every client that opened the Screen from the launcher got its own window, and the taskbar filled with them. A focus shortcut whose window this client never placed does the same instead of opening a second.

### system/apps/terminal

The README runs the terminal tests with `uv run --no-sync pytest`.

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

The README now says the app runs from the workspace venv (its one install), not from its own uv tool.

The pty frame reports typing to the shell's presence (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 4.3): the terminal's xterm lives in a nested frame on the pty's origin, whose key and pointer events never reached the wrapper page that binds the app contract, so a person typing in a terminal read as idle. The pty page now posts a throttled `shell:input` to the wrapper, which hands it up to the shell as the chat root hands up its nested pages'.

A terminal viewed on somebody else's desktop attaches to its tmux session as a viewer from the first moment (the multiplayer spec, section 8.3): a framed wrapper points its pty frame only once the shell's handshake has said whether the window is viewed (attaching plainly after a two-second grace when no handshake comes; an unframed wrapper points at once), and the session script attaches read-only and as a client tmux never sizes the window by (`tmux attach -r -f ignore-size`), so looking at a terminal neither types into nor resizes its owner's. The pty path always carries the workdir argument, so the viewer marker is a fixed third argument, and the viewer attach names its session exactly (`-t =<name>`), so a viewer of a lost `terminal-1` is refused rather than shown `terminal-10`. The agent dispatch script (`agent.sh <name> [view]`, the chat's terminal back face) takes the same viewer marker after the agent name.

### system/libs/app_manifest

`select-tests` prints its test and type-check commands as `uv run --no-sync ...`, so running them never relocks or syncs the workspace.

`select-tests` names the always-run guard tests at their new paths inside the `agents_shared` and `launch_task_skill` packages.

The README points at the name-rule drift test at its new path, `system/scripts/workspace_bare_scripts/forward_port_test.py`.

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor.

`select-tests` no longer names `system/scripts/stdlib_only_scripts_test.py` among the always-run guards; the root `system/test_no_type_errors.py`, which runs with every `system/*.py`, replaces it.

`select-tests` runs a skill's `python/` project as part of the skill's own suite: a change that reaches it (a library it depends on, a `uv.lock` upgrade) selects `.agents/skills/<name>` once, instead of the skill and its `python/` directory as two runs of the same tests.

`select-tests` treats every user package (a standalone project under `system/` that the root workspace does not name) as its own pytest root, so its tests run from its directory against its own venv, and they still run when a library it depends on by path changes. A changed Python package whose own suite has no tests now gets an import check, run in that package's environment, so a change nothing would otherwise load (an undeclared import, say) is still caught.

A launch path may declare a `mention_param` beside `text_param` and `draft_param` (at most one of the three): the declared param the desktop's shell fills with a mention of the person whose tray entry was clicked (`@<handle> `), never a launcher row. The registry row carries it, and `forward_port.py` copies it.

A launch path may declare `app_params = {name = "<param>", display_name = "<param>"}`, two of its params the desktop fills with the name and display name of the app whose window's "Chat about this app" button was pressed (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 9.2); it stands alone like `text_param`, `draft_param`, and `mention_param` (at most one of the four), and the registry row carries it.

An app's `app.toml` may declare `[[keybindings]]`: the actions the keyboard can trigger in it, each with an id, a label, and its default chords (`KeybindingAction`, with the `KeybindingActionId` and `KeybindingActionLabel` rules; ids unique within the manifest). `RegistryRow` carries them as `keybindings`, so the shell's Keyboard shortcuts dialog lists every app's actions from the registry whether or not the app is running (user-profile-state spec, phase 3C).

`find_wiring_sections` accepts a declared wiring program whose supervisord block is an `[eventlistener:...]` section (the Screen's `screen-watch`), attributing it to its drop-in like a program's block.

The README's footprint description uses the Screen (its stack's programs and `screen-watch`, each in its own drop-in) as the `wiring` example in place of the deleted browser app and its `xvfb`.

### system/libs/bootstrap

`bootstrap` runs the env-converge fast phase with `uv run --no-sync`. In a newly created workspace, its window starts it from `.venv/bin` after a `--frozen` sync instead of under `uv run`; a workspace created earlier keeps the `uv run bootstrap` window mngr recorded when it created it. It execs supervisord with the workspace venv first on `PATH` and `VIRTUAL_ENV` set, as `uv run` used to leave it, so supervisord's programs still resolve their entry points (a user-built app's included) in the venv.

The README names the app check by its new path and launch, `uv run --no-sync system/scripts/workspace_scripts/verify_app.py <name> --restart`.

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

The docstring of the environment bootstrap hands supervisord now gives its current reason (bare-named commands such as the agent observer's `mngr` resolve to the workspace venv first), since every app's program line names its entry point by path and no app has a uv tool of its own. No behavior change.

The bootstrap no longer fetches the user's timezone from the Imbue Studio desktop at boot (user-profile-state spec, section 8.4): the client that creates a workspace now writes `data/.state/user_timezone` once, and the boot's `set_timezone` step just applies that file -- the same file the old fetch cached, so workspaces created by older clients keep their zone. Drops the bootstrap's `tenacity` dependency, which only the fetch used.

The README's account of the deferred first-boot installs now names the Screen's stack and the pinned neko binary beside Fortress: both install through the env.d unit `system/scripts/env.d/2000-screen.sh`, which replaced `1000-playwright-fortress.sh`, and the Screen service answers `installing` until that unit is satisfied.

### system/libs/routines

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

`routines migrate-cron` converts a cron line with shell syntax (quotes, `&&`, pipes, `$` expansions) into a routine that runs the line's text through the entry's shell, as cron did, instead of splitting it into words that fail on every run. `\%` becomes a literal `%`, and a line whose bare `%` feeds the command input stays with cron.

It also carries over the state of jobs that never ran on minds-v0.8.7, which the old runner kept under `system/data/.state/jobs/`, so a migrated job keeps its last success and does not run again at update time.

The feed notifier reads the latchkey gateway through the new `latchkey-access` library (`GatewayAccess`) instead of its own copy of the environment and header names; a missing address or password still skips the notification with a warning.

### system/libs/share_grants

New library: the parsers for the workspace's two grants documents, the people's (`data/.secrets/share_grants.toml`) and the visiting agents' (`data/.secrets/agent_access/grants.toml`, with the gateway's last-seen record beside it), shared by the share gateway and the shell so each reads the same files one way.

Tidied the granted-app tests `grants_test.py` took over from the shell (the extra blank line before `test_render_grants_roundtrips_through_parse` is gone), and the README now names the granted-app query (`Grants.granted_app_names`) among the `grants` module's API.

### system/libs/tk_command_parsing

New `tk_command_parsing.uv_run.unwrap_uv_run` returns the program a `uv run` command starts, past the options that leave it unchanged (`--no-sync`, `--frozen`, `--quiet`); the secrets guard and the chat's tk-lifecycle detection both use it, so they agree on which `uv run` forms they see through.

The README and the parser's docstring name the guard checks that import this library at their new home, `system/scripts/workspace_bare_scripts/`; the hooks now reach them through `system/scripts/agent_hook_check.py`.

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

### system/libs/workspace_layout

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

- `workspace_layout.identity` (moved from the shell) parses the `X-Imbue-Identity` header into a `RequestIdentity` and resolves it to a `ParticipantKey` (`owner`, `user:<id>`, `agent:<id>`); `workspace_layout.roster` carries the roster document (`RosterParticipant`, `RosterDocument`), the mention handles, and the participant colour palette.

- The shell client gains `roster()` for `GET /api/roster`, and the client inventory's records name each client's participant.

`ShellLayoutInterface` gains two best-effort posts an app makes to the shell for the taskbar's tray (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, sections 6.4 and 6.5): `post_bubble` (`POST /api/bubbles`, a `BubblePost`: who said what, in which chat, mentioning whom) and `report_chats_activity` (`POST /api/chats-activity`, a `ChatsActivityReport`: every chat's title, status, and kind). The models live in `workspace_layout.feed`, with `ChatActivityStatus` and `ChatActivityKind` in the primitives; `ShellLayoutClient` posts them as it posts a client-activity report, `DisconnectedShell` drops them, and the testing `FakeShell` records them.

`Desktop` (and so the `desktop` object every listing, op answer, and `desktops_updated` carries) gains `owner`: the participant key of the person the desktop belongs to by convention, or `None` for the workspace owner's, which every desktop from before the key was kept is (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 8.1). `DesktopsListing` describes its desktops as being in display order: creation order, as the shell's `POST /api/desktops/order` rearranged it.

- `RequestIdentity` gains `is_header_present`, set only by the header parse: it tells a page's request (a proxy stamped it) from an in-container caller's (a script's, the terminal's), which both read as the owner otherwise -- what lets the chat app annotate the owner's page sends without counting scripts as the owner writing.

- `ClientRecord` (and so the client objects of the clients listing and the inventory) gains `viewport`: a `Viewport` (width and height in CSS pixels) of the backdrop the client's desktop layout last reported its frames as fractions of, or `None` for a client that never has (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, section 8.3); a window viewing one of the client's desktops draws the layout at that size.

- `ParticipantKey` is filename-safe in every form: an `email:` key admits no whitespace, slash, `#`, `?`, or `%`, and a `name:` key no slash or control character, so a key names a mentions file and sits in a route's path without escaping.

- `parse_identity_header` raises `InvalidIdentityHeaderError` (an `InvalidLayoutValueError`) for a present, non-blank header that does not parse, instead of logging it and answering the anonymous owner (the multiplayer spec, section 4.2); a missing or blank header still does, so an in-container caller reads as the owner and a visitor behind a buggy proxy never does.

`WindowState` gains `FULLSCREEN` (the Screen spec's L2 layer: the window fills the whole viewport, taskbar and title bar gone), `PLACEABLE_STATES` includes it, and `workspace-layout place <window> --state fullscreen` sets it; `restore` brings a fullscreen window back to its kept frame like a maximized one.

`workspace-layout open https://...` opens the page through the Screen app's `browser` launch path (`{"app": "screen", "launch": "browser", "params": {"url": ...}}`), since the browser is a launch path of the Screen now and the browser app is gone; the command's help, hints and retired-verb replacements say "the browser on the Screen" and name the Screen service's `POST /browsers/<name>/stop` and `.../start`.

### system/libs/workspace_profile

New `workspace-profile` library: reads the workspace profile snapshot a client (the Imbue Studio desktop, or the hosted web chrome) writes at `data/.state/profile/account.json`, loads the workspace's own per-user override files and the shell's unsent changes under `data/system/profile/`, and resolves account-keyed settings for a request identity (user-profile-state spec, phase 3B).

The snapshot carries no setting keys yet (keybindings arrive with phase 3C); its format and keys are pinned against the desktop's vendored contract fixture.

Keybindings become the first account-keyed setting the workspace consumes (user-profile-state spec, phase 3C).

- New `keybindings.py`: the canonical chord grammar (lowercase tokens joined with `+`, modifiers in the fixed ctrl/alt/shift/meta order, named keys from the lowercased `KeyboardEvent.key` vocabulary, `cmd` normalized to `meta`), validation and normalization, and per-assignment resolution across the user's override, the owner's unsent changes, the snapshot, and an app's declared defaults. The grammar vocabulary is pinned against the vendored desktop contract fixture.

- New `manifest.py`: `load_app_keybinding_actions` reads an app's `[[keybindings]]` from its `app.toml` and refuses a default chord off the grammar, plus the shape of each app's `GET /api/keybindings/me` answer and the resolver the apps share. The library now depends on `app-manifest`.

- `overrides.py` gains the atomic writers of the per-user override files and the shell's `unsent.json` (with the same path-shaped-user-id refusal as the loader); errors move to a new `errors.py`.

- `CONSUMED_SETTING_KEYS` gains `"keybindings"`, matching the desktop's updated contract fixture.

- The library's own `identity.py` is gone: the resolution keys on `workspace_layout.identity`'s `RequestIdentity`, the one definition the shell and the apps read, so the library now depends on `workspace-layout`.

### system/libs/workspace_themes

The README runs the `workspace-themes` commands as `uv run --no-sync workspace-themes ...`, so a one-off never relocks or syncs the workspace.

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

The standard title bar (the chrome a theme without a `[chrome]` table wears) becomes the multiplayer spec's section 9.1 arrangement: the window menu and Refresh lead, the app icon and title sit centred over the bar, and minimize, maximize, and close end at the right edge. Themes that declare their own `[chrome]` keep their arrangement; the one visible change for them is that a centre-aligned title now carries its icon with it into the centre when the chrome names an icon slot.

The colour contract gains two tokens a theme may set: `--c-bubble-other` (a chat bubble that is not the viewer's own, and the chat list's selected row) and `--c-fill-faint` (a hover one step lighter than a selection drawn with `--c-bubble-other`).

The two drawn built-in themes (Classic Mac, Windows 2000) ship a hand-drawn icon for the Screen, a monitor on a stand showing one window, in place of the deleted browser app's globe, and the built-in theme icon test counts the Screen among the apps every drawn theme must cover.

### system/libs/workspace_ui

`describeRequestErrorKind` now recognises mngr's `submission_unconfirmed` send-failure kind (the message was typed and Enter sent, but nothing confirmed the agent took it), so the chat can give it its own notice. mngr's `agent_not_found` still reads as `unknown`: nothing was typed, so the default Retry fits it.

- The app contract reports input: every page that binds it sends `shell:input` (a pointer press or a key, throttled to one message per 20 seconds) up to the shell, whose presence heartbeat reads the client's activity off it -- input inside an app's frame never bubbles to the shell's own window, which is why everyone used to read as idle.

- New colour tokens: the viewer's own chat bubble becomes a green tint (`--c-bg-user-bubble`), a bubble that is not yours (another person's or the agent's) and the chat list's selected row share one 5% grey (`--c-bubble-other`), and `--c-fill-faint` (3%) is a hover one step lighter than a selection drawn with it.

- The shell's handshake carries `isViewing`: whether the window is being looked at on somebody else's desktop (the multiplayer spec, section 8.3), sent again when that changes. A page attaching to something shared (a terminal's tmux session) attaches as a viewer then.

- The icon set gains `mail`, an envelope, which the desktop's tray draws for an invited email, and `user`, a person's silhouette, which it draws for the owner of a workspace that has not shared (the mngr repo's `specs/multiplayer-refinements/spec.md`, sections 6.2 and 6.3).

`embed.ts` carries the embed contract's v12 immersive-mode pair (`IMMERSIVE_REQUEST`, `IMMERSIVE_CHANGED`, probed from the vendored module like the rest) and dispatches `minds:immersive-changed` to its handler; `embed-contract.d.ts` declares both and `MAX_IMMERSIVE_ERROR_LENGTH`.

### system/services/caretaker

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

### system/services/env_converge

The README and the CLI's module help document the subcommands as `uv run --no-sync env-converge ...`.

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

env-converge no longer reinstalls a recorded uv tool whose name is one of this workspace's apps (the `[project]` name of a package under `system/apps/`). Apps now run only from the workspace venv, so such an entry is an old per-app tool, and the package index's project of that name belongs to someone else (`system-monitor` 0.1.0 is one). A record captured before an update removed those tools would otherwise have installed it as root on a rebuilt rootfs.

The `UnitRunResult` example in `data_types.py` names `2000-screen.sh`, the env.d unit that replaced `1000-playwright-fortress.sh` when the Screen's stack took over the browser's install.

The upgrade's apt steps pass `-oDPkg::Lock::Timeout=600`, so an `env-converge upgrade` that runs while the boot-time env-converge is still installing the Screen's stack waits for the dpkg lock instead of failing at once with "Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend".

### system/services/host_backup

Each backup tick refreshes the environment record with `uv run --no-sync env-converge capture`, so a tick can no longer relock or sync the workspace. The slow-backup hint points at `uv run --no-sync host-backup-heavy-dirs`.

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

The comment on the backup's exclusion of the update apply's snapshot directory now lists what that directory holds (the mngr tool's environment, `node_modules` and the built bundles): apps no longer have uv tools of their own to copy aside, and the venv is swapped by link rather than copied. Backups are unchanged.

`data/system/backup.toml` gains a `verification_disabled` key (default `false`): the per-workspace "backup verification off" flag the Imbue Studio app used to keep on each computer now lives in the workspace itself, so every computer agrees on it (user-profile-state spec, phase 3B). The backup service reads the key tolerantly and ignores it; backups run either way.

### system/services/oom_priority

The ledger module's docstring says the launch-task script now imports it from the root venv (a declared dependency) rather than through a `sys.path` edit.

The new `oom_priority.supervisord_testing` module holds `supervisord_commands`, the supervisord program reader the band tests, the app-manifest tests and the supervisord layout test share.

The launch-wrapper and memory-candidates tests import their scripts like the other `bin/` tests instead of loading them by path. Now that the type checker sees `memory_candidates`'s real types, the tests annotate their `Sources` helper and check that the candidate lists are present before reading them.

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

`SERVICE_BANDS` gains `style-guide` (84), the Style Guide app's own band, between Getting Started and System Monitor: a built-in never sits in the user band.

`SERVICE_BANDS` gains `screen = 72` (between `cron` and `files`) for the Screen service, and loses `xvfb`, whose program is gone; the Screen's stack members (`screen-xorg`, `screen-session`, `screen-pulse`, `screen-neko`) and its `screen-watch` listener resolve to the Screen's band by program name through `_NON_SERVICE_PROGRAM_BANDS`, so the backstop never pushes them to the user band.

With the browser's migration onto the Screen (the Screen spec, section 16), `SERVICE_BANDS` loses the `browser` key: the browser app and its coordinator program are gone, and the Screen service (`screen`, 72) is what launches Chromium now. The shared-browser band stays for Chromium's processes, remapped into it by the Screen service's raise-only band sweep (`system/apps/screen/src/screen/band_sweep.py`), which also raises every other program started from the Screen to `AGENT_SUBPROCESS`; the README's band table and "The Chromium exception" say so.

`memory_candidates.py` reads the fleet from the Screen service (`MINDS_SCREEN_SERVICE_URL`, the `screen` registry row, else `http://127.0.0.1:8090`) and lists a running browser as a candidate while no window of the Screen exists on any desktop (the browser's windows are on the Screen, which never stops for emptiness); a candidate's `controller` reads `human` for any human in control of the Screen.

- The Screen's stack (`screen-xorg`, `screen-session`, `screen-pulse`, `screen-neko`) and its `screen-watch` listener move from the Screen service's band (72) to a band of their own, `SCREEN_STACK` (850): above every agent, an abandoned chat's ceiling (800) included, and below `AGENT_SUBPROCESS` (900), so under pressure the desktop an agent or the user launched is shed after the programs on it and before any agent, never before the agent that launched it. The Screen service itself stays at 72. Each stack program passes its own name to `oom_tag_service.py`, which now resolves a key through `SERVICE_BANDS` and then `_NON_SERVICE_PROGRAM_BANDS` (`bands.tag_key_band`).

### system/services/share_gateway

The `template_commit` docstring names `resolve_template_base.py` at its package path, `.agents/shared/scripts/agents_shared/`.

The project requires Python 3.12 or newer (was 3.11), matching the workspace floor: every workspace already runs 3.12, and the lock already required it.

- The grants parsers moved to the shared `share_grants` library; the gateway keeps only the agent key check (`agent_keys.py`).

- A visiting agent's last-seen time is refreshed every 10 seconds instead of every minute, so the shell's roster can show whether the agent is connected.

The share gateway brokers the Screen's stream for visitors (`docs/system/specs/screen/spec.md` section 15, `specs/turn-relay/spec.md` section 7, `specs/screen-studio-integration/spec.md` section 6.3):

- Every relay's frpc config renders a second proxy, `screen-media` of type `tcp`, `localPort` 59000 (neko's TCP ICE mux) and `remotePort` the assignment's `media_port`, when the assignment carries one; none otherwise.

- `GET /shares/assignment` is parsed additively: `media_port` and `published_endpoints` are read when present, and an older connector's answer without them still works (the cache round-trips both).

- The gateway fetches `GET /turn/ice-servers` from the connector with the relay token at stack start and at half life, keeps the credential in memory only, serves an empty list after a refusal or an unreachable connector (retrying five minutes later, and keeping a credential already held until it expires), and never fails the share over it.

- `GET /connect-info` on the loopback port 8791, beside `/_auth/*`, answers the Screen service `{"ice_servers", "candidates"}`: the credential as fetched, and the assignment's `published_endpoints` plus one `tcp` candidate per relay address at `media_port`, each with its `guest_port`. caddy never routes a visitor to it.

- The `screen-media` proxy delivers a visitor's connection to neko's TCP mux at the workspace's own interface address, not loopback: neko's ICE stack (pion) keys its TCP mux by the local address a connection arrives on and gathers a candidate for the interface alone, so a connection spliced to loopback was accepted and then read by nothing, and a visitor of a shared local workspace never got past the screencast. The address is found at render time (`local_address.py`); a workspace with no routable address renders no media proxy.

## [minds-v0.9.5] - 2026-10-30

### .agents

`update-self` carries the Style Guide frontend's bundle like the Routines app's: a change under `system/apps/style_guide/frontend/` rebuilds, snapshots and verifies it, and a worker hands it in with `--worker-bundle style_guide=<path>`.

The `datalib` skill now installs datalib v0.47.0. Requests to Cloudflare-fronted sources (Claude, ChatGPT) and to Slack, GitHub and GitLab are decoded by datalib's own curl: the Imbue Studio gateway hands their compressed replies on as received, which fixes the Slack sync failing on a truncated reply. Notion sources bring everything under a root, databases' rows included, read a page as a document, and link inline databases rather than fetching them as pages. Search narrows by its keys before ranking, gives one fused answer with each document listed once, lands a hit on the message holding the search's words, and reaches eight more sources through `me` and `from:me`. Packages add sources, their renders and applets from a link or a gallery. In the Datalib app, every document has a title bar that stays put, a date chip can serve as T0 so every date reads as its distance from that instant, and charts draw their time axis from it. A Slack routine sync skips quiet channels, and a Google Drive sync of a few changed files takes seconds rather than minutes.

The `datalib` skill now installs datalib v0.48.0. A Slack sync mirrors a channel created since the last sync on the very next run, and shows a first-time poster's name instead of their raw user id. A source keeps at most eight requests out at once, and the Manage screen stays fast as the run log grows. Search ranks whole documents and lands only the page it shows. An agent can now propose contacts, handle links and a `real` (not spam) label to the contacts app in one batch; the user confirms or overrides each in the contacts card's new Review tab. In the Datalib app, a click selects a row and a double-click, Enter or the menu opens it, and Claude Code and Codex syncs show an ETA.

`launch-custom-agent`'s worktree-mode test now expects claude's trust to be recorded under the work dir's realpath, and passes in imbue_cloud workspaces and on macOS. It used to expect `/home/user/worktrees/my-task` as written. Claude checks a folder's trust against the realpath of its cwd, and in an imbue_cloud workspace `/home/user` is a symlink to `/mngr-vol/home`, so the launcher was already writing the key claude reads. The test was the part that was wrong.

- `build-app` shows the design as pictures in the chat when the user asks for pictures, loops on them like any mock, and builds the served mock from the look the user confirms; without such an ask the mock is still a served page, never a picture in its place. The shared interactive-delivery reference says the same of a detached prototype.

- The interactive-delivery reference's "no production state" rule names what it excludes as production-grade work (production scripts, data layers, tests) and says the scaffold a specialization sets up to serve the prototype is fine, so it no longer reads as a ban on serving the prototype at all.

- `build-app` and the shared interactive-delivery reference say the look-and-feel mock is a page the scaffolded app serves, never a picture of one: an SVG, PNG or generated image shown in chat cannot be clicked, shows none of the interactions the user is judging, and is discarded instead of growing into the real page. The skill's description names the served mock page too, so an agent that reads only the description sees it.

Adds the launch-custom-agent skill: a chat agent can now launch a coding agent that works in the user's own repo or directory instead of the workspace checkout, as its own git worktree or in place. The launched agent runs vanilla -- the user's repo conventions govern it, none of the workspace's chat instructions -- but still appears as a chat in the Imbue Studio UI, binds to a signed-in provider account like any chat, and is told where it is running and how to notify the user.

- After a test command is shed, the harden worker reads the free memory the guard acts on with `memory_candidates.py --free-memory`, which prints only that line and reads nothing but the meminfo files, so it is cheap to rerun while memory is short.

- The memory-freeing guides describe a candidate's memory as its processes' own memory, roughly what stopping it frees.

### system

The Style Guide app's frontend joins the npm workspace (`system/package.json`, its lockfile, and the Dockerfile's manifest copies), its built bundle is ignored like the other frontends', and its program runs on port 8060 (`system/supervisord.conf.d/style-guide.conf`).

The Classic Mac and Windows 2000 themes ship the Style Guide's icon (`icons/style-guide.png`): a painter's palette, one bit deep for Classic Mac, in shaded wood with four paints for Windows 2000.

`system/supervisord.conf.d/style-guide.conf` does not autostart.

Bug reports keep more of what they collect when the secret scan finds something.

- The scan now withholds only the files it flags, not the whole group. Before, one chat with a flagged line withheld every chat, and one flagged service log withheld every service log. `collection-notes.txt` names each withheld file, so a partial set never reads as the complete one. A file whose own name was flagged is listed without its name.

- Credentials in URL query strings are blanked before the scan. The value of a parameter like `token=`, `access_token=`, `api_key=` or a presigned link's `X-Amz-Signature=` becomes `REDACTED`, so a newsletter sign-in link in a chat, or a token-carrying URL in a log, no longer costs the report that file. The scan still reads the result, so anything the blanking misses is withheld as before.

The `test-offload` CI sandboxes now give `/home/user` the layout an imbue_cloud workspace has: a symlink to `/mngr-vol/home` instead of the plain directory the image ships. Before this, a test that compared a written `/home/user/...` path with a resolved one passed in CI and failed only in users' workspaces. Coverage records resolved paths, so the chat and system_interface coverage path maps now name `/mngr-vol/home/workspace/...`.

- Pin mngr to the public mirror of the Imbue Studio 0.9.5 release commit, so workspaces built from the `minds-v0.9.5` tag run the mngr the 0.9.5 desktop app ships with.

Adds the `custom` create template backing the launch-custom-agent skill: it keeps an agent launchable from a work dir that is not a checkout of this template by repointing every harness's OOM launch wrapper and codex's plugin provisioning at absolute workspace paths, replaces the per-harness workspace prompt blocks (tk, .agents/skills, data/memories) with one custom-agent context block, and restores claude's native planning and todo tools. Template-stacking tests pin the new template's settings against mngr's live config model.

- Every supervised program (the chat app, routines, the agent observer, the system interface) now runs with `MNGR_ALLOW_UNKNOWN_CONFIG=1`, set once in `system/supervisord.conf`. An update makes the new `.mngr/settings.toml` live before it reinstalls mngr, so for that window the old mngr rejected settings only the new one knows, and a chat create, rename or routine could fail; from the next update after this one, those calls go through. Agents' own `mngr` calls stay strict.

The phone interface plan now says the bottom bar steps aside while the soft keyboard is up, and that the shell's viewport carries `maximum-scale=1` so iOS Safari does not zoom into a focused field.

### system/apps/chat

A Codex reply now shows in the chat while it is being written, as a Claude reply already does. Codex writes an agent message to its rollout file only once the whole message is finished, so on a reply of about 300 words the chat showed nothing for roughly 14 seconds while the agent's terminal was already streaming it. The chat app's live connection to the agent's Codex app-server already hears the reply as it is streamed (its `item/agentMessage/delta` notifications); the app now keeps the message being written from them, and while the chat is open in a window that is shown and focused, the page shows it at the end of the transcript until the real reply, matched by its message id, replaces it. Nothing extra is read for a chat in the background.

The provider chooser now asks again for its provider list when the request fails, waiting a little longer each time for about fifteen seconds before it shows "Could not load providers". The desktop app's connection to a new workspace can drop for a second or two, just as the welcome chat opens the chooser, and a single failed request used to leave a new user on that error screen until they pressed Try again. The chooser's load and the boot-time account load now share one retry loop; only the chooser's gives up, so a failure that persists still reaches the screen.

The screen's Try again button now carries `data-e2e="retry-providers"`, so the Electron end-to-end test in mngr can press it the way a user would.

Signing in to Google (Antigravity) no longer upgrades the workspace's agy. Unless told not to, agy starts a background updater on a regular run, including the bare `agy` the sign-in drives and even a signed-out `agy models`, and that updater replaces the binary it ran from with Google's latest release. The sign-in and the `agy models` check after it ran with the updater on, so one sign-in swapped the image's pinned `/usr/local/bin/agy` out from under every Antigravity chat after it. Both now run with `AGY_CLI_DISABLE_AUTO_UPDATE=true`, the same switch mngr sets for Antigravity agents.

The Claude shoulder tap no longer silently loses a message that its cancel caught mid-turn.

Before: Claude can fold a queued message into the turn that is already running, at its next tool result. If the tap's cancel then lands on that turn, the message is never answered. The tap is built to catch this and send a recovery nudge, but it decided whether a new turn had started from mngr's `active` marker. An interrupt fires no Stop hook, so the cancelled turn's marker was still on disk, and the tap reported success with nothing running.

Now the tap decides from the session ledger. A `dequeue` after the chord means the queued prompt started its own turn. An assistant record counts as that turn's answer only once it follows the interrupt sentinel, because before the sentinel the turn being cancelled is still writing. Without either, the tap sends the recovery nudge, which starts the turn that answers the message.

A new `real_claude` test drives both cases against the pinned Claude Code: the cancelled follow-on gets the nudge and an answer, and a flushed turn that answers slowly gets none.

The browser test of the Compacting strip clearing when its marker goes is marked flaky, so CI retries it while its cause is found (MIND-646).

The coverage path map now names `/mngr-vol/home/workspace/system/apps/chat/`, the resolved path the `test-offload` CI sandbox records now that its `/home/user` is a symlink to `/mngr-vol/home` (the layout of an imbue_cloud workspace). Without it the runner could not combine the sandbox batches against the coverage floor.

The chat list no longer marks an idle chat (it had a hollow ring) or a stopped one (it had a small pause sign): their rows show no mark at all, and a stopped chat's row stays dimmed. Titles keep their place, so every row still lines up. Working, waiting on a background task, needs attention, error, and the green check of a finished turn are unchanged. Each title also sits 2px closer to its mark (6px, down from 8px), giving titles a little more room.

A Pi or Antigravity reply now shows in the chat while it is being written, as Claude and Codex replies already do. Pi writes an assistant message to its session file only once the message is finished; mngr's pi lifecycle extension now keeps the text streamed so far in `pi_reply_draft`, for any model pi runs, and the chat reads it. Antigravity writes a planner step's text into its conversation store while the step is still generating, which the chat used to skip until the step finished; it now shows that text at the end of the transcript until the finished reply replaces it. As before, only a chat open in a window that is shown and focused is read. OpenCode has no chat transcript yet, so it has no draft either.

The OOM prioritizer re-tags every live process of a chat, so a codex chat's TUI and its app-server daemon both follow the chat's activity instead of the TUI keeping its launch band. It also no longer re-tags a process that only reused a stale registry entry's pid, the likely way one workspace's chat app was itself marked as an abandoned chat and shed.

### system/apps/routines

The Routines pages scroll again. The shared base style keeps the page body from scrolling, and the pages had no scrolling area of their own, so anything below the window edge could not be reached. Each page now draws inside a window-tall scroller.

### system/apps/style_guide

New: the Style Guide app, one page cataloguing the workspace's design system. Foundations lists every color token (a swatch drawn with the live value, its utility, its `--c-*` value and the value as declared, under `base.css`'s own groups), the type roles and font stacks, spacing, corner radius, elevation, motion, the stacking layers and widths, and the whole icon set; Components draws every Button variant, size and state, the text fields, the Dropdown and SegmentedControl, the Menu with a submenu, check rows and disabled and danger rows, hover tooltips, badges, banners, activity dots, spinners, the Modal, the notice and delete-confirmation dialogs, toasts, and the surfaces stacked as the apps stack them. The tokens are read out of the shared stylesheet at build time and the components are the library's own, so the catalog follows the library with no edit of its own.

It wears the workspace's theme (`[theming] mode = "tokens"`), opening in it without a flash of the standard look, and serves the themes from its own origin. Under a theme every swatch and control is that theme's, each value caption shows the value the page wears with the standard one struck through when the theme changed it, and the header names the theme. A Theming group lists every part a theme can style, linked to the section that shows it. The shadow values (`--c-shadow-*`) are drawn as elevation rather than as colors, and the font stacks include `--font-display`.

The Tooltips section shows the tooltip's quieter second line (the `detail` option). A Plain pages section frames a page built as plain HTML on the page kit, which the app serves from its own origin (`/page-kit-sample`, and the kit's `/_static/workspace_theme.css` and `.js` from the shell's build); the page hands the theme the shell names on to it, previews included. The parts list names each section by its contents label, and links the tile and list-row parts to that frame.

The contents column runs the full height of the window beside the page, scrolling on its own with a thin bar in a gutter of its own, so on a system that always shows scrollbars the bar never sits against the labels. A long color value (a `color-mix()`) wraps at its spaces in a column of its own width.

The colors are one compact table, a row per color: a swatch (a text color as "Aa" in it, a border color as an outline of it, any other as a frameless chip of it), its name (the utility and its `--c-*` value), and the value the page wears. The page says "color" throughout.

The contents column highlights the section the reader is in from the scroll position (a section jumped to is the highlighted one, not the one above it, and the last at the end of the page), and scrolls itself to keep that entry in view.

The app does not start at boot and is listed once it has been started by hand (`supervisorctl start style-guide`); from then on the shell starts it on the next request for its page.

### system/apps/system_interface

The coverage path map now names `/mngr-vol/home/workspace/system/apps/system_interface/`, the resolved path the `test-offload` CI sandbox records now that its `/home/user` is a symlink to `/mngr-vol/home` (the layout of an imbue_cloud workspace). Without it the runner could not combine the sandbox batches against the coverage floor.

On a phone, tapping a text field no longer zooms the page in. iOS Safari zoomed into any field set smaller than 16px (the chat composer, the start sheet) and stayed zoomed after the field let go; the shell's viewport now carries `maximum-scale=1`, which stops that in every app's page. Pinch-zoom still works in a Safari tab, but no longer in the shell saved to an iPhone's home screen or in Android Chrome.

While a phone's soft keyboard is up, the bottom bar steps aside so the shown page reaches down to the keyboard, and it comes back when the keyboard goes. The keyboard is read off the viewports (a touch screen, a field or an app's page focused, and a visual viewport as wide as the layout and more than a fifth shorter), so a mouse-driven window, a pinch zoom, or a hardware keyboard keeps the bar.

### system/apps/system_monitor

System Monitor counts a process as an agent's only while it is still the process that registered, so a pid that an unrelated process reused, or a thread id, is no longer shown as that agent's chat.

### system/libs/workspace_ui

`components/icons.ts` exports `ICON_NAMES`, every stroke-outline icon's name, which the Style Guide app draws the whole set from.

### system/services/oom_priority

- The agent-pid registry now records each agent process's start time and boot id, and a reader counts an entry only while its pid is still that process: not a thread of another process, and started at the recorded time in the same boot. Under gVisor pids are reused within hours, `/proc/<id>` also resolves for a thread, and the registry outlives a container restart. So a leftover entry could point the chat app's prioritizer at an unrelated process. That is the likely way one workspace's chat app ended up marked as an abandoned chat (`oom_score_adj` 800) and was shed during an update. An entry written before this change, which has no start time, counts while its pid is a process whose environment carries the agent id the entry records, so chats that are already running keep being re-tagged until they next start. The earlyoom kill hook, which reads an entry after its process is gone, no longer names an agent from an entry recorded in an earlier boot.

- `lookup_pids_by_agent_id` returns every live process of an agent, so both of a codex chat's processes (its TUI and its app-server) get re-tagged rather than only one.

- The memory candidates command reports each candidate's anonymous memory (from `smaps_rollup`, or `smaps` under gVisor) instead of summed `VmRSS`. Under gVisor `VmRSS` counts every mapped binary in full and read about two times too high for a claude chat, three for a codex TUI and ten for codex's helper. The JSON field is now `anonymous_kib`. A new `--free-memory` flag prints only the free memory line, reading nothing but the meminfo files.

### system/services/share_gateway

The gateway's access log no longer records query strings. Every sign-in through a share logged the full `/_auth/callback?token=<JWT>` request line, so the handoff token (with the visitor's email) sat in `share-gateway.log`. A bug report's secret scan then flagged that log and withheld the workspace's logs from the report. A request with a query string is now logged as `GET /_auth/callback?<query omitted>`.

Lines already in an existing `share-gateway.log` stay there until the log rotates.

## [minds-v0.9.4] - 2026-10-28

### system

- Bump the Antigravity CLI (`agy`) baked into the image from 1.1.22 to 1.4.7, pinned to the 1.4.7 release URLs and sha512 checksums from Google's release manifest. The installer is renamed from `system/scripts/agy_install-1.1.22.sh` to `system/scripts/agy_install.sh`, so future bumps change only the values inside it. A fresh agent now starts on Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) by default; there is still no model pin of our own.

- Pin mngr to the branch that records agy's reasoning effort in `model_state.json` and confirms agy slash commands as soon as agy handles them, which the chat app's Antigravity model picker relies on.

The claude, codex, pi, and opencode agent types in `.mngr/settings.toml` now pin their `version` to the binary `system/scripts/setup_system.sh` bakes into the image and set `version_mismatch = "WARN"`. Before, only claude was pinned, and a mismatch between the installed claude and its pin failed every create, so a workspace whose claude had drifted could not even create the update chat that would repair it; `message_chat.py --create` worked around that by skipping claude's installation check on every create (through the chat app and in its `mngr create` backoff). Now a mismatch on any of the four only logs a warning and the create goes ahead, so `message_chat.py --create` no longer skips anything. `check_installation` stays off for codex, pi, and opencode, so their baked binaries are still never reinstalled, and a pinned codex no longer runs mngr's provision-time codex update check (its version moves only with the image). A test now fails when a harness pin in `settings.toml` stops matching its `setup_system.sh` default. This needs an mngr that has the `version_mismatch` field: an older mngr refuses to load `settings.toml` because of the unknown key.

- Pin mngr to the public mirror of the Imbue Studio 0.9.4 release commit, so workspaces built from the `minds-v0.9.4` tag run the mngr the 0.9.4 desktop app ships with.

### system/apps/chat

Antigravity chats can now change model and reasoning effort from the model picker, just as Claude, Codex and Pi chats can. Previously the picker only showed the model, and choosing a Gemini model left no way to switch to anything else from the chat.

The picker lists Antigravity's current models: Gemini 3.8 Flash (with a low / medium / high effort control), Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6, and GPT-OSS 120B. A pick is sent to the agent as `/model <slug>`, which sets the model and effort in one step. It is typed by the same worker that delivers queued messages, and only once no turn is open, so a pick made mid-turn takes effect when that turn ends and never lands in a running turn. The chip shows the pick straight away and settles once the agent reports it. A model newer than the list still shows under its own name and can be switched away from.

The switch dialog now offers an Antigravity account's models too, and a new or rebound Antigravity chat starts on the chosen model. The model picker's read-only mode, which only Antigravity used, is gone.

`POST /api/chats/create` no longer takes `is_installation_check_skipped`, and a provisional chat no longer carries it. The chat app used it to skip claude's version check for the update chat, because a claude that no longer matched its pin failed the create. The workspace's settings now set `version_mismatch = "WARN"` for claude and the other pinned harnesses, so a mismatch only logs a warning and every create goes ahead without the flag. A request that still sends the field is now refused as an unknown field. This needs an mngr that has the `version_mismatch` field.

### system/apps/system_interface

Tests only: the layout pipeline tests' `layout_server` fixture no longer chooses the shell's port before it starts its two stand-in apps. When it did, a stand-in could take that port, and the shell's server then failed to start with "Address already in use". `test_context_and_desktops_round_trip_through_the_command_and_endpoint`, which hit this once in CI, is now marked flaky.

### system/libs/workspace_themes

`test_a_path_too_long_to_look_up_makes_only_its_theme_unavailable` no longer fails when pytest's temporary files are under `/var/tmp` in a gVisor workspace, as they were in an update's test run. There, the over-long file is reported as missing rather than unreadable; the test now accepts either problem, as long as it names the file.

## [minds-v0.9.3] - 2026-10-27

### .agents

The `datalib` skill now installs datalib v0.46.0, and tells an agent to start at `datalib-step help`, the one page from which every other datalib doc is reachable: the agent guide, a new guide to reading each source's raw store, and a new guide to building apps on datalib. A data root can now be set up from the shell (`datalib-dag init`, then `datalib-step examples <type> --append` per source), and searched there with no server (`datalib-applet search`). New sources: Todoist, and a calendar source that copies the meetings booked with you on Calendly. A ChatGPT source can be filled from a data export, past the API's rate limit, with the API taking only what changed after it. Gmail label filters keep whole threads, and each email carries Gmail's own ids and labels. In the Datalib app, a clock in the status bar sets the time zone and format of every date. Several sources re-render their documents on the first sync after the upgrade, and an older datalib can no longer open the store.

`record_publish_test.py`'s first-publish test no longer fails in any workspace that has updated, so it stops showing up as a failing test during `update-self`. Its fixture copied the repo's own `docs/VERSION_HISTORY.md`, which in a workspace already has a `created from` line, so `record_publish.py` correctly skipped seeding one and the test's assertion found nothing. The fixture now starts from the ledger the template ships (`update_ledger.VERSION_HISTORY_STARTER`).

A scheduled workspace update no longer stops to ask for memory it is allowed to free.

An update's heaviest moments -- launching its background helper, its test gate, the frontend build -- are the ones the memory guard kills first, and the memory that would unblock them is usually held by the apps. The update could stop only the apps no window was showing, which on a real run freed almost nothing: the memory was in three apps with windows open, and the update waited six and a half hours for the user to say it could stop them.

A scheduled update may now stop any app the memory candidates command lists, windows open or not. That list is the boundary, drawn so everything in it can be brought back: no critical app, nothing internal, nothing sharing a critical app's program, and nothing without a program to start again. A pressed "Update now" keeps the old rule, since the user is at the screen.

`run-status started-by` tells the two apart from the record the app writes when it creates the update chat, matching on the chat's name or its id, either one -- renaming a chat renames its agent, and a scheduled run in a renamed chat would otherwise fall back to asking.

`stop-apps` records each app before it stops the next, and `resume-apps` starts them again. The record matters because the pass stopping them is the one running out of memory, so its own chat may be killed before it restores anything; the next run carries over whatever this one never started. A landed update restarts every program regardless. The pass stops programs and never windows, so a window stays where it is and its page works again once its app is back.

A background helper whose checks were killed now has the update free memory for it under that rule and report the room it made, rather than improvising. It reaches the user only when everything the update may stop is stopped and there is still not enough. Narrowing or skipping a check is never the answer -- and the helper now judges a kill by the figure the memory guard acts on, not the container's `/proc/meminfo`, which reads far more free than the guard sees and sent it straight back into another kill.

New reference: `.agents/skills/update-self/references/freeing-memory-for-an-update.md`. Every other flow still offers the candidates and stops only what the user approves.

### system

`tk` rejects an empty or whitespace-only ticket id with `Error: empty ticket ID`. It used to partial-match every ticket, so `tk close "$UNSET_VAR"` closed the only regular ticket among the step records -- in a workspace, often another chat's editing lease -- and exited 0. The `tk edit` plugin, which carries its own copy of the lookup, gets the same check.

- Pin mngr to the public mirror of the Imbue Studio 0.9.3 release commit, so workspaces built from the `minds-v0.9.3` tag run the mngr the 0.9.3 desktop app ships with.

- Install latchkey 3.19.4 in workspaces (`LATCHKEY_VERSION` in `system/scripts/setup_system.sh`, from 3.19.3), matching the version the desktop app bundles and installs on cloud hosts.

CI runs the chat app's and the shell's browser tests again. Since the suites moved into the workspace image on offload, offload's discovery pass inherited each app's default `-m "not browser and not real_claude"` and dropped every browser test, so none had run in CI. `-m ''` now applies at discovery too, and the group filters leave out only `real_claude`, some of whose tests need a signed-in Claude account.

CI also runs `ruff check` over the root scope, the chat app and the shell, using the locked ruff.
