Like the changelog gate, it is opt-in through a repository variable (`ENFORCE_RUFF`), which the template sets, so workspace repos made from the template do not start linting their own apps. The pre-commit hook runs that same locked ruff instead of whatever `uvx` resolves.

mngr is pinned to a newer commit whose trailing-comment ratchet exempts a bare `# noqa` (or `# noqa: CODE`) ending its line, as it already exempts `# ty: ignore`.

### system/apps/browser

Re-sorted import blocks and dropped one unused import to satisfy `ruff check`, which CI now runs. No behavior change.

`test_http_cast_closes_a_closed_browser_with_the_terminated_signal` is marked flaky, so offload retries it rather than turning CI red.

The test waits for the cast socket's `closed` text frame, which its own comment described as "delivered intact before the close". It is not always: werkzeug corrupts the close handshake by writing a trailing HTTP response after the close frame, and when those bytes win the race the text frame is lost and the receive raises `ConnectionClosed(1005)`. Seen once in CI and gone on a re-run of the same commit. The underlying race is MIND-583, which is about the same close path and had assumed a text frame was the reliable signal.

### system/apps/chat

The app's browser tests run in CI again, and some had gone stale or never passed reliably while they did not:

- The long-chat wheel test waits for each tick's motion to land instead of a fixed 50 ms, which failed on slower machines while the chat was still measuring its history. It still fails if a tick makes the transcript jump.

- Five tests started a new chat through the launcher's primary row with nothing typed, which since the main chat landed sends to the main chat instead. They now start it from the chat list's New chat button, which made the separate test of that button with nothing signed in a duplicate of the provider-chooser test, so it is gone.

- The phone Model submenu test for a Pi chat now measures the menu once its slide has landed, not partway through it.

A Pi chat's model list is now read from the `pi` on PATH and cached per install, rather than cached once for the whole process. Before, a process that had read one `pi`'s models kept serving them after a different `pi` came first on PATH; a test that put its own `pi` on PATH after an earlier test had read the image's saw no model row in the menu.

Fixed the app's `ruff check` findings, which CI now enforces: one import block, three lambda assignments in tests, and a `noqa` on seven deliberate no-op hook methods. No behavior change.

### system/apps/files

Re-sorted two import blocks to satisfy `ruff check`, which CI now runs. No behavior change.

### system/apps/getting_started

Re-sorted one import block to satisfy `ruff check`, which CI now runs. No behavior change.

### system/apps/system_interface

The shell's browser tests run in CI again. One had gone stale while they did not: the avatar test now expects "Design your own..." to post no `window_path`, as it has since the main chat landed.

### system/apps/terminal

Re-sorted import blocks to satisfy `ruff check`, which CI now runs. No behavior change.

### system/libs/app_manifest

Gave the package its own ruff config (one import per line, like its sibling apps), which its code was already written in, and fixed the few findings under it so `ruff check`, which CI now runs, passes. No behavior change.

### system/libs/workspace_themes

The built-in theme icon test checks only the apps the template ships, so it no longer fails in a workspace that has apps the user built (a theme draws those from the app's own icon).

### system/services/oom_priority

The memory candidates command (`system/services/oom_priority/bin/memory_candidates.py`) now reports the free memory the memory daemon actually decides on, and lists the workspace's apps.

Before, it read free memory from the container's `/proc/meminfo`. On a workspace with a memory cap that is not the figure earlyoom acts on: earlyoom reads the headroom file the workspace publishes for its `--host-meminfo`, and the two disagree. On the capped workspace whose stalled update prompted this, `/proc/meminfo` said 3.1 GB free while the real headroom was 1.0 GB, and an agent that believed the first figure kept rerunning a build that kept being killed; a second workspace checked while writing this read 3.3 GB against 1.2 GB at an idle moment. The command now prefers the headroom file while it is fresh, falls back to `/proc/meminfo`, and names which file and which field it read. The rule is the one `oom_priority.meminfo` already applied for the resource sampler and the system monitor.

It also lists the apps the workspace may stop, each with how many windows show it, its supervisord program, whether the shell stops it by itself once no window shows it (`AUTO-STOP`, so an app that may be doing work between requests can be left for last), and the memory its program's process tree holds. A critical app, an app sharing a critical app's program, an internal app, an app with no program and one that is not running are all left out, and so is the browser, whose Chromium processes already have their own section. Before, the apps were missing entirely, so anyone freeing memory had to work out the list by hand.

The apps and the browsers now come from one read of the shell's inventory document rather than two reads of its desktops; a shell that cannot be reached takes both sections to "unknown" together.

### system/services/share_gateway

Gave the package its own ruff config (one import per line, like its sibling apps), which its code was already written in, and fixed the few findings under it so `ruff check`, which CI now runs, passes. Two test helpers now type their response instead of reaching `.headers` through `getattr`. No behavior change.

## [minds-v0.9.2] - 2026-10-26

### .agents

The `datalib` skill now installs datalib v0.45.0. A Gmail source can start from a Google Takeout of the same account and download only the mail newer than it, and ChatGPT keeps archived chats. In the Datalib app a source opens as one card (its documents, with its sync a tab away); sources, people and dates show as chips throughout, every date in a document in your own time zone; you can edit your own contact on its person card; and a right-click on the data root's size (or `datalib-dag --compact`) folds the rendered history to give back disk. Several sources re-render their documents on the first sync after the upgrade; the downloaded data is carried forward as it is, and an older datalib can no longer open the store.

The caretaker and `manage-desktop` now surface a chat with `workspace-layout show chat --path "/?chat=<id>" --showing "/<id>" --repoint /`, which shows it in the pinned chat window. The `open chat --path "/?chat=<id>"` they used before never matched the pinned window, so each run added another chat window.

New `docs/system/themeable-apps.md`: how to make an app themeable (`[theming] mode = "outside"`, serving and loading the page kit, the app's own look in a cascade layer, tokens with today's values as fallbacks, plain controls, `lint-app` to check). Only "Enable theming" points agents at it; app building does not read it.

A preview carries the app's `[theming]` mode from its worktree, and its page hands the shell's theme on to the app it frames, so the preview of a themeable app follows theme changes.

The guide has the agent ask about per-theme icons in the reply that shows the themed app, next to asking whether to keep it.

Skills for workspace themes.

- New `create-theme` skill: makes a workspace theme from a description or a picture -- lays out the folder, writes its tokens, chrome, and part styles (vendoring a CSS library where one fits), validates it, judges it in the theme gallery, and points the user at Desktop settings to try it; it then asks two things about icons: whether to draw one in the theme for each app that has none, in the background, and whether apps built later should get one too, which makes each build cost more and take longer. Only a yes to the second tells app building about the theme, by adding one line naming it to the workspace's `AGENTS.md`; otherwise new apps use their standard icon under every theme.

- New `make-theme-icon` skill: draws an app's icon for a theme with whatever is available -- the harness's image tool, or a pixel grid or SVG the agent writes itself -- then fits, checks, and installs it.

- An icon in a theme's style is drawn only when the user asks for one; until then each theme shows an icon derived from the app's own. An agent drawing icons in a checkout of its own (a background worker) installs and checks them against the live workspace (`--repo-root /home/user/workspace`), since its own `data/` is not the one the shell reads.

- `system/libs/workspace_themes/`, which the shell, the chat, and the terminal run, takes `update-app`'s careful flow like `workspace_ui` and `workspace_layout` (`AGENTS.md`, `update-app`, `update-self`, and the harden-contention reference say so).

### system

The desktop-interface contracts (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/contracts.md`, section 7) list `opensLocalFiles` in `shell:handshake`: whether the Imbue Studio chrome opens its settings for the files shared from the user's computer (`minds:open-local-files`).

The desktop contracts (section 4.5a) describe `offer_tour`, the bootstrap's first-boot mark that decides whether a workspace with no `tour.json` is offered the show-around tour.

- Pin mngr to the public mirror of the Imbue Studio 0.9.2 release commit, so workspaces built from the `minds-v0.9.2` tag run the mngr the 0.9.2 desktop app ships with.

The automation agents' system prompt (`.mngr/settings.toml`) surfaces the agent's chat with `workspace-layout show chat ...` instead of `open chat ...`, so a scheduled run shows its chat in the pinned chat window rather than opening another. The desktop contracts document the shell's new `POST /api/clients/<client_id>/show` route and how a link to an app's pin page with a query of its own is shown through it.

`forward_port.py` copies an app manifest's `[theming] mode` into its registry row as `theming_mode`, and takes `--theming-mode` for a registration with no manifest (a preview of the app), so the shell can tell an app that themes itself, a themeable one, and one that is not themeable yet apart.

Workspace themes become a real feature: a theme is a folder of CSS and a `theme.toml` against a versioned contract (`docs/system/blueprint/workspace-themes/plan-workspace-themes.md`), and Standard, Classic Mac, and Windows 2000 ship as the built-in themes under `system/themes/`. The workspace can also hold its own themes in `themes/`.

- The shared UI library marks its components with the contract's parts (`data-part`), so a theme styles them without depending on class names, and adds the theme client (`themeClient.ts`), the boot plugin that wears a theme before first paint (`themeBoot.ts`), and the page kit for plain-HTML pages (`src/page/`). The app contract's `shell:theme` message (`{theme, revision, isPreview}`) reaches an app's `onTheme(theme, revision, isPreview)`, and `followShellTheme` follows the theme without connecting.

- Each built-in theme carries an icon guide and limits; Classic Mac and Windows 2000 carry pixel-art icons for the built-in apps in `system/themes/<theme>/icons/`.

- The built-in themes ship no font files: Classic Mac sets its type in Chicago, Geneva, and Monaco where the machine has them, and in the nearest installed faces where it does not.

- The terminal's pty page (`terminal_pty`) declares `[theming] mode = "none"`: its xterm takes only the theme's terminal palette, which the terminal app hands it.

- Docs: the desktop-interface and workspace-app-model contracts, `docs/system/app-icons.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, and the library README describe themes.

- The theme contract includes the `avatar` part and the `--desk-avatar-color` and `--desk-avatar-shadow-color` tokens, which both retro themes set.

### system/apps/browser

The browser declares `[theming] mode = "none"`: the pages it shows keep their own look under every workspace theme, and only the window around them is themed.

### system/apps/chat

A Claude reply now shows in the chat while it is being written, instead of only once Claude finishes it. Claude writes a reply to its session file only when the whole text block is done, so a page used to show nothing for the several seconds the agent's terminal was already streaming the answer. While the chat is open in a window that is shown and focused, and a turn is in flight, the chat app reads the reply off the agent's terminal three times a second (with mngr's `stream_snapshot` converter), and the page shows it at the end of the transcript until the real reply replaces it. Background chats (in a hidden or unfocused window, kept loaded out of sight, or not open at all) and agents with no turn running are never read.

A page now recovers transcript events its live stream never delivered. When a chat's turn ends, and when the page is shown again, the page asks for whatever follows its last event: missing events at the end are added in place, and a missing event further up reloads the transcript. Before, such an event stayed missing until the page was reloaded.

Switching back to a chat the chat list already had open now puts the keyboard in its composer, as opening a chat for the first time already did. Before, the keyboard stayed on the list, so that chat neither took typing nor counted as the one being looked at, and its replies did not stream until it was clicked.

No change you would notice: the chat's frame tests hand their windows a `shell:handshake` with the new `opensLocalFiles` flag, as the shell now sends one.

A chat now says where your message is at every moment from Enter to the reply, is usable while its agent is still starting or connecting, keeps every message sent to a chat that is still starting, and keeps the name you give it.

**Where your message is**

A chat now always says where your message is, from the moment you press Enter until the turn is done. One status row sits at the end of the conversation, where the reply will appear:

- Right after you send, a pulsing dot shows under your message at once. If the message is still on its way after a moment, the row says "Sending to Claude Code…"; while the agent is still coming up it says "Connecting to <model> on <provider>…" (this moved here from beside the model chip).

- While the agent works, the row shows "Thinking…" or what the agent is doing, with how long you have been waiting once it passes a few seconds, counted from when you pressed Enter.

- As soon as the reply is in, a check and "Done in 14s" (how long you waited) sit under it, even while the agent is still tidying up behind the scenes.

Before, nothing on the page moved between sending and the agent starting its turn, or between the reply and the turn ending, and nothing said a turn was done.

**Usable while starting or connecting**

A chat is usable while its agent is still starting or connecting.

- Stop is there as soon as a message is sent, including while the chat connects. Pressing it while the message is still waiting for the agent takes the message back into the composer, unsent; once the agent is up it interrupts as before. This also covers the first message of a new chat.

- A chat that is still starting can be renamed and deleted from the chat list and the phone header. The new name shows at once and the agent takes it when it lands; a deleted chat leaves the list at once and its agent is removed as soon as it exists.

- The provider and model of a chat that is still starting can be changed from its model chip. A new model is applied as the agent comes up; another provider moves the chat to it then, carrying the messages already sent.

- "Connecting…" names what the chat waits for, such as "Connecting to Opus 5.5 on Anthropic…".

- Typing into a chat whose agent is stopped starts the agent in the background, so the message usually finds it up and "Connecting…" is rarely seen.

**Starting, switching and renaming show what is happening**

Starting, switching and renaming chats now show what is happening instead of a blank page.

- A new chat's empty page says "Starting your chat…" while the chat is created, then "Your chat is ready." once it is up. The line gives way to the first message.

- Switching to a chat whose page has to load draws the shape of a few turns instead of an empty white page. It fades in only after 400 ms, so a quick switch shows nothing in between.

- Renaming a chat shows the new name in the list, the phone header and the window title as soon as the field closes, instead of after the seconds the rename takes. If the chat app refuses the rename, the old name comes back and the field reopens with the reason.

**Messages sent to a starting chat are kept**

A message sent to a chat that is still starting is no longer lost when that chat's page goes away before the chat is up. The chat app now holds the message itself (answering the send with `202 held`) and delivers it, in order and after any first message the create carried, as soon as the chat's agent lands. Before, the message waited only in the page's memory: the chat list keeps at most four chat pages loaded and drops the oldest, so starting several chats quickly (each typed into while it started) silently dropped the earlier chats' messages, and so did a reload or a closed window.

Every page shows a starting chat's held messages from the chat's record, so a page opened or reloaded while the chat starts still shows them. A create that fails keeps them, shows them above its reason, and its Try again delivers them once the chat starts. Any sender can rely on this, not only a chat page: `POST /api/chats/<id>/message` to a chat whose create is running is held rather than answered 404.

**Chat names**

Chat names are now consistent, and a name you give a chat always sticks.

- A name you type no longer flips back to "Chat N". After a rename, mngr's observe stream sometimes delivered a snapshot it had read before the rename, and the list showed the old name again for several seconds (measured on a staging workspace: back to the old name 0.8 s after the rename landed, for 3.3 s). The chat app now keeps the new name over such a snapshot until the stream reports the rename.

- Your rename wins over the automatic name. Before, the automatic name could be shown over the name you just typed, and its rename could run alongside yours and land last, replacing your name. Now, while your rename runs, no automatic name is shown or made for that chat, and an automatic rename already running finishes before yours. The rail keeps the name you typed until the chat app answers, instead of giving way to the first other name it shows.

In a narrow chat window or on a phone, the settings menu's Model submenu for a Pi chat (OpenRouter, Groq and the other Pi providers) opened as an empty panel, so the model could not be changed there. Focusing its search field scrolled the menu a full panel sideways on top of its slide; the menu now clips instead of scrolling, and the submenu shows its back row, search field and models.

A workspace updated from a version that had no main chat now gets a new chat named "Main" as its main chat, opened on a short message that explains what the main chat is. Before, the main chat went to the chat messaged last, which was usually the update chat itself, so "Update to v0.9.0" ended up pinned at the top of the chat list. The new chat also takes priority over an older app's "Welcome" chat. Fresh workspaces are unchanged.

The note a seeded chat's first agent receives no longer says the conversation happened before the workspace existed. It now says the conversation was written before any agent joined the chat.

The chat wears the workspace's theme: it follows the theme its desktop wears (including Desktop settings' live preview), opens in it without a flash of the standard look, and its inner pages follow the outer one.

- The chat declares `[theming] mode = "parts"` with three parts a theme may style: `chat.user-message` (the user's bubbles), `chat.composer`, and `chat.tool-call`. Classic Mac and Windows 2000 style them.

Turning a chat over to its terminal no longer says "Starting agent..." when the agent is already running, and no longer turns over onto a blank white face while the terminal loads. Until the terminal is on screen the back face shows a line in the terminal's own colors, font and padding, so the terminal that replaces it looks like the same surface: "Starting the agent..." while a stopped agent starts, then "Opening the terminal..." while the terminal loads. The line stays under the terminal once it has loaded, so the moment before the terminal draws never flashes the white card behind it.

When starting a stopped agent fails, the error on its terminal face now wraps to the width of the explanation above it instead of running the full width of the pane.

### system/apps/datalib

Datalib declares `[theming] mode = "none"`: its page is datalib-http's own and keeps its look under every workspace theme, while the window around it is themed. Classic Mac and Windows 2000 draw Datalib with their own pixel-art icon.

### system/apps/files

Files says how each synced folder stands as Imbue Studio reports it, and, inside the Imbue Studio app, opens Studio's settings for what you share from your computer.

- A synced folder's state comes from Imbue Studio on the computer instead of a guess made by comparing names on both sides. While it syncs, the circular arrows on its icon turn, and its tooltip reads "Syncing with Kims-Mac" over how far along it is ("25% done"); once it settles it reads "Up to date with Kims-Mac"; a sync that stopped shows the orange alert, its tooltip ("Sync with Kims-Mac stopped" over the first two lines of Studio's reason) and the folder itself say why, and the folder points to retrying it in Imbue Studio; a sync Imbue Studio has switched on but isn't running, mostly for a moment as Studio starts, reads "Not syncing with Kims-Mac right now"; a sync switched off in Studio leaves the folder a live one. A copy whose computer is asleep, or whose Imbue Studio is closed, is greyed out and reads "Kims-Mac isn't answering" rather than a guess.

- A share whose computer isn't answering, live or synced, is greyed out in the sidebar, icon and all, in place of the crossed-out laptop after its name.

- An empty synced folder that is syncing says so, and how far along it is, in place of "Empty".

- The sidebar, and the folder you have open, keep up with Imbue Studio while a Files window is on screen: they check every few seconds while a folder is syncing and every 15 seconds otherwise, and right away when the window comes to the front. A file you add on your computer shows up in the open folder without leaving it, within a couple of seconds of reaching the workspace for a synced folder. However many Files windows are open, your computers are asked at most once every couple of seconds, and not at all while no Files window is on screen. A computer that is asleep, or whose Imbue Studio is closed, shows its shares as not answering instead of the whole list failing.

- In the Imbue Studio app, Connected ends in "Manage connected files". It opens Studio's Permissions pane at Local files, where you share files and folders from your computer, stop sharing them, or turn syncing on; coming back to Files shows what changed. A plain browser, a phone, or a share link has no Studio around it, so the entry is not shown there.

Files declares `[theming] mode = "tokens"`, since it wears the workspace's theme itself and should not also take it from outside.

Files wears the workspace theme: it serves the theme from its own origin, wears it before the first paint, and follows the shell when the theme changes.

### system/apps/getting_started

The Getting Started page wears the workspace's theme, opening in it without a flash of the standard look. It declares one themeable part, `getting-started.start-glyph`, and its tiles are marked as the contract's `tile` part.

### system/apps/system_interface

A window's page is told whether the Imbue Studio app around the workspace opens its settings for the files shared from your computer.

- The shell keeps what Imbue Studio says with `minds:embedder-capabilities` about `opensLocalFiles` and puts it in every window's `shell:handshake`, so a page opened after Studio spoke still knows. Files shows its "Manage connected files" entry only when it is true.

The show-around tour starts by itself only in a new workspace. A workspace that already existed when an update brought the tour in no longer gets it the next time its agent works: with no `tour.json`, the tour record now reads as seen unless the bootstrap marked the workspace new on its first boot (`data/.state/system_interface/offer_tour`). The launcher's "Show me around" row still starts the tour in any workspace.

A link from an app's page to a chat (the chat root at `/?chat=<id>`) now shows that chat in the pinned chat window instead of opening a second chat window. More generally, a link to an app's pin page with a query of its own goes through the shell's `show`, which raises a window already there, or points the app's on-screen root window or its pinned window at it. Shell pages reach `show` through a new `POST /api/clients/<client_id>/show` route, since the op route is loopback only.

An app the workspace built can be made themeable, and its theming turned on and off by the user.

- The window menu's Theming submenu offers On and Off for a themeable app (`[theming] mode = "outside"`), with theming on by default. While it is off, the shell sends that app's pages the standard theme, so they keep the app's own look; turning it on or off sends every open page of the app its theme again.

- For an app that is not themeable yet, On and Off are greyed and "Enable theming" drafts a request into the main chat to make it themeable, following `docs/system/themeable-apps.md`.

- `POST /api/apps/<app>/theming` `{"is_on"}` turns a themeable app's theming on or off, kept in `app_theming.json`. The inventory carries each app's `theming`: `on`, `off`, `unthemed`, or null for an app that wears the theme itself or is not themed.

Workspace themes: Desktop settings has a **Theme** choice listing every theme the workspace has -- Standard, **Classic Mac**, **Windows 2000**, and any theme made in the workspace -- with a live preview (Save keeps it, Cancel puts the saved one back). A preview is never remembered, so a reload mid-preview comes back in the saved theme. Settings opened for a desktop that is not on screen say to switch to it to see a theme before saving; until the themes have been read the row says they are loading.

- A theme can be the workspace's default ("Make this the workspace default") or one desktop's own; a desktop with no choice of its own wears the default. A desktop whose own theme is no longer available wears the standard look, and its Theme row says so.

- Window title bars are drawn from the theme's chrome: which controls sit left and right, and whether the title is centred (Classic Mac puts the close box first and centres the title).

- Under a theme, each app's icon is the theme's drawn icon, one the workspace generated, or one derived from the app's standard icon in the theme's style (pixelated, reduced to the theme's colors, or in two colors), so a new app is never left with a blank or out-of-place icon.

- Editing a theme's files, or an app manifest that changes which themes are available, updates every open window at once, with no restart.

- New routes: `GET /api/themes`, `POST /api/themes/default`, `GET /api/themes/<id>/icons/<file>`, `POST /api/desktops/<id>/theme` (any available theme id, or null for the default), and `/_static/themes/` for theme files. `desktop_themes.json` holds `{"version": 1, "default", "desktops"}`. The socket sends `themes_changed`. An unavailable theme lists no icons, and every icon is answered with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (an svg icon also with a script-free `Content-Security-Policy`).

- `/theme-gallery?theme=<id>` shows every part of the interface under a theme, for judging one; a theme that fails validation is shown in the standard look with its problems listed.

- The shell's build also produces the page kit (`/_static/workspace_theme.css` and `/_static/workspace_theme.js`), which a plain-HTML app page loads to wear the theme.

- A window's title-bar controls take every press on them, even where a resize corner reaches into the title bar; the corner still resizes from its rim, just outside the window.

- Desktop settings' Theme row ends with **Make your own...**, which closes the dialog and drafts a theme request into the pinned chat window, where the agent makes the theme; with no window that takes a draft, the row says to describe the look in a chat instead.

- The pinned chat's avatar wears the theme too: it is the contract's `avatar` part, in the avatar chooser as well, and the workspace character draws its body and shadow from `--desk-avatar-color` and `--desk-avatar-shadow-color`. Classic Mac draws it solid black with a hard edge and no soft shadow; Windows 2000 in the caption bar's navy; the standard look is unchanged.

### system/apps/terminal

The terminal theme test now expects the wrapper page's unthemed background to be ttyd's dark grey (`#2b2b2b`), the background #950 gave the page. It still expected black, so CI on `main` failed it once #950 merged.

The terminal theme test expects the wrapper page's own `#2b2b2b` background (ttyd's default, which the page moved to) instead of black, so the test suite passes again.

The terminal theme test expects the terminal page's new dark grey background (ttyd's #2b2b2b) instead of black, matching the page since the source-view startup change.

The terminal's colors follow the workspace's theme: a theme's terminal palette (`--term-*` tokens) recolors the terminal live, and the terminal keeps its own colors under a theme that sets none. The terminal declares `[theming] mode = "none"`, so its output and its own page are otherwise left alone: the palette is read without the theme's rules styling the page.

The terminal page's background is now ttyd's own dark grey instead of black, so the moment before a terminal draws (and the terminal's messages, such as "The terminal is starting...") sit on the same surface as the terminal itself.

### system/libs/app_manifest

`[theming] mode = "outside"`: the app has a look of its own, written on the design tokens with that look as their fallbacks, and loads the page kit; the user turns its theming on and off from its window menu. `RegistryRow.theming_mode` records the manifest's mode; it is absent for an app that declares none.

`app.toml` takes a `[theming]` table saying how far an app takes part in workspace themes: `mode = "tokens"` (the default: built from the shared parts and design tokens), `"parts"` (also declares named parts a theme may style, as `parts = [{ name, description }]`, each description one line), or `"none"` (content with its own look). `registry.py` names the page kit's built paths, `SHELL_THEME_SCRIPT_PATH` and `SHELL_THEME_STYLESHEET_PATH`.

### system/libs/bootstrap

A workspace's first boot now writes `data/.state/system_interface/offer_tour`, the mark that lets the system interface's show-around tour start by itself. A workspace that already carries a first-boot signal (`workspace_main_branch_initialized`, or the older `initial_chat_created`) never gets it, so updating an existing workspace does not start the tour.

### system/libs/workspace_layout

`workspace-layout`'s hints for the retired `chat:` and `chat-terminal:` spellings, and `open --path`'s help, now point at `show chat --path "/?chat=<id>" --showing "/<id>" --repoint /`, which shows a chat in the pinned chat window. `open chat --path "/?chat=<id>"` opened a second chat window, because the pinned window's own path stays `/`.

`InventoryApp.theming` reads where an app's Theming submenu stands (`AppTheming`: on, off, or unthemed); it is absent for an app that wears the theme itself or is not themed.

`DesktopView` (the `desktop` object the shell answers and broadcasts) carries `theme`: the desktop's own workspace theme id, or null when it wears the workspace's default theme.

### system/libs/workspace_themes

- `workspace-themes lint-app` checks an app's own `assets/` folder too, where build-app keeps a page's hand-written CSS and scripts; built output (`static/`, `dist/`, `build/`) is still skipped.

- `workspace-themes lint-app` lints outside-mode apps too, and takes a token's `var(--token, fallback)` fallback as the look the app keeps with no theme, not as a literal. An id selector that starts like a hex color (`#add-form`) is no longer read as one.

New library and CLI, `workspace-themes`, for workspace themes (`docs/system/blueprint/workspace-themes/plan-workspace-themes.md`).

- Reads theme folders from `system/themes/` (built in) and `themes/` (made in the workspace), resolves each theme's base chain, chrome, and icons, and validates every theme against contract 1: only contract tokens and parts, metrics within range, no classes, ids, imports, or remote URLs (including through a namespace prefix, any selector function, a backslash, or a URL put in with `var()` or `if()`), and only allowed file types and sizes (a hidden file, or a file in a hidden folder, that a theme never serves, such as a `.DS_Store`, an editor's swap file, or a `.git` folder, is ignored); each selector of an app's overlay (`apps/<app>.css`) names one of that app's parts, and an overlay defines no `@keyframes` or `@font-face`, since every overlay is in every app's bundle. `validate <id>` reports every folder with that id.

- Serves a theme's bundle and files from any app's own origin (`register_workspace_theme_route`), with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on every answer and a script-free `Content-Security-Policy` on an svg (`theme_file_security_headers`). A theme folder, an icon, or an icons folder that is a link is never read or served, and a style file may not be named `theme.css`, the bundle's name. A relative `url()` inside a custom property's value (a wallpaper token such as `--desk-default-wallpaper: url("assets/bubbles.svg")`) is sent rewritten to `/_static/themes/<id>/<path>`, since the browser resolves it where `var()` puts it rather than against the style file.

- Icon tools that work with any image model or none: `icon spec` (what to draw, and which apps lack an icon), `icon fit` (trim, scale, and quantize any drawing onto the theme's limits; one already at the theme's size keeps its pixels one for one), `icon grid` (draw from a text pixel grid), `icon check` (an svg icon may hold no script, event handler, `foreignObject`, or reference outside itself), and `icon install` (which, for a built-in theme, fills only an icon the theme does not ship); `fit` and `grid` take `--preview` for an enlarged copy.

- `new` lays out a theme folder, `validate` checks themes, `bundle` prints a bundle, `list` lists themes, and `lint-app` finds literal colors, fonts, and shadows in a tokens-mode app.

- `scripts/vendor-css-library.mjs` adapts a CSS library (system.css, win95.css, ...) onto the contract's parts from a pinned, digest-checked source; it refuses two library assets with one file name, and never reads text inside an attribute selector or string as a class.

- `workspace-themes icon missing [<id>...]` lists, for every theme with icons of its own, the apps it has no icon for (naming the folder too when two folders share an id), and exits 1 when there are any. A theme that keeps the standard icons has none to draw.

- When it sends a theme's style file, the server gives each rule for the `button`, `field`, or `select` part a second selector for the bare `<button>`, text `<input>`, `<textarea>`, or `<select>` of a page built on the page kit (`:root[data-page-kit]`), at the element's own weight, so such a page wears the theme without marking its controls and an app's own class rules still win.

### system/libs/workspace_ui

The app contract and the embed contract carry what Files needs to open Imbue Studio's settings for the files shared from your computer.

- `shell:handshake` has an `opensLocalFiles` flag, read as false when the shell does not send it: whether the Imbue Studio chrome opens its settings for the files shared from the user's computer.
- `embed.ts` probes the contract v11 `minds:open-local-files` (workspace to embedder), which asks Studio to open its Permissions pane at Local files.
- A tooltip can carry an optional second line in quieter text under the first (`hoverTooltipAttrs(text, placement, { detail })`), for a detail worth a glance -- a reason, a time -- without stretching the first line. It shows at most two lines, ending in an ellipsis past that. A tooltip without one is unchanged.
- `laptop-off` leaves the shared icon set: Files greys out a share whose computer isn't answering instead, and nothing else drew it.

The shared UI library takes part in workspace themes (`docs/system/blueprint/workspace-themes/plan-workspace-themes.md`).

- Its components carry the contract's parts (`data-part`), so a theme styles them without depending on class names.

- New theme client (`src/themes/themeClient.ts`), which loads the theme a page wears from the page's own origin, and boot plugin (`src/themes/themeBoot.ts`), which wears the remembered theme before first paint.

- New page kit (`src/page/`), a stylesheet and a script every app serves at `/_static/workspace_theme.css` and `/_static/workspace_theme.js`, so a page built as plain HTML wears the workspace's theme too. On such a page a plain `<button>`, text `<input>`, `<textarea>`, or `<select>` wears the theme as its part does, with no marking; `data-variant` on a plain button still gives it emphasis.

- The app contract's `shell:theme` message (`{theme, revision, isPreview}`) reaches an app's `onTheme(theme, revision, isPreview)`, and `followShellTheme` follows the theme without connecting.

## [minds-v0.9.1] - 2026-10-24

### system

- Pin mngr to the public mirror of the Imbue Studio 0.9.1 release commit, so workspaces built from the `minds-v0.9.1` tag run the mngr the 0.9.1 desktop app ships with.

## [minds-v0.9.0] - 2026-10-23

### .agents

Building an app no longer runs an extra background process alongside it.
Workspaces that never had that process see no change.

The `datalib` skill now installs datalib v0.44.0. The Datalib app can now be shown inside Studio's windows: this is the datalib that reads the `DATALIB_FRAME_ANCESTORS` the launcher already sets, while every request still needs its API token. It adds Google Drive (Docs, Sheets and Slides with every revision, Docs rendered with their comment threads) and Linear sources; attachments and people's photos are linked from the source's own store instead of copied beside each page; sources appear as chips on the Dashboard with the same Sync, Stop, history and Reset actions as their row; and `datalib-step help` and `datalib-step examples <type>` walk an agent from an empty directory to a first sync. An existing store is upgraded on the app's next start; an older datalib can no longer open it.

- `publish-template` is restructured for progressive disclosure. `SKILL.md` is the lead's checklist (about 400 lines, down from 1,445); the worker's assembly instructions moved to `references/assembly-worker.md`, and every failure and what to do about it to `references/failures.md`. The task file the lead writes now carries only the template's parameters.

- The deterministic steps are scripts, shared with `update-published-template`: `github_access.py` probes and waits for the GitHub grants, and reports UNKNOWN rather than "not permitted" when the gateway cannot reach the user's Imbue Studio app, so the user is asked to open the app instead of being sent requests for access they may already have granted (the permission requests stay inline, since the chat builds its approval card from them), `github_repo.py` creates the repo, locks it down, points the README's Open in Imbue Studio button at it and sets its topic, `push_snapshot.py` runs the pre-push gate and pushes one snapshot commit as a fast-forward (with an optional version tag), refusing to publish from the live workspace or any other main checkout, and `record_publish.py` writes the `docs/VERSION_HISTORY.md` entry. `update-published-template`'s `references/ledger-entry.md` is gone.

- The pre-push gate is one command, where it was a validator run plus three greps: every `validate_template.py` run now checks that the thumbnail is inert (no script, embedded HTML or event handlers), and `--pre-push` adds the check that the README's repo-URL placeholder was replaced.

- The worker and the lead run the publish tools from the publishing workspace's copy rather than the copy inside the assembled tree, which is the base's and can be older. A workspace whose base predates a tool fix no longer fails at the worker's or the lead's validation.

- Fixed stale instructions: renaming after assembly edits the title in both manifest files (the old step renamed slug-named files that no longer exist, and then failed validation); the README is reviewed by pasting it into chat (the preview-tab step was removed in August); the published-page check after the push is now a step; the generated manifest points adopters at `connect-external-service` instead of the retired `latchkey` skill; and `update-installed-template` names `update_ledger.py` as where the ledger starter lives. `update-self`'s ledger helpers (`VERSION_HISTORY_STARTER`, `origin_line`, `insert_under_workspace`, and `pad_note`, the note-padding rule both ledger sections use) are public, for `record_publish.py`.

`publish-template` no longer fails on every publish with "runs under data/.secrets/restic.env, but no included app.toml [[secrets]] or SKILL.md secrets: entry declares that file" (and the same for `share.env`). The check that every secret file a template runs under is declared now looks only at the supervisord programs and `mcp-servers.json` the template's include paths cover, not the base's own programs, which run under files Imbue Studio provides. It reads program configs the way supervisord does, so a file named only in a comment is not a reference. The manifest writer now uses the validator's copy of this check rather than its own, and runs under `uv run --no-project --with 'pydantic>=2'` to load it.

An update's run record (`data/.state/update-apply/run.json`) now carries `applied_at`, the time the apply went live, until the next run starts. Imbue Studio reads it to say the update is finishing while the run wraps up its checks, instead of going back to "Preparing an update" between the landing and the verdict.

Chat agents are now told to describe the work rather than name the skill they are following, whether as code (`fetch-process-show`) or dressed up as a noun ("this workspace's fetch-process-show process"). Codex's own skill rules tell the model to announce which skills it is using; the output style and `.agents/shared/references/user-facing-language.md` now override that explicitly, and the style's "a rule fights the harness" override no longer lets that announcement through. The style reaches codex as developer instructions, the same level as those rules. A skill's name may be repeated only after the user has used it (they typed `/assist`, or named one of their own skills), or when they ask which skill was used. The language reference gains a short "Skills in particular" section with rewrites, and its plumbing table now lists skill names, which ends its contradiction with the output style; the word "skill" stays fine for the user's own creations.

A new `use-from-phone` skill walks the user through using the workspace from a phone: turning on sharing, getting the link onto the phone (the Share panel's "Email me a Mobile Access Link" button, or a copied link), and adding the workspace or an app to the home screen on iPhone/iPad and Android.

A harden pass now covers one change, not one creation: every app, skill, service or shared script the change touched is hardened by a single pass with a single worker.

- **One pass per change.** `update-creation` and `heal-creation` dispatch one pass for every creation the change (or the gap or failure being healed) touched, so two apps edited to work together, or an app and the skill that drives it, no longer get a worker each. The pass is named by `$SLUG`, its ticket title lists every creation, and the single-flight check and go-live run per creation. The worker may still split the work, by job rather than by creation.

- **Task files name their creations.** A task lists `creations` as `<type>:<name>` (`app`, `skill`, `service`, or `shared` for `.agents/shared`) plus one `scope_file`; `crystallize-creation` uses the same form. `parse_task_frontmatter.py` and `pass-scope` refuse a malformed task, a malformed creation, or one named twice. The worker computes the pass's footprint with the new `app-manifest pass-scope`, loads a `type-<TYPE>.md` per type, and writes one final-gate block per creation; the stale `system-interface` type is gone.

- **Critical apps.** A change touching a critical app takes `update-app`'s careful flow as a whole: ordinary creations it also touched are edited, hardened and applied in the same pass, and checked by the lead afterwards. `update_self.py apply --keep-rollback-point --pass-scope <file>` records the pass's other apps and services in the rollback point, so the notice names them and a rollback restarts them; only critical apps gate the verdict.

- **Go-live** tells an app to refresh its window and a service to restart its programs (noting that a routine-run service has none, and naming `oom_priority`'s), instead of telling a service to refresh a window.

- **The test gate runs only the pass's own tests.** The worker writes its scope file with `--lead-ref` and runs `app-manifest select-tests --scope-file`, which selects what the pass's footprints and its own branch changed. Other chats' commits in the same window no longer pull in their suites (one takeover had been running the chat, shell and full root suites for ~470 unrelated commits) or show up as `Outside footprint:`.

Update the file-sharing prompt a little bit.

- The build-app and update-app skills, `verify.md` and `service-processes.md` verify an app after a code change with one call, `verify_app.py <name> --restart --marker ... --screenshot ... --open` (or `--refresh` without `--screenshot` for an app already on screen), which restarts the program without the 30 s `startsecs` wait, checks the marker, renders the page and surfaces it. `supervisorctl restart` remains the way to bounce a daemon with no port. `check-app-errors` points a restart after a fix at `update-app` step 2 with the same split.

The `manage-routines` skill replaces `manage-scheduled-tasks`, `enable-caretaker` and `disable-caretaker`: anything that runs on a schedule is a routine, made and changed with the `routines` command (`routines add <id> --every 1d --at 07:30 --skill <name>` or `-- <command>`), never a cron line; the Routines app is where the user sees, runs, pauses and retimes them. The `caretaker` skill carries the role its create template used to hold and retimes or switches itself off through the `routines` command; `build-app` says periodic work in an app is a routine with `--app <name>`, not a loop in the service; `check-app-errors` reconciles routines through `routines list` and `routines log` instead of reading cron logs. `update-self` carries the Routines frontend's bundle like the Files app's: a change under `system/apps/routines/frontend/` rebuilds, snapshots and verifies it, and a worker hands it in with `--worker-bundle routines=<path>`.

The `datalib` skill's folder, `data/.skills/datalib`, is now a libraries folder laid out like the desktop app's `~/Datalib`: one folder per library. The data root the skill works with is the `Default` library, `data/.skills/datalib/Default`, and `scripts/sync_request.py` reads the API token from there. The skill's shell preamble now runs the install script before it creates the data root, so the Datalib app has moved an older store into `Default` before the agent touches it. A store a workspace wrote at `data/.skills/datalib` itself is moved into `Default` by the app's launcher the next time the app starts; nothing is lost and the API token stays the same.

The build-app skill's port note calls port 8040's app by its new name, System Monitor.

A background pass whose base moved before it could land is now caught up instead of thrown away. Before, any commit from another chat while an update-self, update, heal or critical-app worker ran discarded the finished pass and started over; for update-self that meant redoing a ~40-minute validation.

- **Catch-up.** The lead keeps the worker and asks it to merge the current `HEAD` into its branch (worker guide §7). The worker resolves conflicts (regenerating lockfiles rather than picking a side), hardens what came in that touches the pass, and re-runs its test gate over only what the catch-up changed for the pass, from a scope file written for the catch-up (`pass-scope --diff-base <pre-merge tip> --lead-ref <lead HEAD>`, then `select-tests --scope-file`). A note naming a creation outside the pass also makes it stale: the catch-up adds that creation, and the lead records it in its task file and ticket title. A fresh pass replaces a stale one only when its worker is gone, or no chat is left to lead it.

- **update-self.** Before the apply, the lead waits for other chats' in-progress edits to settle instead of refusing, then catches the worker up if its branch no longer fast-forwards, messaging it in a way that starts a stopped worker rather than replacing it. The exit-1 guidance in SKILL.md, `apply-outcomes.md` and the apply's refusal now says to catch the worker up and never to destroy it.

- **Orphaned passes are taken over.** A pass whose holder chat stopped while its worker is still there is adopted by the next chat as lead: it reassigns the ticket, relabels the worker, acts on the last report the gone holder read, and drives the pass to the end.

- **Abandoned work is kept.** `create_worker.py destroy --delete-branches` refuses while a branch it would delete holds commits no other local branch has, and prints a `git branch superseded/<name> <branch>` command to keep each (`--discard-unmerged` overrides). The lead keeps those branches and lists them in the new pass's task under `## Carried work`, and the new worker merges and hardens them.

- A milestone the lead provisionally merged and then reverted is brought back by the worker on its own branch, rather than re-applied by the lead on the served tree.

A freshly scaffolded app (`build-app`'s `scaffold_flask_lib.py`) passes its own generated tests again. Its `/_csp-report` view had no docstring, so the generated `runner_test.py` failed with `these routes have no docstring ... POST /_csp-report`, and it logged blocked resources with `print`, so the generated `test_prevent_bare_print` ratchet failed at count 1. Every new app hit both failures before the agent added any code. The view now has a docstring and logs through loguru (`logger.error`, with `setup_logging()` in the runner's `main()`, like the Routines app), and loguru is a declared dependency of every scaffolded app. The supervisor log line now carries loguru's prefix (`ERROR    | <module>:<function>:<line> - `) before the same text, so `check-app-errors` still finds it.

The scaffolder's tests now scaffold an app into a throwaway repo and run that app's own tests (everything except its type-check ratchet, which an existing test already covers), so a change to the template that breaks the tests it writes fails here instead of in the next agent's new app.

`update-self`'s results message no longer tells the user that parts of an update "only take effect when this workspace is rebuilt" when a rebuild would change nothing. The worker now marks each image-level `Dockerfile` hunk *covered live* or *pending recreate*. A hunk is covered live when its effect already reaches the running workspace through the merged tree or the apply's `setup_system.sh` re-run, or when it only shapes the image build (a layer-cache `COPY`). A hunk is pending recreate when the running workspace lacks something until a recreate. The lead's §5c and the results message's Caveats section now mention only pending-recreate items, and say what the workspace lacks until then. Before this, §5c said to call out every image-level hunk, while the Language rules said a consequence-free item was "one line at most, or nothing". The lead followed §5c and told the user about COPY lines for manifests and an installer that the apply had already made live.

The `datalib` skill now installs datalib v0.43.0. It adds time series: Garmin's daily metrics, weigh-ins and each activity's per-second samples, and YoLink's and AirVisual's sensor readings, are kept as time series, which a new Time series card in the Datalib app charts, and documents draw their charts from them. The unified index is renamed the unified document index; an existing store is moved over on the app's next start.

An update-self pass can now run start to finish with nobody watching, started by the Imbue Studio app's in-workspace schedule or "Update now".

- **Runs without the app.** When the app's message pins the target and ceiling, the pass uses them and never asks the app for its version. The lead may clear the way without asking: pausing other chats and background agents, stopping the browser and windowless apps, pruning dead workers' worktrees, unused apply snapshots and tool caches, saving a dirty tree as one work-in-progress commit, and taking over an abandoned "updating workspace" lease. The results message names each such action with its undo.

- **Chats are paused, not waited on.** Right before the apply, `run-status stop-chats` pauses busy chats and background workers and saves their work; afterwards `run-status resume-chats` starts each again with a "Workspace updated" note. The run record gains `started_by` and `stopped_agents`.

- **New `NEEDS_DECISION` verdict.** A customization the update cannot keep ends the pass, with the worker stopped and its branch kept, instead of waiting; the user's answer in the chat, whenever it comes, resumes the kept pass.

- **Verdicts mean what they say.** `STUCK` is only for a fault the pass cannot recover from: a dead worker is restarted first (in every lead, per `dead-worker-recovery.md`), an app a pinned pass cannot reach is not a fault, and an apply that ends in an emergency records `STUCK`. `references/apply-outcomes.md` says when each verdict is recorded.

- **Survives restarts and stops on request.** A lead restarted by the app's watchdog (a workspace restart stops every chat) finds where the pass got to and carries on. A request to stop ends the pass `REFUSED`, with the worker's branch kept, leases released and paused chats brought back.

- **Rollbacks and critical apps.** A rolled-back apply's retry goes back to the same worker, which catches up, reverts the rollback on its branch and reports again (worker guide §8). A user's critical app whose probe fails blocks the update instead of being patched by the lead.

- update-self's `SKILL.md` is slimmer, with resuming, stopping and migration in references of their own; Step 6 shows the update chat in an existing window rather than opening a new one; and `manage-routines` says never to make a routine that runs update-self or the app's update dispatcher.

### system

Reverts the build-app plan recorder (#530).

Removes `system/scripts/imbue_plan_extra/` (the `write_plan.sh` wrapper and its
`build-app` prompt) and the exemption for `write_plan.sh` in
`agent_require_steps_pretool.sh`. A workspace that added its own prompt under
`prompts/` and a `write_plan.sh <flow>` line to one of its skills keeps both,
but the command now fails with "No such file or directory"; remove the line
from the skill.

Keeps `data/.imbue/plans/CLAUDE.md`, moves its note into an `AGENTS.md` beside
it that the `CLAUDE.md` imports, and keeps the `.gitignore` rules that
track both and the `data/README.md` line. Workspaces that ran the recorder
still hold run folders under `data/.imbue/plans/<flow>/`, each with `brief.md`,
`plan.md`, `meta.json` and `log`. Only `plan.md` carries its own warning;
`brief.md` and `log` both contain the calling agent's description of the
user's request. A nested `CLAUDE.md` is loaded only once an agent reads a file
in that folder, so a shell search across `data/` can still print matching
lines before any note is seen.

- Upgraded offload from 0.9.14 to 0.10.0 on both pins the `test-offload` CI job
  keeps in lockstep: the runner's `OFFLOAD_VERSION` in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
  and the one the image bakes in via `system/scripts/offload_sandbox_init.sh`.

- 0.10.0 identifies a cached base image by a content *recipe* (builder, copy
  dirs, `sandbox_init_cmd`, and digests of the inputs that escape the checkpoint
  tree) rather than by the path of the TOML config that asked for it. The three
  configs at the repo root -- `offload-modal.toml`, `offload-modal-chat.toml`,
  `offload-modal-system-interface.toml` -- are identical in every field that
  determines the image and differ only in pytest working directory, args and
  output dir, so under 0.9.14 each built and cached its own copy of the same
  image: three full base builds per job on a cold checkpoint, run one after
  another. Under 0.10.0 they resolve to one recipe, so the first suite builds and
  the other two reuse it.

- The note entry now also carries the recipe, the config path, the offload
  version and a build timestamp, so `git notes --ref refs/notes/offload-images
  show <sha>` says what an image was built from rather than only its id.

- The first run after this lands is cold by construction, twice over: bumping
  `offload_sandbox_init.sh` is itself a checkpoint build input, and 0.10.0 cannot
  match note entries written by 0.9.14 (they carry no recipe), so every existing
  cache entry misses once.

- CI's pytest runs, on the runner and in the three offload configs, now carry a fake agent identity (`MNGR_AGENT_ID`, `MNGR_AGENT_NAME`, `MINDS_CHAT_ID`), as an agent's test run has one. The pytest-workspace-env plugin clears it before any test code runs, so it only shows when a pytest root fails to load the plugin, and then that root fails in CI instead of in an agent.

- The script tests' own fixture that cleared `MINDS_CHAT_ID` and `MNGR_AGENT_ID` is gone: the plugin now clears the whole agent environment for every test run.

- The root pytest configuration requires the pytest-workspace-env plugin (`required_plugins`), so a root run that cannot load it stops before collecting anything.

`AGENTS.md`'s "Using crystallized skills" section gains a rule to describe the work rather than name the skill being followed, even when the harness says to announce which skills are in use; a skill's name is repeated only after the user has used it. It points at the new "Skills in particular" section of `.agents/shared/references/user-facing-language.md`.

AGENTS.md now tells agents that the user may be reaching the workspace from the Imbue Studio desktop app or through a sharing URL in any browser, desktop or mobile, which the whole workspace and each of its apps has once sharing is on, and points them at the new `use-from-phone` skill for setting it up.

Downloads from the workspace's built-in pages work inside Imbue Studio. Before, downloading a folder or file in Files, an image from the chat lightbox, or the avatar chooser's original SVG offered to save `download.txt` (or the file's name with `.txt` in place of its extension), and the download failed.

- Imbue Studio frames the workspace from another site, so the workspace's session cookie is partitioned, and the browser sent a `download` link's request without it. The new shared `startDownload` helper in `workspace_ui` loads each download in a hidden frame instead, whose request carries the cookie.

- A download the server refuses now says why, in a toast or in the lightbox's title, instead of offering to save the refusal.

`docs/system/workspace-internals.md` describes a harden pass as covering one change: every creation it touched, with one worker, each loaded with its own type reference.

The workspace app model's contract for the update notice (`docs/system/blueprint/workspace-app-model/contracts.md`, section 5) says its `apps` include every other app of the harden pass the apply landed, not only the critical ones.

Bump the Latchkey version to 3.19.3.

- `system/scripts/smoketest_app.py` is renamed `verify_app.py`, since it restarts, checks, renders and surfaces an app rather than only smoke-testing it; every skill, reference and README that named the script now uses the new name.

- `verify_app.py <name> --restart` bounces an app's supervisord program without waiting out its `startsecs` window: it starts the program through supervisord's RPC socket without waiting, reads readiness from the port, and fails at once with the last lines of the stderr log when the program dies on start. `--open` and `--refresh` surface the verified page through `workspace-layout` in the same call.

- `AGENTS.md` makes app verification in a chat turn one `verify_app.py --restart ... --open|--refresh` call and leaves new test files to the background harden pass (a change to hardened code still extends its tests) and suite runs to the background test gate.

- The standalone-tk hook allows a tool call made only of `tk create`, `start` and `close` commands joined by `;`, `&&` or a newline, so a step boundary (`tk close <id> "<summary>"; tk start <next>`) is one tool call. A `cd` prefix, real work, a pipe, `||`, `&` or a redirect alongside a start or close is still blocked. `AGENTS.md` has the agent start a step in the same message as its first command and move between steps with one `tk close ...; tk start ...` call.

- The pipe-into-head/tail hook reads through a line continuation after the pipe, so `cmd | \` followed by `tail -30` on the next line reaches the checker instead of running unchecked.

- `verify_app.py --restart` reaches supervisord on the socket named by `MINDS_SUPERVISOR_SOCKET` when that variable is set (the shell app's liveness probes read the same one), else on `/var/run/supervisor.sock`.

Routines: everything that runs on a schedule is now a routine, one tracked TOML file under `system/routines/<id>.toml` (the root `routines/` symlink), run by the new routines library and shown by the new Routines app. The design is `docs/system/specs/routines/spec.md`.

- The hand-written cron entries, the `run_job.sh` runner and the `run_automation.sh` wake script (`system/libs/automations`) are gone; the bootstrap writes one `routines` cron entry (the once-a-minute tick) at every boot and converts a workspace's old `data/.state/cron.d` entries into definitions, once.

- The Caretaker is the routine `caretaker` (`system/routines/caretaker.toml`), off by default and turned on from the Routines app; its own create template is gone (the `automation` template serves every skill routine), and its check now also reports routines that are failing, overdue, broken or waiting on the user.

- The Routines app (`system/apps/routines`, port 8050, launcher rank 45, its own memory band) joins the built-ins and the npm workspace; the root `uv.lock` and `system/package-lock.json` follow.

The changelog gate keys a project by its parent and name (`libs/routines`, `apps/routines`), so a library and an app of the same name each owe their own entry; before, both collapsed into one project whose entry was always the library's.

The image's dependency layer copies the two new workspace members' `pyproject.toml`s and the Routines frontend's `package.json` with the other manifests, so the cached install sees them.

- Pin mngr to the public mirror of the minds 0.9.0 release commit, so workspaces built from the `minds-v0.9.0` tag run the mngr the 0.9.0 desktop app ships with.

`docs/system/avatar-designs.md`: "Design your own..." drafts into the selected chat, else the workspace's main chat, else the most recent one.

The desktop-interface, post-launch-paths and element-reference-menu plans now name the main chat as the fallback ahead of the most recent chat, for the chat root with nothing selected and for a `current_chat` intake or draft from a window that shows no chat.

The post-launch-paths plan adds the `main_chat` intake target and the chat's `main` launch path, the launcher's Enter.

The Datalib app (`system/apps/datalib`) now serves `data/.skills/datalib/Default`: the skill's folder is a libraries folder laid out like the desktop app's `~/Datalib`, with one folder per library. The launcher moves a store that an earlier workspace wrote at `data/.skills/datalib` itself into `Default` on the app's next start, keeping its contents and its API token; the library is known by where it is on disk, whatever spelling of its path the launcher is given.

- Pin mngr to the paired mngr change that lets Imbue Studio hand custom-scheme links (`slack:`, `vscode:`) to the workspace (embed contract version 10), so the vendored contract and link vectors include them.

Added `docs/system/specs/system-monitor.md`, the design of the System Monitor app and its resource sampler, and the `resource_sampler` supervisord program in `system/supervisord.conf.d/`. The docs and the manifest contract tables follow the app's new name.

The spec gained the breakdown's accounting rules (anonymous memory, a System row that makes the memory and CPU columns add up), the Workspace row's items, the disk walk's items, and a section on the Stop buttons (with `POST /api/stop` in its route table); the disk view's figure is documented as the machine's whole disk.

The desktop interface contracts (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/contracts.md`) describe the show-around tour: its record (`tour.json`, section 4.5a), the `GET` and `POST /api/tour` routes, the `minds:highlight-chrome` message the shell sends (section 5), and the tour's markers (section 12): `data-tour-card`, `data-tour-badge`, `data-tour-paused`, `data-tour-exit`, `data-tour-back`, `data-tour-next`, `data-tour-link`, and the launcher's `data-tour-row`. The pinned window's first frame is now most of the backdrop (sections 4.2 and the pinned-taskbar-entries plan), and the launcher plan and the stop-when-no-windows spec record that Getting Started's first-visit window is gone.

The shared `workspace_ui` library's `HIGHLIGHT_CHROME` export is described in its own changelog (`system/libs/workspace_ui/changelog/`).

Workspaces stop trusting the compromised emSign/eMudhra CA chain (`emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, eight intermediates whose private keys are trivially recoverable), and `uv.lock` stops churning.

- The provisioner installs uv 0.13.4 (was 0.11.7), Node 24.22.1 (was 22.23.2), Claude Code 2.1.307 (was 2.1.293), modal 1.6.2 (was 1.4.2) and OpenCode 1.19.4 (was 1.18.19; built on Bun 1.4.4, which drops the root and blocks the eight intermediates). The venv's certifi is 2026.10.19. The apt snapshot moves to `20261021T180000Z` with a matching base image, which brings `ca-certificates` 20250419+deb13u1. Existing workspaces get all of this from a normal update: the changed provisioner and apt timestamp re-run it, and the changed lock re-syncs the venv. Moving a workspace off Node 22 removes the old bundled npm first, so npm keeps working. The old uv's cache buckets stay on updated workspaces (about 0.9 GB on one measured workspace); fresh workspaces have none.

- Workspaces, CI and mngr's pin bump now all write `uv.lock` with the same uv. Before, a workspace's uv 0.11.7 rewrote the lock's header and markers on every re-resolve, so agents threw the diff away, and real new entries went with it. `system/toolchain_pins_test.py` fails when CI's setup-uv or setup-node version differs from the provisioner's, or when setup-uv is referenced at more than one commit SHA.

- uv tool installs and the venv stay on Python 3.12 (`UV_PYTHON=3.12` in the provisioner and build scripts), even though uv 0.13 defaults open-ended requests to 3.15. The runtime environment is unchanged.

- Fortress (the workspace browser) gets a managed `CADistrustedCertificates` policy listing the eight intermediates, written on every boot. Its bundled Chromium still trusts the bad root and never receives Chrome's CRLSet, because Playwright disables component updates. Run against a chain signed with a recovered intermediate key, Fortress 151 accepts it with no policy and rejects it with the policy in place. A Fortress that is already running usually picks the policy up within about 10 seconds, without a restart (13 of 14 trials; the other was still accepting the chain after 60 seconds).

Test runs in a workspace no longer leave their temporary files piling up in `/tmp`. The root pytest config now sets `tmp_path_retention_policy = "failed"` and `tmp_path_retention_count = 1`: a passing test's `tmp_path` is deleted as soon as it finishes, and only the latest session's leftovers are kept. pytest's default kept every test's directory for the last three sessions. `/tmp` is a tmpfs, and under gVisor each file or directory there also holds sandbox memory until it is deleted. After a couple of suite runs, the leftovers (73,000 entries in one measurement) held about 300 MB of the container's memory. Because this is ordinary pytest config in the checkout, existing workspaces pick it up with their next update.

earlyoom's supervisord program (`system/supervisord.conf.d/earlyoom.conf`) runs it through a wrapper that timestamps every line of its log; see the oom_priority entry.

`system/scripts/install_earlyoom.sh` no longer tells a version bump to move `minds-admin hotpatch-earlyoom`'s pin too; that command is removed in mngr.

Datalib can be shown in Studio's windows: its launcher sets `DATALIB_FRAME_ANCESTORS` to the places Studio frames it from, the desktop app's local origins and, for a shared workspace, Imbue's content domains and hosted chrome origins. It takes effect with a datalib that reads the variable (imbue-ai/datalib#1318); an older one ignores it.

Bug reports include the update flow's records from `data/.state/update-apply/` (schedule, run record, last dispatch and its create attempt, watchdog state, apply and emergency markers, provisioning-incomplete record, kept rollback point, and the dispatcher log's tail) as their own secret-scanned class; pre-apply snapshots and the dispatcher program are never included.

`docs/system/blueprint/unattended-workspace-updates/` points to the unattended workspace updates plan in the mngr repo, and the routines spec (section 12) says the cron migration leaves the app's `update-self-dispatch` entry with cron.

### system/apps/chat

The pytest configuration requires the pytest-workspace-env plugin (`required_plugins`), so a test run that cannot load it, and would let a test see the environment of the agent running it, stops before collecting anything.

The real-claude background-task test names the Claude account it runs on: the default signed-in Claude account from the workspace's account store, passed to claude as its config dir. It used to rely on the agent's own `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, which the pytest-workspace-env plugin clears, so in a workspace it failed with "Not logged in". It is skipped when no Claude account is signed in.

A background task's report that arrives while a chat is switching account or harness now shows as its one-line notice from the start. It used to appear as a raw message bubble until it reached the transcript.

Automatic chat names are more reliable. The small model that names a new chat from its first message used to answer that message instead of titling it ("what's 2+2?" named the chat "4", and a translation request named it "Bonjour"), or obey instructions inside it. Now the message is handed to the model as text to describe, with worked examples. In testing on Claude Haiku 5.5, five of twenty tricky opening messages went wrong this way before the change and none of 105 did after it.

Chat names are shorter and no longer repeat themselves. A name used to come in two halves that often said the same thing twice ("Map app: build a simple map application"), and was usually cut off in the chat list. A chat is now named with a short title such as "Simple map app", which fits the list whole. When another chat already has that name, the new one is numbered ("Simple map app 2") instead of keeping "Chat N".

Chats opened in Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Russian, Arabic or another non-Latin script now get a name. Such a name used to come back in that script, which a chat's name cannot hold, so the chat kept "Chat N". The name is now written in English for those messages, and in the message's own language without accents (for example "Vacances en Italie") for languages that use the Latin alphabet.

Claude chats are still named on the `haiku` alias, which the pinned Claude Code resolves to Claude Haiku 5.5, and Codex chats on the newest Luna model the account offers; neither needed a model change. When Haiku fails, a Claude chat is now retried only on the account's default model, no longer on Sonnet first, so a failure that no model can fix (a rate limit, an expired login) costs at most two calls instead of three.

The image lightbox's Download works inside Imbue Studio. Before, it asked for the image with a `download` link, whose request went without the workspace's session, so the download failed.

- Download of the workspace's own image goes through the shared `startDownload` helper, and the server serves an image asked for with `?download` as an attachment under its own name.

- A failed download says so in the lightbox's title; a missing image is answered in plain words ("There's nothing at ..."), which the title shows. An image from another site still opens in a new tab.

- Fixed the flaky `test_websocket_replays_the_provisional_chats_before_the_agent_list`. The tests' WebSocket client (`simple_websocket` 1.1.0) handles only the accept from the socket read that completes its handshake. If the server's first messages arrived in that same read, they stayed unread, and since the server sends nothing more, `receive` timed out. The tests now use a client that also delivers those messages.

- The P6 tool-call policy allows a `tk start` or `tk close` to share its tool call with other `tk create`/`start`/`close` commands joined by `;`, `&&` or a newline; the progress view applies the `Updated` lines of one output in order.

The workspace now has a **main chat**, where a message with no chat of its own goes. The chat the Mind app seeds is the main chat to begin with, and is now named "Main" instead of "Welcome"; that name is kept rather than replaced by one drawn from the first message, until you rename it:

- The chat list always leads with it, alone above a thin rule and in a medium weight, instead of sorting it by recency. Helper chats it started sit right under the rule.

- The main chat never sleeps: whenever it is found stopped (stopped from elsewhere, by a routine, or shed by the memory guard), the chat app starts it again. Its menu offers no stop or restart.

- With no chat selected, the chat list opens on it rather than on the most recently messaged chat; deleting the chat on screen also returns you to it.

- Pressing Enter in the desktop's launcher sends the text to the main chat ("Send to main chat"). "New Chat" moves to the second row, so Cmd+Enter (Ctrl+Enter elsewhere) starts a new chat, and "Send to chat..." stays in the list without a key.

- A draft or message sent to the "current chat" from a window that shows none (the desktop's "Design your own...") lands in it.

- Any chat you started can be made the main chat from its right-click menu (and the phone layout's kebab): "Make main chat". It moves to the top in place of the old main chat.

- The main chat can be deleted like any chat. Another chat becomes the main chat right away (the one messaged most recently, never a helper chat an agent started) and moves to the top; with no chat left, the new chat the list opens becomes the main chat.

The main chat is kept as a pointer in `data/.apps/chat/main_chat.json`, not as a property of any chat. `chats_updated` pushes and `GET /api/chats` carry it as `main_chat_id`.

- A chat that is still waiting for its first message (the new workspace's Main, or the empty chat the list opens) can now be renamed, made the main chat, and deleted from the list; only a chat whose agent is being created offers none of these until it is up.

Hovering the Fast mode row in the model card now explains it: the same model, just as smart, only quicker, and it costs more to run.

- A custom-scheme link in a message (`[channel](slack://channel?id=C1)`, `sms:`) is now a link, opened by the app of the workspace registered for its scheme or else by the app of the user's system it belongs to. Before, it was unwrapped to its text. A file and line (`q4.md:12`) or a host and port with no scheme (`localhost:3000/app`) written as a link target still renders as text, by the shared link classifier's rule, and so does a custom-scheme link of that shape (`sms:5551234`; `sms:+15551234` is a link).

The welcome chat's agent starts as soon as the user signs in to a provider, rather than on their first message: the sign-in the chat's "Connect an AI provider" chooser produces launches a chat still awaiting its first send with no message, so the agent is up before the user has typed. The first message sent to it then carries the seeded onboarding conversation ahead of the user's words (as the launch used to), once it has gone through: a send the harness refused or could not take yet leaves the conversation for the next, and a slash command sent first goes as typed and leaves it for the next message too. The chat record carries `is_seed_pending` for this; a record written before it reads as delivered. One send carries the conversation at a time: a send that overlaps the carrying one goes as typed. A message sent while the sign-in's launch is still on its way waits for the chat and goes to it, rather than launching the chat a second time (which the chat app refuses).

A new chat starts with fast mode off unless the workspace's default was changed in the model picker; it used to start in auto (fast for the first two turns). Auto and on are still there to pick, and a workspace whose settings file already names a default keeps it.

The chat app's baked Claude model catalog is regenerated from Claude Code 2.1.307, the version workspaces now run. Models, aliases, display names and fast mode are unchanged; each model only gains a `total_tokens_reminder` capability.

Signing in to an account again no longer starts every chat on it. The restart that makes chats pick up the new credentials now skips agents that are stopped, which read the credentials whenever they next start. On a workspace with a couple of dozen old chats on one account, a single sign-in used to start all of them within five minutes, and earlyoom shed them as fast as they came up until the container ran out of memory and was killed.
