A body carrying a key its route's model does not name (on the accounts, the account flows, the secret requests and `POST /api/chats/create`) is now refused the same way, where it used to be ignored. The harness catalogs route answers a model too, and the richer failures (a send failure with its kind, the converging refusal with its phase) are listed on the routes that answer them, so the document shows them. The harness catalog answer models live in `imbue/chat/api_models.py`.

### system/apps/datalib

The README no longer compares the app to Files, which is now a Python package.

The Datalib manifest carries a one-line `description` of what the app is for, which the visiting-agent primer shows; datalib-http is another program's server, so the app declares no API document of its own.

New app: Datalib, datalib's web UI (`datalib-http`, the Manage screen and the Add/Edit source wizard) over the store the `datalib` skill writes at `data/.skills/datalib`.

- `launch_datalib_http.py`, a standard-library launcher, registers a copy of `app.toml` whose one launch path carries datalib's API token as a preset, so a window opens signed in, and then becomes `datalib-http`. The token is the one at `data/.skills/datalib/system/api-token`, kept across restarts.

- `datalib-http`, and every sync step it starts, runs in the agent-subprocess memory band (`oom_score_adj` 900): under memory pressure datalib is shed before any agent or service.

- The app is not announced to users yet. Its program has `autostart=false`, and an app is listed only once its program has registered it, so no workspace shows a Datalib app until the `datalib` skill starts the program.

- The app is not a uv workspace member (`system/apps/datalib` is excluded in the root `pyproject.toml`).

The app's supervisord program is defined in `datalib.conf` here and is not in `system/supervisord.conf.d/` until the `datalib` skill's install script copies it there on first use. It autostarts from then on. `test_datalib_pin.py` checks that no tracked file under `system/supervisord.conf.d/` defines the program, that the installed copy is gitignored, and that the program still starts in the `user` memory band.

### system/apps/files

The File Viewer is now Files, rebuilt to feel like Finder or the Windows Files app instead of a directory listing.

- A resizable sidebar with Shortcuts (Workspace, Uploads) and Connected: every file and folder shared from your computers. Each one's icon carries a small badge saying whether it is linked (opened live from your computer) or synced (a copy kept here), and the same badge marks it wherever a folder lists it. After the name, a "Read-only" badge, an orange alert when a synced copy hasn't caught up, or a crossed-out laptop when your computer isn't answering; hovering says how it syncs and how it stands. With nothing shared yet, it says to share from Imbue Studio on your computer. Dropping something from your computer onto a shared folder's row uploads into it. A toolbar with the path, a view switcher, a + button, and view options.

- Files has a server of its own in place of dufs: it serves the workspace's files, downloads a folder as a zip as it is written, saves an upload whole or not at all (a cut-short upload leaves the old file), keeps an edited file's permissions and links, reads the shares through the latchkey gateway, opens unsynced ones live from your computer, and keeps file names with unusual characters (like the narrow space in macOS screenshot names) from breaking their preview. dufs is no longer installed.

- Three views: icons (images as thumbnails), a list with Name, Date Modified, Size, and Kind columns that sort, and columns that open to the right as folders are chosen and end in a preview of the chosen file. The view, the sort order, and whether system files show are remembered.

- Click to select (Cmd/Ctrl and Shift to select several), double-click or Enter to open, F2 to rename in place, Delete to delete after a confirmation, and keyboard arrows, Cmd/Ctrl+A, Cmd/Alt+Up, and type-to-find.

- Right-click an item for Open, Open in New Window, Edit, Download (folders as a zip), Rename, Copy Path, and Delete; right-click empty space, or use +, for New Folder, New File, Upload Files, and Upload Folder.

- Drag files or folders in from your computer to upload them into the folder under the pointer, with progress shown as they go (the panel tidies itself away once they are done); a name already there asks whether to replace it or keep both. Drag items onto a folder to move them.

- A file opens in a window of its own, to be closed when you are done: it previews pictures, video, audio, and PDFs, shows text, and edits it (the Edit icon beside Download) with Save or Cmd/Ctrl+S; it also offers Rename, Copy Path, and Delete.

- On a phone-sized window the sidebar floats over the folder from a toolbar button, the column view steps aside, a tap opens, and each item has a "..." menu.

The column preview of a text file and a text file's own page use the shared type scale (helper and body sizes) rather than hand-set pixel sizes, and the list's sortable column headers drop the medium weight, as buttons do.

A note Files leaves when something fails (a move, a save, a copy) rises at the foot of the window like the desktop's, several stack rather than replace one another, and each can be closed. The pointer hides while you type, as everywhere else in the workspace.

Files describes its own API: `GET /__files/api/schema` answers an OpenAPI document built from its routes, and its manifest carries a one-line `description` and the `api_schema_path`, which the visiting-agent primer links.

Files names what every route exchanges in a route table its API document publishes: the connections listing answers the `Connections` model and refuses with the shared `{"detail": ...}` shape (a 502 when Imbue Studio cannot be read) rather than plain text, and every file route (a path's page, bytes, zip or `?json` page data, and the verbs that change it, in the workspace or live on a connected computer) is declared schemaless with what it answers, since a served file can be of any kind. Every view carries a docstring, so the document summarises each route.

### system/apps/getting_started

The manifest's note on launcher order calls the File Viewer by its new name, Files.

The Getting Started page now carries a `Content-Security-Policy`: scripts only from its own origin, fetches only to its own API, images from its own origin and from the catalog's (the template thumbnails live beside the catalog), no plugins.

Getting Started describes its own API: `GET /api/schema` answers an OpenAPI document built from its routes, every route's view carries a docstring the document shows as the operation's summary, and its manifest carries a one-line `description` and the `api_schema_path`, which the visiting-agent primer links.

- The "create a workspace from this template" prompt names the `imbue-studio` skill, which replaces the retired `minds-api` skill.

Getting Started's routes are typed: `GET /api/health` answers a `HealthResponse` (`status`, `is_frontend_built`) and `GET /api/templates-catalog` a `TemplatesCatalogResponse` whose `catalog` is a `CatalogDocument` of `TemplateEntry` rows (each template's listing with its drawing resolved to a `thumbnail_url`) and `CatalogShelf` rows, or null when no catalog is configured; its 503 is the `{"detail": ...}` error shape. The page, the bundle's assets and the app contract module are declared schemaless. The API document at `/api/schema` publishes the models, and every answer is checked against the route table.

### system/apps/system_interface

The avatar keeps working while a chat waits on a background task. An agent that ends its turn to wait on a command it started through `run_in_background.py`, or on one of Claude's own background tasks, reads WAITING to mngr, so the avatar used to go idle though the task's completion would start the agent's next turn. Its mood is now working when any agent but the services agent is running, as before, or when any chat holds a live background task marker under `data/.apps/chat/background_tasks/`. The shell watches that directory as it watches mngr's agents event file, so a marker written or removed shows within the debounce, and its periodic re-check catches a marker whose process died without removing it.

The shell's test fixtures call the File Viewer Files, and its end-to-end tests open files in Files windows by double-click and the item menu, as the rebuilt app does.

The style guide lists the new `type-tag` role (10px, for word badges such as "Read-only").

The toasts come from the shared workspace-ui library, which now carries them for Files as well; on the desktop they look and act as before, wrapping at 480px.

The shell's pages (the desktop and the not-built placeholder) now carry a `Content-Security-Policy`: scripts only from the shell's own origin plus the placeholder's inline script by hash, fetches and sockets only to the shell, frames of any http(s) page (the apps it shows), images from its own origin (its wallpapers and icons), no plugins. Who may frame the shell stays the proxy's `frame-ancestors` policy. The page a parked port answers for a stopped app carries one too, admitting its inline stylesheet and nothing else.

The shell describes its own API: `GET /api/schema` answers an OpenAPI document built from its routes (the inventory, layout and presence routes among them), every route's view carries a docstring the document shows as the operation's summary, and its manifest carries a one-line `description` and the `api_schema_path`. The shell is internal, so the visiting-agent primer never lists it; a workspace-scope agent reaches the document on the shell's loopback port.

The shell's routes are typed: every route is in a route table the API document publishes, each JSON body is read through the shared `parse_request_body` and each JSON answer through `model_response`, so the document shows a request and response schema for every one of them (the desktop, window, placement, client, avatar, wallpaper, update-notice and presence routes, and the agent-facing op route's bodies and answers as a choice), and every refusal is the shared `{"detail"}` shape. Two wire shapes changed: `GET /api/updates/pending` answers `{"notice": <notice or null>}` instead of the bare notice or null, and the embedder-message relay's answer carries `detail` as an explicit null when every app took the message, and its deliveries carry `shown`, `has_no_desktop_window` and `window_id` as explicit nulls when no page was shown.

### system/apps/system_monitor

Memory & disk describes its own API: `GET /api/schema` answers an OpenAPI document built from its routes, every route has a docstring the document carries as its summary, and its manifest carries a one-line `description` and the `api_schema_path`, which the visiting-agent primer links.

Memory & disk's routes are typed: `GET /api/stats` answers a `StatsResponse` (the memory and disk figures, the breakdown's rows and their items, the usage mode, the memory guard's stops, and the graph's history) and `GET /health` a `HealthResponse`; the page and the shell's browser-side modules are declared schemaless. The API document at `/api/schema` publishes the models, and every answer is checked against the route table. Every row of the breakdown now carries a `limit` field (null except on the Temporary files row).

A new built-in app, Memory & disk (`system-monitor`): one page showing how much memory and disk the workspace is using, which chats, code checkers, apps, and workspace programs hold the memory, and which programs the memory guard stopped in the last 24 hours, each described in plain words with its exact command behind Details.

- It started as a user app built in a cloud workspace and keeps that app's page and readers. As a built-in it serves on 8040 (below the 8080 the build-app scaffold starts handing out), runs in its own memory band, sits last in the desktop's seeded shortcuts and the launcher (`launcher_rank = 50`), and declares `system = true`, so the Share tab lists it under its System group.
- A chat on any agent type (claude, codex, pi) counts under Chats with everything it started: its main processes come from oom_priority's agent-pid registry, with claude's command line as the fallback.
- Memory per row is exact where the kernel has `smaps_rollup`: each row is its programs' private memory, memory several programs share is one Shared row, the files in the scratch space (`/tmp`, a tmpfs) are a Temporary files row with its size limit and an info popup, and the rest is a System row, together adding up to the memory in use. Where it has none (gVisor) the rows fall back to resident sizes scaled down by one factor, and the page says they are approximate.
- The memory graph covers the last 10 minutes on a 0 to 100 percent scale, draws readings the app itself records every 5 seconds while it runs (so the line stays whole while a window is hidden or reloaded), and leaves blank any stretch with no readings.
- The memory and disk bars label their used share on the filled side and their free amount on the empty side.
- From 80% memory used, the bar and a note turn orange: the note gives the percentage, says the memory guard stops programs once less than 10% is free, and names the largest kind of memory the user can free (chats, their apps, code checkers, or temporary files) with what frees it. Under 80% the note appears only to report programs stopped in the last 24 hours.
- The app keeps its own overhead low: it asks supervisord over its control socket with no `supervisorctl` process per refresh, every open window shares one snapshot taken at most every 4 seconds, the stop history and the guard's log are read only from their last 256 KB and 1 MB, and only again once they change (on a stop), and a hidden window stops polling. One refresh costs about 25 ms of CPU (it was about 80).
- The page takes its colours, type sizes, fonts, radii, and tooltip style from the workspace's design tokens (`system/libs/workspace_ui/src/base.css`), copied by name since the page has no build step.
- The icon is the gauge it shipped with, now inked cream on a terracotta tile per `docs/system/app-icons.md`. The exported glyph named no fill, so it drew as an empty tile.
- The code is split by topic: `memory` (totals, disk, the graph's history), `programs` (the running programs and who they belong to), `usage` (the breakdown's rows), `stops` (what the guard stopped), and `stats` (the shared snapshot). It reuses oom_priority's agent-pid registry, ledger path and headroom-file path, and app_manifest's shell module paths.
- Tests cover the /proc and smaps_rollup readers, the grouping, the exact breakdown and the scaled fallback, the temporary files row, the pairing of the guard's records with its log, the supervisord socket (and that its path matches `system/supervisord.conf`), the shared snapshot, the memory history, and the routes.

### system/apps/terminal

The terminal's wrapper pages now carry a `Content-Security-Policy`: the page's own inline module script by hash, frames of any http(s) page (the pty origin), fetches only to the terminal app, no plugins.

The terminal describes its own API: `GET /api/schema` on its pages origin answers an OpenAPI document built from its routes, every route's view carries a docstring the document shows as the operation's summary, and its manifest carries a one-line `description` and the `api_schema_path`, which the visiting-agent primer links.

The terminal's routes are typed: `POST /new` reads a `NewTerminalRequest` (an optional `workdir`) and answers a `NewTerminalResponse` (the new terminal's page path), `GET /api/sessions/{name}` answers a `SessionPage`, `GET /api/health` a `HealthResponse`, and `POST /api/window-closed` reads the shell's `WindowClosedHint` and answers 204; the page and the app contract module are declared schemaless. The API document at `/api/schema` publishes every model, every parse and answer is checked against the route table, and a body of another shape than a route's model (a window-closed post that is not the shell's hint included) is refused as a 400 `{"detail": ...}` rather than tolerated.

### system/apps/terminal_pty

The terminal pty manifest declares a one-line `description` (it is ttyd, another program's server, so it serves no API document of its own).

### system/libs/app_manifest

The manifest and registry tests' sample app is called Files, as the File Viewer now is.

`app_manifest.content_security_policy` is new: `attach_document_policy(app_or_blueprint, overrides=None)` gives every HTML page an app serves a `Content-Security-Policy` (same-origin scripts plus the page's own inline `<script>` blocks admitted by hash, inline styles, images from the page's own origin plus `data:` and `blob:`, frames of any http(s) page, same-origin fetches and sockets, no plugins, no `<base>` retargeting, no cross-origin form posts), leaving a response that sets its own policy alone. The workspace's Flask apps (the shell, the chat, the terminal, Getting Started, the browser) attach it; `app_manifest.testing.assert_document_policy_admits_page` checks a served page against its header, `url_origin(url)` gives the source for one origin an app opens a directive to, and `inline_source(text)` gives the `'sha256-...'` source for one inline script or stylesheet (the shell's parked-port page uses it for its stylesheet). The library now depends on Flask and Werkzeug.

The manifest and the registry row gain two optional keys: `description`, one line (at most 200 characters) saying what the app is for, and `api_schema_path`, the path under the app's origin that answers an OpenAPI document describing its HTTP API (contracts.md sections 2 and 3). `forward_port.py` copies both onto the row.

### system/libs/app_schema

New library: an app's self-description. `register_api_schema_route` serves an OpenAPI 3.1 document built from the app's Flask routes, Flask's own static routes (the app's and a blueprint's) left out (a docstring's first paragraph as the operation's summary and the whole of it as its description, a blank one counting as none; path parameters; and optional pydantic request and response models) at the path the manifest names in `api_schema_path`; `assert_api_schema_describes_app` is what each app's tests assert about it, and it fails for a route whose view has no docstring, so a route cannot be added without saying what it does.

The library now owns how a route exchanges JSON, so an app's API document cannot drift from its routes. Every app keeps a route table: a `RouteModels` entry (request model, response model, status, alternate successes) for each route that exchanges JSON and a `SchemalessRoute` entry, with its reason, for each that serves a page, a file, a stream or a socket. `parse_request_body` validates a body with the model the table names (a body off the shape is a 400 `ErrorResponse`, the one error shape every route now answers, logged with the method, path and problem) and `model_response` answers the model the table names; either disagreeing with the table fails the request with `RouteModelsMismatchError`. The document shows every table entry (an alternate answer under a failure status, such as a relay's 502, is described as a failure rather than a success), `x-no-schema` with the reason for a schemaless route, and `ErrorResponse` as every operation's default response. `assert_api_schema_describes_app` now also requires every operation to be in the table, the table to name no route the app lacks, and no modelled view to read its body around the helper. A HEAD request is checked as the GET operation that serves it, so a probe's HEAD of a modelled route answers as before. A check on every answer fails a modelled route that answered JSON around `model_response` or succeeded without reading its body through `parse_request_body`; a failure richer than `ErrorResponse` must be listed as one of its route's answers; `merge_route_tables` joins an app's module tables and refuses a route two of them name; the 400 handler and the answer check are installed app-wide even when the document is registered on a blueprint.

### system/libs/bootstrap

The bootstrap announces each step it runs as an event under the agent's state directory (`events/bootstrap/events.jsonl`, one JSON line per event under the standard envelope, appended to on every boot): a `bootstrap_step_started` and a `bootstrap_step_completed` (with the step's duration) for each of its steps, in order, and a final `bootstrap_completed` as it hands off to supervisord. The desktop that created the workspace tails these while it waits for the system interface, so its progress bar moves through the boot instead of sitting on one long "waiting" step. Outside an agent (no `MNGR_AGENT_STATE_DIR`) nothing is written and the boot is unchanged.

### system/libs/chat_background_tasks

New stdlib-only library holding the background tasks each chat waits on: the marker files under `data/.apps/chat/background_tasks/<chat-id>/` and their liveness rules (`markers`), and the chat-app-first listing with its fallback to the files (`listing`). A task's `source` is `run_in_background` or `harness`, and a harness task names its harness (`claude`). The chat app, the shell's avatar, `memory_candidates.py`, `create_worker.py`, `system/scripts/background_tasks.py` and `system/scripts/claude_background_task_hooks.py` import it.

### system/libs/workspace_layout

The `open` help names the file browser Files, its new name.

`parse_window_closed_hint` is gone: the browser and the terminal, its only readers, now take the shell's close hint as a `WindowClosedHint` through `app_schema.routes.parse_request_body`, which refuses a body of another shape as a 400 instead of ignoring it.

### system/libs/workspace_ui

The shared icon set gains the glyphs Files draws its chrome with: layout-grid, list, columns, plus, upload, ellipsis, folder, house, inbox, file-plus, copy, info, panel-left, link, and laptop-off (a laptop struck through, for a computer that is not answering).

`alertDotIcon()` is a filled disc with a white exclamation in the current colour.

A hover tooltip can ask for a narrower bubble (`hoverTooltipAttrs(text, placement, { maxWidth })`), so a sentence or two of explanation wraps instead of running out in one long line.

The type scale gains its smallest step, `--font-size-tag` (10px), and a `type-tag` role on it, for a word badge set beside other text such as "Read-only".

The shell's toasts move here, as `models/toasts.ts` (the queue) and `components/toasts.ts` (the stack), so Files shows its notes with them too. A page may pass `onDismiss` to give each toast a close button; the shell passes none, so its toasts still take no press.

`SegmentedControl` is a few choices side by side in one outlined well, the chosen one filled, each a glyph or a label. It is a radio group, moved along with the arrow keys. Files' view switch is the first.

The `folder` glyph is redrawn in the Files app icon's hand-drawn shape, and a matching hand-drawn `page` glyph joins it.

A menu row that opens a submenu stays highlighted with the hover fill (`bg-fill-hover`) while its submenu is open, so it still reads as the row the flyout belongs to after the pointer moves into the flyout.

The icon set gains lucide `package-open` and `package`, the chat transcript's chips for a compaction of the agent's context starting and finishing.

### system/services/oom_priority

`memory_candidates.py` no longer offers an agent whose chat is waiting on a background task as safe to stop. Such an agent has ended its turn, so mngr lists it as `WAITING`, but the task's completion will start its next turn, and stopping it would lose the work in flight. A candidate must now be `WAITING` and in a chat that is not busy: no live marker under the chats' background task directory, read through the `chat_background_tasks` library for the agent's `chat_id` label, else its own id. That includes a chat waiting only on a `run_in_background.py` command: stopping the agent stops the command too. The table's heading says so ("waiting, not on a background task"), and the README's "Memory candidates" section describes the rule.

The service bands and README call the File Viewer by its new name, Files.

The shed-notice SessionStart hook now starts Python only when the shed ledger names the agent (`bin/claude_shed_notice_hook.sh`), so the usual case adds no Python startup to the time before a new chat can take its first message.

`SERVICE_BANDS` gains `system-monitor` at 85, just above Getting Started's 80: the new Memory & disk app is one polling page that stores nothing, so a shed costs a reload and it becomes the most expendable built-in service. The built-in gets a band of its own because `test_app_manifests.py` refuses a built-in app in the `user` band.

### system/services/share_gateway

The README calls the File Viewer by its new name, Files.

Shared workspaces now answer every request with the browser hardening headers a security scan expects, whatever the service behind the origin sends:

- caddy stamps `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on every response of the share and strips the `Server` header, so a service's own (the Flask development server's `Werkzeug/x Python/y`, for one) no longer reaches a visitor. The operations are deferred, so they apply after the service's response headers land, and the auto-retrying loading page caddy serves for an unreachable backend carries them too. One visible consequence of `nosniff`: a script or stylesheet a service serves under the wrong MIME type is no longer sniffed into working by the browser.

- The gateway's own pages (loading, "Not shared with you", "Sign-in link expired", "Sharing is misconfigured") carry a full `Content-Security-Policy` admitting only their inline stylesheet by hash, beside the `frame-ancestors` policy caddy adds to everything.

A service's own `Content-Security-Policy` is still left in place and composed with the gateway's `frame-ancestors` policy; the gateway sets no page policy for services, since only a service knows what its pages load.

The primer's apps table says what each app is for and where it describes its API: the gateway reads the manifest's `description` and `api_schema_path` off the registry row and renders the schema's address over the share beside the app's origins.

Visiting agents: a coding agent running outside the workspace can be invited in with a one-time code and then works through the workspace with the workspace's own authority. The gateway gains the `/_agent/*` surface on the auth origin (join, me, primer, skills, changes, invites, grants) and admits a bearer admission token beside the session cookie, resolving it against a new agent grant kind kept in `data/.secrets/agent_access/grants.toml` and scoped to the whole workspace (every origin, exec authority through owner-exec via a reconciled `authorized_keys` line) or to named apps. A served single-file Node helper (`wsvisit`) joins, signs owner-exec requests, verifies responses, refreshes the skills index daily, and heals moved coordinates. The `agent-access` CLI exposes invite, list, revoke, primer, skills, changes, and reconcile for the desktop and the terminal; with `--json` its refusals are JSON on stderr, and its events record whether the gateway or the CLI asserted the granter. Every writer of `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` (the gateway's reconcile and the desktop's SSH grant) now holds `authorized_keys.lock` around its read-and-write. Caddy routes `/_agent/*` on the auth origin and strips `Authorization` before every backend. Design: `specs/studio-agent-access/spec.md` in the mngr repo. The CLI refuses a non-positive `--expires-in-days` the way the invite route does; the helper refuses a state directory that is not private when it reads from it, tells an app-scope agent that inviting needs the whole workspace instead of calling it revoked, and names the clock skew behind a signature refusal. The helper no longer runs a command a second time when the run's stream trailer fails verification: it refreshes the workspace's addresses for the next command and reports the failure after the output. The helper drains its stdout and stderr before exiting, so a large answer read through a pipe (where Node writes asynchronously on macOS) keeps its tail. The join route bounds the body it reads rather than the body it has already read, and the grants and invites files escape every control character a stored string carries, so a trusted caller's odd input can no longer leave the files unreadable. The marker lines that bound the exec-only passages of the primer and the instruction block are removed from the rendered text for workspace scope, not only (with the passages) for an app scope. The helper refuses a `--timeout` that is not a positive number of seconds (one given without a value used to run the command with a one-second timeout). The gateway replaces `last_seen.json` atomically, so a listing that reads it mid-write no longer blanks every agent's last-seen time.

The helper refuses an `--expires-in-days` on `wsvisit invite` that is not a positive number of days (a bare flag used to mint a one-day grant, and a word a grant with no expiry at all), the way it already refuses such a `--timeout`.

When the helper cannot reach the workspace, it says the workspace may not be published right now and that its owner publishes it from the Share panel, since an unpublished workspace is the usual reason the share's addresses stop answering.

A workspace record the gateway cannot read (a truncated host `data.json`, an unreadable host public key) is logged rather than silently read as empty, so a join answer with no host id or host key can be traced to its cause; an absent record still reads as empty quietly.

A join or a revoke that drops an expired grant records the `expired` event for it, as the gateway's start-up reconcile already did, so a grant's event trail always ends with its expiry or its revocation.

The auth-origin label is created atomically: the gateway starting the stack and the `agent-access` CLI minting an invite can both create it on a workspace's first publish, and the one that loses now answers the label the other stored, instead of a second label the running gateway would not serve.

The orientation renderers log what they fall back from: a git invocation that fails or times out, a skill file that cannot be read, a skills-index cache that cannot be parsed, and a missing primer or instruction-block reference file each leave a line in the gateway's log beside the degraded answer they still render.

The helper an invite installs is pinned to a published source: the instruction block fetches it from the template repository at the workspace's exact ref (`raw.githubusercontent.com/imbue-ai/default-workspace-template/<tag or commit>/...`) and checks the SHA-256 the block carries, with the workspace's own `/_agent/helper` as the fallback for an unpublished commit; `/_agent/helper` answers an `X-Helper-SHA256` header, the join and `me` answers carry a `helper` object (`version`, `source_url`, `sha256`), and the helper warns on stderr when its own hash is not the one the workspace publishes, naming where to reinstall it from.

The helper's published address, the `X-Helper-Version` header, and the `template_ref` the orientation routes report now name the workspace's template commit (the one it was created from, or the upstream commit its last `update-self:` merge brought in) rather than the workspace's own HEAD, which bootstrap's initial commit puts past anything GitHub has, so the pinned download no longer 404s. The helper gains `wsvisit get <app>/<path>` (or a URL on one of the workspace's origins): the admission token goes with the request as a bearer and to those origins only, and an app that answers 503 with `Retry-After` while it starts is waited out.

## [minds-v0.8.6] - 2026-10-13

### .agents

The `claude_p.py` helper in `use-ai-integration` now works with prompts that start with `-`. It used to pass the prompt as a bare argument, so a prompt starting with `---` (any file with frontmatter, such as a SKILL.md) failed with `unknown option`. The prompt now goes after `--`, and both `claude_p_completion` and `claude_p_task` accept any prompt text. Apps that copied `claude_p.py` in earlier keep the old behaviour until they copy it again.

The `find-transcripts` skill now reads current transcripts. Its jq recipe only knew the old `user_message` / `assistant_message` / `tool_result` records, so it printed nothing useful for agents writing today's `step` / `observation` records. The recipe now handles both formats. The skill points to `mngr transcript --preserved-only` for destroyed agents instead of claiming `mngr transcript` cannot read them, and mentions `--full` for untruncated tool inputs. Its `find` no longer lists the transcript converter's log as a conversation.

Workers exploring the lead's transcript now read with `--role user --role agent`. The guide said `--role assistant`, a role the current transcript format no longer has, so the lead's replies were silently left out. The detailed re-read now adds `--full`, since the default view cuts long tool inputs short.

`claude_p.py` works from a supervisord service or a cron job again. A service that copied `claude_p.py` in earlier keeps both failures below until it copies the file again.

- Every call failed with "OAuth session expired and could not be refreshed". With `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` unset, the helper read credentials from the workspace's default account, but the `claude -p` it launched still looked in `~/.claude`, which holds no sign-in. The child now runs on the same account the resolver reads: the agent's own account inside a chat, else the workspace default.

- Every call also waited 3 seconds. Under supervisord the child inherited a stdin that never closes, so `claude -p` waited for input before proceeding. The helper now gives it a closed stdin.

- The helper's docstring and `references/billing-and-credentialing.md` no longer say `claude -p` authenticates from the shared `~/.claude`, and neither the skill's litellm sketch nor the `migrate-workspace` layout reference says the resolver reads the shared Claude settings.

- With `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` unset, the helper now picks the workspace's default Claude account the way a new chat does: the pinned default, else the most recently used one. It used to take the most recently used one even when another was pinned as the default.

`manage-desktop` explains popped-out windows: how to spot one in `desktops` (each client's `popped_out`), which ops refuse to move one and exit `4`, what `--force` does, and when to pass it (only when the user asked for exactly that change) rather than telling the user the window is popped out and how to bring it back. `build-app`'s surfacing step says an `open --beside` a popped-out chat opens unpaired, which needs no `--force`.

The update-app skill now tells agents to run `uv sync --all-packages` in a worktree before booting an app preview from it, and again before `refresh` after changing a dependency or entry point. Without that step, a preview booted from a fresh worktree served the live app's code with no error or warning: the worktree had no environment of its own, so the app's command fell through to the live install.

The build-app scaffolder pins a new app's type-check ratchet to `ty` 0.0.85 (was 0.0.24), the version every committed project now uses.

The build-app scaffolder makes every new app type-checked: its `pyproject.toml` gets an empty `[tool.ty]` table and a `ty==0.0.24` dev dependency, and its ratchets get `test_no_type_errors`. The scaffolder's tests hold a scaffolded app's ratchets to the same set of tests every committed project's ratchets define, and check that a scaffolded app passes `ty`.

update-self's worker guide reserves `stuck` for a provisioning change whose absence would break the running workspace. A global pin bump cannot be held back (the apply re-runs the provisioner with every pin from the merged tree), so a user-created dependent of one is `done`, reported as "applied live, unverified in the worktree; the lead checks it after the apply".

The test gate for a commit is exactly what `select-tests` prints for it; a suite it did not print is a widening that goes through the worker's `question` gate. The shared harden guide says so once, and the lead's gate rule now says a `select-tests` output is never the "silence" its more-coverage fallback applies to.

Before changing a test that failed, a harden worker runs it on the tree before its change and reports whether the change caused the failure or it was already there (shared harden guide, "The test gate"); update-self's worker names `$MERGE^1` as that tree.

`create_worker.py reply` is now the one way to bring a worker back: its send already revived a worker that `stop` stopped, one that crashed, and one the OOM daemon shed (mngr's send relaunches a shed agent's lingering session, the same stop-then-start as `mngr start --restart`), and once the message is delivered it blanks the `archived_at` label a `stop` set. lead-proxy's "Resuming after the user overrides a failure" and the shed and crash recovery docs send the reply rather than running `mngr start` first; update-self's "Resuming after `stuck`" lists only the flow's own preconditions (lease, run record, history bridge). launch-task's recovery docs treat a STOPPED worker as deliberately stopped only when `archived_at` is non-empty.

`reply --name` is gone: it reached workers whose task file predates the `worker_agent_id` stamp, which shipped in minds-v0.6.0. A `launch` whose `mngr create` reports no agent id now fails before sending the task (exit 2, with the worker named for `destroy`) instead of sending it by name.

update-self's Step 1 no longer triggers a backup and waits for it. It runs `host-backup-now --check`, which reads the backup service's log and reports whether a recent restore point exists, with the same exit codes as before; the apply has no backup step.

build-app's Step 5 says the background test-gate run AGENTS.md asks of a chat is not the harden worker's thorough pass, so a chat still runs it before handing a new app to a worker that may never be dispatched.

Skills name `uv run --no-sync workspace-layout` for the desktop's window ops instead of `python3 system/scripts/layout.py`, which is removed; `manage-desktop` also documents the new `show` subcommand.

- The isolated-instance preview's hint names the new command.

- `manage-desktop` places windows with `workspace-layout place --state snapped-left|snapped-right|maximized`.

- `update-app` and `update-self` treat a change under `system/libs/workspace_layout/` as a change to a critical app: it is made in an isolated worktree, never the served tree, takes the `system_interface`, `chat`, and `terminal` editing leases, counts in the freshness check, and previews as the shell with the chat.

- `migrate-workspace` lists every `layout.py` call it carries over among the legacy paths to fix, since the script it names is gone and its flags changed.

- The show-files-in-chat skill links files (and folders) by absolute path or `file:///` URL, so a click opens them in the File Viewer.

- AGENTS.md says to link a registered app by the `link` `workspace-layout list` prints for it, and other local services by their localhost URL.

- The build-app skill's public URL reference says where an app's share address comes from (`workspace-layout list`) instead of telling agents to ask the user for it.

- The build-app skill says a scaffolded app's links are followed by the app contract (plain `<a href>` links, no link handling of its own), that its `window.open` to a workspace address is routed the same way and returns `null`, and tells a wrapped third-party tool that can serve a static file and add a script to its pages to load the contract too.

- The manage-desktop skill says `workspace-layout list` gives each app the `link` to write for it.

Adjust the file-sharing skill and add a new "devices" skill so
that agents can work with multiple user devices.

Let agents know how to send permission requests to all of user's desktops.

Adjust the latchkey skill to elt agents know that they can request traffic to be proxied through user's computer.

- The notify-user script now asks the chat app which pages are watching the chat (shown and focused) and sends their ids as `watched_by`, so the Imbue Studio app can file the notification as read instead of showing it to a user who is already reading the chat. If the chat app does not answer within 2 seconds, the notification goes out without the field and the script prints `notify-user: could not check who is watching this chat (...); sending anyway` to stderr; the exit code still says whether the notification was accepted.

- The notify-user skill no longer describes how the app displays and files a notification (bell, badge, toast, banner, read and cleared states), which the agent does not act on. It now says only that the message goes to the app's notification menu, that clicking it opens this chat, and that it is one-way.

Skills now refer to the user's workspace as a "workspace" rather than a "machine" where they tell the agent what to say to the user or describe the workspace itself: file-sharing (synced copies live "in this workspace", including the example request rationale), connect-external-service's latchkey reference (the Permissions tab of "this workspace's" options), update-self (what "the workspace" is waiting on during a hold), and manage-scheduled-tasks (jobs fire while "the workspace is running" and are skipped "while the workspace is stopped"). "Machine" stays where it means compute, such as running low on memory.

The app and service worker references (`type-app.md`, `type-service.md`) now run an app's suite by path from the repo root (`uv run pytest system/apps/<package>`), not from inside the app's directory. An app resolves its paths against the repo root, so a run from inside its directory could not find the shell's built modules, and its browser tests failed even in a built checkout. `type-app.md` also says to build the frontends once in a fresh worktree before running an app's browser tests.

### system

The shared UI library (workspace-ui) carries the media queries that tell a phone from a desktop, `device_queries`: the phone-sized viewport (a short side at most 500px and a long side at most 1000px, either way round) and the touchscreen query. Apps that draw a phone layout import them, so they all switch together.

The stop-when-no-windows spec's description of the services event stream now lists the display name among the registered fields a `service_registered` event compares, alongside the URL, label, and icon. Documentation only; the behavior it describes is the system_interface change in the same PR.

Claude Code bumped from 2.1.280 to 2.1.293, the current `latest` release (`stable` is still 2.1.285), in both places that pin it: `CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION` in `system/scripts/setup_system.sh` and `[agent_types.claude].version` in `.mngr/settings.toml`. 2.1.284 added Claude Sonnet 5.5 (`claude-sonnet-5-5`) and 2.1.293 added Claude Haiku 5.5 (`claude-haiku-5-5`), and the `sonnet` and `haiku` aliases now resolve to them, so a claude agent switched to Sonnet or Haiku runs the 5.5 model. 2.1.293 is the first release that carries Haiku 5.5, which is why this pin is ahead of `stable`. Since 2.1.281, a recursive `rm` whose target is command-substitution output (such as `rm -rf "$(pwd)"`) asks for confirmation even under `--dangerously-skip-permissions`; an unattended agent waits 2 minutes for an answer, then the command is denied with a hint to rewrite it.

Codex CLI bumped from 0.157.0 to 0.161.0 (`CODEX_VERSION` in `system/scripts/setup_system.sh`). New codex agents now start on GPT-6.1 Sol: `[agent_types.codex]` pins `model = "gpt-6.1-sol"` instead of `gpt-6-sol`. Codex's bundled catalog has GPT-6.1 Sol from 0.159.1 and lists it for every ChatGPT plan GPT-6 Astra is listed for, including `promax`, which GPT-6 Sol was not. An account that is not offered it still starts on the account's default model. GPT-6.1 Sol's own default effort is `low` (GPT-6 Sol's was `medium`), so `[agent_types.codex]` now pins `model_reasoning_effort = "medium"` and a new codex agent keeps starting at medium effort. Its default speed tier is standard, but `service_tier = "default"` stays pinned for models such as GPT-6 Sol whose default is the fast tier.

mngr is pinned to `3d1687adc4`, the public export of mngr-internal#1684, the paired mngr change. It moves mngr's own Claude Code pins and dialog snapshot to 2.1.293 and prices Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol. Once that PR merges, the twice-daily bump moves the pin to the mirror of mngr `main`.

The ai-driven-services plan now shows the `claude -p` helper's invocation with the prompt last, after `--`, matching `claude_p.py`. It used to show the prompt right after `-p`, the form that fails with `unknown option` for a prompt starting with `-`.

The `test_workspace_claude_config.py` docstring no longer lists `claude_p.py` among the callers that land on the shared `~/.claude`: with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` unset, `claude_p.py` reads the workspace's default account and runs its child `claude -p` there.

- The chat presence contract (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/contracts.md` section 7) now names the report's `sequence` field: the page numbers its reports from 1 in the order it sends them, and the chat app drops one numbered at or below the page's standing report. A `closed` report no longer deletes the page's report outright; the page counts as neither open nor visible after it.

New plan `docs/system/blueprint/popped-out-layout-ops/plan-popped-out-layout-ops.md`: how agents' layout ops treat a window the user popped out into its own Imbue Studio window. The desktop-interface contracts describe it: section 8 gains `force`, the 423 refusal and exit code `4`, the ops that raise a pop-out instead, the unpaired `open --beside`, and the answer fields; section 5.5's inventory lists each client's popped-out windows; section 10's placement notes say which verbs an agent's op reaches on one.

`uv.lock` records `ty` 0.0.85 (was 0.0.24) for every project's type-check ratchet.

`uv.lock` records the `ty==0.0.24` dev dependency every project now declares for its type-check ratchet.

AGENTS.md now says a chat runs the `select-tests` gate itself, even for a change it will hand to a harden worker (which may never be dispatched), but only through `system/scripts/run_in_background.py`, never in the foreground. That run checks the change against its existing tests; new tests and review gates stay the worker's. In the foreground the chat verifies the change as a user would.

The root conftest overrides pytest-playwright's session `playwright` fixture to fail with a pointer to `module_browser`, so a root-suite test that asks for `page`, `context` or `browser` errors on its own instead of leaving an asyncio loop running that breaks every later browser test in its xdist worker. The chat and shell suites, which run their own sessions, are unaffected.

The agent-facing desktop command is now `uv run --no-sync workspace-layout` (from the new `system/libs/workspace_layout` library) instead of `python3 system/scripts/layout.py`, which is removed; the root project depends on the library so the command is always in the root venv.

- AGENTS.md, the automation agents' system prompt, and the docs name the new command.

- `refresh_workspace_view.py` stays stdlib-only; a test now checks the body it posts against the shell's own request models.

- The desktop contract's op route table gives `place` a `state` or a `frame` record and a shortcut op's `cell` as a record, and says the arguments and answers are the `workspace_layout` models.

Links clicked inside a workspace open inside the workspace: files in the File Viewer, local addresses as the window of the app on whose `<label>.localhost` host or registered port they are, or else in the workspace's browser, an address on the workspace's share domain as that app's window, and external links in an app of the workspace registered for them, or else outside the workspace.

- The File Viewer registers `open:file`, shown on the file's (or folder's) view page and raising a window already there.

- AGENTS.md tells agents to link files by absolute path, a registered app by the `link` `workspace-layout list` prints for it (its share address once the workspace has been shared, else its port-less `<label>.localhost` address), and other services running in the workspace by their localhost URL.

- The desktop-interface contract describes each app's `share_url` in the inventory, the recorded share domain, and the `open:web`, `open:mailto` and `open:tel` messages external links become.

- The desktop-interface and workspace-app-model contracts describe the new message handler forms, `shell:message`, `shell:open-link`, the app contract's link rule, and `minds:open-link`, and drop the reserved `handles` table.

- `fetch_mngr_assets.sh` also fetches the desktop app's URL externality vectors, which the link classifier is tested against, and the template pins mngr to the export carrying embed contract version 8.

- The desktop-interface contracts (section 7) now describe chat presence: reports keyed by a per-page instance id with the document's focus, the 30-second heartbeat, what counts as watching a chat, the loopback-only watchers route, and the read call the chat app makes when someone starts watching. The workspace-app-model phase 6 spec points there for the current shape.

The create gate's refusal now reads "No provider account is signed in for this workspace." (was "on this machine"), matching the minds app's return to calling the user's unit a "workspace".

`forward_port.py` copies the new `system` manifest key onto the registry row. Both `contracts.md` files and the workspace app model plan document the key and the services event's `system` and `internal` fields, and say the share gateway admits a per-app grant on any app that is not internal. The stop-when-no-windows spec and the desktop-interface contract now exempt an app with a per-app grant from the automatic stop only when it is not internal.

- Pin mngr to the public mirror of the minds 0.8.6 release commit, so workspaces built from the `minds-v0.8.6` tag run the mngr the 0.8.6 desktop app ships with.

The desktop interface contracts (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/contracts.md`) describe the new desktop-switch protocol: `client_state` reports carry a `report_id` and an `is_following` flag, client records carry a `desktop_revision`, and `active_desktop_changed` carries the `revision` and `report_id` of the move it announces.

The contracts also describe how the shell orders a page's desktop moves against the moves it had not heard of: a moving `client_state` report carries a `page_id` and the `revision` it was made at, and the client record keeps `desktop_moved_by`, the page whose report wrote the current revision; the shell answers a report it does not record by sending that connection the client's record as an `active_desktop_changed`.

The scaling design's memory-lifetime section now says that a chat whose agent stops is dropped by the release that runs after every observe event, which spares a chat someone is streaming, rather than evicted at the stop itself; destroying an agent, or an archived member stopping, still evicts directly.

earlyoom now sheds at the workspace's own memory cap on a local docker workspace under runc: a new `publish_cgroup_meminfo` program publishes the container's cgroup limit and headroom into the `--host-meminfo` file earlyoom already reads (the gen-2 slice VM publishes it from outside under gVisor; under runc the container can read its own cgroup). Before, under runc earlyoom watched the whole machine's memory and the cgroup OOM killer struck first.

earlyoom's swap gate is held open (`-s 100,100`): it acts only when memory and swap are both below their thresholds, and under runc the container sees the host's swap, which on a laptop with swap kept earlyoom from ever acting. A workspace container can never swap, and the gen-2 and lima VMs have no swap, so nothing changes elsewhere.

- New `system/scripts/minds_browser_shim`, the `$BROWSER` a provider sign-in CLI runs in the workspace: it records the page to open for the chat app to hand to the minds desktop app.

The post-launch-paths plan now says a chat with nothing signed in asks for a provider itself: a first message from an intake waits in the chat's composer, and the chat's page opens the provider chooser.

Removed the unused `pyright` dev dependency and the dead `[tool.pyright]` tables from the root, chat, and system-interface pyprojects; type checks run with `ty`. Having `pyright-langserver` on every workspace's PATH is what made Claude Code offer its pyright LSP plugin in every Python-touching session, and one accepted offer installs the plugin for the whole account, putting a language server of several hundred MB behind every later chat.

Claude agents (chats, background workers, automations) are told to give every Bash call a `description` again (a line added to the Claude-specific instructions in `[agent_types.claude].append_system_prompt` in `.mngr/settings.toml`). Since workspaces moved to Claude Code 2.1.280 and Opus 5.5, most chats had stopped writing one: whether a chat does is settled by its first Bash call (usually a `tk create` batch), and a chat that skips it there never writes one afterwards. The chat's activity strip and tool chips then showed the raw shell command instead of a plain-language description. On one production workspace, 38 of 50 chats since the switch had no descriptions at all, against 1 of 45 before it. Replaying a real chat's opening message, 3 of 6 Opus 5.5 chats started without descriptions; with the new line, 0 of 8 did.

### system/apps/chat

The chat list is resizable: drag its right edge (or focus the edge and use the arrow keys) to make it between 100px and 480px wide; a double-click on the edge puts it back to the default 180px. The width is kept per browser across reloads. A chat's title now runs to the end of its row; the rename pencil only takes room, shortening the title, while the row is hovered.

In a narrow chat window on a desktop (a mouse rather than a touchscreen), the header's list button now opens the chat list exactly as the wide window shows it -- dense rows, a rename pencil on hover, "New chat" spelled out -- at the width it was dragged to, instead of the phone's finger-sized drawer. Phones and other touchscreens keep the finger-sized drawer.

Under a mouse, the narrow layout's header is denser (36px, smaller buttons) to match the desktop's chrome; touchscreens keep the 44px bar. The drawer, on every device, now floats with the same soft shadow as menus over an undimmed chat, and a click or tap beside it still closes it.

The narrow layout's header menu (the three dots) now offers everything a right-click on the chat's row in the list does: Rename, Stop or Restart, Delete, and Copy reference, Explain... and Modify..., which point at the chat's title in the header. The narrow layout now follows the device: on a touchscreen it is on whenever the screen is phone-sized either way round (by the desktop shell's own phone rule, a short side at most 500px and a long side at most 1000px), so a phone keeps it turned sideways and a tablet never gets it; under a mouse it starts at 500px wide or less, down from 700px.

The Claude model picker's Sonnet and Haiku entries now select Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5. On the new Claude Code 2.1.293 pin, the `sonnet[1m]` alias resolves to `claude-sonnet-5-5` and the `haiku` alias to `claude-haiku-5-5`, so the entries are labelled "Sonnet 5.5" and "Haiku 5.5" and their `harness_reported_model_id`s move with them. Sonnet 5 (`claude-sonnet-5`) and Haiku 4.5 (`claude-haiku-4-5`) stay in the catalog as hidden options, so a chat created on an earlier pin still shows its model's name. Sonnet 5 is ordered after the offered Sonnet 5.5 key because `claude-sonnet-5` is a prefix of `claude-sonnet-5-5`, and Haiku 4.5 sits ahead of the `claude-haiku-4` family catch-all.

The baked model catalog fixture (now `baked_model_catalog_v2_1_293.json`) and the list of model ids the binary carries were regenerated from the 2.1.293 executable.

A Codex chat whose effort was never picked now shows the effort it is running at, the model's default (Medium for GPT-6-Sol), instead of none.

Before, the model menu's effort control showed no current effort for such a chat: the slider sat at Low and the model chip left the effort out. Codex records no effort until one is picked, and the chat app did not pass on the per-model default that Codex reports in its model list. Each model option now carries that default, and the menu shows it whenever the chat has recorded no effort.

Switching a chat like this to another model now keeps the default effort it was running at, if the new model offers it, instead of dropping to the lowest.

Starting a new chat from such a chat on another account of the same provider, keeping its model, now starts it at that default effort too, instead of failing to apply the model because no effort was named.

Fast mode can now be turned on or off for such a chat, including the switch Auto makes after its turn limit. The change was refused because it carried no effort, so fast mode stayed as it was. A model with a default effort no longer needs an effort named.

A newly picked model that does not offer the current effort, in the model menu or the switch dialog, now starts at its own default effort instead of the lowest one.

- The chat frontend's vitest run no longer fails with "EnvironmentTeardownError: Closing rpc while "onUserConsoleLog" was pending" while every test passes. Two `ModelProviderMenu` tests open the menu on a dynamic picker, which loads the chat's offerable models; the test file let that request go out to jsdom's `localhost:3000` unanswered, and its failure was logged after the file's environment had been torn down. The tests now answer the request themselves.

- A chat page's presence could be stuck as hidden (so not watching) while it was shown and focused, until its next heartbeat up to 30 seconds later. A page sends `hidden` when the shell's handshake lands and `visible` a moment later on `shell:shown`, each as its own request, and the threaded server could record them in the reverse order. Presence reports now carry a `sequence` number the page counts up from 1, and the chat app drops a report numbered at or below the page's standing one. A `closed` report is kept as the page's standing report until it expires (counting as neither open nor visible), so a report it overtook cannot reopen the page either. This was the cause of the flaky `test_a_chat_page_watches_its_chat_only_while_shown_and_focused` e2e test.

The type-check ratchet runs `ty` 0.0.85 (was 0.0.24). 0.0.85 checks the objects the chat builds with `cls.__new__(cls)`, which 0.0.24 typed as unknown, and its findings are fixed:

- The OOM prioritizer reads a chat's process start through `_read_active_process_started_at`, which answers `None` for a chat with no active agent instead of passing `None` on as an agent id.

- The antigravity watcher's `build` assigns its attributes without re-annotating them; the class body already declares each one.

- The codex endpoint tests' fakes are subclasses (`_FakeCodexLedger` of `CodexMessageLedger`, and a `CodexHarnessSession` subclass that overrides `ensure_live` and `_live_ledger`) instead of lambdas assigned over a session's methods.

- `@contextmanager` functions are annotated as returning `Generator[X, None, None]` rather than `Iterator[X]`, which 0.0.85 reports as a deprecated overload.

- The e2e test that records launcher dialogs registers a named `Dialog` handler returning `None`; the tuple-returning lambda matched none of `Page.on`'s overloads.

- An inert mypy-style `type: ignore` in the config tests is gone.

The chat reaches the shell through the shared `workspace_layout` library's client instead of its own: the auto-open reactor, the focus-chat route, and the client-activity reports behave as before.

- A send whose client or desktop id the shell would refuse is no longer reported to the shell (a warning is logged instead of the shell refusing the body).

- The auto-open reactor logs a warning, rather than an info line, when the shell answers its show of a chat with something other than a show's answer; the chat stays held and is retried as before.

- The shell's answer to a show is read as the library's whole show answer (the desktop, the client's layout, the window, and a known `shown` outcome); an answer missing any of them, or naming an outcome the chat does not know, is malformed rather than passed through.

- The focus-chat route answers 400 for a client id the shell would refuse, instead of passing it on.

- The paths the chat shows (its root with a chat selected, a chat's own page) are typed window paths and pages, checked before they are sent to the shell.

- Frontend comments name the `workspace-layout` command in place of the removed `system/scripts/layout.py`.

Links in chat open inside the workspace instead of downloading or doing nothing.

- A link to an absolute path, or a `file:///` URL, opens the file or folder in a File Viewer window (raising one already showing it) instead of downloading it.

- A link to `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`, or a `*.localhost` address is clickable again. A link to `<label>.localhost` (or `<name>.localhost`) of an app registered with the workspace, or a `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `[::1]` link at that app's port, opens as that app's own window; any other opens in the workspace's browser.

- External web, mail, and phone links go to an app of the workspace registered for them, of which there is none yet, and otherwise open in your own browser or mail or phone app (Imbue Studio asks first for mail and phone links). A link to one of the workspace's share addresses opens that app's own window. All links look the same, and hovering or copying one shows its real address; Cmd/Ctrl-click and middle-click do what a plain click does, and the chat itself never navigates away.

- The chat has no link code of its own: clicks follow the app contract's link rule, as in every app. It only renders an absolute path as the file's `file:` URL.

- Opened on its own outside the workspace, the chat leaves its links to the browser: a web, mail, or phone link opens in a new tab, and a file link does nothing (it no longer downloads the file).

- Chat presence is now tracked per page rather than per client. Every chat page mints an id when it loads and names it on each presence report, so a pulled-out chat and its hidden copy in the main window no longer overwrite each other's report (which made the chat flicker between shown and hidden for the memory prioritizer). Reports also say whether the page's document has focus, are sent again on every focus and blur, and heartbeat every 30 seconds instead of every 60.

- A chat page that is shown and focused, and has reported in the last 90 seconds, is *watching* its chat. The new `GET /api/chats/<chat-id>/watchers` (loopback only) lists the watching pages as `{"watched_by": [...]}`, which the notify-user script passes on to the Imbue Studio app so it can show nothing to a user who is already reading the chat.

- When a chat goes from nobody watching to someone watching, the chat app tells the Imbue Studio app the chat was read (`POST /api/v1/agents/<agent-id>/notifications/read` through the latchkey gateway, as the chat's current agent), so its notifications from that chat are marked read. The call runs off the request thread; an app without the route (404) or an unreachable gateway is ignored. A secondary (preview) chat makes no such call.

The permission card for a request to act on the user's other workspaces is now titled "Other workspaces" instead of "Other machines", matching the minds app's return to calling the user's unit a "workspace" (a "machine" is only the compute it runs on).

The manifest declares `system = true`: it is part of the workspace itself rather than an app built on it, so the minds Share tab lists it under its collapsed System group instead of offering it up front. It can still be shared on its own from there.

The transcript can always be scrolled all the way to its bottom, however tall the composer is. Before, a draft long enough to grow the composer pushed the last message under it: the transcript sat short of its bottom and kept getting pulled back up, so scrolling down could not reach the end.

- The composer no longer collapses to one line for a moment each time it measures its text (every redraw), which made the browser pull the transcript's scroll position up to fit that one-line layout.

- When the composer shrinks back (a draft cleared or sent), the transcript keeps following new messages at its bottom. The browser's adjustment as the transcript grew taller was read as the user scrolling up, which stopped the follow.

An open chat no longer stops showing new events after its agent is briefly reported stopped.

Before, the moment the observer reported a chat's agent dead, the chat app dropped the chat's transcript watcher. That watcher is the only thing feeding the page's live stream, and the stream kept sending keepalives, so the page looked connected while nothing new appeared until a reload. A live agent can be reported dead for a moment: an automatic rename moves the agent's tmux session before it rewrites the agent's name, and a listing in between finds no session. The next message sent from the chat rebuilt the watcher, but everything written in the gap never reached the page.

Now a chat whose agent dies is released only when nobody is streaming it: as soon as its last stream closes, rather than at a later observe event. A stopped chat that no window shows is still dropped at the observe event that reports its stop.

Removing a chat's active agent now drops the whole chat's resident transcripts, archived segments included, and ends the chat's open streams. A chat whose active agent is gone never reads as stopped, so nothing else would release those segments; and with its watcher gone nothing feeds the stream, so the chat page reconnects and resyncs once the agent is listed again (an open subagent panel does not reconnect yet) instead of looking connected while nothing arrives.

Opening a stopped chat now counts as streaming it before its transcript is loaded, so an observe event landing while the stream opens no longer drops the transcript the new stream depends on.

- Signing in to Claude or ChatGPT no longer needs a pasted code when the chat runs inside the minds desktop app. Picking Claude or ChatGPT hands the sign-in page to the desktop app, which opens it in your browser and relays the provider's callback back into the workspace; the chooser says "Finish signing in to <provider> in your browser", with "Try again" and "Try another way" buttons, and closes by itself once you are signed in. Without the desktop app, Claude falls back to pasting the code its page shows, and ChatGPT to its one-time-code login. While you are in the browser, "Try another way" shows Claude's code steps for the same sign-in or starts ChatGPT's code login, and lists the other ways in; a failed sign-in offers the same, next to "Try again". If the desktop app can no longer open the page, the chooser moves to another way in by itself.

- ChatGPT signs in through a short-lived Codex app-server rather than by scraping `codex login --device-auth`: "Use your ChatGPT plan (runs on Codex)" in the browser, or "ChatGPT with a code" from any device.

- New `POST /api/accounts/flow/<flow_id>/callback` delivers a relayed browser callback to the sign-in CLI: only the callback with the flow's `state`, once, while the flow is waiting. Only the workspace's owner can deliver one (a visitor gets 403). It answers with the flow's status once it settles (or `pending` after 20 seconds) and the provider's name, which the desktop app shows the browser. When a flow ends, the chooser sends `minds:provider-sign-in-end` so the desktop app frees the callback port.

- Signing in again no longer takes the account's old credential away first; the account keeps working until the new sign-in lands, and a sign-in is not counted as landed while the old credential is all the account holds. A credential an older build parked mid-re-auth is put back at boot. A Claude sign-in is decided by the CLI's clean exit with its "Login successful" line, or its own probe when the line was reworded. "Sign in again" on an API-key account asks for a key rather than opening a browser sign-in (`reauth_method` on each account row). A Claude browser sign-in that lands removes the key or long-lived token the account held in its settings, which Claude would otherwise keep using over the new sign-in.

- Clearer sign-in failures: a Claude sign-in whose browser callback reports a denial says "Access wasn't approved on Claude's page." (claude.ai's own Deny sends nothing back, so the chooser keeps waiting with Try again and Try another way); a code Anthropic refuses says to start over; a ChatGPT sign-in denied or refused says which in plain words (codex's own error is logged, not shown); a ChatGPT code login that cannot start says to turn on device code sign-in for Codex in ChatGPT's security settings; and a sign-in stopped by a restart says it stopped rather than that it was replaced.

- While ChatGPT's browser sign-in waits ("Finish signing in to OpenAI in your browser"), the chooser notes that "Enable device code sign-in…" has to be turned on first, at the bottom of the ChatGPT settings page. A sign-in method can carry such a note (`note` on each method in `GET /api/lanes`, as Markdown), shown on that waiting screen.

With nothing signed in, a chat now asks for an AI provider before anything else: the provider chooser opens in the chat as soon as it is shown, instead of after the first message has been typed.

This is the only way the chooser opens for a missing provider. A chat waiting for its first message shows "Connect an AI provider to start chatting." and a "Choose a provider" button above the message box, which stays in view (keeping anything already in it) but disabled until a provider is signed in; the button opens the same chooser in the same place. The New chat button opens that waiting chat instead of a chooser of its own, and a message sent in from the launcher waits in the chat's message box, with no "Failed to start the chat" dialog, until a provider is signed in.

Removed the dead `[tool.pyright]` table from this app's pyproject; its type checks run with `ty`, and the template no longer installs pyright.

No behaviour change. A comment on the tool chip's label order no longer claims Claude always writes a description for its shell calls; the description is optional and Opus 5.5 often leaves it out, which is why the workspace's Claude instructions now ask for it.

### system/apps/files

The README names the `workspace-layout` command in place of the removed `system/scripts/layout.py`.

The File Viewer opens links to files and folders clicked elsewhere in the workspace: its manifest registers the `open:file` message, so a chat's link to an absolute path (or a `file:` URL) opens that file or folder on its view page in a File Viewer window, or raises a window already showing it (however that window reached it) instead of opening another.

The File Viewer now speaks the app contract every app speaks: its pages load the shell's contract module from its path in the workspace, so its links follow the contract's link rule, and its location beacon and file windows go through the contract.

### system/apps/getting_started

The first-visit window counts as delivered when the user already has it popped out into its own Imbue Studio window: the app leaves it there instead of trying to place it on the desktop, which the shell now refuses, and retrying every few seconds, which raised the pop-out each time.

The type-check ratchet runs `ty` 0.0.85 (was 0.0.24). `@contextmanager` functions are annotated as returning `Generator[X, None, None]` rather than `Iterator[X]`, which 0.0.85 reports as a deprecated overload of `contextmanager`.

The project is type-checked: its ratchets run `test_no_type_errors` (`ty`, pinned to 0.0.24 as the shell and the chat pin it), and its `pyproject.toml` makes the directory its own `ty` project (an empty `[tool.ty]` table).

The first-visit window is opened and placed through the shared `workspace_layout` library's client instead of the app's own HTTP code; when and where it opens is unchanged.

- The first-visit window's frame is sent as a frame record rather than an `x,y,width,height` string.

The template detail page's second action is now "Create a new workspace from this" (was "Create a new machine from this"), and the chat it starts asks for a new Imbue Studio workspace rather than a machine.

The manifest declares `system = true`: Getting Started is part of the workspace itself rather than an app built on it, so the minds Share tab lists it under its collapsed System group instead of offering it up front. It can still be shared on its own from there.

### system/apps/system_interface

The shell's phone rule and touch query now come from workspace-ui's shared `device_queries`, which the chat app uses too; when the shell switches to its phone layout is unchanged.

The services event stream now carries each app's display name, so the Imbue Studio desktop can call an app what the workspace calls it.

A `service_registered` event gained a `display_name` field, the manifest's `display_name` (empty for a row registered with `--name`/`--url` and no manifest). A change to it alone re-announces the app, exactly as a change to its URL, label, or icon does. Until now the desktop learned only an app's registered name, so its share panel could offer "files" where the workspace shows "File Viewer"; the name a user reads could not leave the workspace at all.

The field is additive and older consumers ignore it.

An agent's layout ops no longer quietly undo a window the user popped out into its own Imbue Studio window.

- `restore`, `maximize`, `place`, and `minimize` on a window the target client has popped out (while it is connected) are refused with 423 and change nothing, including the switch `args.desktop` would make. With `force` they apply and bring the window back onto its own desktop without switching the client's desktop window; a forced `minimize` brings it back minimized, so it actually goes out of sight instead of only its ghost. A disconnected client's pulled-out window is moved without `force`, so the pop-out reopened at its next launch closes.

- `focus`, and an `open` that finds the window at the path, raise the pop-out's own window instead of pulling it back. `open --beside` a popped-out window opens unpaired unless forced. `close`, `navigate`, `refresh`, `show`, and the rest are never refused.

- The op answers say what happened: raised in its own window, brought back, not paired, and whether the client has only pop-outs open (so a window shown on its desktop waits for a desktop window). The inventory lists each client's popped-out windows with whether their ghost is hidden.

- A pulled-out window's own page raises its window when a `show`, a `focus`, or an `open` that finds it names it, so the raise works with the main window closed.

The type-check ratchet runs `ty` 0.0.85 (was 0.0.24); the pin's comment no longer claims newer versions are off limits.

The test server and File Viewer helpers are annotated as returning `Generator[...]` rather than `Iterator[...]`, which 0.0.85 reports as a deprecated overload of `contextmanager`. Finding the nearest free desktop cell answers `None` for no candidates before taking the `min`, rather than passing `min` a `default=None` that 0.0.85 folds into the key's parameter type.

The op route's request models, the client, desktop, and window ids, the wallpaper reference, and the client-activity report now come from the shared `workspace_layout` library, so the shell and its callers read one definition. Every argument is read through those models, so a value off its rule is answered with a 400: a client, desktop, or window id as before, and now also a `client` or `desktop` that is not a string (ignored before), an empty `app`, `path`, `desktop`, or `beside` (read as absent before), and a `window` or `beside` that spells no window, which is now refused before a named `desktop` switches the client to it.

- The op route's hints for an unknown or unsettled client name `workspace-layout context` instead of the removed `layout.py`.

- The op route reads each body into its op's own body model from `workspace_layout`, and the dispatcher matches on the body exhaustively, so an op added but not handled fails type checking instead of reaching a runtime "no handler" error. An argument the op does not take is refused with a 400 naming it (a `refresh` of an `app` with a `client` or `desktop`, and `reload_system_interface` with any argument, were accepted before; a `wallpaper` op must name its `wallpaper`, null to clear it, where one without the key cleared it before), and the 400 names every argument it refuses rather than the first; `context`, `desktops`, and `list` still ignore their arguments.

- The shell's records (windows, desktops, placements, frames, cells, client records) and every answer it gives (the op answers, the inventory, the desktops and clients listings, the `context` answer, and the `layout_op` message) are `workspace_layout` models the shell builds its JSON from, rather than dicts it writes by hand; the JSON is unchanged but for timestamps, which now end in `Z`.

- The op route's `place` takes `state` (`SNAPPED_LEFT`, `SNAPPED_RIGHT`, `MAXIMIZED`) or a `frame` record; `zone` and a string `frame` are refused with a 400, as is a shortcut op's string `cell`. `context` is answered by the same dispatcher as every other op.

The desktop delivers messages that apps send each other, and opens the links apps and Imbue Studio hand it.

- An app's page can send the desktop a message (`shell:message`) for whichever app registered its type. A handler that shows a page has the desktop build the page from the message and raise a window already on it, or open one; a message from a pulled-out window lands on the main desktop, and when the main Imbue Studio window is closed a notice says to reopen it.

- When a message cannot be delivered, a notice says why in the words of the app that refused it (for example, that Chromium is not installed yet).

- A link an app's page hands over (`shell:open-link`, which the app contract sends for every link that is not the page's own), and a popup to a local address that Imbue Studio now turns back into the workspace, open where they belong: a `file:` URL in the File Viewer (`open:file`), a local URL on an app's `<label>.localhost` host or at the port it registered (`http://localhost:8095/...`) as that app's window at the URL's path, any other local URL in the browser (`open:url`), and one of this workspace's app addresses as that app's window; another workspace's address is refused with a notice.
