Both now wait for the list first, and read it again when it names no account, because a sign-in made in another chat (for example the Welcome chat) does not reach the chat list's own copy. The chooser only appears when no provider is signed in.

- The Chat window is never open empty. With nothing selected, it shows your most recent chat. With no chats at all, it shows a new chat ready to type, which starts on your configured provider when you send its first message. Nothing is created before that message, and several Chat windows opening empty at once share the one new chat. A new route, `POST /api/chats/awaiting`, hands the chat list that waiting chat. The phone layout still shows the list alone when nothing is selected.

### system/apps/files

The File Viewer's manifest declares `stop_when_no_windows = true`: the viewer holds nothing between windows, so the shell stops the program a minute after its last window closes and starts it again on the next request, answering that request with a loading page that reloads into the viewer (`docs/system/specs/stop-when-no-windows.md`).

### system/apps/getting_started

Getting Started's manifest declares `stop_when_no_windows = true`: the shell stops the program a minute after its last window closes and starts it again on the next request. The first-visit window is unaffected: the shell stops nothing before a client has arrived, and the app is running by then (`docs/system/specs/stop-when-no-windows.md`).

### system/apps/system_interface

Bringing a window to the front by clicking its content, or by any other route that is not a press on its title bar, its edges, its taskbar entry, or a shortcut (an agent focusing it, a link opening it, a menu's Focus last), now takes the keyboard off the window it covered. Before, that window kept the keyboard: typing went into a window you could no longer see, and switching to another application and back put it back on top of the one you had chosen (the chat window resurfacing over a maximized app).

The launcher menu now moves in the same frame as the launcher field when the field grows or clears. Before, the menu followed one frame late: for that frame a grown field overlapped the menu's foot, and a cleared field left a gap under it. That lag also made `test_the_launcher_field_grows_upward_out_of_its_row_and_lifts_the_menu` flaky, because it reads the menu's position right after the field changes.

Fix the flaky floating-entry drag-and-reload e2e test (`test_a_floating_entry_toggles_its_window_drags_to_a_position_that_survives_a_reload_and_returns_to_the_bar`). The entry's icon grows by a tenth under the pointer through a transition that reduced motion leaves on, and the test read the entry's box with the pointer resting on it, so each read caught the growth at an arbitrary point and the post-reload box sometimes came out more than the 4px tolerance wider than the post-drag one. The test now moves the pointer off the entry and waits for its animations to finish before each read. Test-only; no product change.

- New workspaces now show a Chat shortcut on Home whether they are created locally or leased from the cloud pool. Home is still made on the first read of the desktops after the app registry is read, but an app that registers afterwards (the chat registers last) now has its default shortcut added to every desktop: a desktop still as it was seeded is laid out again in launcher order, so the Chat shortcut comes first; any other desktop gets it at the next free cell with nothing moved. This happens as soon as the registry changes, announced to every open window, and again on every read of the desktops.

- The shell records the apps whose default shortcut it has offered in `data/.state/system_interface/default_shortcuts_offered.json`, so a shortcut the user removed stays removed when its app registers again, on every boot and across restarts. `desktops.json` keeps its shape. When `Home` is seeded again over a missing or unusable `desktops.json`, the record starts over from the apps `Home` is seeded with, so a late app still reaches it.

- An app with a pinned window that registers late (the chat's avatar window) now gets that window on every desktop as soon as the registry changes, rather than on the next read of the desktops.

- Existing workspaces get the Chat shortcut back once: with no record yet, the apps with a shortcut on any desktop count as offered, so the chat, missing from every desktop of a workspace seeded before it registered, is added once. So is any other registered app's default shortcut that is on no desktop: a built-in one the user had removed from every desktop comes back once, and an app built with a `default_shortcut` after the desktops were made gets its shortcut once.

The shell owns app lifecycles (`docs/system/specs/stop-when-no-windows.md`):

- A lifecycle manager parks the loopback port of every stoppable app that is stopped and wakes the app on the first connection, answering it with a loading page that reloads until the app is up; wakes are budgeted (3 per 5 minutes per app, counting only wakes the app did not come up from: a wake after which the app ran, or was stopped on purpose while still starting, spends nothing, so an app opened and closed or Quit a few times in five minutes is woken every time) and a wake that ends in FATAL is answered with a "could not start" page. A POST launch to a stopped app wakes it first and waits for it to answer.

- An app whose row carries `stop_when_no_windows` is stopped once no window on any desktop has shown it for 60 seconds, and only once a client has arrived at the shell since it started. An app with a per-app share grant (a `[services.<name>]` table of `data/.secrets/share_grants.toml` that names anyone, while the workspace is shared) is exempt: its visitors reach it without loading the shell, so no window of theirs exists to count (`shell/share_grants.py` reads the grants document; one the gateway would refuse grants no app, warned about once per version of the file). The close hint an app declares is no longer posted to a stopped app.

- `POST /api/apps/<name>/quit` closes every window of the app on every desktop and stops its program; the window menu offers "Quit <app>" in place of Stop and Start. A stoppable app's window keeps its page while the app is stopped (the parker answers it); the stopped placeholder, without its Start button, survives only for rows the shell cannot start.

- The registry read announces registrations to the minds desktop (`app_announcements.py`, formerly the `app-watcher` service), and the inventory's sweep re-reads the registry when its mtime moved. The `app` wire object carries `stop_when_no_windows`.

- The liveness sweep answers a supervised row from supervisord alone: when supervisord cannot answer for it, the row keeps its last liveness instead of being TCP-probed, since a connect on a stopped app's port would now wake it through the parker. Rows without a program are still probed over TCP.

Taskbar and launcher refresh.

- A taskbar entry is a labelled chip: the app's icon with the window's title
  beside it at body size. The chip tints under the pointer and for the window
  you are in; a window that is out of sight -- minimized, or shown in a window
  of the chrome's own -- dims until the pointer reaches it, and the hover bubble
  carries the whole of a title the bar had to cut short.

- The bar itself is solid, with no line along its top and no blur behind it, and
  everything in it sits in one element that can be dressed on its own.

- Icons carry a cast sized for where they sit: a tighter, darker one for the
  desktop's tiles, which fall on the bar's white as often as on a photograph, and
  a quieter one again for the row of them in the bar.

- The launcher field wears a plus rather than a magnifier, asks to "Open an app
  or send a message", takes body text, and is rounded to match the card above
  it; that card now takes the field's width and the chrome's menu styling.

- An app that declares no launch path of its own is offered by its name rather
  than as "Open <name>", so a verb in that list means a different kind of row.

### system/libs/app_manifest

The footprint command's diff can now run to a ref other than HEAD, and reports what the footprint accounts for as well as what it does not.

Before, `app-manifest footprint --diff-base` always diffed up to HEAD and listed only `outside_footprint`, so a caller standing on a merge commit could not read either side of it, and had to work out for itself which changed files were the creation's own.

Now `footprint` takes `--diff-ref` beside `--diff-base`, and the scope file's `diff` gains `ref` (the full sha the diff runs to) and `inside_footprint` (the changed files the footprint accounts for; excluded files are in neither list). One tree can answer for a range that does not end at HEAD, which is what the update-self worker needs to read a merge commit's two sides over the same footprint.

`app.toml` gains `stop_when_no_windows` (bool, default `false`): whether the shell may stop the app's program once no window on any desktop shows it. `critical = true` forces it `false`, and a manifest declaring both fails to load. `RegistryRow` reads the key `forward_port.py` copies from the manifest.

### system/services/oom_priority

The `app-watcher` service band is gone with the service: the shell announces app registrations to minds itself. The built-in service order loses that entry and is otherwise unchanged.

### system/services/share_gateway

The rendered Caddyfile serves the gateway's auto-retrying loading page for a registered service whose backend caddy cannot reach (`handle_errors 502`) instead of a bare 502: the moment between an app stopping and the shell parking its port, or between the shell releasing the port and the app binding it (`docs/system/specs/stop-when-no-windows.md`, section 5.7). The share-gateway program runs as its own process (`exec .venv/bin/share-gateway`) rather than under a resident `uv run`.

## [minds-v0.8.0] - 2026-09-29

### .agents

The icon a new app is asked for is a tile now, not line art.

- `build-app` describes the icon it requires by pointing at `docs/system/app-icons.md` -- a 216x216 two-layer tile, a flat background under one fill-only glyph in a centred 144x144 box, coloured from the pair palette that doc carries -- in place of the monochrome `currentColor` line-art frame it used to spell out. Both the pre-flight step and the `forward_port.py` CLI reference say so, so an agent scaffolding an app draws the same thing the built-in apps wear.

- The tile is authored at 216 rather than 48, and `docs/system/app-icons.md` now says what the mark should look like as well as what it must be. It is one everyday object, drawn by hand rather than constructed: no perfectly straight line, no machine-drawn curve, and no mirror symmetry -- whatever is symmetric in the object comes out slightly off in the drawing. The deviation is slight and lives in the shape, never in the quality of an edge, which stays smooth however much the line under it moves. At 48 there was nowhere to put the points that carry a deviation that small, so every glyph came out as smooth as a logo. Drawing is one pass and never revised -- a second pass averages the deviation back out.

- `manage-desktop` names arcs as the bundled wallpaper that ships, in place of dawn, and points at `GET /api/wallpapers` for the current list rather than spelling one out that will rot.

`manage-desktop` and `build-app` now cover `layout.py open --beside`, which lays
a newly opened window beside the chat that asked for it (that window on the left
half, the new one on the right half and focused) instead of dropping it over the
conversation. `build-app`'s surfacing step uses it by default.

The `engineering-subordinate` output style no longer asks chat agents to give time estimates for how long building something or finishing a task will take. Its "Give specific time estimates" rule is replaced by "No unfounded time estimates": give a duration only when hard data backs it (a measured run, a progress count, a known duration), and otherwise say what happens next. The examples and the harness-override note that modeled guessed durations ("back in ~5 minutes", "About 15 minutes ... An afternoon if not") are removed.

- `serve_isolated_instance.py up --copy` (which app previews use for their copy of an app's data) now checks that the copy fits before making it. A copy that would leave less than 6 GiB free on its disk (above the space a cloud workspace's disk quota holds back) is refused before anything is written, failing the boot with a message saying what to do instead, and a copy that fails part way is removed rather than left holding the space.

- The `update-app` skill no longer tells an agent to copy an app's data into `/tmp`, which is now a RAM disk capped at about 1 GiB. The copy an agent tests a change against is made with `serve_isolated_instance.py up --copy`, which puts it on disk and deletes it on `down`, and a snapshot before an in-place change goes to `/var/tmp` after a fit check. The `file-sharing` and `minds-api` skills send large files and backup exports to `/var/tmp` as well.

A rolled-back update apply no longer leaves behind what the forward apply added outside its snapshots, which left the workspace unable to take any later update. The restore of a tool environment now puts its bin-directory entrypoints back to the restored receipt's set: it removes a link the apply added (a dangling `terminal-pty`, over which every later `uv tool install --reinstall` refused with "Executable already exists") and relinks one the failed reinstall had removed. A reinstall also clears a link into its own tool that the receipt does not list, so a workspace an earlier rollback already left in that state recovers on its next apply. Recovery no longer demands a bundle the restored tree has no frontend for (getting_started's, on a tree from before that app), which had turned a clean rollback into an emergency. The rollback also removes the fetched `system/vendor/mngr-assets` from a restored tree that has no fetch script, where it was an untracked directory that refused the next apply. The user-requested rollback of a kept rollback point gets the same cleanup.

A lead now waits for its background agent's report the same way on every harness. The skills that dispatch a worker (`launch-task`, `crystallize-creation`, `update-creation`, `heal-creation`, `fetch-process-show`, `migrate-workspace`, `publish-template`, `update-self`, and the shared `lead-proxy.md`) start `create_worker.py await` through `system/scripts/run_in_background.py` instead of claude's background tool, and the report arrives in the lead's chat as a message. Before, a codex lead had no way to be woken by the report. It improvised its own notifier, and the chat showed the report as a "Browser fleet" message.

`update-self` carries its own copy of `run_in_background.py`, kept identical to the one in `system/scripts/` by a test, so the copy of the skill it takes from the release it is updating to brings the runner with it. The workspace being updated may be too old to have the script. In one too old to have `message_chat.py` as well, the runner delivers through `mngr message` instead.

`migrate-workspace`'s two backups and `publish-template`'s wait for the GitHub approval also run through `run_in_background.py` now, so no skill waits on claude's background tool any more.

update-self now works out which earlier updates' rollbacks still need undoing with a new `update_self.py pending-rollbacks` command, which the worker runs before it merges, and the apply refuses a merge that leaves one in place by the same rule. Before, the worker guide reverted the newest rollback it found. That could be an earlier release's rollback that its own retry had already undone, and the worker then stopped on an empty revert. Now each rollback nothing has undone is reverted, newest first, whether the pass retries that release or moves to a newer one. An update's rollback now names the release it rolled back in a `Rolled-back-update:` trailer, which is how it is told apart from a user's rollback of an app change: that one carries the same subject and is left alone. A rollback made before the trailer is recognised by the history it undid instead, including the rollback of a failed retry of a release already in history, where all the retry landed was the revert of the first rollback. Before, the apply caught a skipped revert only on a retry of the same release; now it catches it on any pass.

`update-self` now updates to the template branch you picked. Choosing a branch name (not a release) as the update target used to fail quietly when the workspace only had that branch from the template upstream. The update then ran the workspace's own older update steps instead of the branch's, so fixes that shipped on the branch were skipped. The name now resolves to the upstream branch (`upstream/<branch>`), and that wins over a stale local branch of the same name. A target that names nothing the workspace has fetched now stops the update with a clear error, instead of being staged silently as the workspace's own copy.

Skills now call the desktop app Imbue Studio and the thing you talk to "your agent". The desktop app is now called Imbue Studio, and the noun for the thing you talk to is now "your agent" rather than "your mind".

The template skills carry most of this: publish-template, use-template, update-installed-template, update-published-template and migrate-workspace describe adopting, publishing and importing in the new vocabulary, and the README that publish-template generates for a published repo now says "a published Imbue Studio template" with an "Open in Imbue Studio" button, matching the badge the build script already emitted.

update-self's user-facing error text now names Imbue Studio ("could not reach the Imbue Studio app", "Update the Imbue Studio app itself first"), with its test assertions moved in lockstep.

The Caretaker introduces itself as "a Caretaker for your workspace" rather than for your agent: under the new vocabulary the Caretaker is itself an agent, and what it looks after is the workspace.

Nothing machine-readable moved. The `minds-api` skill keeps its directory name and gateway route, the `minds-template` GitHub topic and the `(minds template v2)` repo-description marker stay verbatim (both are read by the catalog generator and the publish flow), and `MINDS_*` environment variables, `~/.minds` paths, `minds-placeholder-thumbnail`, the betterleaks rule ids and the `minds-v*` release tags are untouched.

The published-template README's call-to-action now reads "Open in Imbue Studio" and links to the Studio trampoline page, `https://studio.imbue.com/open?git_url=<repo url>`, a route the connector serves on the web chrome origin, instead of the external GitHub Pages trampoline; that page's button carries the app's new `imbue-studio://create` deep link. The fallback line under the button says "Create a Studio workspace". `build_template.sh` generates the new link and badge, and the README recipe names the new scheme. The `SKILL.md` prose still says "Open in Mind" until the product-name sweep.

update-self now updates a workspace created before the template's history was rewritten to drop the vendored mngr directories. Such a workspace shares no commit with a newer release, so the update's merge had no base. The lead's new `bridge-history` step (end of Step 3a, right after a forced tag fetch) finds the workspace's fork point and its rewritten twin in the target (same author, committer, dates and subject, same tree once the vendored paths are removed) and adds a `git replace` graft naming the fork point as the twin's extra parent. The ordinary worker merge and fast-forward apply then run unchanged, and the workspace's own history is never rewritten. Teardown drops the graft whatever the outcome (`bridge-history --drop`); a retry rebuilds it. Every other workspace sees a no-op.

The update's tag fetches now accept moved tags (`git fetch upstream --tags --force`), and the worker guide says to report `stuck` rather than merge unrelated histories when no merge base exists.

- The careful flow for critical apps takes one lease per critical app it touches (`editing critical app <name>`, a `workspace_ui` or npm-file change counting as both the shell and the chat), rather than one `editing critical apps` lease for all of them, so a chat edit and an unrelated shell edit no longer block each other. A pass takes its leases all or none, so two passes that need the same apps at entry never hold one each, and a pass that later grows to a held app surfaces it along with the leases it already holds. The go-live freshness check now also fails when any file the pass changes moved on the served branch, and the lead re-checks for another pass's "recently updated" notice before applying. `update-self` takes the per-app leases, all or none, for the critical apps an update touches (and its release step no longer names the stale `editing service system_interface` lease), and `harden-contention.md` tells a merging pass to wait out a critical app's lease too.

- `update-app`'s `preview_app.py` has an integration test (`test_preview_app_lifecycle.py`) that boots a fixture app from its manifest's `[preview]` table through the real `serve_isolated_instance.py` and `forward_port.py`, refreshes a rebuild in place, and tears it down. The existing tests stub the shared script and hand-write its state file, so a renamed flag or state key there used to pass both suites.

### system

The rules every app icon is drawn to, and the docs and scripts that point at them.

- `docs/system/app-icons.md` is new, and is now the one statement of what an app icon is: 48x48, two layers, a flat background under one fill-only glyph in a centred 32x32 box, a 32 per cent corner radius, and a colour pair from the palette it carries. It also says what the file may and may not hold (no shadow, no strokes, a root `fill="none"`, a clip only for a glyph drawn to the tile's edge), how a glyph is drawn, and what the workspace draws behind one (nothing) -- and it says outright that this look is the workspace's default rather than a fixed law, with this doc as the place to change it.

- `AGENTS.md` and `forward_port.py` point at that doc rather than describing a house style of their own: the registration error an app with no icon raises names it, and the module's own docs say the markup check here is about safety, not style.

- The file viewer's icon is Courage on Inspiration, built to those rules, replacing its `currentColor` line glyph.

- `test_app_manifests.py` pins the order of the built-ins the desktop seeds its shortcuts in and the launcher lists -- chat 10, Getting Started 15, the file viewer 20, the browser 30, the terminal 40 -- rather than asserting one app's rank on its own.

`layout.py open` takes `--beside [window]`: bare, it pairs the opened window with
your own chat; with a window argument, with that window. The desktop contract's
`open` row documents the new `beside` argument.

- Local Docker workspaces' `/tmp` tmpfs is now capped at 1 GiB (`[providers.docker]` start args `--tmpfs /tmp:exec,size=1g`), matching cloud workspaces, whose `/tmp` mngr caps at an eighth of the VM's RAM. A large write to `/tmp` now fails with "No space left on device" instead of filling the container's memory and taking the workspace down. AGENTS.md tells agents `/tmp` is a small RAM disk and where large files go.

- The workspace app model contract (section 17) and the desktop interface contract (section 13) say an isolated instance's `copies/` also hold what its `--copy` flags name.

A new script, `system/scripts/run_in_background.py`, runs a command in the background and, when the command exits, sends its exit code and output to the calling agent's own chat as one message. That message starts the agent's next turn, so it works on every harness. Only claude's own background tool wakes the agent when its command finishes; codex, pi and opencode have no such tool. The chat shows the user only a one-line summary. The report tells the agent to act on it before ending its turn even when it arrives in the middle of other work, since a harness can hand it over mid-turn. The run's output and exit code are also kept in `data/.tasks/run-in-background/<task>/`.

If the report can't be delivered, the runner keeps retrying with backoff for up to four hours. That covers a chat that is mid-handoff, and an agent that was shed for memory and is waiting for its lead to restart it. It gives up at once only when the chat no longer exists. The runner also outlives a stop of the agent that started it (a handoff retiring it, or its restart after a shed), which kills every process tagged with that agent's id: the runner drops the tag, and only the command keeps it, so the command still ends with the agent and the report says how. `message_chat.py` now exits 8 when the chat app doesn't know the chat and `mngr` has no agent with its id. Before, `mngr message` exited 0 for an id that matched nothing, so a message to a chat that no longer existed looked delivered. The runner also lowers its own OOM priority to the user-service band once its command has started, so under memory pressure every agent but the workspace's primary is shed before it. The command itself keeps the caller's band.

`message_chat.py --system` is now `--browser-fleet`, after what it does: it wraps a message in the browser fleet's tag, which the chat shows as a "Browser fleet" chip. A codex lead had used `--system` to report a worker's result, and the chat showed that report as a browser-fleet message. `--system` still works, for a browser app that is still running the code from before an update; it goes once every release the app updates from passes the new name.

Codex CLI bumped from 0.154.0 to 0.157.0 (`CODEX_VERSION` in `system/scripts/setup_system.sh`). 0.155.0 is the first release that can use GPT-6 Sol (`gpt-6-sol`) and GPT-6 Luna (`gpt-6-luna`); on 0.154.0 an account's model list does not offer them at all.

New codex agents now start on GPT-6 Sol: `[agent_types.codex]` pins `model = "gpt-6-sol"`. Without a pin, codex starts on the first model of the account's server catalog, which is GPT-6 Astra. A chat can still switch to any model its account offers from the model bar. The catalog lists GPT-6 Sol for every ChatGPT plan GPT-6 Astra is listed for except `promax`; on an account without it, a new codex agent starts on the account's default model instead. Codex agents also now pin `service_tier = "default"`: GPT-6 Sol's catalog entry defaults to the fast (`priority`) tier, which codex's terminal UI would otherwise apply to any turn typed directly in the agent terminal. The `fast` create template still overrides it.

Codex agents can no longer type into a running command. `features.unified_exec = false`, which was meant to remove `write_stdin` (a tool that fires no PreToolUse hook, so typing commands into a shell skipped every command guard), has been silently ignored since codex 0.154: codex forces unified exec back on unless a managed requirements file pins it. `[agent_types.codex]` now sets `features.unified_exec_tty = false` instead, so every command runs with its stdin closed and `write_stdin` can only poll a running command or interrupt it. Long-running commands still yield and can be polled.

`suppress_unstable_features_warning` moved from codex's `[features]` table, where codex ignored it, to the top level of the config. Left where it was, codex 0.157.0 starts every session with two error items: "Codex is ignoring 1 unrecognized configuration setting" and "Under-development features enabled: code_mode_only". At the top level, neither appears.

The first codex agent in a workspace no longer turns `/tmp` into mode 0700. codex 0.154.0 forced the parent directory of its app-server socket (`/tmp/mngr-codex-<hash>.sock`) to 0700, and since codex runs as root that made `/tmp` unwritable for other users, such as apt's `_apt` sandbox user. codex 0.157.0 keeps its sockets under `/tmp/codex-daemon-<uid>/` and leaves the parent alone.

A codex account whose plan does not offer GPT-6 Sol no longer gets a codex agent that fails every turn. `[agent_types.codex]` now sets `fall_back_to_account_default_model = true` alongside its `model = "gpt-6-sol"` pin, so before mngr starts a new codex thread it reads the account's model list, and if GPT-6 Sol is not in it (the catalog leaves it out for `promax`) the thread starts on the account's default model instead. A chat whose thread already exists keeps its model.

mngr is pinned to the public export of mngr's `gabriel/codex-model-fallback` branch, which adds that setting.

The workspace now installs earlyoom v1.9.0-imbue.3 and runs it with `--host-meminfo /mngr-vol/.host-meminfo`. The release never picks a gVisor zombie or exiting task (v1.9.0-imbue.2 could signal one over and over until the sandbox was killed), and under gVisor it counts each process's smaps `Anonymous:` total rather than the inflated `VmRSS`. On a gen-2 slice VM, `--host-meminfo` reads the headroom the VM publishes into the workspace's volume, which includes the memory gVisor itself is charged, so earlyoom sheds before the container's cgroup kills the whole sandbox. Where nothing is published there (local docker, lima), earlyoom logs that once and uses `/proc/meminfo` alone.

The desktop's contracts record the shortcut drag as it now behaves: the rule for where the shortcut you drop onto steps aside to (the nearest free cell, as before, now searched over the grid and shown live) and why nothing else on the grid moves, where that leaves the drag and the shell's own move route disagreeing, and the `data-lifted` marker plus what `data-cell` means on the icon a drag is holding.

`forward_port.py` copies a manifest's `message_handlers` onto its registry row. The shared embed module (`system/libs/workspace_ui`) lets a page observe every message the Imbue Studio chrome sends it, whatever the type, which is how the shell relays one to the app that registered for it; `FOCUS_CHAT` is no longer exported. The desktop interface and workspace app model contracts describe the manifest table, the relay route, and the `show` op.

- Pinned mngr to public commit `d90339cba2` (the mirror of mngr `1b632f1f19`) for the minds 0.8.0 release (`minds-v0.8.0`).

The `[providers.docker]` comment on the tmpfs `/run` and `/tmp` mounts no longer says the AWS provider's start args apply the same mounts: mngr_vps now adds them itself on every cloud VM provider whenever the container runtime is runsc, so the template's copy covers the local docker provider only. No setting changes.

The shared frontend library (`system/libs/workspace_ui`) gains `hideCursorWhileTyping.ts` and a matching rule in `base.css`: the mouse pointer hides while a keystroke inserts or deletes text in a focused field and comes back on the first real pointer movement, press, or scroll, so it never sits over what is being typed. Shortcuts such as Cmd+C, bare modifier presses, keys pressed outside a field, and Space on a checkbox or radio leave the pointer alone; keystrokes an input method editor is composing hide it. Because `cursor` never crosses a frame boundary, the shell, the chat page, the chat root, and the Getting Started page each install it on their own document.

The `[providers.lima]` comment in `.mngr/settings.toml` no longer says the trixie image pin exists because `mngr_lima` defaults to bookworm: the library default is the same trixie release from the same artifact mirror now, and the comment explains why the template still pins it and lists the library default among the sites to bump together. Comment-only; no behavior change.

Prose across the workspace now calls the desktop app Imbue Studio and the thing you talk to "your agent". The desktop app is now called Imbue Studio, and the noun for the thing you talk to is now "your agent" rather than "your mind".

The root README, AGENTS.md, the `data/` READMEs, the workspace-internals doc and the `.mngr` create templates are reworded, including the five systemd unit `Description=` strings that a user sees in `systemctl status`.

The unit names themselves (`minds-autostart.service`, `minds-autostart.path`), the `minds-caretaker` cron drop-in, the `bootstrap@minds.local` git identity, the `minds patch` marker blocks that `install_dufs.sh` re-applies by name, and the `minds-v*` tag scheme are all unchanged: they are identifiers and live state, not display text.

`docs/system/blueprint/` and `catalog/` are deliberately untouched -- the first is dated design history, the second is generated and carries third-party authors' own project names.

Lima workspaces keep their regenerable caches on the resizable btrfs data disk: the lima create template now runs `system/scripts/lima_cache_on_data_disk.sh` before the dependency install, which makes `~/.cache` a nested btrfs subvolume on the data disk (skipped by the home tree's btrfs snapshots, as restic already skips `**/.cache`) and turns `/var/cache/user` (the `XDG_CACHE_HOME` / `npm_config_cache` target) into a symlink to it, carrying over whatever the pre-baked image held there. The VM's boot disk stays the pre-baked image's 20 GiB, now holding only the OS and toolchain; `.mngr/settings.toml` documents which disk each `--disk` refers to and points at `mngr lima resize` for changing a workspace's CPUs, memory, or data disk afterwards.

Merges `mngr/cloud-provider-updates` (the companion to mngr-internal's gen-2 learnings series): comment-only updates to `.mngr/settings.toml`. The `[providers.docker]` tmpfs comment no longer says the AWS provider start args apply the same mounts (mngr_vps adds them itself on every cloud VM provider under runsc), and the `[providers.lima]` comment explains why the template still pins the trixie image now that `mngr_lima` defaults to the same release. No setting changes. See the `mngr-cloud-provider-updates` and `mngr-host-sizing-debian-13` entries. The comment now also says the cloud providers cap their `/tmp` tmpfs and that this block's is memory counted against the container's limit (mngr-internal #1402).

Local docker workspaces are now sized: `[providers.docker]` in `.mngr/settings.toml` sets `default_cpus = 4` and `default_memory = "8g"`, rendered by mngr as `docker run --cpus` / `--memory` (with swap capped at the memory cap) on every new workspace container, so a runaway workspace can no longer take the whole machine down. The CPU cap is clamped to the daemon's CPU count on smaller machines. A per-create `-s --cpus` / `-s --memory` overrides the defaults, `mngr list` reports the recorded size as `host.resource`, and `mngr docker resize <host>` changes a workspace's size afterwards.

The desktop-interface contracts document the `is_detached` placement flag, the tear-out, detach, and reattach rules, and the shell's solo mode (`/?solo=<window-id>`), for windows pulled out of the desktop into a desktop window of the Mind app's own (mngr's `specs/pull-out-window/spec.md`).

The workspace build's mngr asset fetch now runs its checkout with the private-repo credential too, so a template pinned to mngr-internal builds instead of failing on the lazy blob fetch of the vendored files.

The template-env-manifest blueprint names the Studio trampoline page (`https://studio.imbue.com/open?git_url=<repo url>`) and the `imbue-studio://` deep link scheme where it described the published README's call-to-action.

The critical-app-editing spec and test plan describe the per-app `editing critical app <name>` leases that replace the single `editing critical apps` lease, the spec says a pass takes them all or none, and the spec describes a secondary chat's OOM prioritizer as inert (no writer) rather than handed a refusing one. The spec's integration tests name `update-app`'s `test_preview_app_lifecycle.py`.

### system/apps/chat

A new icon: the imbuman as a two-layer tile.

- The chat's icon is the imbue figure in Confidence on Comfort, built to the rules in `docs/system/app-icons.md` -- a flat 216x216 background under one fill-only glyph, with the 32 per cent corner radius the shell's `--desk-icon-radius` computes. It replaces the `currentColor` line glyph, so the chat wears its own colours wherever the workspace draws it.

- It is the one icon in the set that carries a `clipPath`: the figure stands on the tile's bottom edge rather than inside the centred 144x144 box every other glyph fits, so the tile's rounded corners have to cut its feet.

Increase the default background autocompact command timeout from 30 seconds to 120 seconds, giving context compaction runs on active chat agents more time to complete without timing out.

The report that `system/scripts/run_in_background.py` sends an agent when its background command finishes shows as a one-line notice ("Background task: <what it was> (finished)"), like claude's own background-task notices, instead of as a message the user seems to have typed. The full report still reaches the agent. A report waiting in the chat's queue, because the agent is still mid-turn, shows as the same notice rather than as its raw text. Stopping the agent no longer drops a queued report into your composer: it is sent straight back to the agent, which starts its next turn with it. It only lands in the composer if that send fails, so it is never lost. When codex, pi or antigravity flush their queue as one message, a report merged into your turn is hidden from the bubble, which shows only your words, and reports flushed together with nothing else show as one notice naming each; the agent still gets every report. A secret or permission notice flushed together with a report still resolves its card, with the report kept out of the card's note, and a report whose output happens to print a notice's tag does not hide your words.

A message sent to a chat that is destroyed while the send is in flight now answers "chat not found" (404) instead of an internal error (500), so a background task's report to a deleted chat stops retrying at once.

A Codex chat's model bar now keeps the effort level you pick between messages.

Before, changing the effort between turns was undone within a moment: the bar went back to the effort the previous turn ran at (often none, if that turn ran at the default), while the agent itself was set to the new level. Codex logs every settings change to its session file, and that write made the chat app re-apply the last turn's effort over the pick it had just saved.

The chat app now leaves the saved pick alone until the next turn runs. A turn that falls back to a different model or effort still shows in the bar.

Switching a chat to an account on another provider now makes that account the most recently used one, as a switch within the same provider and a new chat already did. Before, the workspace's default stayed on the account the chat had just left. Workers, automations and every other `mngr create` that names no account kept launching there, even when it was the account the user had moved away from because it hit its usage limit.

Retrying a failed switch on a different account likewise makes that account the most recently used one.

Opening a chat's notification in the Imbue Studio app now shows the chat in the full chat window (the chat list beside the chat): a window already showing the chat is brought forward, else the chat is selected in the chat list window on screen, else in the pinned one, else a new chat list window opens with it selected. The chat app handles the Imbue Studio app's `minds:focus-chat` itself: its manifest registers the message, and the new `POST /api/focus-chat` asks the shell's `show` op for the chat list with the chat selected, counting the chat's own page as already showing it and naming the chat list as the one page whose window may be moved to it. A chat the Imbue Studio app starts (the welcome, update, and help chats) now reaches the screen through the same op, naming no page to move, so a window already showing it is brought forward, else the pinned window takes it, else a chat list window opens. A refusal from the shell is reported as an error rather than a success.

The mouse pointer hides while you type into the composer (and the chat root's own fields) and comes back the moment the mouse moves, is pressed, or scrolls, so it never sits over the words being entered. Shortcuts such as Cmd+C leave it alone.

Chat now calls the desktop app Imbue Studio. The desktop app is now called Imbue Studio, and the noun for the thing you talk to is now "your agent" rather than "your mind".

The welcome and update chats, the permission cards, the message renderers and the agent-manager prose all name Imbue Studio, and the three assertion-bearing strings moved together with their tests.

The `minds:` postMessage event names and the `@minds/embed-contract` module specifier are unchanged -- they are the wire protocol shared with the desktop app's own `embed_contract.js`, so only the prose describing that contract was reworded. Recorded harness fixtures under `testdata/` keep the text they captured.

The provider chooser describes Opencode Go and OpenRouter in our own words instead of echoing the providers' marketing, and no longer quotes their prices: Opencode Go is "A subscription to a selection of open models." and OpenRouter is "Models from many providers on one key." The Opencode Go key screen now reads "One key for every model on your Opencode Go subscription."

A message you queue while a Claude agent is working no longer disappears when the agent's reply comes in. The agent looks idle the moment its reply lands, but Claude only picks up the queued message after its end-of-turn hooks run; in that gap the chat used to drop the message and show it again once its turn started. It now stays below the reply, shown as being sent, until its turn arrives. A message still queued 10 seconds after the agent went idle is treated as stranded and removed. Messages queued behind one that just started its turn go back to showing as queued, and wait there for their own turn.

The row under the composer (the model and provider on the left, Source view on the right) now always takes up the same space, so the composer no longer shifts when the row fills in. A new chat shows the provider it will start on from the moment it opens, instead of an empty row until its agent exists. With no provider signed in, the row says "Not connected", and pressing it opens the provider chooser.

A chat whose account is no longer signed in (typically: its account was signed out, then signed in again as a new account) no longer stays stuck. Its "Sign in again" link used to try to re-authenticate the account that was gone, or open a plain sign-in that left the chat unbound, so the chat kept saying it was not signed in however often you signed in. Now signing in, or picking an account already signed in, moves the chat onto that account. The model menu's Provider row for such a chat reads "No account" with "Pick one to move this chat to it" instead of "Not signed in", which contradicted the signed-in accounts listed right under it.

A secondary (preview) chat's OOM prioritizer now has no writer and is inert: it accepts every presence, message and lifecycle report but resolves no pids, computes no bands, and runs no staleness sweep. Previously it did all of that work every time and then dropped each write through a stub that always failed.

### system/apps/getting_started

A new icon: the flag as a two-layer tile.

- Getting Started's icon is a planted banner in Confusion on Energy, the only yellow tile in the set, built to the rules in `docs/system/app-icons.md` -- a flat 216x216 background under one fill-only glyph inside a centred 144x144 box, with the 32 per cent corner radius the shell's `--desk-icon-radius` computes.

- The flag is a bowed pole under a cloth that droops unevenly, so the line reads as drawn rather than ruled. The line glyph it replaces was the last `currentColor` icon left.

- Getting Started's `launcher_rank` moves from 5 to 15, which puts it after the chat and before the file viewer. The desktop seeds its shortcuts in this order too, so the built-ins read Chat, Getting Started, File Viewer, Browser, Terminal both on the backdrop and in the launcher, and the chat leads, since it is what the workspace is for.

The mouse pointer hides while you type into the search field and comes back the moment the mouse moves, so it never sits over what is being typed.

The getting-started tiles and template pages now name Imbue Studio. The desktop app is now called Imbue Studio, and the noun for the thing you talk to is now "your agent" rather than "your mind".

The "Learn about Imbue Studio" tile and its chat prompt, the template-detail page's create request, and the catalog config comments are reworded. The prompts are still written as plain-language requests so the agent's own skills match on them.

### system/apps/system_interface

A new bundled wallpaper, an app's icon drawn as the tile it now is, and a title bar that recedes behind the window you are in.

- A new bundled wallpaper, arcs, in a warm taupe colourway, and the default every desktop wears until it picks one of its own. It is the only one the shell bundles: dawn, the wallpaper it replaces, is no longer shipped, so a desktop that never chose one moves to arcs and a desktop that had chosen dawn draws arcs too, by the rule below.

- A desktop's chosen wallpaper is painted *over* the default rather than instead of it. A reference outlives the file it names -- a bundled wallpaper the shell stops shipping, a file taken back out of `data/.apps/system_interface/wallpapers/` -- and the desktop goes on holding it, since the choice is still the choice and the file may come back. A background layer whose image does not load is simply not painted, so what shows in the meantime is the default, which is what a desktop with no wallpaper of its own already wears. Before, such a desktop fell all the way to the flat page colour and read as a broken shell rather than as a wallpaper that had gone missing.

- A desktop shortcut paints nothing behind an app's icon. Every icon is a tile now (`docs/system/app-icons.md`), with its own background and its own 32 per cent corner, so the white surface and the 8px of padding the icon box used to carry -- there to make a transparent line glyph legible -- were framing each tile in a second one and drawing it at 32px inside a 48px box. The box keeps the matching rounding and `--desk-icon-shadow`, since the shadow and the hover are what it still owes the tile.

- An app that registered no icon wears its monogram on a tile too: its initial in Courage on Strength, the most neutral pair on the board, built to the same rules. With nothing painted behind it, the outlined `currentColor` letter it used to draw would have been left floating on the wallpaper.

- A window's title bar carries the app's icon at 20px rather than 14, starts 6px from the window's edge, and leaves 6px between the icon and the title. At a control's size the tile read as mud; 20 in a 36px bar leaves it 8px of clearance and makes it a picture again. The title is bold while the window is focused, and stays at medium when it is not -- the shade of grey that said which window you were in does not read from across the screen.

- An unfocused window's bar recedes further: its icon fades to half, its title to seven tenths, and the refresh and window-menu buttons beside the title are dropped rather than greyed, so a background window reads as a name and the controls every window owes you. The icon has to be faded by hand, since a tile that paints itself cannot take the bar's colour the way a line glyph did. The buttons return with the click that focuses the window, and nothing to their right moves when they do; the taskbar entry's own menu still reaches a window you are not in.

- The desktop settings dialog reads a wallpaper the workspace no longer offers as Default, and saves it as one. Every swatch sat unlit before, which said nothing about what the desktop was actually wearing -- the backdrop had already fallen back to the default, and the picker now agrees with it. Saving what the picker shows clears the dead reference in passing, so a desktop stops carrying a name nothing answers to.

- An app that brought no tile of its own is given one, and the monogram and the older glyphs are given the same one: `#492222` on `#F5D6A0`. The monogram wore the board's most neutral pair, which turned out to be the arcs wallpaper's own colour -- a tile in it vanished into the backdrop and left the letter and the shadow standing for the app alone.

- An icon drawn before `docs/system/app-icons.md` is put on that tile rather than left as a bare stroke on the wallpaper. Such a glyph has no filled shape and takes `currentColor` from the text beside it, which is nothing to take now that no surface paints behind an icon. It is drawn into the same centred 144 box a drawn icon's mark sits in, since it was authored to fill its own frame edge to edge and at full bleed it crowded the corner and outweighed every icon next to it. An icon with a filled shape is left exactly as it is.

- A floating entry paints nothing behind the app's icon either. The surface, the border and the 8px of padding it carried framed each tile in a second one -- the pale edge around the drawing when a pinned avatar is switched to the app's icon -- so what is left is the shadow that says raised and the corner it is cast around, the tile's own 32 per cent rather than a fixed radius. The hover is the tile growing and an open menu is a ring, since a tint behind the tile can no longer be seen.

- A new desktop's shortcuts are laid out along its top edge rather than down its left. The blind grid -- the one the shell assumes when it seeds a desktop or places a shortcut an agent added with no cell of its own, since it knows no backdrop at that point -- is one row eight columns wide rather than one column down the side. Eight columns is 784px of backdrop, and a stored cell past the last column a narrower one holds is re-packed where it is drawn, so a long row never runs off the screen.

- Those shortcuts are seeded in launcher order (`launcher_rank`, lowest first, registry order breaking a tie) rather than in registry order. Registry order is the order the apps happened to finish registering in, which is boot order, so which icon sat at the top left was nobody's decision; one manifest key now says where an app sits on the backdrop and in the launcher alike.

**`open` takes a `beside` argument.** It names a window (a window id, `self`,
`pinned`, or an app name, resolved the way the window verbs resolve one) that
the opened window should sit next to. The opened window takes half the
backdrop's width against it, at the named window's own height and its place down
the backdrop, and lands on top of the stack, for the target client alone.

The named window is disturbed as little as the room allows, which is usually not
at all: it is left exactly as it stands, down to its state, when either side of
it has half the backdrop free; moved, keeping its width and height, by the least
that opens half the backdrop on one side when neither does -- the side that
already has more of the room, ties going right -- rather than travelling to an
edge for space that was a nudge away; and narrowed to half the backdrop only when
it is wider than that, since no amount of moving opens that much beside it. Nothing
ever changes its height or where it sits down the screen. A `beside` that matches no window on the desktop -- a chat the user
closed, a requester that is nobody's chat -- leaves the opened window where it
would have landed rather than refusing the open: the pairing is the open's
courtesy, not its point.

This is the desktop's answer to what the tabbed shell did when an agent opened
something it had just built: dock it beside the chat that asked for it, rather
than over the conversation the user is reading.

**A window travels to its new rectangle instead of appearing at it.** Any move
the pointer did not make -- a snap from the size menu, a restore, a `place`, the
pairing above -- now runs as a 180ms transition (`--desk-window-move`). Only the
chrome transitions: its live page is positioned by measuring the chrome, so it
has nothing to transition towards and is re-measured every frame of the travel
instead. A press sets `data-window-motion="off"` on the desktop's root for its
whole length, so a dragged window is held by the pointer rather than trailing
it; the snap a release commits lands after the press is over, so it travels the
last step like any other move. `prefers-reduced-motion` turns the travel off
entirely.

Dragging a shortcut around the desktop is a different gesture now. Before, the icon you pressed faded to a fifth of its strength and stayed in its cell while a copy of it followed the pointer, and a dashed rectangle drew itself over the cell you were about to drop into. The copy, the fade, and the rectangle are all gone. The icon you pressed **is** the one that moves: it lifts out of its own cell at full strength, grows a tenth, casts a deeper shadow, and tracks the pointer exactly, with nothing eased so it never lags behind the hand.

What tells you where it will land is the shortcut in the way getting out of it. Hold the icon over a cell another shortcut is in and that shortcut steps aside, live, under your hand, and steps back if you move on. Hold it over an empty cell and nothing else moves at all: the gaps you leave between your shortcuts are yours, and closing them up behind a drag would be the desktop rearranging itself rather than making room. Nothing but the shortcut you are dropping onto ever moves -- a shortcut that merely happens to sit between where you picked the icon up and where you are dropping it is left alone. The stepping aside is motion, so a machine set to reduce motion does not get it: the shortcut simply appears in its new cell, the way a window moved from the size menu does there.

Where it steps to is unchanged: the nearest free cell, ties settled by the lower column then the lower row, which is what the desktop has always done on a drop. The cell the icon in your hand is leaving counts as free, so a short drag often just swaps the two. What is new is only that you see it happen before you let go.

Nothing at all is written while you are still holding the icon -- what you see under your hand is the desktop showing you the result, not saving it. The drop is one request naming the shortcut you dragged, exactly as before; where the displaced one goes is the workspace's own answer, the same rule the drag drew. Both cells are drawn the moment you let go rather than after the round trip, so there is no flicker back to where they started, and the icon settles into the cell your hand left it in rather than sliding there from the cell it was picked up in.

Two smaller things came with it. The cursor is an open hand over a shortcut and a closed one for as long as one is in your hand, wherever on the desktop the pointer has got to -- the icon under it has been lifted, so its own cell is no longer what the cursor is over. And a drag redraws the desktop only when the pointer crosses into a new cell, since that is the only thing that changes what the other shortcut is doing; the lifted icon's own travel is written straight onto it, a frame at a time.

Dropping a shortcut back into the cell it came from now asks the shell for nothing, where before every drop wrote a move whether or not anything had changed.

Opening a chat's notification in the Imbue Studio app now brings forward a chat window that already shows that chat, switching desktops if it is on another one. A chat window pulled out into its own window stays out: its own window is brought forward, as its "Show" does, rather than the chat window being pulled back onto the desktop. Otherwise the chat is selected in the chat list window you have on screen on this desktop (else the pinned one), and only when there is neither does a new chat list window open with the chat selected. Before, a chat selected in the chat list never counted as already showing it, and the pinned chat window was sent a path it could not read, which cleared its selection.

The shell no longer decides any of this about chats. It relays a message from the Imbue Studio app to the app whose manifest registers its type, through the new `POST /api/embedder-messages`, and that app asks the op route's new generic `show` op for the window: `show` takes an app, a path, the other paths that count as already showing it, and the pages whose windows it may point at the path, and answers which of raised, navigated, pinned, or opened it did. The shell reads no meaning into a query string: a window is moved only when its page is one the app named. A preview shell relays nothing: its registry copy names the live apps, so it refuses the relay as it refuses stopping and starting an app.

The mouse pointer hides while you type into the shell's own fields (the launcher, the desktop settings) and comes back the moment the mouse moves, so it never sits over what is being typed. The framed pages do the same for themselves.

The shell now calls the desktop app Imbue Studio in its own prose and docstrings. The desktop app is now called Imbue Studio, and the noun for the thing you talk to is now "your agent" rather than "your mind".

This covers the window menu, the desktop store's close-chord documentation, the relay's boundary comments, the share-profile modules and the embed ratchet rule descriptions.

The embed contract itself is untouched: every `minds:` event name and the `@minds/embed-contract` import keep their spelling, because the desktop app matches on them.

A window can be pulled out of the desktop into a desktop window of the Mind app's own.

Drag a window's title bar past the edge of the Mind window and it comes out: the app opens a window of its own under the cursor holding that page, and the desktop keeps a ghost of the window where it was, with "Show" (raise or reopen that window) and "Bring back". "Open in its own window" in the window menu does the same without a drag; a pulled-out window's taskbar entry is marked and offers "Show" and "Bring back to desktop" in its menu. Dragging back inside before letting go, or pressing Escape, puts the window back. The desktop's shell is the one writer during a drag: it saves the detach the moment the window goes out (with the drag's raise, so the window keeps its place on top) and the return the moment it comes back, and the pulled-out window's own view of the desktop only reads, waiting for that word rather than writing a stale layout over it; a return dropped back onto the desktop through the app goes through the desktop's shell too, so a quick drop no longer leaves a ghost behind. The pulled-out window's own view still takes the window back when no desktop is open to do it, reporting the return only once it is saved. The gesture and the menu item appear only where the app can make windows (the Mind desktop app), never in a plain browser.

Under the hood: placements gain `is_detached` (a file without it reads as attached; every verb that shows a window clears it), the shell gains a solo mode (`/?solo=<window-id>`) that shows one window edge to edge for the app's own window, and the shell announces every title-bar drag to the app (`window-drag-started`), which watches the cursor and says when the window is out, back in, or released (`tear-out`), since the shell's own pointer events stop at the app window's edge on some platforms; and the shared embed library learns the pull-out set of the minds embed contract (`pop-out-window`, `window-drag-started`, `window-drag-ended`, `detached-windows`, `embedder-capabilities`, `reattach-window`, `tear-out`), probed with fallbacks so the shell builds against the pinned older contract too. Design: mngr's `specs/pull-out-window/spec.md`.

A window being dragged or resized now stays on top of the stack for the whole gesture: a raise of another window that arrives meanwhile is dropped rather than applied. Dragging a window out of the Mind window and back in used to leave it under the pinned chat, because the Mind window's focus comes back mid-drag, the chat's page (still holding the document's focus from an earlier click) reported it, and the shell raised the chat over the dragged window.

Pressing a window's title bar or resize edge, a shortcut, or a taskbar entry now takes the document's focus back from any other window's page that holds it, as a plain click would (the shell prevents the press's default so a press inside a text selection cannot start a native drag, which also stopped the browser from moving focus). Before, clicking into the chat and then bringing another window to the front left the chat's page focused underneath, and it jumped back on top whenever the Mind window lost and regained focus (switching to another application and back).

The ghost of a pulled-out window gains a third button, "Hide", which puts the ghost out of sight while the window stays in its own desktop window; clicking the window's taskbar entry shows the ghost again (a second click shows the window's own desktop window, as before), and the entry's menu offers "Hide placeholder" / "Show placeholder". Minimizing a pulled-out window (the entry's menu, an agent's `layout.py minimize`) now hides its ghost the same way rather than pulling the window back minimized.

A pulled-out window no longer comes back to the desktop when the Mind window is clicked after the window was pulled out from its own keyboard focus (the chat, dragged out while its composer had focus): the browser restored focus to the window's hidden page in the desktop, which reported it, and the shell raised the window, which brings a pulled-out one back. The shell now ignores a focus report from a page it is not showing, and takes the document's focus off a page as it hides it; the same held for a minimized window, which un-minimized on a switch to another application and back.

### system/apps/terminal

A new icon: the prompt as a two-layer tile.

- The terminal's icon is Comfort on Envy, built to the rules in `docs/system/app-icons.md` -- a flat 216x216 background under one fill-only glyph inside a centred 144x144 box, with the 32 per cent corner radius the shell's `--desk-icon-radius` computes. It replaces the `currentColor` line glyph, so the terminal wears its own colours wherever the workspace draws it.

Terminal comments now call the desktop app Imbue Studio, including the tmux config header for the in-memory persistent terminals feature. The desktop app is now called Imbue Studio, and the noun for the thing you talk to is now "your agent" rather than "your mind".

### system/libs/app_manifest

The manifest gains `[[message_handlers]]`, each `{type, path}`: a message type the app takes from the Imbue Studio chrome (`minds:` and a lowercase kebab-case name, unique within the manifest) and the route under the app's origin the shell posts each such message to. `RegistryRow` carries them, and `MessageHandler` and `MessageType` are the new model and primitive.

### system/libs/bootstrap

Bootstrap docstrings now call the desktop app Imbue Studio, including the timezone fetch from the desktop client and the clean-branch guarantee for a new workspace. The desktop app is now called Imbue Studio, and the noun for the thing you talk to is now "your agent" rather than "your mind".

### system/libs/workspace_ui

The shared library gains `hideCursorWhileTyping.ts`: a page installs it once on its document, and the mouse pointer hides while a keystroke inserts or deletes text in a focused field (a writable input, textarea, or editable region), coming back on the first real pointer movement, press, or scroll. Shortcuts such as Cmd+C, bare modifier presses, and keys pressed outside a field leave the pointer alone. `base.css` carries the matching rule, `html.typing-hides-cursor * { cursor: none !important }`. Because `cursor` never crosses a frame boundary, every page installs it for itself.

The shared embed library learns the pull-out set of the minds embed contract (version 6): `pop-out-window`, `window-drag-started`, `window-drag-ended`, and `detached-windows` (workspace to embedder), and `embedder-capabilities`, `reattach-window`, and `tear-out` (embedder to workspace), each probed on the vendored snapshot with a literal fallback so a frontend builds against the pinned older contract too.

### system/services/env_converge

Template-manifest field descriptions and the service README now use the new vocabulary: a manifest records what an agent adopted or built on, rather than what a mind did. The desktop app is now called Imbue Studio, and the noun for the thing you talk to is now "your agent" rather than "your mind".

Only the human-readable descriptions changed; every manifest field name is the same, so published manifests stay readable by older and newer workspaces alike.

### system/services/host_backup

The backup's default excludes now cover a throwaway instance's copies of an app's data and its scratch directory (`data/.state/isolated-instances/*/copies` and `*/scratch`). The data they copy is backed up where it lives, and one app's store can run to many GB, so without this every hourly snapshot taken while a preview or test instance was up swept a second copy of it. The instance's own state (`instance.json`, its logs) is still backed up.

The README's manual restore now targets `/var/tmp/restored` instead of `/tmp`, which is a RAM disk capped at about 1 GiB that a full restore would overflow.

Backup documentation and messages now call the desktop app Imbue Studio -- it is Imbue Studio that writes `data/.secrets/restic.env` and runs `restic init` from outside the workspace. The desktop app is now called Imbue Studio, and the noun for the thing you talk to is now "your agent" rather than "your mind".

The `minds-v<X>` tag scheme and the `backup-update: minds-v<X>` commit-subject convention are unchanged: the desktop updater matches on both, so renaming them needs a coordinated release rather than a text edit.

### system/services/oom_priority

The OOM drill now predicts the victim the way earlyoom v1.9.0-imbue.3 picks it under gVisor. It counts each process's smaps `Anonymous:` total in place of `VmRSS`, since gVisor's `VmRSS` counts whole mapped ranges (every claude process carries the whole claude binary). It also treats a `VmSize` of 0, gVisor's zombie or exiting task, as a process earlyoom cannot pick. The README and `bands.py` describe the counted memory, including what stays approximate.

The README now describes `--host-meminfo`, which the workspace's earlyoom runs with from this release on.

Documented what MemTotal is for a lima workspace (the VM's own RAM, set by the lima create template's `--memory` and changeable with `mngr lima resize`), so earlyoom's thresholds follow the VM's size. No code change.

Documented how the container memory cap that local docker workspaces now run with interacts with earlyoom: under gVisor the container's `/proc/meminfo` reports the cap as MemTotal, so earlyoom sheds relative to the workspace's own limit; under runc it still sees the whole machine. No code change.

### system/services/share_gateway

Sharing documentation and state descriptions now call the desktop app Imbue Studio -- it writes `data/.secrets/share.env` and reads the gateway's retry state. The desktop app is now called Imbue Studio, and the noun for the thing you talk to is now "your agent" rather than "your mind".

The `minds_session` cookie name and the gateway's route names are unchanged.

Sharing now starts as soon as the minds app writes the share materials, instead of up to ten seconds later. The share gateway watched `data/.secrets/share.env` through `inotifyx`, which was never a declared dependency and is not installed in the workspace, so the watch silently fell back to a blind ten-second sleep between polls and every share enable (and unshare) waited out the remainder of a tick before anything happened. The gateway now watches through `inotify_simple`, the library the app_watcher service already uses and the template already ships.\n

## [minds-v0.7.4] - 2026-09-26

### .agents

The `latchkey` skill is replaced by `connect-external-service`, one skill for reaching anything outside the workspace on the user's behalf. Its SKILL.md is a routing table: one row per method, in order (a builtin latchkey service; a custom latchkey service the user pastes a key into; the service's own MCP server; a custom latchkey service the user signs in to, capturing the session the service's website uses; its direct API with a key the user supplies through a secret card; the browser), each with the cheap test that says whether it is workable, the sentence to say, and the reference to read; the tests start from `latchkey services list` and `mcpc`, which name the connections that already exist. The agent takes the first workable row and explains rather than asking, and does not rule a row out from a probe made without the user's credential. The latchkey text lives on as `references/latchkey.md`, with the custom-service `header` and `credential_instructions` options (the latter puts the agent's directions to the key beside the input in the approval window, which covers the chat), a section on choosing between the cookie and token sign-in flows (and on where the sign-in window and the gateway's requests run), and a pointer to the direct-API row where it used to say to have the user type credentials into a file. `references/direct-api.md` is new, and so is `references/mcp.md`, which reaches every MCP server through `mcpc`, one MCP client the whole workspace shares, instead of any harness's own MCP config: servers are listed in `mcp-servers.json` at the repo root, each gets a session through `mcpc connect`, and tools are called with `mcpc @<name> tools-call`, so a newly connected server works in the same turn, from any chat on any harness, from an app, and from a scheduled job, with no chat restart. An MCP server the service does not publish itself is never run, hosted or local: it would be a stranger's code holding the user's key, or a middleman on their data; its source only informs a key or direct-API connection. A hosted server's OAuth sign-in runs through `mcpc login`, held open in the background while its consent page is handed to the user in a workspace browser; a hosted server that takes a key names it as `${VAR}` in its header, records the secret file it needs as `secretsFile`, and is connected under `with_secrets.py`.

The skill ships `scripts/request_secret.py`, which files a secret request with the chat app and prints it; the chat renders a card with one password input per variable, the user submits, and the agent is told the file and the variable names, never the values. A value reaches a program only through `python3 system/scripts/with_secrets.py data/.secrets/<name>.env -- <command>`.

Alongside: the eight skills that named the latchkey skill now point at the new one; `agentic-browser-fleet`'s description says to arrive through connect-external-service rather than load it directly; it says the window `new` opens is minimized, that `handoff` brings it up in front of the user, and that the agent shows it with `layout.py open browser` whenever else the user should watch, rather than telling the user to open it from the launcher; and it no longer says a launch-task worker runs in an isolated container (it runs in a worktree of the same workspace); `use-ai-integration` says to delete and re-snapshot `anthropic.env` rather than edit it; `build-app` takes `--secrets-file` and documents `[[secrets]]` in `app.toml` and the wrapped program command, and `update-app`'s preview runs such an app under the same wrapper for each declared file; `manage-scheduled-tasks` and the service-processes reference say how a job or program runs under a secret file; the worker reports a needed secret instead of requesting one; and `migrate-workspace`'s `retired-skill` audit now flags a migrated workspace's own references to the old `latchkey` skill.

Templates carry their secrets: `publish-template` aggregates every app's `[[secrets]]` and every skill's `secrets:` front matter (plus the files the snapshot's `mcp-servers.json` servers and supervisord programs run under) into `[[requirements.secret]]` entries with `file` and `variables`, refuses to assemble when a referenced file is undeclared or a declared variable is missing from the publishing workspace; `use-template` files one secret card per entry up front, and connects each MCP server once the file it runs under is stored, once the user has signed in, or at once when it needs neither.

Three build-app scaffolder tests no longer fail when run inside a live workspace. They asserted which port the scaffolder would pick automatically, but it skips any port something on the machine is already listening on, and a live workspace has apps across that range, so it picked 8091 instead of the 8081 or 8082 the tests expected. The scaffolder now takes that listening-port check as an argument, and the tests pass one that reports nothing listening. The two tests that a requested port held by another app is refused now use the same check, so they can no longer pass just because the machine happened to be listening on that port. A new test runs the real scaffolder and confirms the port it picks is the one written into both the app's program file and its runner. Another hands the scaffolder a check that reports one port in use and confirms it skips that port when picking and refuses it when asked for it.

The `submit-upstream-changes` mngr-changes reference now names the real recipe (`just dwt-mngr-pin`, not the nonexistent `just pin-template-mngr`) and describes how a developer with both checkouts iterates on a paired change: pin a template branch to an unmerged mngr commit on the private mngr-internal repo (`just dwt-mngr-pin-internal`), then move the pin to a public export of that branch before merging (`just dwt-mngr-pin-export`). Neither is something an agent in a workspace does.

The `welcome` skill is removed: new chats no longer open with a greeting or hints. `publish-template` no longer writes a template-specific welcome into the snapshot it publishes, so a mind created from a template starts on an empty chat like any other.

The manage-desktop skill's file viewer examples use absolute paths (`open files --path /home/user/workspace/data/notes/`): the viewer now serves the filesystem root and opens at the workspace folder, so a folder is no longer named relative to `data/`.

The file-sharing skill can now ask for a synchronized copy of a folder in the same permission request that asks for access, by adding a `sync` object (with an optional `conflict` rule) to the request payload. The skill explains what the user can do with the ask in the approval dialog, where the copy lands on the machine (`~/synced_folders/<device id>/<path>`), and that the resolution message says whether the copy was enabled. It also calls the app Mind throughout.

The build-app scaffold's pages carry a module script that connects the page to the workspace shell, reports its location on the handshake, and installs the element context menu, in place of the old location beacon; the runner serves `/_static/app_contract.js` and `/_static/context_menu.js` from its own origin. The skill says to keep both on every page and to give list rows and controls stable ids or data attributes so a reference resolves to one thing. `shared/references/element-references.md` is the agent's guide to a `REF-<id>.json` attachment: what it holds and how to find the element it names.

### system

AGENTS.md now tells agents to write workspace file paths in chat replies in code formatting rather than linking them, and to suggest the File Viewer for files under `data/`: the chat renders only web links and absolute-path download links.

The `agent_block_pipe_tail_head.sh` guard now blocks a pipe into `head`/`tail` only when the output it truncates would have to be regenerated. A new `agent_block_pipe_tail_head_check.py` splits the command with the shared shlex parser and judges each pipeline on its own. The pipe is allowed when everything feeding it only reads files, directories or git history (`cat`, `grep`, `rg`, `sed`, `ls`, `find`, `git log/show/diff/status`, ...), or prints `--help`/`--version`, or when a `tee FILE` upstream keeps the full output. Anything else is blocked, including a pipe into `head`/`tail` the checker cannot see as a pipeline stage (inside quoted text such as `bash -c '...'`, or a substitution). So `cd x && cat f | head`, `git diff --stat | tail -40`, `grep x /tmp/saved.txt | tail -3` and `pytest 2>&1 | tee /tmp/out | tail` now run. `pytest | tail`, `uv sync | tail`, `git fetch | tail`, `curl ... | head`, `python3 -c ... | head`, and anything fed by a command or process substitution are still blocked.

The guard no longer mistakes `||` for a pipe (`grep x f || tail -4 f` was refused), and it now catches `|& tail`, which it used to miss. The wrapper checks for a pipe into `head`/`tail` with bash's built-in regex, so the 95% of commands with no such pipe never start Python.

Replayed against the 4,540 Bash commands in one production workspace's agent history, the old guard blocks 214 and the new one blocks 80, and nothing the old one allowed. All 53 blocks of test runs, dependency syncs, fetches, network calls and commits are kept.

pi agents now get every command guard from this repo, the same way claude, codex and agy do. `.pi/extensions/policy_guards.ts` feeds the same hook scripts claude runs (`agent_prevent_commit_rewrite.sh`, `agent_block_pipe_tail_head.sh`, `agent_latchkey_request_standalone.sh`, `agent_secrets_guard.sh`, `agent_tk_standalone.sh`) the payload they read on stdin (the secrets guard on pi's file tools too), then prefixes an allowed command with `agent_rewrite_bash_command.py --prefix-only`. Until now the pipe-into-`head`/`tail` block, the git history-rewrite block and the OOM/git-identity rewrite were copied into mngr's pi extension, so a change to any of them needed a matching mngr release, and pi's refusal messages had drifted from the scripts' wording. `agent_hook_wiring_test.py` now fails if pi's list of scripts differs from claude's. A guard or rewrite that fails (a missing script, a crash) lets the command run and is logged to `pi_policy_guards.log` in the agent's state dir.

`setup_system.sh` now fails the build if the installed codex npm package does not hold the native binary for this machine at `node_modules/@openai/codex-linux-<arch>/vendor/<triple>/bin/codex`, the one codex's npm entry point would run. The OOM launch wrapper execs that binary directly, so a codex version bump that moves it would otherwise quietly bring back unattributed OOM kills. The `.mngr/settings.toml` comment on the codex launch command now says the wrapper execs the native binary.

- Drop the `ssh_bind_address = "127.0.0.1"` pin from the `[providers.docker]`
  block. With a user config that points docker at a remote daemon
  (`host = "ssh://..."`), the pin produced a loopback bind mngr cannot reach, so
  docker workspace creation failed; with an mngr pin older than
  imbue-ai/mngr-internal's matching fix, every `mngr create` run from the
  template (imbue_cloud included) failed while loading config. Local-daemon
  containers still publish sshd on loopback only, since that is mngr's default.
