Secrets an agent needs now enter the workspace through a chat card and leave it only through a wrapper. `system/scripts/with_secrets.py data/.secrets/<name>.env -- <command>` loads the file's variables into a child process's environment and execs the command; it is the one sanctioned reader of `data/.secrets/`, and it refuses a file outside that directory or readable by more than its owner. `data/.secrets/README.md` now says what lives there (the minds app's files, the secret card's files, and mcpc's store) and that only the wrapper reads a file, for an agent's commands, `mcp-servers.json` servers, supervisord programs, and scheduled jobs alike.

Two tool-call policies enforce that. P9 (`agent_secrets_guard.sh`, `agent_secrets_guard_check.py`) refuses any shell command that mentions `data/.secrets` (or `~/.mcpc`, which links into it) unless it runs the wrapper or the request script, `ls`, or `rm` (a `bash -c` string is judged by the same rule, so a supervisord program passes), and refuses claude's, codex's, and pi's file tools on a path under the directory; the README stays readable. P10 holds the connect-external-service skill's `request_secret.py` to the same one-per-tool-call rule as a latchkey permission request, in the same checker. Both are registered for claude, codex, the agy shim, and pi, where the secrets guard is the first checker to run on every tool call rather than on bash alone.

The workspace image installs `mcpc` (`@apify/mcpc`, pinned as `MCPC_VERSION` in `setup_system.sh`), the MCP client every agent, app, and scheduled job shares, and removes its native keyring binding so it keeps credentials in its file on every provider; with the binding, a lima VM would hold them in the kernel keyring, which a reboot empties. A new env.d unit, `1300-mcpc-home-link.sh`, links `~/.mcpc` (mcpc's state directory) to `data/.secrets/mcpc` under both homes a process can have, `/home/user` and `/root` (which lima's boot unit gives system-services after a reboot), moving in anything mcpc stored before the link existed; env-converge runs it on every boot and during an update, and the first-boot seed runs it too, so mcpc's sessions, OAuth sign-ins, and stored headers sit under the secrets guard and survive with the rest of `data/` in new and updated workspaces alike.

The `ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS=false` comment in `.mngr/settings.toml` now says what it does and does not forbid: claude.ai's connector sync is a side channel around latchkey for services latchkey supports; a service's own MCP server, for a service latchkey does not support, is fine, connected through mcpc. `AGENTS.md` sends any request to reach something outside the workspace on the user's behalf straight to the new skill, with no `latchkey` command to run first and no direct route to the browser fleet; its two browser sections become one Playwright note for testing a workspace app or checking a public page. The build-app planning prompt points at the new skill too.

The chat progress-view spec now describes a system chip or notice as a break in the timeline (the reply before it stays above it, the resumed work renders below it) rather than an inline chip that never splits a turn, and says that a step still open across two back-to-back breaks shows once, under the later one.

Fixed three tests that fail on a real workspace or developer machine while passing in CI, because they read live machine state instead of isolating it.

The lead-address test no longer depends on which providers the host has enabled. It resolves a name that should be gone, but a name that resolves nowhere reports the first provider that could not be reached rather than "not found" -- and the docker provider is on by built-in default with no daemon to reach inside a workspace container. It creates a local agent, so both providers that answer over a network are turned off, matching the block the repo's other real-mngr tests already write.

The agy shim's OOM-tag test is skipped where there is no tag to apply. It asserts the tag by reading `/proc/self/oom_score_adj`, and both the tag and the file are Linux kernel interfaces, so off Linux it failed for the absence of the mechanism rather than for the shim's behavior. It now asks whether that file is writable, which is the gate the OOM service's own test already uses for the same interface -- a platform name would still have run it on a Linux host where the file is absent or read-only.

The strict-mode bash ratchet no longer checks gitignored scripts. It scanned every `.sh` file on disk, and in a live workspace that includes the shell scripts the terminal app generates under `data/` -- machine state, not template code, whose style is not this ratchet's business. It now asks git for the scripts it would consider (tracked, or untracked but not ignored), so a new script is still checked before it is staged.

The shared menu (`system/libs/workspace_ui`) gained two things the desktop's new size menu needed, both available to any menu:

- **Hover triggers** (`hoverTriggerAttrs`): a control that already does something on its click can offer a menu as the slower way in. It opens and closes on the pointer exactly as a submenu does, and lays no sheet under itself, so the chrome around the trigger stays hoverable; a press outside, Escape, and `close` still take it down.
- **`center` alignment** in `placeMenu`, on both axes, for a menu hanging off something too small to align an edge to.

Claude agents in the workspace no longer pin an effort level: each model runs at Claude Code's own default for it (medium on Opus 5.5, the workspace default; high on Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5).

The workspace build's mngr asset fetch now runs its checkout with the private-repo credential too, so a template pinned to mngr-internal builds instead of failing on the lazy blob fetch of the vendored files (`fatal: could not fetch <blob> from promisor remote`).

The mngr pin in `pyproject.toml` may name a commit of the private mngr-internal repo on a branch iterating on a paired mngr change, not only the public mirror; `main` always pins the public mirror.

A build from a private pin reads a credential from `/run/secrets/mngr_internal_git_token` (a BuildKit secret on docker, an uploaded file on lima and modal) through the new `system/scripts/_mngr_git_auth.sh`, which scopes it to the commands that fetch mngr; the lima and modal templates delete the file right after the workspace build. A public pin builds exactly as before, with no BuildKit requirement: the `--secret` build arguments and Dockerfile `--mount=type=secret` lines exist only while the pin is private.

New `system/scripts/set_mngr_pin.py` moves the pin and those BuildKit lines together (`--public`/`--internal <commit>`) and checks that a tree agrees with itself (`--check`, `--require-public`). `list_mngr_plugins.py --kind` reports whether the pin is `public` or `internal`.

CI gains a `pin-is-public` job that refuses a private pin (meant to be a required check on `main`), the `test` job refuses one up front with the same script, and a new `release-pin-gate.yml` fails a `minds-v*` tag that carries one.

- Pinned mngr to public commit `2a53294cf2` (the mirror of mngr `141922ce33`) for the minds 0.7.4 release (`minds-v0.7.4`).

The new-chat greeting is gone: the `welcome` create template is removed from `.mngr/settings.toml`, as are the codex and pi system-prompt instructions for `/welcome`, and `system/scripts/welcome_count.py` (the counter that varied the greeting's hints) is deleted. `data/.state/README.md` names the first-boot marker the bootstrap writes, `workspace_main_branch_initialized`, instead of describing a welcome chat.

The File Viewer now opens at the workspace folder (`/home/user/workspace/`) and can browse upward from there: dufs serves the container's filesystem root instead of `data/`, so the breadcrumb reaches the workspace's own folders (`system/`, `skills/`, `docs/`) and anything above them that the workspace user can read. Folder paths given to the viewer (`layout.py open files --path ...`, the `path` launch parameter, the `open=files:` deep link) are absolute paths now rather than paths under `data/`.

Pi chats on OpenRouter now start on GLM 5.3 instead of pi's own first pick (Kimi K2.6): the workspace seeds pi's `defaultProvider` / `defaultModel` into `~/.pi/agent/settings.json` at boot. Pi only honors that default when an OpenRouter key is present and otherwise falls back to its usual choice, and the seed never overwrites a default you saved yourself from pi's model picker.

The pi coding agent baked into the image moves from 0.83.0 to 0.87.1. That release bundles OpenRouter's GLM 5.3 in pi's model catalog, which is what lets the seeded default actually take effect: 0.83.0 only knew GLM up to 5.2, so pi ignored the saved default and fell back to its first available model.

Every page of the workspace gets an element context menu (`docs/system/blueprint/element-reference-menu/`): a right-click opens a menu with the browser's own edit, link, and image rows and then "Copy reference", "Explain...", and "Modify...", which attach a JSON description of the clicked element (its tag, id, classes, attributes, a checked selector, the selection, and the app, window, and page it is on) to a chat message as a `REF-<id>.json` file, with a prompt that names it, so a user can point at anything on screen and an agent knows which element they mean. `.agents/shared/references/element-references.md` tells the agent what the file holds and how to find the element.

The app contract gains `shell:draft-text` (a page asks the shell to draft a text into the chat on screen, as "Design your own..." does) and the handshake carries the window's `app`; every app serves `/_static/context_menu.js` beside `/_static/app_contract.js`. The build-app scaffold's pages connect to the shell and install the menu in place of the old location beacon, and serve the two modules from their own origin.

### system/apps/chat

Clicking a file path linked in a chat message no longer replaces the conversation with an error page. Absolute-path links still download the file, and a missing file fails as a download instead of navigating the chat. http(s), mailto and tel links are unchanged; any other link (a relative path, a fragment, another scheme) now renders as plain text.

A permission request a Codex chat files from a code-mode script now keeps its permission card after the request's result arrives.

When the script printed the whole command result (`text(result)`) rather than just its stdout, the result came back wrapped in a JSON envelope that escaped the request's details, so the chat could not find them. The card showed while the request was pending, then turned into an ordinary tool call once the result landed, even though the request was filed and granted. The envelope is now unwrapped before the request is looked for, the same way task titles already were. The raw output shown on expand is unchanged.

The tool-call policy for piping into `tail`/`head` (P1) now states the rule the guard enforces: a pipe is blocked only when the output it truncates would have to be regenerated. Reads of files, directories and git history, `--help`/`--version` output, and pipes downstream of a `tee FILE`, are allowed, and each pipeline in a compound command is judged on its own.

`tool-call-policies-state-of-things.md` now records that pi reaches every command guard and the OOM/git-identity rewrite through this repo's `.pi/extensions/policy_guards.ts`, which runs the same scripts as the other harnesses. mngr's pi extension no longer carries any command policy. A pi agent created by an older mngr keeps that mngr's extension (mngr writes it at create time), so for those agents `policy_guards.ts` judges the command the older extension records as `mngrOriginalCommand`, and replaces that extension's prefix with its own.

The tool-call policies state-of-things doc now records how codex's `write_stdin` guard bypass is actually closed: `features.unified_exec_tty = false` (stdin closed for every exec'd process), since `features.unified_exec = false` is ignored by codex 0.154 and later.

The chat renders a secret card when an agent runs the connect-external-service skill's `request_secret.py`, modelled on the permission card. The script files the request through the new `POST /api/secret-requests`; the card shows the agent's rationale, the target `data/.secrets/<file>.env`, a note naming any existing variables a submit overwrites, one password input per variable (masked, with a Show/Hide button beside each so the user can check what they typed), and Submit and Decline (with an optional note). Submit writes the file (mode 0600, POSIX single-quoted so any value survives `with_secrets.py`, merged into whatever the file already held) and sends the agent a message naming the file and the variable names; Decline sends the verdict and the note. The values reach the file and nothing else: not a log line, not the persisted request, not the transcript.

Requests persist under `secret-requests/` in the chat's data directory (`data/.apps/chat/` for the live chat, the scratch copy for a preview) so a restart keeps a pending card live, and a preview chat refuses to submit or decline a card, since it runs from an editing worktree and the answer belongs to the live chat; a second request for the same file supersedes the first, and only the newest accepts input (a superseded request in another chat is told by a message). The card flips from the transcript's notice, from the page's own submit, or from a status fetch after a reload, and a transcript recorded by an older backend shows an honest can't-read state.

Every harness's parser recognises the call from its input (`display: "secret_request"`) and lifts the echoed request out of its result (`secret_request`), through the one `stamp_echoed_requests` call that also lifts permission requests; the classifier reads the stored / declined / superseded notice by its tag (`display: "secret_resolution"`). The transcript walk lifts a secret request out of any open step as it does a permission request and resolves each card by its own request id.

The tool-call policies (`core-contracts/tool-call-policies.md`) gain P9, that only `with_secrets.py` reads a file under `data/.secrets/` (a mention of `~/.mcpc`, the link to mcpc's store there, counts as a mention of the directory), and P10, that a secret request is the only thing in its tool call.

A system notification in a chat (a finished background task, Stop-hook feedback, a browser-fleet nudge) now shows up in the order it happened. The work the agent did after being woken used to be drawn inside the step above the notification, so nothing appeared below it and the spinner and latest caption sat higher up the page. And for the few seconds before the agent's first tool call, the reply it had given before the notification jumped below it. The timeline now breaks at a notification the way it does at a permission verdict: the reply stays above it, and the agent's next work renders below it, in the step carried over from before. A notification that lands during a handoff summary stays with the handoff, as before. And when two messages or notifications arrive back to back while a step is open, or a message is followed straight away by a fresh start on another agent, the step now shows once, under the later one, instead of also as an empty step under the first.

Answering a secret card no longer uses up one of the chat's fast-mode turns: like a permission verdict, the notice the app sends the agent is not a turn the user took.

A new chat opens as a blank, ready chat: no "Starting the chat...", "Loading events...", "No events yet for this agent." or "Send a message to start this chat." placeholder at any point. While it waits for its first send, while the agent is created, while its transcript loads, and once it is up with nothing in it, the page is the transcript's own empty list with the composer ready, so nothing changes on screen as the chat comes up. Nor does a new chat flash "No conversation data": a transcript that is not found before the chat app has sent its chat list, or while the reload that follows the chat coming up is still running, is a chat not known yet and reads as an empty one; only a chat the app lists (or has no record of) with no reload pending shows that screen.

A message sent while a new chat is still starting stays where it was typed instead of sitting at the bottom of the screen and jumping to the top once the chat came up.

New chats are no longer greeted: a chat started with nothing to say is created without a first message and waits for the user's, so a message sent during startup is no longer queued behind a `/welcome` turn. Older chats' transcripts still hide the `/welcome` turn they began with.

The e2e test for a chat the root created staying shown through a late socket replay now starts its chat from the root's New chat button instead of loading `/new`, which the chat app no longer serves (it answers 404). It had failed on every run since the two changes met on main.

A new chat's auto fast mode now runs fast for the first 2 of your turns instead of 5 before switching to standard speed (the limit is still adjustable in the model picker).

The one-time notice shown when that switch first happens now reads "Fast mode is off now: this chat ran fast for its first N turns. Change this in the model picker." and, for a Claude Code chat only, adds "Fast mode always uses API billing, not subscription usage."

Every chat page and the chat root draw the element context menu (`docs/system/blueprint/element-reference-menu/`): a chat page drafts a reference into its own composer, the root into the selected chat's composer (else through the shell), a sub-agent view through the shell (its `shell:draft-text` relayed by the root), and the rail's row menu ends with the reference rows. A reference entering a composer is attached as a `REF-<id>.json` file through the ordinary upload path, with a chip that says what it points at, and the prompt in the composer names it ("Explain what I attached in REF-..."). Ready attachments now persist across a reload beside the draft text.

### system/apps/files

The File Viewer opens at the workspace folder (`/home/user/workspace/`) and can browse upward from there: dufs now serves the container's filesystem root instead of `data/`, so the breadcrumb reaches the workspace's own folders (`system/`, `skills/`, `docs/`) and anything above them that the workspace user can read. It stays bound to loopback with all operations enabled; the workspace origin is still what gates access.

- The manifest's `new` launch path is `/home/user/workspace/` (it was `/`), so a plain launch lands in the workspace folder.

- Folder paths given to the viewer are absolute now rather than paths under `data/`: `layout.py open files --path /home/user/workspace/data/notes/`, the `path` launch parameter (`--param path=/home/user/workspace/data/notes/`, a window at `/home/user/workspace/?path=...`), and the `open=files:` deep link.

### system/apps/getting_started

The Getting Started page draws the element context menu; "Explain..." and "Modify..." draft through the shell's `shell:draft-text`.

### system/apps/system_interface

A wallpaper of your own now displays. An image placed in the workspace's own wallpapers directory (`data/.apps/system_interface/wallpapers/`) was offered by the picker and could be set on a desktop, but every request for the image itself failed, so the desktop rendered with no backdrop at all; the wallpapers that ship with the shell were unaffected. That directory is configured as a path relative to the workspace root, and the route that sends the image resolved it against the shell's own package directory instead, looking for the file somewhere it had never been written. A configured directory is now resolved to one absolute place where the shell's state is built, so the listing and the image both name it; the avatar catalog directory, configured the same way, is resolved there too.

The desktop's shortcuts, the window chrome, and the menus that hang off them have had a pass.

**Shortcuts.** An icon's drawing sits inside its tile rather than filling it, and the tile's corner is a fraction of the icon's size, so an icon shown larger or smaller keeps its shape. A name is bold at the label size over a softer shadow, and the icon and the name start at the top of their cell, so every icon sits on one line across the grid and every name starts on one -- a two-line name no longer lifts its icon off its neighbours' line. Hovering an icon grows it; the tinted box now says only *selected*, in the accent colour under an accent outline, and it wraps the icon and its name rather than filling the cell. Right-clicking an icon selects it, so the menu names something that looks picked. Dropping a dragged icon lands it where it was dropped, instead of showing it back where it started until the move is recorded.

**Window chrome.** The taskbar is translucent over a blur, which needed the wallpaper to carry on behind it. Refresh has left the window menu for a button of its own beside the window's name, followed by the three dots, which stand vertically. The controls are sized from the bar rather than the touch target, and share one box so their hover targets line up; the app's icon takes the title's colour and dims with it. The bar shows the open hand, and the closed one while a window is dragged. A window's frame has no border: the shadow is what separates it from the desktop.

**Move and resize.** New: a grid of nine places a window can take -- the whole backdrop, the four halves, the four quarters. Rest on the maximize control to open it, or find the same grid under *Move and resize* in the window's menu. Each tile's picture is drawn from the placement it performs, so the two cannot disagree.

Marked the e2e test `test_an_independent_pinned_window_keeps_a_path_per_client_and_an_agent_navigates_one_client` flaky: it failed once in CI on a navigate the page never followed, and passes locally.

The README's `layout.py open files --path` example now names a folder by its absolute path (`/home/user/workspace/data/notes/`): the file viewer serves the container's filesystem root and opens at the workspace folder, so a folder is no longer named relative to `data/`.

An app's page can now declare that it owns the close chord (Ctrl+W): the desktop then only tells the page, and leaves its window open. The browser uses this to close a tab rather than its window; every other app closes as before.

The desktop draws the element context menu over its own chrome: a right-click the views leave alone opens it, and the taskbar entry, shortcut, and desktop menus end with its reference rows after a divider. A page's `shell:draft-text` is answered by drafting the text into the pinned window that takes a draft (the avatar dialog's "Design your own..." path), else through the first draft row of the machine, else by telling the user no app takes a draft. The handshake carries the window's `app`, and the shell serves `/_static/context_menu.js` beside `/_static/app_contract.js`.

### system/apps/terminal

A terminal now opens at the right size for its window instead of needing a nudge. The terminal used to size its grid once, before switching to its faster renderer whose characters are slightly narrower, so the grid came up short of the pane until you resized the window. The terminal page now gives the terminal that resize itself shortly after it loads.

### system/libs/app_manifest

An app declares the secret files it runs under in `app.toml`: `[[secrets]]` entries with `file` (the `<file>` of `data/.secrets/<file>.env`), `variables` (at least one POSIX identifier), and an optional one-line `note` for the adopter. `publish-template` aggregates the declarations into a template's `[[requirements.secret]]`. Two entries may not name the same file.

`SHELL_CONTEXT_MENU_PATH` and `CONTEXT_MENU_ROUTE` name the element context menu module the shell builds beside the app contract, which every app serves from its own origin.

### system/libs/bootstrap

The every-5-minutes update-apply recovery guard runs again on containers whose `/run` is a tmpfs, which is every gen-2 imbue_cloud slice and every desktop docker workspace. Its cron entry took its `flock` lock at `/var/lock/update-apply-recover.lock`. In this image `/var/lock` is a symlink to `/run/lock`, and a tmpfs `/run` starts out empty, so `flock` failed with "No such file or directory" on every tick and the guard never ran. An interrupted update apply was then never recovered unless the container restarted. The lock is now `/run/update-apply-recover.lock`, directly under `/run`, which exists on every container.

The README no longer says first boot creates a welcome chat agent with `/welcome`: the bootstrap only moves the workspace onto a clean `main` branch, and chats are created by the chat app.

### system/libs/tk_command_parsing

The pipe-into-`head`/`tail` guard (`system/scripts/agent_block_pipe_tail_head_check.py`) is now a third consumer of the parser, imported under a bare `python3` like the tk and latchkey gates. The README's consumer list and the module docstring now name it, since it is one more reason the package must stay stdlib-only.

### system/libs/workspace_ui

The app contract gains a `closeChord` capability: a page that declares it (and gives `onCloseRequest`) owns the shell's close chord, so the shell sends `shell:close-request` and leaves the window open. Declaring it without a handler is refused at connect, like `navigation` without `onNavigate`.

The element context menu (`docs/system/blueprint/element-reference-menu/`): `element_reference.ts` describes a right-clicked element as JSON under a random `REF-<id>` (its tag, id, classes, attributes, a selector checked to match it alone, the selection and field value, the click and the viewport, and the app, window, and page from the shell's handshake), `context_menu_rows.ts` builds the menu's rows (Cut, Copy, Paste, Select All, the link and image rows, then "Copy reference", "Explain...", "Modify..."), and `context_menu.ts` is the installer every page runs, with a framework-free renderer for pages without Mithril and `components/contextMenuOpener.ts` for pages with it. `app_contract.ts` gains `draftText` (`shell:draft-text`) and the handshake's `app`.

### system/services/env_converge

A template's `[[requirements.secret]]` entry now names a `file` (the `<file>` of `data/.secrets/<file>.env`) and its `variables`, which is what `use-template` files a secret card for; the legacy bare `name` still loads until no published template predates the change. `validate_template_tree` flags a supervisord program or an MCP server in `mcp-servers.json` that runs under a secret file no entry declares, so an adopter is never left with a program that starts without its credential.

### system/services/host_backup

A host_backup snapshot test no longer fails when run inside a live workspace. Its fake outer helper decided whether a request was new by the request file's modification time. Under gVisor, which workspaces run on, the modification time the sandbox reports for a file it just wrote changes to the host's slightly different value once the sandbox drops its cached copy of the file's details, which a busy test run makes likely. The helper then handled the same snapshot request twice, and the test saw `cleanup, snapshot, snapshot` instead of `cleanup, snapshot`. The fake now goes by the request id, the same way the real helper and the backup service match a result to its request. The backup service itself is unchanged.

Hourly backups on remote workspaces no longer re-read the whole home tree. restic skips an unchanged file only when the previous snapshot holds it at the same path inside the snapshot, and each tick reads from a new timestamped snapshot path (`<mount>/snapshots/<timestamp>/home`). So no file ever matched, and every backup opened, chunked and hashed everything, even though deduplication then uploaded almost none of it. restic now runs from inside the snapshot and backs up `.`, which stores the tree at the snapshot root, with `--group-by ''` so the newest snapshot is the parent and `--ignore-inode` so files are compared by size and mtime. A local test of two ticks over the same 20 files went from re-reading all 20 to re-reading only the one that changed. The first backup after this lands still reads everything once, because its parent has the old layout.

Every restic command also runs with `GOMAXPROCS=1` and `RESTIC_READ_CONCURRENCY=1`, so a backup or prune uses one core and reads one file at a time instead of competing with the workspace's agents and UI. `nice` cannot do this on remote workspaces: gVisor accepts scheduling priorities but ignores them.

Restoring a snapshot taken after this change needs a minds app that knows the new layout (it restores from `<snapshot>:/`). An older app reports that the snapshot "does not contain a machine". Snapshots taken before the change restore as before. Downloading a new snapshot likewise gives a zip with the home tree (`workspace/`, ...) at its top level, rather than nested under the snapshot path it was read from.

Backup retention no longer thins away a snapshot from the last hour. `restic forget` now runs with `--keep-within 1h`, which keeps every snapshot taken within an hour of the newest one. Before, any extra tick in the same hour as the previous one (a restarted service, a changed `restic.env`, a manual backup) made keep-hourly drop that previous snapshot. A minds restore rewrote `restic.env` just before it ran, so restoring the newest backup of the current hour failed with "failed to find snapshot": the tick the restore itself triggered had forgotten the snapshot the user picked. Seen on a staging workspace.

Backup retention runs again after a container is replaced mid-backup. A `restic backup` killed with its container leaves its non-exclusive lock in the repository. New backups still work alongside it, but `restic forget` and `restic prune` need an exclusive lock, and restic refuses one while any other lock exists, stale or not. The runner only cleared stale locks when a backup was blocked, which never happens in this case, so every hourly tick failed `forget` and `prune` with exit 11. Old snapshots were never thinned and the repository kept growing.

`forget`, the restore-marker age-out and `prune` now do what the backup step already did: on a lock error they run `restic unlock` and retry once. Plain `unlock` removes only stale locks: one whose process is gone on this host, or one that has not been refreshed for 30 minutes. A running restic refreshes its lock every 5 minutes, so a concurrent `host-backup-now` is left alone.

### system/services/oom_priority

A codex agent shed by earlyoom is now recorded against that agent, so a lead waiting on a codex worker is told the worker was shed instead of waiting on a report that never comes.

Before, codex's npm entry point (`bin/codex.js`) ran the native binary as a child process. The launch wrapper registered the entry point's pid, but earlyoom killed the native child, whose pid nothing had registered. The kill hook wrote the shed with no agent, so the worker report watcher never matched it. The chat app's engagement re-tag had the same problem: it raised or lowered the band of the small `node` entry point, not the codex process holding the memory.

Now the wrapper execs codex's native binary directly, picking the one for this machine's platform the way the entry point does, with the same `CODEX_MANAGED_BY_NPM` and `CODEX_MANAGED_PACKAGE_ROOT` environment the entry point sets, so the registered pid is the one earlyoom kills. If `codex` on the PATH is not an npm install, the wrapper execs `codex` as before. If it is the npm entry point but this machine's native binary is not where the entry point would look, the wrapper says so on stderr and falls back to the entry point.

### system/services/share_gateway

The share gateway no longer retries a failed bring-up every 10 seconds. When the connector cannot issue the certificate or hand out the relay assignment, attempts are spaced 15s, 30s, 1m, 2m, 8m, then 15m apart (a longer connector `Retry-After` wins), and a refusal the connector marks as permanent (any 4xx other than 408/429) halts retries until `share.env` changes. This keeps one stuck workspace from hammering the connector, its Cloudflare DNS token, and the certificate authorities behind it.

Each outcome is reported in `data/.state/share_gateway/status.json` (`up` / `retrying` / `halted`, the last error, the next retry time), which the minds desktop client reads to explain a share that is not live yet. The file is removed at unshare.

## [minds-v0.7.3] - 2026-09-24

### .agents

The `use-ai-integration` skill's `claude_p_completion` no longer leaves a Claude project directory behind on every call. Each completion runs `claude -p` from a throwaway working directory, and Claude persisted every one of those sessions under the account's `projects/` tree, which is what the chat app watches and scans (839 of 841 project directories on one workspace were completions). Completions now pass `--no-session-persistence`; `claude_p_task` still persists its sessions. Apps that copied `claude_p.py` in earlier keep the old behaviour until they copy it again.

The `manage-desktop` skill's vocabulary explains GET and POST launch paths (a POST launch path is posted its parameters by the shell and answers the page to open), and its `desktops` description drops the retired `is_settling` window field.

The manage-scheduled-tasks skill now says that a boot whose timezone fetch fails keeps the last applied zone (from `data/.state/user_timezone`), and that a timezone set by hand should also be written there so later boots keep it.

### system

Codex agents no longer load the ChatGPT account's apps/connectors. Before, a codex agent signed in with ChatGPT got a hosted `codex_apps` MCP server carrying every connector the user had added on chatgpt.com (52 tools on a test account), an OAuth side channel to third-party services that bypasses the latchkey gateway. `[agent_types.codex]` now sets `features.apps = false`, codex's counterpart of the `ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS=false` claude already runs with. Plugin skills and hooks (code-guardian) are unaffected.

earlyoom now sheds in priority-band order under gVisor. gVisor reports every process's `oom_score` as 0, so the stock earlyoom shed the largest process first whatever its band: a chat or the chat app could go before a runaway pytest. The workspace now installs the imbue-ai fork of earlyoom (`system/scripts/install_earlyoom.sh`, chained from `setup_system.sh`), which computes the kernel's badness from `oom_score_adj` and memory itself. On runc hosts (lima, local Docker) the order is unchanged. The apt `earlyoom` package is no longer installed; a re-provision purges it, and on systemd hosts masks its unit, which was running a second, unconfigured earlyoom. The plan is in `docs/system/blueprint/earlyoom-gvisor-shed-order/`. `AGENTS.md` now says how to check for gVisor instead of listing which providers use it.

The shared pulsing activity dot (`activityDotClass` in `system/libs/workspace_ui`) takes an optional tone, `"accent"` (the default, unchanged) or `"warning"`, so a caller can pulse in the warning colour without restating the pulse timing. The chat's new "Connecting…" indicator is the first caller.

The chat-agent-split plan now describes the messages a switching chat holds as ordinary sent messages, matching the chat app, which no longer fades or captions a not-yet-delivered message, and its wire snapshot lists the new `active_agent.is_connecting`.

Launch paths that start something are POSTs now, so no page URL has a side effect any more (issue #646; the spec is `docs/system/blueprint/post-launch-paths/`).

An app's manifest may declare `method = "POST"` on a launch path, along with fixed `presets` sent with every launch and a `draft_param` (the counterpart of `text_param` for text that is drafted rather than sent). `forward_port.py` copies the three onto the registry row. The names `client_id`, `desktop_id`, and `window_path` are the shell's envelope and are refused as param or preset names.

`layout.py open --launch` works unchanged: a POST launch path is posted the `--param` values by the shell and the window opens at the page the app answers. Windows no longer carry `is_settling`; `desktops` and `list` stop printing it.

The desktop-interface, pinned-taskbar-entries, launcher-and-getting-started, and window-bound-resources documents are amended where the spec's section 13 says.

The `data/.state/` README now lists `user_timezone`, the bootstrap's record of the last timezone it applied.

Bump the pinned Claude Code version from 2.1.269 to 2.1.280 in both places that carry it -- the `CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION` default in `system/scripts/setup_system.sh` and the `[agent_types.claude].version` pin in `.mngr/settings.toml`.

2.1.280 adds Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`) and makes it what the `opus` alias resolves to, so on this pin the chat's Opus entry reaches Opus 5.5 instead of Opus 5. It also removes the deprecated `TaskOutput` tool and stops running agent-type `PermissionRequest` hooks; neither affects this workspace, whose hooks are all `command` type and which names `TaskOutput` only in the read-only tool list `agent_require_steps_pretool.sh` exempts from its step check.

The chat app's baked model catalog fixture is now tied to the pin: `system/test_workspace_claude_config.py` requires the one `baked_model_catalog_v*.json` to be the pinned version's, so a future bump that forgets to regenerate it fails instead of passing every catalog test against the old binary's models.

- Pinned mngr to public commit `efd062971a` (the mirror of mngr `b703070921`) for the minds 0.7.3 release (`minds-v0.7.3`).

### system/apps/chat

A turn's tool calls now read as one message instead of one message per call. A harness emits an event per model response, so the sentence an agent says before it works and the calls that carry that work out arrive separately -- and each became its own top-level row, stacking one lone chip per row a full message gap below the last. A row is now a run: one head event plus every chip-only event after it, so a turn lays out as the one message it is (the sentence, the chips tucked under it, then the result as its own message). Prose ends a run and heads the next, as does a sub-agent card. The chip row's spacing is deliberately uneven -- tight above, where it belongs to the line that introduces it, and a full message gap below, where the agent has moved on to what it found -- and collapses at a message's edges so it never adds to the message's own margin. The row also stops on the same edge as the prose now, including inside a progress block, which was the one place on that thread where a reply ran the full column while everything beside it stopped at the gutter.

A failed call is no longer painted red. Whatever the failure means, the agent explains it in prose a line or two below, which is the form a reader can act on; colour on a chip now says only which one is open.

Opening a tool call gives you a header naming the call with a control to close it, a dashed seam between the input and the output, and -- for an output past 20 lines, or past 2000 characters when it has no line breaks at all -- its first part with a "View all N lines" control rather than a whole log dumped into the transcript. Unfolding one is forgotten when the chip is closed, so reopening it starts short again.

A path named in a tool chip keeps a trailing slash when it had one, so a directory reads as `chat/` rather than as a file with no extension. The slash is kept, never added: a directory written without one still reads bare, since nothing else in the path distinguishes the two.

Loading a Claude chat, and every live refresh of it, no longer scans the account's whole projects tree. The watcher looks for a session's file where Claude files it for the chat's work directory first (one or two file checks), and only falls back to a scan of the project directories directly under `projects/` when the file is not there. A session the history names but whose file never appears is scanned for at once, then after 1s, 2s, 4s and so on up to once a minute, instead of on every refresh forever; on one production workspace two such sessions made every refresh of every chat walk 841 project directories, and loads of those chats took 17-22 seconds.

A transcript watcher now refreshes at most once every 0.25 seconds. Every chat on an account watches the same projects tree, so one chat's writes woke every chat's watcher once per write; a burst of writes now costs each watcher one refresh.

A new chat started from the chat window's New chat no longer vanishes when the window's live connection is slow to catch up. The window created and showed the chat, then took the first chat list the connection delivered, which could predate the chat, as meaning it was gone, and closed it: the window went blank and stayed blank. It now keeps a chat it created until a list names it.

A sent message no longer sits in a faded bubble under a "Sending…" caption while it is delivered. It shows at once as an ordinary sent message, solid and uncaptioned, the same way everywhere a not-yet-delivered message appears (a fresh send, a message held while the chat switches harness, a message re-sent by a shoulder tap). This makes the chat more optimistic than before: a message now looks sent before the chat app has confirmed it, and the message-lifecycle contract says so. A send the chat app refuses still leaves the transcript and returns to the composer with a notice.

When the delivery has to wait for the agent to come up -- the agent was stopped and the send starts it, or it has just launched and is not taking input yet -- "Connecting…" shows with a pulsing orange dot beside the model name until the message goes through. A message sent to a chat that is still being created reads the same way. The chat app decides this from the agent's lifecycle and the harness's own ready signal (claude's `session_started` marker, pi's `pi_session_started`, codex's live connection) and reports it as `active_agent.is_connecting` on each chat's snapshot. The message-lifecycle contract describes it as the Connecting sub-state of Sending.

Every text that enters a chat from outside a chat page arrives through one route, `POST /api/chats/intake`: the text, how the receiving chat is chosen (`target`: `new_chat`, `current_chat` from the window's path, `chat_selector`, or an explicit `chat`), whether it is sent or drafted (`is_draft`), an optional `account_id`, and `is_delivery_awaited` to wait for the harness to accept the send. The route answers the pure root path the shell opens a window at: `/?chat=<id>` when it finished the work, `/?chat=<id>&intake=<token>` or `/?intake=<token>` when the page has to finish it (a draft, a pick, or a first message with nothing signed in). Pending intakes are held in memory for fifteen minutes under `GET`, `POST .../apply`, and `DELETE /api/chats/intakes/<token>`.

The manifest declares `new`, `send`, and a new `draft` launch path as POSTs onto that route with presets; `GET /new` and `GET /send` are gone (a stale link answers 404), and the root takes no `draft` query parameter. Loading or reloading any chat page creates or sends nothing.

A new chat that cannot start at once (a draft into a new chat, or a first message with no account signed in) is minted as an unseeded provisional chat in the `awaiting_first_send` phase; its page shows an empty conversation over the composer and the first send launches it, through the provider chooser when nothing is signed in.

The Claude model picker's Opus entry now selects Claude Opus 5.5: the `opus[1m]` alias it switches with resolves to `claude-opus-5-5` on the new 2.1.280 pin, so the entry is labelled "Opus 5.5" and its `harness_reported_model_id` moves to `claude-opus-5-5`, which is what the live model-state read is matched against. Opus 5 (`claude-opus-5`) stays in the catalog as a hidden option so a chat created on the previous pin still shows its name instead of falling through to the shrug case; it is ordered after the offered Opus 5.5 key, because the prefix pass would otherwise let the shorter key claim the new id. Fast mode is declared on both, following the `fast_mode` capability the binary's own model table gives Opus 5.5, Opus 5 and Opus 4.8.

The catalog's three binary-derived facts -- what each alias resolves to, what each model is called, and which models can go fast -- are now pinned against a fixture lifted from Claude Code's own baked-in model catalog (`baked_model_catalog_v2_1_280.json`) rather than transcribed from release notes. A pin bump that repoints an alias, renames a model or changes its fast support now fails a test naming the specific disagreement, which is the failure this release would otherwise have shipped silently: the picker would have offered a switch labelled "Opus 5" that landed on Opus 5.5.

### system/apps/system_interface

The update-notice watch test no longer flakes on Linux. Its helpers rewrote `last-good.json` in place, so the file watch could wake on the truncation, read an empty file and announce no notice. The real apply script replaces the record atomically, and the helpers (`write_rollback_point` and the stub update-self script's `rollback-last`) now do the same. The test's `flaky` mark is removed.

The shell runs launch paths through a new route, `POST /api/desktops/<id>/launch`, with a target of `new`, `focus`, or `window` (point a named window at the page). A GET launch path opens at its path with the presets and params as the query; a POST launch path is posted the presets, the params, and the shell's envelope (`client_id`, `desktop_id`, `window_path`) and the window opens or is navigated at the page the app answers. An app's refusal (a 4xx carrying a `detail`) is answered as a 400 naming the app and its reason; an app that cannot be asked (unreachable, or a 4xx with no detail), or answers no path, as a 502. Undeclared params are refused.

Every place that ran a launch path uses the route: the launcher's rows and free-text rows (a draft launch path is a free-text row too), shortcuts, the `?launch=` deep link, `shell:start-with-text`, the avatar dialog's "Design your own..." (which now looks for the pinned app's launch path with a `draft_param` and targets the pinned window), and the op route's `open`. A free-text row of an app with a pinned window points that window at the page whatever its scope, since the page is pure. Only GET free-text rows are bounded by the window path length.

Settling is gone: windows have no `is_settling` (a stray one in an old `desktops.json` is dropped on read), the windows route takes no `launch`, no restore is deferred, and no taskbar entry dims for a window mid-launch. A visitor's seeded desktop copies every window of the first desktop.

### system/apps/terminal

The `new` launch path is a POST: the shell posts `workdir` to `/new` and the terminal answers `{"path": "/?session=terminal-<N>"}` after allocating the session, so no window ever sits at a URL that creates a session and a reload creates nothing. A `GET /new` answers 405.

### system/libs/app_manifest

A launch path may declare `method = "POST"` (default `GET`), `presets` (fixed string name-value pairs the shell sends with every launch), and `draft_param` (one of its params, the one filled with text to be drafted rather than sent; at most one of `text_param` and `draft_param`). Preset names may not repeat a param's, and the reserved envelope names `client_id`, `desktop_id`, and `window_path` are refused for both. The registry's launch path rows carry the three fields, reading old rows as GETs with no presets.

### system/libs/bootstrap

The container keeps the user's timezone when the boot-time fetch fails. Before, a boot that could not reach the minds app on the user's computer (it was asleep, offline, or its tunnel to the workspace was still coming up) left a freshly created container on UTC, so cron schedules ran in UTC until some later boot's fetch succeeded. The bootstrap now records each zone it applies in `data/.state/user_timezone` and re-applies that zone whenever the fetch fails or returns a zone the container cannot apply.

### system/services/oom_priority

Each `process_shed` line in the shed ledger now records why earlyoom picked the victim: its `oom_score_adj`, `badness_kib`, `vm_rss_kib` and the `ordering` earlyoom used (`kernel_badness`, or `upstream_fallback` when its startup self-check could not read those inputs and it chose the victim the way upstream earlyoom does). Each field is null when earlyoom did not report it, as on a workspace still running the stock earlyoom. A new drill, `bin/oom_drill.py`, checks the shed order live on a disposable workspace: it sheds memory-holding sleepers at the bands you name and fails on the first victim that was not the predicted one. The README, `OOM_DRILL.md` and `bands.py` now describe the badness earlyoom actually uses instead of `/proc/<pid>/oom_score`, which gVisor serves as 0.

## [minds-v0.7.2] - 2026-09-23

### .agents

An update no longer fails and rolls back when the npm dependencies are not installed. The apply ran `npm ci` only when the merge touched `package.json` or `package-lock.json`, but ran the frontend build whenever frontend source merged -- so a merge that changed neither manifest built into a tree with no `node_modules` at all, died with `sh: 1: tsc: not found`, and rolled the whole update back. Whether the manifest changed says nothing about whether the dependencies are there; either is now reason enough to refresh. "There" means an install that finished, which npm records in `node_modules/.package-lock.json`: the directory itself proves nothing, since `npm ci` empties it but leaves it standing. A tree that does have its dependencies, with no manifest change, still skips the refresh -- it is the slowest and most memory-hungry step of the apply. A rollback that has to rebuild the frontend follows the same rule: when the forward pass installed a worker's prebuilt bundle (and so never ran `npm ci`), or its `npm ci` died after emptying `node_modules`, recovery now installs before it builds instead of dying on the same `tsc: not found` and escalating a clean rollback to an emergency.

The `build-app` scaffolder no longer keeps its own copy of the registry's reserved-name list. It carried a third copy that had drifted, so names the registry refuses, such as `share` and `host`, scaffolded cleanly and then failed to register -- the scaffold would mint a half-built app package that died at manifest validation. It now asks `forward_port.py` itself whether a name can be registered, and keeps only the names of its own built-in apps, which the registry has no reason to know about.

Finding a defect in built-in code is now itself a reason to escalate it upstream, rather than something the user has to think to ask for. `update-self`'s review gates are built to surface exactly this class of finding, and they deliberately do not fix it locally -- a fix to a file that is byte-identical to the release only manufactures divergence the next update must reconcile. But the flow then had no outlet: findings were labelled "submit-upstream-changes candidate" and recorded in the workspace's own ticket tracker, which cannot reach the code that needs changing. Every workspace that hit the same bug rediscovered it and buried it again. `update-self` now has a terminal step that submits those findings or surfaces them to the user with the submission offered, and AGENTS.md states the general rule and names both channels.

`/assist` now sends exactly one report per pass, covering every built-in issue it found, instead of one report per issue. Each report pops a modal over the user's workspace, so a report per issue meant a queue of modals to read and submit one at a time for a single session's work. Issues can be split apart upstream; they cannot be un-popped here. The one-report rule and the POST that opens the modal now live in one shared reference, `.agents/shared/references/report-built-in-issues.md`, which `/assist`, `update-self` and the mngr-changes reference all point to, instead of each pointing at `/assist`'s step 6 by number.

A workspace's second `update-self` pass no longer fails to start with `fatal: a branch named 'mngr/update-self' already exists`. Destroying the previous pass's worker left its branch behind, and the new worker is created on a branch of that same name, so every pass after a workspace's first failed at launch. The pass now deletes the old branch first when it is already part of the workspace's history, which it is after both a landed update and a rolled-back one. A branch still holding commits the workspace lacks is kept under an `archive/update-self-<timestamp>` name, and the results message says so.

Update the Latchkey skill to tell users to try restarting their Minds app if necessary.

This branch carries the desktop-interface work merged from the `mngr/desktop-ui-*` branches; their own entries (`mngr-desktop-ui-*.md`) describe the changes in full. The skills gain nothing new for the shared-desktop work yet.

### system

`system/scripts/message_chat.py --create` makes a new chat through the chat app, the way it already messages one: the chat app mints the id, binds the workspace's default account and harness, takes `--name` and `--label NAME=VALUE`, waves the claude version check on every create (so a workspace whose claude no longer matches its pin can still make the update chat that repairs it), sends the message as the chat's first, and the script waits for the create to finish, printing the chat's `chat_id`, `name`, and `display_name` as one JSON line on exit 0, or the create's own failure on exit 1. A plain `mngr create --template chat` with the same name, labels, and message is the backoff, taken only when the chat app cannot be reached, has no create route, or has one from before these fields (which refuses them by name); both backoffs (this one and the send's) now answer in the script's own three codes rather than handing mngr's status back, so mngr's own exit 2 can no longer be read as the script not being there. The Minds app's assist and update chats use it (falling back to their own `mngr create` on a template without it).

Fixed a family of app-name bugs found while updating a workspace to minds-v0.6.2.

The reserved-name set is carried in three places, because two of them cannot import the one that owns it: `forward_port.py` is stdlib-only by contract, and `layout.py` is an agent-facing script. `layout.py`'s copy had drifted to just `localhost` and `auth`, so a bare word like `share` or `host` waited five seconds for a registration that could never happen instead of being refused at once. The drift test that was supposed to catch this sampled a fixed list of names rather than comparing the sets, so it could not see the gap; it now compares the set held by every carrier in this repo. One further copy lives in the mngr repo, outside this tree, and still holds the old two-name value; the test says so, and it has to be corrected there.

`github` is now reserved. Enabling GitHub sync writes a `github-sync` supervisord program, and an app named `github` would have claimed it as a sidecar -- so turning GitHub sync on would have failed the manifest suite in that workspace.

Apps can no longer collide with *another* app's programs: an app named `pr` would have claimed a second app's `pr-review` program as its own sidecar. The existing guard only covered collisions with programs that belong to no app. An app matching itself is not a collision -- a manifest may set `program` to its own `<name>-<role>` form, and that program is its sidecar. Nor is a program the claiming app's own package runs: `terminal_pty` is only the manifest of an origin the `terminal` package registers and runs, so `terminal-pty` is the terminal's sidecar in fact as well as by name. That excuse needs the run to be established, which is one app package declaring the program's console script; where several declare it, which of them runs is not something the supervisord config decides, and the collision stands. Two app packages declaring one console script is now caught on its own: every app installs as its own uv tool into one shared bin directory, so a shared name leaves a single file there for whichever installed last -- and, until now, a suite reporting that as a name collision between two apps that were fine.

`layout.py`'s tests now run without any part of the ambient agent identity. They already ran with the chat id hidden, but `layout.py` falls back from it to `MNGR_AGENT_ID`, and nothing hid that one -- so a test asserting on an address `layout.py` derives could still be reading whoever ran the suite rather than its own inputs. Both are cleared now, in one fixture rather than two, matching what the browser app's tests needed.

The agy shim's open-steps reminder no longer depends on GNU `stat` or on bash 4, and its tests no longer depend on the kernel's inode allocator. Two separate things kept it from ever firing off Linux, each on its own enough: the turn key is the `active` marker's inode, read with `stat -c`, which only GNU stat understands; and the reminder script did not parse under bash 3.2 -- what `/bin/bash` is on macOS, and what the shim runs it with -- because an apostrophe inside its heredoc opens a quote that version reads as unterminated. The shim discards that script's errors, so both failures were silent, and the suite looked broken rather than unportable. Both `stat` spellings are asked now, and the apostrophe is gone.

The test that checks the reminder returns on a new turn used to recreate the marker and hope for a different inode, holding the freed number down with 64 files. When the kernel reused it anyway the reminder correctly stayed quiet and the test failed -- a red that was reported as a shim bug. It now renames a confirmed-new inode into place, and says so plainly if it cannot get one.

The fixture those tests share also never started the step it created, so the tickets dir held a declared-but-unstarted step rather than an open one, and the shim emitted the "none is currently in_progress" reminder instead. It now starts the step, and checks both tk calls rather than discarding their output.

AGENTS.md now states that finding a defect in built-in code is itself a reason to escalate it upstream, names the two channels (a report when you have a diagnosis, a PR when you have a fix), and says plainly that a local ticket is not a valid end state for one. It points at the shared report reference and at `/assist`'s "Classify the cause" section by name, not at another skill's step numbers, which move whenever that skill is edited.

A workspace container mounts `/tmp` `noexec` (Docker's default for a bare `--tmpfs`), so nothing written under `/tmp` can run. That broke every test that puts a stub executable on `PATH` from pytest's `tmp_path`: the stub was skipped, and the real tool it stood in for ran instead. One update's validation reached the user's live `tmux` this way and killed their terminal sessions. Every pytest run from the workspace's own venv now loads the new `pytest-executable-tmp` plugin, which keeps temporary files somewhere they can run. CI now runs the Python suites with `/tmp` remounted `noexec`, as a workspace container has it, so a pytest root that stops loading the plugin fails in CI rather than only in a workspace.

A new workspace container's `/tmp` is now executable (`--tmpfs /tmp:exec` in the docker provider's start args), matching mngr's gen-2 start args. Docker mounts a bare `--tmpfs` with `noexec`, so nothing written under `/tmp` could run: a stub executable a test puts on `PATH` from pytest's `tmp_path` was skipped and the real tool ran instead (one update's validation killed the user's terminal sessions this way), and OpenCode's TUI could not start. `nosuid` and `nodev` stay. The mount applies when a container is created, so existing containers keep `noexec` until they are recreated.

Every desktop in the workspace shell is shared, and a signed-in visitor arriving for the first time gets a desktop of their own, seeded from the first one (the system interface's entry has the details). The desktop-interface blueprint documents (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/`) drop the sharing mode, add the arrival route, the `users.json` file, and the `user_id` on client records, and describe the per-user desktop in a new plan section 3.10; they also list the presence routes, the `presence_updated` push, and the Presence tray widget from the merged sharing identity cleanup. The branch also carries the desktop-interface work (`mngr-desktop-ui-*.md`) and, in the share gateway, the sharing identity cleanup (`mngr-sharing-cleanup.md`).

### system/apps/chat

Render Codex CLI context compaction events in the chat transcript.

- **Status indicator:** Codex CLI `ContextCompaction` items are parsed and emitted as inline status messages ("Context was compacted").
- **Compaction summary display:** When a compaction summary is provided, it is attached as expandable display body content on the status tag, allowing users to inspect what was retained across compaction.

Render Pi agent context compaction events in the chat transcript.

- **Status indicator:** Pi agent `compaction` entries are parsed and emitted as inline status messages ("Context was compacted").
- **Compaction summary display:** When Pi provides a compaction summary, it is attached as expandable display body content on the status tag, allowing users to inspect what was retained across compaction.

`POST /api/chats/create` can now make a chat on a caller's terms from outside the chat page: `labels` puts extra labels on the chat's agent (`auto_open=true` has the shell surface its window; the labels the app sets itself are refused), `is_installation_check_skipped` waves the claude version check the in-container mngr would otherwise fail the create on (`message_chat.py --create` sends it on every create, so the update chat that repairs a pin mismatch can still be made), and `should_wait` holds the answer until `mngr create` has finished, answering with the chat when it landed, a 500 carrying the create's own reason when it failed, or a 504 when it is still running at the wait's ceiling. Before this, a chat the Minds app started from outside (the assist and update chats) had to be a bare `mngr create` inside the workspace, which the chat app only learned about from the observe stream.

The first agent of a welcome chat now starts with the conversation that chat opened on.

A workspace's first chat is seeded with the conversation the Mind app had before the workspace existed, and the page showed all of it. The agent the user's first message started did not: it was launched with that message alone. So a reply like "1", picking one of the numbered options the last seeded turn offered, reached an agent that had never read the options and could not tell which one was meant.

The launch now carries the seeded conversation ahead of the user's words, in one message, so the agent answers the turn in its context. The chat still shows only what the user typed -- the context block is stripped for display and never appears as a bubble.

This app's test suite now loads the `pytest-executable-tmp` plugin. A workspace container mounts `/tmp` `noexec`, so a stub executable a test writes under `tmp_path` and puts on `PATH` was skipped, and the real tool it stood in for ran instead. The plugin moves temporary files somewhere they can run, or stops the run before any test starts.

This branch carries the desktop-interface work merged from the `mngr/desktop-ui-*` branches; their own entries (`mngr-desktop-ui-*.md`) describe the changes in full.

### system/apps/system_interface

This app's test suite now loads the `pytest-executable-tmp` plugin. A workspace container mounts `/tmp` `noexec`, so a stub executable a test writes under `tmp_path` and puts on `PATH` was skipped, and the real tool it stood in for ran instead. The plugin moves temporary files somewhere they can run, or stops the run before any test starts.

Every desktop is shared, and each signed-in visitor gets a desktop of their own.

- The `sharing` mode (`shared` or `personal`) is gone from desktops, the settings dialog, the settings route, and the desktop record; a `desktops.json` that still carries the key is read with it dropped. A window holds a resource for everyone, so a private desktop was never private.

- A shell page now posts its arrival (`POST /api/clients/<client_id>/arrive`) before reading the desktops, and lands where the shell answers. The owner and any request without a user id land as before. A visiting user (the `X-Imbue-Identity` header's `owner` false with a `user_id`) landing on the owner's desktop would open and close the owner's windows, so on their first arrival the shell makes them a desktop named after them (display name, else the email's local part, else `Guest`, made unique), with the next free glyph and its colour, seeded from the first desktop: its shortcuts, its wallpaper, and a new window at the path of each settled window open there (one still mid-launch is skipped).

- The shell remembers each visitor's desktop in `data/.state/system_interface/users.json` and the user on each client record (`clients.json` gains `user_id`, as does `GET /api/clients`). Later clients of the same user land on that desktop; a returning client keeps the desktop it was on. If the desktop was deleted meanwhile, the next arrival seeds another and the page shows a notice naming the deleted one.

- The presence strip from the share identity work is a tray widget (`data-tray-widget="presence"`) beside the Desktops widget rather than a fixed overlay in the corner of the window, and the `presence_updated` push reaches the desktop store through the shell socket like every other message. The identity header's record and parser moved to `shell/identity.py`, shared by presence and the arrival.

- Presence is now mtime based. Each user has one file, `data/.state/presence/users/<user_id>.json`, holding their identity snapshot (`user_id`, `email`, `owner`, `first_seen`); a heartbeat touches the file's mtime instead of rewriting it, a user is connected while the mtime is within 70 seconds, and the mtime is their last seen. Files are never removed, so whoever is gone is still the record of who was last here. The per-tab session id, the `sessions` map, `POST /api/presence/leave`, the page's leave beacon, and the `data/.state/presence/events.jsonl` join/leave log are gone; the heartbeat takes no body. A sweep every 10 seconds broadcasts `presence_updated` when someone's heartbeats have stopped, so every window learns of a silent departure. A present user on the wire is `user_id`, `email`, `display_name`, `profile_picture_url`, `owner`, `first_seen`, `last_seen` (no `session_count`).

- Display names and profile pictures come from imbue_cloud, not the identity header. The `X-Imbue-Identity` header is read for `owner`, `user_id`, and `email` only (a header that still carries `display_name` or `avatar_url` is read the same way). The shell fetches `GET {SHARE_BROKER_URL}/users/<user_id>/profile` from the broker `data/.secrets/share.env` names, with a 2 second bound, and caches each answer -- and each failure -- for 5 minutes under `data/.state/presence/profiles/<user_id>.json`; the presence route, the `presence_updated` push, and the tray get `display_name` and `profile_picture_url` from there, and a visitor's desktop is named after their profile's display name (else their email's local part, else `Guest`) on their first arrival, the profile resolved before the arrival takes the state lock. A workspace that is not shared, or whose connector is unreachable, shows no names and names desktops by email; no request fails or hangs on a profile.

- The shell page boots from REST. After posting its arrival it reads `GET /api/inventory` once, taking the desktops, the apps, and its own client record from that one answer, in place of the separate desktops and clients reads; the apps no longer wait on the WebSocket's first `apps_updated`, so a shortcut is never drawn for an app the page does not know and a desktop is complete even when the socket is slow to connect (the socket still sends `apps_updated` on every connect, for the resync). Until the inventory answers, a shortcut whose app the page cannot look up draws faint as "Connecting to the workspace..." (`data-connecting="true"`) and running it says "Still connecting to the workspace" instead of that the app is not registered; once the apps are known, a genuinely missing app is reported as not registered, as before.

- The "Refresh my sign-in" link is gone from the Presence tray widget (the gateway's identity refresh route it pointed at is removed with it); nothing in the shell links to a sign-in.

- The Presence tray widget is drawn only while two or more users are connected (one is just you), everyone else first and the requester's own entry last, with an accent ring, "(you)" on its hover text, and `data-presence-self="true"`; the own entry is the one whose `user_id` the heartbeat's answer names.

- A user's picture is their "profile picture", not their "avatar" (the avatar is the workspace's creature). The connector's public profile route answers `{"user_id", "display_name", "profile_picture_url"}`, and the shell's `UserProfile`, the profile cache under `data/.state/presence/profiles/`, the presence route, and the `presence_updated` push carry `profile_picture_url` in place of `avatar_url`.

The shell now knows who is here. Every open shell window heartbeats `POST /api/presence/heartbeat` (every 30 seconds while visible, with a leave beacon on unload), and the shell records each signed-in user's identity -- as the request's `X-Imbue-Identity` header carries it -- under `data/.state/presence/users/<user_id>.json`, appends `user_joined` / `user_left` events to `data/.state/presence/events.jsonl`, serves the connected set at `GET /api/presence`, pushes it as `presence_updated` over the WebSocket, and draws one avatar per connected user in the corner of the window. Over a share the strip links to the gateway's identity refresh. The owner of an unshared workspace carries no identity and is not recorded.

### system/apps/terminal

This branch carries the desktop-interface work merged from the `mngr/desktop-ui-*` branches; their own entries (`mngr-desktop-ui-*.md`) describe the changes in full.

### system/libs/app_manifest

An app's supervisord wiring is found again. `find_wiring_sections` read only `system/supervisord.conf`, but every program now lives in a `supervisord.conf.d/` drop-in, so the app footprint silently lost its wiring -- and the browser app, which declares an `xvfb` sidecar, failed outright with "supervisord.conf does not define program:xvfb". It now reads the main config and its drop-ins, and attributes each block to the file it is actually written in, so a footprint names the file a change would have to edit -- which is what the README's footprint example now shows.

This branch carries the desktop-interface work merged from the `mngr/desktop-ui-*` branches; their own entries (`mngr-desktop-ui-*.md`) describe the changes in full.

### system/libs/bootstrap

This branch carries the desktop-interface work merged from the `mngr/desktop-ui-*` branches; their own entries (`mngr-desktop-ui-*.md`) describe the changes in full.

### system/libs/pytest_executable_tmp

New test-only pytest plugin that keeps a session's temporary files where they can be run. A workspace container mounts `/tmp` `noexec`, so a test's stub executable written under `tmp_path` and put on `PATH` was skipped, and the real tool it stood in for ran instead. One update's validation run reached the user's live `tmux` this way, killed their terminal sessions, and failed 110 tests. The plugin checks, before any test runs, that a file written under the temp root can run; a root where the check's script cannot even be written counts as one that cannot run it. If it can't, it moves temporary files to `/var/tmp`; when the root was chosen explicitly, or `/var/tmp` fails too, it stops the session and says to point `--basetemp` or `PYTEST_DEBUG_TEMPROOT` at a directory that allows running files.

### system/services/caretaker

This branch carries the desktop-interface work merged from the `mngr/desktop-ui-*` branches; their own entries (`mngr-desktop-ui-*.md`) describe the changes in full.

### system/services/host_backup

`host-backup-now` no longer gets killed by the OOM watchdog before it does anything. Its first step reads the backup events log to see whether a tick is already in flight, and it read the whole file to look at the last 200 lines. Every event embeds the stdout of the restic command it reports, so the log reaches gigabytes on an old workspace: the command was killed within seconds, every time, with memory to spare. It now reads only the end of the file.

This mattered beyond the command itself. `update-self` takes a backup first and treats a non-zero exit as "no confirmed restore point", so on any workspace with a grown log, every update ran and reported that it had no restore point -- while the hourly snapshots were in fact healthy the whole time.

The log that grew is now bounded. Each field of an event is stored with at most 16 KB, keeping the head and the tail with a marker naming what was dropped, so a command's opening lines and its final summary both survive -- an uncapped `restic backup --json` progress stream was adding megabytes a day. And the log is rotated: at the start of a tick, once it has reached 8 MiB, it is renamed to `events.jsonl.<timestamp>` and only the two newest rotated files are kept (a workspace had grown one to 1.22 GB). `host-backup-now` follows the file it opened across a rotation, so a tick that starts a fresh log still ends the wait.

### system/services/oom_priority

This branch carries the desktop-interface work merged from the `mngr/desktop-ui-*` branches; their own entries (`mngr-desktop-ui-*.md`) describe the changes in full.

### system/services/share_gateway

This branch carries the share identity cleanup merged from `josh/sharing-cleanup` (`X-Imbue-Identity`, user-id grants); that branch's own entry (`mngr-sharing-cleanup.md`) describes the changes in full.

- Removed the identity refresh route (`GET /_auth/refresh?next=<url>`) and its Caddyfile handle. With profiles read on demand from the connector, the route had no remaining purpose beyond a manual re-login; a visitor whose account record changed simply signs in again when their session ends.

- Fixed the Caddyfile so caddy really strips a client-supplied `X-Imbue-Identity` header *before* `forward_auth` injects the verified one. Caddy's built-in directive order runs `forward_auth` ahead of `request_header`, so the strip was deleting the value the gateway had just injected and no backend ever saw an identity over a share; the rendered global options now carry `order request_header before forward_auth`, which a test pins.

- The login callback now says what went wrong instead of one generic refusal, and logs every denial (never the token). A callback whose nonce or handoff token no longer verifies (a reopened link, the back button, a redirect that outlived the 60-second token) heals itself: a visitor who already holds a session is sent on to their destination, and anyone else is sent through the broker exactly once more; only a failed retry shows the new "Sign-in link expired" page (403). A missing or malformed grants file shows "Sharing is misconfigured" (503, also from `/_auth/verify` for non-owners) telling the visitor the owner must fix the workspace's sharing settings; a verified account without a grant still gets "Not shared with you".

- The identity record shrank to `owner`, `user_id`, and `email`: the session cookie and the `X-Imbue-Identity` header no longer carry `display_name` or `avatar_url`. Profiles live in the connector and are fetched on demand by whatever renders them; profile claims from an older broker's handoff token or an older gateway's cookie are ignored.

- The workspace session cookie now lasts 30 days instead of 24 hours.

- Unsharing deletes the session-cookie signing secret (`data/.secrets/share_gateway_signing_key`), so every existing session -- the owner's included -- is invalidated the moment the share ends; the next share mints a fresh secret. The secret file records the SHA-256 of the relay token it was minted under and is reused only under that token, so a secret an unshare left behind while the gateway runner was down never signs the next share (which always carries a new relay token): it is discarded when the runner next starts without share materials, and replaced at start when the runner comes back to find the next share already set up. The TLS key and cert still persist for a fast re-share.

Shared workspaces now hand every backend the requester's whole identity in one header, and grants can name accounts rather than only emails:

- `X-Share-Owner` and `X-Share-Email` are replaced by a single `X-Imbue-Identity` header, a JSON record carrying `owner`, `user_id`, `email`, and (when the account has them) `display_name` and `avatar_url`. The owner's requests carry the owner's own record over a share; the desktop no longer writes `data/.state/share/owner_email`. caddy strips any client-supplied copy before authorization and injects only the value `/_auth/verify` verified, exactly as before.

- The session cookie carries the whole identity record, copied from the broker's handoff token (which gained `display_name` and `avatar_url`). A cookie minted before the record carried a user id opens no session: an HTML navigation is silently bounced through the broker again.

- `share_grants.toml` scopes gain a `users` list matched (by user id) before `emails` and `email_domains`. An `emails` entry is now an invitation: once a visitor with that verified email is admitted, the gateway rewrites the document to hold their user id instead, under an exclusive `flock` on `data/.secrets/share_grants.toml.lock` that every writer of the file holds.

- `/_auth/refresh?next=<url>`, served at every origin of the share, re-runs the broker handoff so a user who changed their name or avatar gets a session carrying the new record.

## [minds-v0.7.1] - 2026-09-22

### .agents

Speed up the `build-app` workflow when creating and iterating on initial app mocks:

- Adds `--start` to `scaffold_flask_lib.py` to register the new app with supervisord and wait for `/health` in one step, removing the need for separate supervisorctl commands.
- Adds `references/frontend-choices.md` with baseline design defaults (typography, cards, dark mode, copywriting) and removes the requirement in `build-app` and `update-app` to invoke external frontend design skills before writing markup.
- Updates verification guidance in `build-app` and `references/verify.md` to recommend `smoketest_app.py` for sub-second HTTP readiness and content verification.

A scaffolded app's supervisord program now carries `startsecs=30` and `startretries=5`, so a broken app gives up instead of restarting forever.
