An app that dies before it has stayed up 30 seconds counts as a failed start, which sends supervisord into backoff and then FATAL; one that runs for a while and then exits is still restarted as before. Built-in services keep retrying indefinitely, which is deliberate -- the workspace is unusable without them -- so a user app's block now differs from theirs, and `build-app`'s documented program blocks (scaffolded, inline wrap-existing, and wrapper-script) carry the same two settings. The shared program-format reference that `update-app` and `build-app` both point at now documents that split too, so an app added by hand through `update-app` gets the bound policy rather than the built-in services' `startretries=1000000`.

The scaffolder wrote `startretries=1000000` copied from the built-in services, and supervisord's default `startsecs` is one second, so an app that stayed up just over a second and then died was treated as a clean exit and restarted immediately, at full speed, for as long as the workspace lived. On one production workspace an app did that 46,939 times in a single day and kept going for four days; nobody was told, because a crash loop is only visible to someone who runs `supervisorctl status`. Each restart also re-registered the app, which is what drove that workspace's service event log to 1.1 GB.

`scaffold_flask_lib_test.py` pins the property rather than the numbers: a scaffolded program must declare a finite retry count and a `startsecs` long enough that a fast death counts as a failed start.

Surfacing a crash-looping app to the user (rather than only bounding it) is still open. The shell already reads every program's supervisord state name, but `fetch_supervisor_program_states` collapses FATAL into the same `False` as a program the user stopped on purpose, so telling them a broken app gave up means widening that bool into a state the inventory can render.

Apps already scaffolded into existing workspaces keep `startretries=1000000` in their own drop-in; this changes what new ones get, and does not rewrite them.

update-self's apply now refuses to land an update (`--target-ref`) without `--ff-only`. Landing with an ordinary merge puts the worker's `update-self: merge upstream template (<ref>)` commit on a second parent, which the version read and `resolve_template_base.py` never look at because they follow only the first-parent line. After such a landing, the Mind app kept reporting the previous version and offering the same update again. An update that also asks for `--keep-rollback-point` is now refused with a message that says to drop `--keep-rollback-point`, not `--ff-only`. The old message led one update run to drop `--ff-only` and land with an ordinary merge.

- The update-self refresh reinstalls the `mngr` tool from the public-repo commit
  `pyproject.toml` pins for `imbue-mngr`, and adds the plugins
  `system/config/mngr_plugins.toml` assigns each tool from that same commit. A
  workspace built before the pin, whose tool receipt names editable paths into
  the vendored tree the update deletes, is refreshed from the manifest alone
  rather than failing on those paths.

- `submit-upstream-changes/references/mngr-changes.md` describes mngr as a pinned
  dependency: there is no git checkout of it in a workspace and no way to run
  another mngr there, so mngr changes are developed in an mngr-internal checkout on
  a developer's machine, land as their own mngr PR, and reach the template by a
  pin bump.

- `classify-merge` no longer emits the `editable_tool` path class: no release diff can
  touch a vendored mngr tree, so nothing classifies as one.

- The `assist` skill treats an mngr issue as report-only: it needs an mngr change and a
  template pin bump, not a workspace fix or a new desktop-app build.

- The `publish-template` skill drops its Google-OAuth push-protection note: the client id
  it described lived in the vendored tree, which the template no longer carries.

The update-self apply learns the Getting Started app's frontend bundle (`system/apps/getting_started/frontend` built into `system/apps/getting_started/src/getting_started/static`) beside the shell's and the chat's, so an update that changes the app's frontend rebuilds it; there is no boot preflight for it, as an update's bundle is all it needs. The `update-self` and `update-system-interface` landing steps, the update-self worker's report, and the apply's `--worker-bundle` flag name it as the third bundle (`getting_started=<path>`), since the apply installs the worker's bundles only as a complete set.

`update-self` now updates a workspace to the release its Mind app was built against, and says nothing about releases beyond it.

It used to take the newest release at or below the app's, and when that left something on the table it told the user "there's a newer version available, but it needs a newer Mind app", offering `--override` to take it anyway. Under release channels and staged rollout that names a version the user's own updater may not offer for days: the app said "up to date" while the workspace pointed elsewhere. The app announces its own updates; the workspace stays quiet about them.

Matching the app exactly also turns two silent substitutions into faults the agent reports: the upstream not carrying the release the app names, and the app naming no release at all (a dev build reports its branch). Neither picks a different release to update to. An operator testing a dev build passes the ref they want as `--override`, unchanged, as is the confirmation for an override the app cannot vouch for; an app on a release candidate now takes the matching candidate template, the pairing that was verified. The code calls the app's version that now -- `AppVersionUnavailableError`, `AppVersionNotReleasedError`, `--app-version` (`--ceiling` still works) -- and keeps "ceiling" only where something can pass it, in `exceeds_ceiling`.

The `minds-api` skill's create recipe reads a `branch` from `GET /api/v1/app/version` and sends it, and `migrate-workspace` step 0 says the same. Its documented body carried only `git_url`, which builds the new workspace from the template's default branch -- unreleased code, recorded as the app's release -- and an agent picking a version unaided would reach for the newest tag upstream, which the app may not support.

### system

- Add `system/scripts/smoketest_app.py` and its test suite: a fast CLI tool for smoke testing web applications. It resolves application ports automatically from service names or configurations, polls `/health` and HTTP endpoints with response marker validation (<0.1s), and optionally captures headless Playwright screenshots.
- Streamline instructions in `AGENTS.md` for within-Mind workflows.

`forward_port.py` no longer rewrites `data/.state/apps.toml` when the registration changes nothing. It renders the registry first and compares it against what is already on disk; an identical result leaves the file, and its mtime, alone. A real change still lands through the same atomic replace as before.

Every app re-registers each time it starts, and the readers of the registry key off the file's mtime, so an app that crashes and restarts in a loop handed them a "changed" registry several times a second for a registry whose bytes never moved. Measured on one production workspace: 46,371 rewrites in a day, which the app watcher fanned out to 602,823 service-registration events and a 1.1 GB event log.

- mngr is no longer vendored. `system/vendor/mngr/` (a copy of the private
  mngr-internal monorepo) is gone; mngr and its plugins are installed as Python
  packages from the public mngr repo, https://github.com/imbue-ai/mngr, at the
  one commit `pyproject.toml` pins under `[tool.uv.sources]`.
  `system/scripts/build_workspace.sh` derives the `mngr` tool
  (`system/scripts/install_mngr.py`), each app's tool, and the workspace venv
  from that pin; `system/config/mngr_plugins.toml` lists each plugin's package
  and repo subdirectory.

- The few files the workspace needs from mngr that no published package carries
  (the embed contract and service icons the UI bundles, the style guide) are
  fetched at build time by `system/scripts/fetch_mngr_assets.sh` into gitignored
  `system/vendor/mngr-assets/`.

- There is no way to build a workspace against any other mngr: the build reads
  the pin and nothing else. A workspace built by the mngr repo's dev loop or CI
  harnesses runs the pinned mngr too.

- `system/test_mngr_pin.py` pins the shape: public repo, full commit, every locked
  mngr package at the pin, nothing tracked under `system/vendor/mngr`.
  `system/test_supervisord_layout.py`'s evals-capture release gate, which could
  only read the capture from a vendored tree, is gone; mngr-internal's own
  `evidence_collection_test.py` covers that capture.

- `system/scripts/pull_upstreams.sh` and `push_upstreams.sh` are gone: they existed to
  split vendored-mngr edits from workspace edits, and there is no vendored mngr to
  split. mngr changes are their own PR on the mngr repo.

- The root dev group depends on `imbue-common[testing]` (the extra that declares what
  `imbue_common.ratchet_testing` needs) instead of naming `import-linter` itself.

A new blueprint, `docs/system/blueprint/launcher-and-getting-started/plan-launcher-and-getting-started.md`, specifies the launcher's next shape and a Getting Started app, and this branch implements it: the taskbar's field opens a compact menu of rows in which one row is always highlighted (Enter runs it; with no match, Enter starts a new chat with the typed text and Ctrl+Enter sends it to an existing chat, both in the chat's pinned window); a launch path declares which param takes typed text (`text_param`); and the "Start something" intents and the template catalog leave the shell for a Getting Started app that starts chats through one new contract message, `shell:start-with-text`, and opens its own window once per workspace, on the first desktop, for the first client that connects.

Repo-level wiring for the new app: `system/supervisord.conf.d/getting-started.conf`, the `getting-started-frontend` member of the npm workspace, `forward_port.py --manifest` copying a launch path's `text_param` into the registry, and `test_app_manifests.py` checking the new built-in and the chat's text params. The desktop-interface blueprint (concepts, plan, contracts), the window-bound-resources spec, the shell and apps READMEs, and `catalog/README.md` are amended as the plan's section 12 lists: the launcher is a menu, the New Tab sections are the Getting Started app's, `GET /api/templates-catalog` is the app's, and the catalog's cache lives under `data/.state/getting-started/`.

After a first pass in a real workspace: the Getting Started window opens at `0.07,0.05,0.38,0.9` (the width it was resized to, a hair short of the pinned chat) with its tiles two to a row and a page that scrolls; the launcher field is a growing text area (Shift+Enter breaks the line), its `Enter` caption follows the highlight, and "Send to chat..." shows only with text to send; the terminal, file viewer, and browser launch paths are labelled by their app's name. The plan's sections 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 4.1, 4.2, 4.5, 4.8, and 13 and the built-in manifests table in the desktop contracts are amended accordingly.

- Pinned mngr to public commit `39d7ba77e5` (the mirror of mngr `c132c9b8ff`) for the minds 0.7.1 release (`minds-v0.7.1`).

### system/apps/chat

The chat app's supervisord entry now sets `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=4`, capping how many per-thread allocator arenas glibc spreads the app's heap across. Folding the agent stream allocates and frees continuously -- every event arrives as JSON, becomes pydantic models, is folded into the agent view, and is dropped -- and glibc keeps the freed pages in whichever arena they came from, so the app's RSS tracked the high-water mark of every arena at once (eight per core by default) rather than what it holds.

Measured by replaying the same 300 seconds of agent stream at each setting: RSS grew 193 MB at the default, 88 MB at 4, and 59 MB at 2. 4 is the setting here because 2 costs 55% more CPU per MB against this allocation pattern while 4 costs 9%.

This lowers the plateau a long-lived chat app settles at; it is not what made the app in the incident grow for six days. That growth is retention -- the app keeping the whole `mngr observe` output stream, and one watcher per agent -- which two separate open changes address.

Stopping a file watcher now reliably releases the OS watch it holds.

The watcher creates its watchdog observer on its own background thread, but `PathWatcher.stop()` ran on the caller's thread and read the observer as its very first act. In a single `start()` / `stop()` pair that read almost always landed before the background thread got as far as creating the observer: measured over 50 iterations, `stop()` saw no observer 48 times, and in all 48 the background thread went on to start one -- plus its emitter thread and an OS-level watch -- a fraction of a millisecond later, then exited, leaving nobody to stop them. Watchdog's threads are daemons, so the process still shut down cleanly and nothing ever surfaced the leak; the watches simply accumulated for the life of the process.

`stop()` now joins the watch loop's thread before reading the observer, and observer creation is guarded by a lock that `stop()` also takes and by a check of the stop flag. The two outcomes are now exhaustive: either `stop()` sees the observer the loop thread created and stops it, or the loop thread sees the stop request and never creates one. Repeating the same 50-iteration measurement leaves zero observers running.

- The chat frontend bundles the embed contract and the service icons from
  `system/vendor/mngr-assets/` (fetched from the pinned mngr commit by the npm
  workspace root's `prebuild`/`pretest`) instead of a vendored mngr tree.

The chat's `new` launch path declares `text_param = "message"`, which makes it the launcher's primary free-text row: Enter in the desktop's field with no row matched starts a new chat whose first message is the typed text, in the chat's pinned window.

A new launch path, `send` ("Send to chat...") at `/send` with the same `message` text param, is the launcher's secondary row (Ctrl+Enter). The chat root handles `/send?message=<text>` on load and on `shell:navigate`: it opens a picker over the chats that are agents (a typeahead over their titles, one row highlighted, Enter or a click picks, Escape dismisses), sends the text to the chat picked through the ordinary send, selects that chat, and reports `/?chat=<id>` as its location so a reload sends nothing again; dismissing reports the selection alone, and a `send` with no text is a no-op that reports the selection.

The chat's e2e helper that started a chat from the launcher presses the menu's row instead of the retired tile.

With one chat to send to, the `send` launch path sends the text there at once and selects it, with no picker; with no chat at all it starts a new chat with the text.

Model-choice tracking no longer spends a dedicated filesystem watcher on every agent. Each observed agent -- workers included, running or stopped -- used to get its own watchdog observer for its `model_state.json` (a poll thread, dispatcher, emitter, and inotify buffer: four OS threads and one kernel inotify instance per agent, held for the agent's whole life), so a host accumulating agents grew the chat app to hundreds of threads and eventually exhausted the inotify instance limit, at which point new agents' model watchers silently failed to schedule. Tracking is now one shared poller thread that stats every known agent's model-state file once a second and recomputes only the choices whose file stamp changed. The path set is re-resolved from ground truth on every pass, which also fixes a latent bug where a watcher built before the agent's harness was known kept watching the guessed path forever.

### system/apps/files

The `new` launch path's label is "File Viewer" rather than "New File Viewer": the launcher's row is the one place the label shows (shortcuts read the app's display name), and it reads as the app's name there. Nothing about what the launch path does changes.

### system/apps/getting_started

A new built-in app, Getting Started (`getting-started`, port 8030, `launcher_rank = 5`, `critical = false`, a focus-mode default shortcut, its own `getting-started` memory-shedding band): the page the New Tab launcher's "Start something" intents and "Start from a template" shelves moved to, with a search field over its own content and each template's detail as a page inside the app (a back control, "Make it mine", and "Create a new machine from it"). Every tile and both actions start a chat with a seeded text through the shell's `shell:start-with-text`, so the app names no chat app.

The app fetches the template catalog itself (the shell's `template_catalog.py` moved here whole: the fetch from `SYSTEM_INTERFACE_TEMPLATE_CATALOG_URL`, the six-hour reuse, the last-good copy on disk, `GET /api/templates-catalog`), keeping its cache under `data/.state/getting-started/`.

It opens its own window once per workspace: a poller watches the shell's connected clients and, for the first one, opens a Getting Started window on the first desktop through the op route (`open` with `if_present = focus`, then `place` at the frame `0.07,0.05,0.38,0.9`, to the left of the pinned chat, a hair short of it), recording the delivery in `data/.state/getting-started/first_window.json` so no later client or restart opens it again.

The page lays its "Start something" tiles two to a row, shows four before "See more", and scrolls itself, since the shared base styles pin the body to the viewport.

Its manifest declares a `[preview]` table for `update-app`'s `preview_app.py`: `getting-started --no-register --state-dir {scratch}/state` on a free port. The new `--no-register` flag skips the registration and the first-visit opener, so a preview neither re-points the live `getting-started` row nor opens a window in the live desktop.

### system/apps/system_interface

A window you drag stays where you let go of it, even when the desktop never sees the release. A drag interrupted that way -- the button comes up outside the window, or over a live page while the window has lost focus -- used to be thrown away on the next pointer move, snapping the window back to where the drag started; it now settles at the last point the pointer held it, which is where you let go. A resize loses its size the same way and is kept the same way. A drag the browser itself cancels still returns the window to where it was.

Dragging a window's edge out into the desktop starts as readily as dragging it inwards. A press becomes a drag only once it travels the drag threshold, and the pages of the windows around it are live until the drag begins, so the pixels before the threshold could be spent inside a neighbouring app's page, where the desktop sees nothing at all and the threshold is never crossed. Since an edge strip lies mostly inside its window (it overhangs the frame by less than the threshold), outward drags were the ones that left the strip early and stalled. The pages are now inert from the press rather than from the drag, so the threshold is measured against moves the desktop can always see. The pages are live again the moment the press ends, whether it became a drag, a click, or a long press.

- The frontend build reads the embed contract from `system/vendor/mngr-assets/`
  (fetched from the pinned mngr commit by the npm workspace root's
  `prebuild`/`pretest`) instead of a vendored mngr tree.
  `update_staleness.py` no longer treats a vendored mngr path specially.

The launcher is now a menu (launcher-and-getting-started plan sections 3 to 6). The taskbar's field ("Start app or send message...") opens a compact card above itself with one row per launch path of every app, a row per window of every desktop while typing, and at the foot the free-text rows: one per launch path that declares a `text_param`, which run that launch path with the typed text. One row is always highlighted; the arrows and hovering move it, Enter or a click runs it, and Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on macOS) runs the secondary free-text row whatever is highlighted. A free-text row of an app with an independent pinned window points this client's view of that window at the path (restoring and raising it) rather than opening a new window; a text whose encoded path would pass the window path bound is disabled with "Too long to send from here". Typing filters the rows with the library's `matchesQuery`; free-text rows always stay.

The shell answers a new contract message, `shell:start-with-text` (`startWithText(text)` on the connection `connectToShell` returns): it runs the launcher's primary free-text row with the text, so a framed page starts a chat without naming the chat app, and notifies "No app on this machine can start a chat" when nothing on the machine declares one.

The "Start something" intents, the template shelves and detail, and the template catalog (`template_catalog.py`, `GET /api/templates-catalog`, `Config.system_interface_template_catalog_url`) left the shell for the Getting Started app; `LauncherOverlay.ts` and the tiles' `.launcher-tile` class are gone. The registry wire form of a launch path gains `text_param`. The menu's width is the theme token `--desk-launcher-menu-width`. Selectors: `data-launcher-overlay` names the menu, `data-launcher-row`, `data-launch`, `data-launcher-window`, `data-text-action`, `data-highlighted`, and `data-disabled` its rows (contracts section 12).

The field is a one-row text area that grows with its text (to eight lines, then scrolls): Shift+Enter breaks the line, and a text with a line break is a message rather than a query, so the menu keeps the free-text rows alone and the arrows move the caret. The field grows upward out of its one-row footprint in the taskbar, over the backdrop, and the menu rises with it, so the taskbar's entries hold still and the text being written stays in view rather than running under the menu and below the viewport; the break just typed already makes the text a message. The secondary free-text row ("Send to chat...") is listed only while there is text to send. The `Enter` caption sits on whichever row is highlighted, of any kind, rather than always on "New Chat"; the secondary row keeps its `Ctrl+Enter` (`Cmd+Enter` on macOS) caption.

### system/apps/terminal

- The terminal app depends on `imbue-mngr-ttyd` (at the mngr commit `pyproject.toml`
  pins) and reads the OSC 52-capable ttyd web client from that package's resources
  (`importlib.resources`) instead of a file path into a vendored mngr tree;
  `--ttyd-web-client` is now an optional override.

The `new` launch path's label is "Terminal" rather than "New Terminal": the launcher's row is the one place the label shows (shortcuts read the app's display name), and it reads as the app's name there. Nothing about what the launch path does changes.

### system/libs/app_manifest

A launch path may declare `text_param`, naming one of its `params` as the parameter the launcher fills with typed text (launcher-and-getting-started plan section 3.1); naming a param the launch path does not declare fails to load with an `InvalidManifestValueError`. `LaunchParamName` is the primitive for a launch param's name, on `LaunchParam.name`, `LaunchPath.text_param`, and the registry row's `RegistryLaunchPath.params` and `text_param`.

### system/libs/workspace_ui

`matchesQuery` (every whitespace token of a query occurring in one of the given texts, case-insensitively) moves from the shell into the library as `src/search.ts`, so the launcher's rows and the Getting Started page's search filter the same way.

The app contract gains `shell:start-with-text`: `connectToShell` returns `startWithText(text)`, which asks the shell to run the launcher's primary free-text row with the text (start a chat with it, on a machine whose chat declares one), so a framed page seeds a chat without naming the chat app.

### system/services/oom_priority

`SERVICE_BANDS` gains `getting-started` at 80, just above the file viewer's: a shed Getting Started page costs one reload, so it is the most expendable built-in service. The built-in gets a band of its own because `test_app_manifests.py` refuses a built-in app in the `user` band.

## [minds-v0.7.0] - 2026-09-22

### .agents

`service-processes.md` describes the `agent-observer` program: the workspace's one `mngr observe`, a manifest-less supervised service with no app directory, which every chat instance follows and which a chat never starts on its own.

The build-app scaffold writes the `[preview]` table into every new app's `app.toml`: the library's default for the name spelled out (`<PACKAGE_UPPER>_PORT`, `_HOST`, `_DATA_DIR` over a copy of `data/.apps/<name>`), so an edit to the runner's env names has the table to keep in step beside it. The scaffolded runner imports `os` for the environment reads it makes at import; it crashed with a `NameError` before serving anything.

`update-app` boots any app's preview from its manifest: `preview_app.py up --app <name> --worktree <dir> [--with <sibling>]... [--instance-key <key>]` reads the worktree's `app.toml`, resolves its `[preview]` table, boots the siblings first, writes the app's registry copy with each sibling's row pointing at its preview (under the preview's own origin label), and surfaces the app as the labeled `<name>-preview` app, whose window frames it; `refresh` re-boots the inner process in place after a rebuild and `down` tears the preview and its siblings down -- including after a boot that failed with siblings already up, or a re-`up` that named fewer siblings, whose record keeps every sibling so they stay tearable-down rather than being stranded. One preview per app at a time: a different worktree's live preview is refused rather than hijacked. A sibling re-upped or taken down on its own (a chat under a shell preview) is written into the registry copy of every live preview that frames it, with its new port or with the live app's row back, so the shell preview follows without a re-up of its own. A terminal preview is booted `--with terminal-pty`, since its pages frame the pty the registry names. The skill's isolated-instance section points at it for any app with a manifest and keeps the raw `serve_isolated_instance.py` invocation for manifest-less services.

`serve_isolated_instance.py` carries the old live-editing branch's work forward and gains what the preview table needs. Carried: `refresh --name` re-boots the inner server on its existing port after stopping the old process (SIGTERM, escalating to SIGKILL as `down` does) and waiting for it to release the port, recording the new pid before the health wait; `down` escalates SIGTERM to SIGKILL and removes the state directory only once every recorded process group is gone, keeping the state and exiting non-zero for a survivor (`up` refuses to boot over a stale instance it could not clear); a failed boot quotes the log since the last boot marker and the health probe's response body, and copies the log to `data/.state/isolated-instances/<name>-failed.log`; both the inner server and the wrapper launch through `oom_tag_service.py user`. New: `--port-env NAME=ENVVAR` and `--port NAME` for named free ports, `--copy KEY=SOURCE` for a directory copied into the instance's scratch space, `{port:...}`, `{copy:...}`, `{scratch}`, and `{host}` filled in the launch argv and `--env` values, and `--inner-path` for the page the preview frame opens (`preview_wrapper_server.py --inner-path`; a path without a leading slash is refused before anything boots, rather than after the dead wrapper's whole health budget). The state file records ports, copies, and the inner path, so `refresh` and `down` need nothing but the name. The health probe reads the route's own verdict too: a 200 whose JSON says `is_frontend_built` is false (a shell or chat booted from a worktree with no bundle) is not up, since a preview of it shows the "not built" placeholder, and the failure says so. A preview now puts one app in the launcher rather than two, reading as the app it previews: the labeled frame registers `--preview-title` as its display name, and the inner service registers `--internal`, since the frame is how it is meant to be reached and its bare origin serves the same page with nothing marking it as a preview. An instance registered with `--service-name` alone, whose own origin is the surface, stays an app to open.

`update-app` routes by manifest. Its first step finds the app the change touches and reads its `app.toml`: `critical = true` (the shell, the chat, the terminal, and any user app that declares it), or a change under `system/libs/workspace_ui/`, follows the new `references/critical-app.md`, the careful flow that replaces the `update-system-interface` skill: one `editing critical apps` lease held from entry through go-live or abandonment, an isolated worktree provisioned in the background, the live loop through `preview_app.py up`/`refresh` and `layout.py open <name>-preview` (what to point the user at per app, the screenshot fallback when no client can show the window), the two handoff shapes to a harden worker created at approval on the lead's branch, the freshness check over the app, the shared library, and the npm lockfile, the apply with both bundles and `--keep-rollback-point`, the exit codes, the notice only a person closes, and the teardown (the preview's window is closed before `down`, since nothing takes a window away when its app leaves the registry). A pass on an app whose notice is still open proceeds and says the new apply replaces its rollback point. Each round of the live loop closes the preview's window before editing and re-opens it when the round is ready, so "verify before the user can see it" holds every round rather than only the first, and a half-built or broken round is never on the user's screen; the preview itself stays up throughout on its same ports and registrations, so this costs only the window. The reference also says what a preview shell can and cannot do: everything that edits its own copy of the state or reaches only its own windows stays live, and only an app's stop and start and the update notice's verbs are refused. The skill's verify step says to verify before the user can see it, the turn-end section drops the system-interface pointer, and the isolated-instance section says to refresh in place rather than re-`up`. `update-system-interface` and its `reveal_system_interface.py` are deleted.

`update-self`'s apply keeps a rollback point when asked. `update_self.py apply --keep-rollback-point` (the careful flow's flag; update-self's own applies never pass it, and it is refused beside `--ff-only`, whose landing leaves no merge commit for a rollback to revert) leaves its snapshots in place on success and writes `data/.state/update-apply/last-good.json`: the merge it landed, the tree it landed on, the copies it kept, the critical apps whose program or bundle it changed (read off the merged tree's manifests: a changed path under the app, both frontend bundle owners whenever the frontend is rebuilt or installed -- a chat-only edit may therefore include the shell, avoiding a separate source-stamp comparison just to minimize restarts -- an app whose tool environment the apply reinstalled, since a shared backend manifest moves every tool's closure and the copies a rollback puts back include those environments, and the shell when its process's code changed), the supervisord programs a rollback restarts, and whether the diff reached the workspace's own setup (the provisioner, `system/Dockerfile`, the bootstrap). Any later apply replaces the record and its copies; a merge that changed no files keeps no point, since it landed no commit for a rollback to revert. Two subcommands close it: `rollback-last` forward-reverts the merge (work committed since is kept), restores the copies, re-reads supervisord's table when the config or any of its drop-ins changed, restarts exactly the recorded programs (none when the update touched no program's code or bundle, a supervisord drop-in alone, say; or, when the diff reached the workspace's own setup, restores the files and names `mngr start --restart system-services` for an agent), waits for the workspace to settle, asks the shell's page and each restored app's health route whether the restored bundle is actually served (a copy that restored no page is an emergency, not a rollback that worked), refreshes every open view, and writes its progress and outcome into the record for the shell's notice; a rollback that ends in an emergency, or whose revert conflicts and is aborted, keeps the copies, which its outcome says; `confirm-last` drops the record, and the copies with it only when no rollback ran on the point, so closing a failed rollback's outcome leaves the copies its outcome and `emergency.json` point an agent at (the next apply discards them). A settled record is refused a second rollback and closed by `confirm-last`; a rollback holds a lock for its whole run, so a second one started beside it (a double press of the notice's button), or a `confirm-last` or a new apply that would discard the copies it is restoring from, refuses without touching the record or the copies, as does a run over a record an earlier rollback left mid-way; a failed rollback probe takes the apply's existing emergency exit, and a rollback that dies in a way nobody predicted settles the record with what failed (keeping the copies) rather than leaving the notice reading as a rollback still in flight, which refuses every verb. The apply, its recovery, and the rollback now share one "settled" verdict: several consecutive healthy answers from the shell and from the health route of every critical app the user can open, on supervisord pids that hold still across all of them for every critical program (the internal `terminal-pty` included), a pid that turns over restarting the count rather than failing it.

`launch-task`'s `create_worker.py launch` and `launch-sync` take `--branch <spec>`, passed through to `mngr create`, so a worker can check out and extend a branch the lead already built up; `launch-sync` reads the worker's branch back from `mngr ls --format json` (`initial_branch`) rather than assuming `mngr/<name>`, from the payload rather than the exit code, fails fast and destroys the worker when it cannot, and validates the worker name before interpolating it into the CEL filter. `destroy`'s unmerged-work warning counts commits on the worker's recorded branch, so a `--branch` worker is checked against the branch it actually committed to.

`update-creation`'s `type` is `skill`, `app`, or `service`; a critical app is `type: app` reached only from the careful flow, its task carries no `## Change origin` marker (stated where the task-file format is defined), and its go-live belongs to the careful flow. `heal-creation` says a heal of a critical app is a live edit at the agent's own risk and points at the careful flow for the safe path; both spell `create_worker.py await` with its required `--name`. The worker references: `type-app.md` gains a "Critical apps" section (build both bundles at the npm root, report both paths, never `networkidle` against a shell or chat instance, verify against your own instance), `type-system-interface.md` is deleted, and `op-update.md`'s and `op-heal.md`'s system-interface exceptions are retargeted at the critical-app handoff. `interactive-delivery.md` phase 5 names the two demonstrative-prototype types and the wiring-cost versus restart-cost choice, allows commits on an isolated throwaway branch, and says not to test the prototype yourself. `manage-desktop`, `build-app`, `assist`, `update-self`, and `harden-contention.md` name the new flow, and `manage-desktop` says `layout.py open` shows the user something live.

Acceptance focuses on practical recovery rather than minimal restart scope, complete isolation of real terminal sessions, or exact outage and banner timing. Worker-bundle source verification remains required; rollback targeting no longer compares the installed bundle stamp with its kept copy.

A rollback that cannot restore one of its recorded copies now reports incomplete recovery, retains the copies and writes emergency state before restarting services. It no longer treats a copy failure as a warning that later health checks can turn into success; this also protects points that require a full workspace restart.

Added the `notify-user` skill for chat agents: at the end of every turn in which it did work, a chat posts a one-sentence summary into the Mind app's notification feed (bell, badge, toast card, and a system banner when the user is looking elsewhere). Clicking the notification lands the user in that chat. A Stop hook asks for one at the end of every turn; it is a suggestion, and a turn that does not warrant a notification declines by replying with nothing at all. The skill is for chats only, not launch-task workers, whose results reach the user through their parent chat.

Its script posts to the app's existing per-agent notifications route through the latchkey gateway's minds API proxy, addressing it with `MNGR_AGENT_ID` rather than `MINDS_CHAT_ID` -- Latchkey authorizes the runtime agent, and the app derives the stable conversation destination from that agent's `chat_id` label, so the notification is not refused when the conversation and runtime agent ids differ. It exits non-zero with the reason on stderr when the app cannot be reached, so the agent can say in its reply that the notification did not go out.

An update no longer installs a tool that nothing on PATH can run, and it now removes the stale copies of app tools that older workspaces carry.

When the apply could resolve neither the tool it was refreshing nor `mngr` to a uv tool on PATH, it let uv pick the tool directory. uv's default follows `$HOME`, which in a workspace is `/home/user` -- a directory the image's PATH, the login profile and supervisord all leave out. The install then exited 0 and the apply reported UPDATED, so a workspace whose `mngr` had been deleted, or an old lease that never had a uv-tool `mngr` to resolve in the first place, could update itself into having no working `mngr` at all. The apply now falls back to the same pinned tool home the build installs under, taken from the `tool_env` module both trees share. Reading a tool's recorded plugins follows the same directory rather than asking `uv tool dir`, and the pre-apply copy-aside takes the same resolved destination as the reinstall, so a failed update puts back the environment its refresh rebuilt instead of leaving a rollback to re-resolve it over a network the workspace may not have.

Workspaces created before tools were pinned under `/root` also carry a second copy of every app tool under `/home/user/.local`, and an interactive shell (the terminal app) reaches those first -- one production workspace ran a `system-interface` a month older than the one each update refreshed. The apply already swept that leftover copy for `mngr`; it now sweeps each app's tool too, but only when its own PATH already reaches the pinned `/root` installation, so the copy PATH runs and the pinned one are never the ones removed. Every console script the stale copy installed goes with it, so none is left on PATH with a dead interpreter. A tool whose only copy is under `/home/user` is left in place.

The apply's tests now run with the pinned home redirected at a temporary directory, so a test that resolves nothing from its fake PATH can no longer reach the real `/root` of whatever machine runs the suite.

Make sure agents prefer prompting users over asking them to perform actions in the UI.

The `manage-desktop` skill documents pinned windows (listed with `is_pinned` and `scope` by `desktops`, never closed: `close` is refused, `minimize` instead) and that `navigate` on an independent window (the chat's pinned root) moves the target client's page alone. The `build-app` skill's `forward_port.py --manifest` notes cover the `[pin]` table.

The `manage-desktop` skill's listing notes name `client_paths`.

The `manage-desktop` skill names the `pinned` window argument.

The build-app skill's registration notes list `launch_paths` among the manifest fields `forward_port.py` copies onto the registry row.

- The `manage-desktop` skill says `layout.py desktops` and `list` print JSON (they no longer print YAML by default).

The update-system-interface, update-app, and assist skills and the system-interface worker reference describe the shell's frontend as the desktop (its windows, taskbar, and launcher) rather than the dockview shell, the sidebar, and the New Tab launcher, which phase 5 of `docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/plan-desktop-interface.md` deletes; the update skill's verification step opens the motivating chat through the launcher field or a deep link instead of the tab bar's add-tab dropdown.

Phases 6 and 7 of the desktop interface (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/plan-desktop-interface.md`), the skills:

- A single `manage-desktop` skill replaces `manage-layout` and `manage-projects`: the desktop's vocabulary (desktops, windows, placements, clients, launch paths, shortcuts), which client an op targets, how to name a window (`win-<hex>`, `self`, an app name), and the `layout.py` verbs for opening, arranging, closing, navigating, and editing a desktop's shortcuts and wallpaper. Every skill that cited `layout.py` (update-app, update-system-interface, build-app, agentic-browser-fleet, caretaker, crystallize-creation, heal-creation, update-creation, migrate-workspace, manage-scheduled-tasks) speaks the desktop's verbs.

- The update apply's post-restart probes poll `/api/health` on every critical app the user can open (`critical = true` and not `internal = true`; the chat and the terminal), at the URL each app's registry row names, in place of the retired instances API.

- `update-self` no longer rebuilds a files app tool (the app has no Python package) and no longer runs the layout migration on apply; its `surface-chat-tab` command opens the chat's window through the desktop's `open` (`layout.py open chat --path "/?chat=<id>"`); `build-app` documents the manifest without the retired `instances` and `actions` keys.

- `manage-desktop`: `open --minimized`, an `open` with no client to target landing unplaced, and closing a window as the way a terminal or the browser is ended. `agentic-browser-fleet`: the fleet holds one browser that `new` gives you, opened as a minimized window the user can see; the browser stops once no window shows it, and `close` (which deletes the profile) is rarely what you want.

Comments, docstrings and skill prose refer to mngr as mngr, not as "the vendored mngr" or the `system/vendor/mngr` path, where the sentence holds however mngr is installed.

### dev

The root uv workspace excludes `system/apps/terminal_pty`, a manifest-only app directory whose program is an entry point of `system/apps/terminal`.

The workspace app model contract (`docs/system/blueprint/workspace-app-model/contracts.md`) describes the terminal as it now runs: the instance URL is the wrapper page `/?session=<key>&tab={tab}`, the built-in manifests table lists `terminal-pty`, and the `ttyd-focus` note says the wrapper passes the message on to the pty frame.

### system

The shared workspace UI library gains the pieces the chat transcript's restyle needs. `system/libs/workspace_ui/src/base.css` adds the `--width-agent-gutter` token (how far the agent's side of a conversation stays clear of the column's right edge), the `--c-step-done` and `--c-step-pending` progress-bullet colours with their `text-step-done` / `text-step-pending` utilities, and a `--spinner-width` knob on the shared ring spinner. `system/libs/workspace_ui/src/components/icons.ts` adds the small tool glyphs the chat's inline tool chips draw (terminal, sparkle, bot, globe, wrench) and repaints the progress status badges from the new tokens.

`system/scripts/scroll_verification/verify_scroll.py` expands an inline tool chip where it used to expand a full-width tool-call block, matching the chat's new tool-call rendering.

`.DS_Store` is now gitignored, and the stray `.agents/.DS_Store` that had been tracked is removed.

The chat-agent-split plan now lists "switch to another provider" under an auth-failed turn, and "+ Add a provider", as ways to start a handoff or rebind.

`system/supervisord.conf.d/agent-observer.conf` adds the `agent-observer` program: the workspace's one `mngr observe --quiet`, run from the primary agent's work dir in the chat's memory band, restarted on exit like every service. A work dir that is unset or gone falls back to the workspace root with a line in the program's log, rather than failing the command and leaving supervisord respawning something that never observes. The chat app no longer runs an observer of its own; every chat instance follows the event file this program writes. `supervisorctl restart agent-observer` bounces it, and a chat rides the outage out (its `/api/health` reports it) rather than freezing. `agent` joins `forward_port.py`'s reserved app names, since an app by that name would claim the program as its `agent-<role>` sidecar.

`system/vendor/mngr` is refreshed from the paired mngr branch `gabriel/critical-app-editing`, which carries the observe read side (`ObserveEventFollower`, `is_observe_writer_running`, `find_last_full_state_offset`), the follower's start-without-a-writer mode the chat relies on, and the `initial_branch` widening.

The workspace app model's contracts record the chat's `agent_events` health field and the observer's band; the chat, apps, and services READMEs describe the program.

`forward_port.py --display-name <label>` gives a manifest-less row the label users read, instead of the raw service name the workspace falls back to. Like `--internal` and `--program`, every call is authoritative, so a re-registration that stops passing one leaves no stale label behind; a label the shell would reject on read (empty, or over 64 characters) is refused at registration, since such a row is skipped and the app disappears rather than showing a bad name.

`system/test_app_manifests.py` checks that every critical built-in's `[preview]` table names the app's own console script.

The workspace app model's contracts describe `--display-name` and where a row's `display_name` comes from, what a preview shell refuses (an app's stop and start, and the update notice's verbs) and what stays live, the manifest's `[preview]` table and the built-ins' tables (the terminal's pty included), the preview shell's meta tag, `is_preview` on the inventory document, and where an isolated instance's copies and scratch space live. The desktop interface's contracts carry the shell-side additions too: the manifest's `preview` row and the built-ins' tables, the update routes and the JSON 404 for an unknown `/api/` path, what a preview shell refuses and its meta tag, `is_preview` on the inventory document, the `update_notice_changed` socket message, and the new files under `data/.state/`.

`AGENTS.md` says `layout.py open` puts a window on the user's screen the moment it returns (and points at `manage-desktop`, which carries the same rule), and that `update-app` reads the app's manifest first and takes its careful flow for a critical app; `docs/system/workspace-internals.md` names the careful flow in place of the removed `update-system-interface` skill; `system/scripts/agent_rewrite_bash_command.py`'s note names app previews. `docs/system/blueprint/critical-app-editing/plan-critical-app-editing.md` and `test-plan.md` are the branch's plan and hand-run test plan, written against the tabbed shell and headed by a note on what the merge onto the desktop interface changed.

The shared embed module (`system/libs/workspace_ui`) now handles the minds embed contract's new `minds:focus-chat` message (contract v4): the Mind app sends it when the user opens a chat's notification, and the system interface shows that chat. Its payload names the chat by `chatId` (a chat's id is its first agent's id).

The module also announces `minds:workspace-ready` (contract v5) once the page's endpoint is listening. The app holds a focus-chat ask until that arrives, instead of guessing when a freshly-mounted frame's page is live; a send into a page whose listener is not up yet is simply lost. Like the other newer contract types, both constants are probed off the vendored snapshot so a build against an older snapshot still compiles.

Chat agents now tell the user when they finish. A Stop hook (`system/scripts/agent_notify_user_stop_nudge.sh`) asks for a notification at the end of every turn; a turn that does not warrant one declines by replying with nothing at all, so the judgement stays with the agent instead of being guessed from the outside. The reminder reaches the agent by refusing the stop, and claude's `stop_hook_active` is what lets the resulting continuation through, so the hook keeps no state of its own. Workers, automations and claude subagents are never asked -- it gates on `MNGR_AGENT_ROLE=chat`, which the `chat` create template now sets. Wired for claude only; codex is left unwired until it is known whether it reports a continuation the same way. `AGENTS.md` carries the rule for every harness.

The shared tool-environment sweep in `tool_env.py` takes the tool to sweep as a parameter instead of handling `mngr` only, so the update apply can reuse it for app tools, and it removes every console script that points into the environment it deletes rather than only the one named after the tool. The build's `drop-shadowing-mngr` still sweeps only `mngr`, but now also takes any other script left pointing into the stale copy.

The safe-update-apply plan describes the environment snapshots the way the apply resolves them -- from the console script behind a tool, else the mngr tool's directory, else the build's pinned tool home -- instead of via `uv tool dir`, a command the apply no longer runs anywhere and never used to pick a snapshot target.

- Refreshed `system/vendor/mngr` from mngr `9be21fb42c` for the minds 0.7.0 release (`minds-v0.7.0`), carrying the changes since `minds-v0.6.2`.

Phase 9 of the chat-agent split: the plan (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/plan-chat-agent-split.md`) now covers a rebind that takes a model pick.

- Principle 24: after a switch the chat runs on the model the user picked, else on what the switch implies.

- 4.2, 4.6, and 5.2: the pick sits on the shared transition record, and the switch route takes it for either kind.

- 5.1: why a rebind stays armed on the press rather than opening the dialog, what its dialog variant says, and that a harness with a read-only model bar gets no picker.

- 5.12 and 6: the rebind's apply step, its retry while the agent comes up (a codex pick checked only against the old account's options included), `failed_step: model`, and the resume marker.

- 4.2 and 6: account binding is one class per harness registered on `HarnessSpec`, and the rebind record's sessions field is the harness-neutral `sessions_dir`.

- Chat agents no longer get a Stop hook prompt at the end of every turn asking them to send a finish notification: `agent_notify_user_stop_nudge.sh` is removed from `.claude/settings.json` and deleted. Claude Code can only deliver a Stop hook's text by refusing the stop and injecting it as a user message, which every chat turn rendered as a "Stop hook feedback" chip followed by a second, duplicated agent reply (found in the minds-v0.7.0 staging rehearsal). The rule itself stays in AGENTS.md and the notify-user skill, where the agent applies it without a hook.

A new blueprint, `docs/system/blueprint/pinned-taskbar-entries/plan-pinned-taskbar-entries.md`, specifies pinned taskbar entries and the chat avatar for the desktop interface: an app's manifest may declare a `[pin]` whose window exists on every desktop and is never closed; each client shows that window's taskbar entry in the bar or floating above the windows, plain or drawn as an avatar whose image says whether any agent is working (read from mngr's observe event file, with no mngr import); and a window's location scope may be `independent`, so a pinned chat root keeps a separate path per client.

`forward_port.py` copies a manifest's `[pin]` table onto the registry row (the `path`, and each of `style`, `scope`, and `default_mode` the manifest wrote), refusing a malformed one the way it refuses a malformed `default_shortcut`.

`layout.py desktops` and `list` show each window's `is_pinned` and `scope`; a `close` of a pinned window prints the shell's refusal ("minimize it instead"). The desktop-interface concepts, plan, and contracts documents carry the pinned-window, independent-scope, presentation, and avatar amendments the pinned-taskbar-entries plan lists in its section 9, and `docs/system/avatar-designs.md` is the authoring guide for a design drawn through chat.

`layout.py desktops` and `list` show each window's `client_paths` (each client's own path for an independent window). The window-bound-resources spec's reader section and the desktop contracts' desktops route describe the field.

`layout.py` accepts `pinned` as a window argument (your app's pinned window on the target desktop).

Added the blueprint for the desktop-style system interface under `docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/`: `concepts.md` (the agreed vocabulary and decisions: desktops, windows, placements, backdrop, shortcuts, taskbar, launcher, system tray, theme, compact and touch modes), `plan-desktop-interface.md` (the V1 spec: model, behaviour, shell backend, frontend architecture, app contract v2, manifest changes, the built-in apps, testing, phases, deferred work), and `contracts.md` (identifiers, manifest, registry, state files, routes, WebSocket, contract messages, agent ops, geometry rules, theme tokens, test selectors).

Phase 1 of that plan: the browser-side app contract (`system/libs/workspace_ui/src/app_contract.ts`) gains the desktop interface's additions, all additive: a `title` on `shell:location`, a `shell:capabilities` announcement on connect, a `shell:navigate` message with an `onNavigate` handler for pages that can move in place, and `openPath(path, ifPresent)` beside `open(address)`. The tabbed shell ignores what it does not know.

Phase 2: `system/scripts/forward_port.py` copies a manifest's `launch_paths` and `default_shortcut.launch` onto the registry row.

- `system/scripts/layout.py` imports only the standard library again: the registry is read with `tomllib` and the read verbs (`context`, `desktops`, `list`, `shortcuts`, and the shortcut writes' output) print indented JSON. Inside a workspace the script runs under the system `python3`, which has neither `tomlkit` nor `yaml`, so every documented `python3 system/scripts/layout.py ...` call had been failing with `ModuleNotFoundError`. `--json` is still accepted and changes nothing.

- A new test in `system/scripts/` (`stdlib_only_scripts_test.py`) parses the imports of every script the documentation runs with a bare `python3` and fails on anything outside the standard library, so this cannot recur.

- The desktop-interface contracts (section 7) and plan (section 7), the workspace-app-model contracts (section 10), the shell's README, and the `workspace_ui` README and `app_contract.ts` docstring record that every app serves the app contract module from its own origin: a cross-origin module import carries no cookie, and the desktop client's forwarder and the share gateway refuse it.

- The desktop-interface contracts (section 11) list the resize handle tokens (`--desk-resize-edge`, `--desk-resize-corner`, `--desk-resize-overhang`, `--desk-resize-edge-inset`) and how the handles overhang the window's border.

Desktop interface phase 3 (the apps): the built-ins gain the pages of the desktop plan's section 9 while the tabbed shell still runs them.

A new `terminal-pty` supervisord program and manifest (`system/apps/terminal_pty/app.toml`, internal and critical, in the `terminal-pty` memory band beside the terminal) runs ttyd on its own origin, framed by the terminal app's wrapper page.

The browser-side app contract module reads a shell handshake that carries only a client id, so pages keep working under a shell that sends no tab, view, address, or device kind.

Added `docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/geometry_vectors.json`, the shared test vectors for the desktop interface's geometry rules (cascade, clamping, snap frames, fit, snap zones, un-snap, the grid, reading order, nearest free cell, shortcut placement) that both the shell's Python editor and the desktop frontend's TypeScript geometry run.

The plan's phase 6 and phase 7 items now name the gaps phase 4 leaves for them: the desktop store's duplicated name, colour, and glyph validators and the client record's tabbed-shell fields (phase 6), and the op route's read-only verbs answering the desktops rather than the inventory document (phase 7).

Phase 5 of the desktop interface (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/plan-desktop-interface.md`), the parts outside any one app:

- The shared browser-side app contract (`system/libs/workspace_ui/src/app_contract.ts`): the shell's handshake now carries `windowId`, `desktopId`, and `path` (the window the page is in, its desktop, and the path the window is at), read as `""` from a shell that does not send them; the tabbed shell's `deviceKind`, `address`, and `tabId` stay until phase 6 deletes them, and `viewId` still carries the desktop id for the chat's client-activity report.

- `contracts.md` gains the `--desk-shortcut-label-shadow` theme token, the text shadow the backdrop's shortcut labels wear over a wallpaper.

- The shared `postJson` helper (`system/libs/workspace_ui/src/models/http.ts`) throws an `HttpError` carrying the response status alongside the server's detail, so a caller can tell one refusal from another (the desktop's placements save reads a 409 as a stale save through it).

- `dockview-core` leaves the npm workspace lockfile along with the tabbed frontend that used it.

Phases 6 and 7 of the desktop interface (`docs/system/blueprint/desktop-interface/plan-desktop-interface.md`), the parts outside any one app:

- `system/scripts/layout.py` is rewritten around the desktop's verbs (`context`, `desktops`, `list`, `load`, `open`, `focus`, `minimize`, `restore`, `maximize`, `place`, `close`, `navigate`, `refresh`, `shortcuts`, `shortcut set|move|remove`, `wallpaper`); it names apps and windows (`win-<hex>`, `self`, or an app name), opens at `--path` or a launch path (`--launch`, `--param`), targets one client (`--client`, else the client that last messaged the requester, else the one connected client), and refuses the tabbed shell's `app:`/`chat:`/`terminal:` addresses and its retired verbs with a pointer to the replacement. The read verbs print the shell's inventory document.

- The `app_instances` library (instance records, the JSON store, the blueprint, the nudge, the sidecar) is deleted, as is `system/scripts/migrate_workspace_layouts.py`.

- The shared contract module (`system/libs/workspace_ui/src/app_contract.ts`) loses `open(address)` and the handshake's `deviceKind`, `address`, `tabId`, and `viewId`; the handshake is `{clientId, windowId, desktopId, path}`. `ClientIdentity` keeps the active desktop id beside the client id (`getActiveDesktopId`, `adoptClientIdentity({clientId, desktopId})`). `addresses.ts` and `views.ts` are deleted, and the stale dockview comments in the library describe the desktop.

- `system/scripts/forward_port.py --manifest` copies `display_name`, `critical`, `priority`, `program`, `internal`, `launcher_rank`, `default_shortcut` (which now needs `launch` and `mode`), and `launch_paths` onto the row; the tabbed shell's `instances`, `instances_url`, and `actions` keys are no longer read, and a re-registration strips them from a row an earlier release wrote (a `CLEANUP:` note says when that can go).

- The files app's supervisord program runs dufs directly after registering the app; the root `pyproject.toml` no longer lists the deleted packages, and `uv.lock` follows.

- The auto-open in `.mngr/settings.toml` posts the desktop's `open` of the chat at `/?chat=<id>`.

- Docs: `docs/system/README.md` points at the desktop plan as the current direction; the plan records that every phase has landed; `contracts.md` describes the contract module without `open(address)`; `system/apps/README.md` and `system/libs/README.md` describe the desktop-era layout.

- Adds the spec `docs/system/specs/window-bound-resources.md`: every seeded shortcut opens a new window of its app (the chat's is its chat list), a terminal and the one browser live as long as a window shows them and are collected by their own apps, and agents open a window for what they use.

- `forward_port.py` copies `window_closed_path` onto the registry row; `layout.py open --minimized`, an `open` with no client landing unplaced, and the retired `delete` verb's advice naming the apps' own collection. The desktop-interface contracts, plan, and concepts record the window-bound-resources design (`docs/system/specs/window-bound-resources.md`, now implemented).

- `docs/system/specs/window-bound-resources.md` and the contracts record that an app takes the close hint's `path` as proof a window showed the resource it names, closing the gap where a resource closed within its first sweep interval was never collected.

- The desktop-interface blueprint records that the tray ships the Desktops widget alone; the Running apps widget is gone.

Pin the workspace image's base (`system/Dockerfile`) to the `python:3.12-slim-trixie` index digest whose Debian 13.6 packages match the pinned apt snapshot `20260725T000000Z`, instead of the floating tag. Docker Hub had moved the tag to a Debian 13.7 build whose `libc6`, `perl-base` and `libsqlite3-0` are newer than the snapshot's, so apt could not install `libc6-dev`, `perl` or `sqlite3` without a downgrade and every fresh image build (pool seed bakes, new desktop Docker workspaces, CI) failed (imbue-ai/mngr-internal#1138). No package version changes: the pinned base is the one every 0.6.x image was built from before the tag moved. The digest must be bumped together with `.mngr/apt-snapshot-timestamp` from now on.

Comments, docstrings and skill prose refer to mngr as mngr, not as "the vendored mngr" or the `system/vendor/mngr` path, where the sentence holds however mngr is installed.

The shared frontend library gains a menu component, a dropdown, and the geometry both place themselves with. Every menu in the workspace is built on it: the chat app's, and the desktop's, whose own second menu system goes.

`components/menu.ts` is the Menu: `createMenu(options)` owns opening, closing, the invisible sheet under an open menu, Escape, placement against the trigger, and submenus, and a caller describes rows (`action`, `submenu`, `value`, `check`, `divider`, and `custom` for content that is not a plain row). The rules are the component's rather than a setting: a menu opens on a click and closes on a press outside or on Escape, never on a drift, a scroll or a resize; a row may open one submenu, which opens on hover (or keyboard focus) after a short intent delay, is protected on the pointer's way across by a safe triangle, and closes when the pointer leaves the menu-and-submenu pair; a submenu cannot open another, held by the types. Every menu portals to <body> on a new `--z-popover` layer above the modal overlays, because a popover is the most recently opened thing on screen and one opened from inside a modal has to paint over it; `--z-dropdown` goes. A Menu has `dispose()`, which its owner calls from `onremove` -- a menu still open when its owner unmounts would otherwise keep its Escape listener on the window for good, and swallow Escape for every menu after it. An action row may `keepsOpen`, for an action that reports its failure on a line under the rows.

`components/dropdown.ts` is the form control that looks like a menu and is deliberately not one: it picks one value from a list and nothing else, behind the same sheet, with the same Escape.

`flyout-position.ts` becomes `menu-position.ts`, and gains `placeMenu` beside the renamed `placeSubmenu` and `isInSafeTriangle`. `placeMenu` gains `above` and an `end` alignment, and one gap and one margin serve every menu. `placeSubmenu` lines a submenu's first row up with the row that opened it and slides the box up, by exactly as much as it takes, when holding that line would run it off the bottom of the screen; the safe triangle is what tells a pointer travelling to the submenu apart from one changing its mind.

`menuCardClass` puts every menu on the 16px radius, the step the scale keeps for the largest surfaces, and `menuRowClass` draws a row's highlight as an inset rounded slab, 4px in from the card's edges with the 12px radius that corner leaves once you step 4px inward. `placeTooltip` gains `above` beside `below` and `right`, as an addition rather than a change of default.

`--shadow-overlay`, the one shadow every floating surface casts, becomes a 2px contact shadow under a halo 3px down with an 8px blur and a 2px spread, both at 8% black, in place of the 1px contact under a 12px blur with no spread: the same lift, with a firmer edge and a halo that ends sooner.

The Menu learns to hold a submenu open over unfinished work: a caller may answer `holdsSubmenuOpen`, and while it does, neither the pointer drifting off the menu-and-submenu pair nor another row taking the hover closes the submenu -- a click or Escape still does. A submenu that has filled its height cap keeps that height for as long as it stays open, so a list filtered shorter shrinks inside the box instead of shrinking the box and sliding it down under the pointer. A menu taller than the window scrolls between the margins instead of running its far rows off the screen. Two hover-path fixes ride along: a pending hover-intent dies when the pointer settles on a plain row, rather than opening a submenu under a row the pointer has already left, and a submenu opened from keyboard focus paints at once instead of waiting for the next event to redraw it.

An open menu follows a window resize rather than sitting where its anchor used to be: `open()` and `toggle()` take the anchor element as well as its box, a resize re-measures the element and re-places the card, and an open submenu's first-row alignment follows its row's current top. An action row's `trailing` content sits BESIDE the row's button rather than inside it -- buttons cannot nest, and a trailing control may be a button of its own -- with the wrapper carrying the slab and the hover so the row still lights as one piece. The dropdown's option rows borrow `MENU_ROW_SLAB` and `MENU_ROW_FOCUS`, the menu's own row shape, rather than restating them.

`loginSpinnerIcon` takes a size, the way `warningIcon` already did, so a caller can set the disc and its glyph together.

`anchorForEvent` and `anchorForPoint` join the geometry in `menu-position.ts`: an anchor off the element an event fired on, and a zero-width one at a pointer position, which is what a context menu hangs off. They came from the desktop's own menu module, which the shared component replaces.

# Codex review plugin provisioning

Provision native code-guardian in each Codex agent's isolated home before launch,
including its first session and re-provisioning. Preserve existing reviewer
policies and warn on plugin outages, as the Claude installer does. Requires the
code-guardian 0.6.0 release to land on main first.

### system/apps/chat

The chat transcript is restyled and an agent's tool calls now render as a row of inline chips instead of a stack of full-width blocks.

The agent's side of the conversation stops short of the column's right edge (a new `--width-agent-gutter`): its prose, its wrap-up reply, and the timeline's task rows, so a reply reads as one side of a conversation rather than full-bleed text. An opened-up timeline step drops the left rule and indent that read as a nested timeline. A task title takes its colour from its state -- only a closed one greys out, and the live one shimmers together with its narration -- and the status bullets soften (a done step's check is the accent pulled toward grey, a pending one sits below faint, the live spinner runs a thinner ring). The bullet is re-centred on the title's x-height so it lines up across rows regardless of the glyphs a title contains. Type moves back onto the design-system scale (body titles, helper captions) from the sizes the prototype had invented.

A turn's tool calls collapse into one wrapping row of small chips, each a glyph and a short phrase, and only the chip a reader picks opens its detail below it. The detail opens directly under its own chip even when the row has wrapped onto several lines. A run of calls merges into one row even across the separate assistant messages a harness emits, so a sequence reads as a single line of what the agent did; a sub-agent call and a permission request stay as their own cards. What a chip says comes from the agent's own words when the tool records them (a shell command's or a delegation's `description`), otherwise a past-tense verb and the thing the call acted on -- a file by its name, a search by what it looked for. The name is never inferred for a tool that records no reason; those chips read from the live activity strip's present-tense caption, then the bare tool name as a last resort. Opening a chip shows the tool's input as readable text rather than the raw JSON object, led by the verb where the chip is showing the note instead, with the field the chip already said dropped so it is not printed twice. Claude's parser stamps `action_verb`, `action_target`, and `action_note` onto each tool call; the other harnesses fall back to their existing caption.

The "switch to another provider" link under a failed chat turn now moves that chat to the account you pick, the same way the provider menu does, instead of opening a new chat. Picking an account on another harness opens the switch dialog, so the conversation is handed off; picking another account on the same harness and provider arms a rebind, which keeps the agent and its conversation. Either way your next message carries out the switch. The link appears once the page has loaded the chat, including when the chat arrives after the failed turn is already on screen, so the chooser always knows which account to mark "Not working". "+ Add a provider" in the composer's provider menu now marks the chat's current account "Current" and does not let you pick it.

The chat app no longer runs its own `mngr observe`. The workspace's one observer is the `agent-observer` supervisord program, and every chat instance follows the agent lifecycle event file it writes through mngr's `ObserveEventFollower`. supervisord starts the two in no guaranteed order, so the chat starts without the observer and picks the stream up on its opening snapshot rather than retrying; until then the routes that need the agent list answer `503` as they did until the first list. When the observer dies mid-run (a memory shed, a restart) the chat keeps serving its last known list and reports degraded, where before its agent view froze for good; the returning observer's opening snapshot replaces the folded view. `GET /api/health` gains `agent_events` (`{"is_stream_healthy", "detail"}`) saying whether lifecycle events are reaching this instance; `status` stays `ok` either way.

`chat-app --secondary` boots a second chat beside the live one, the preview of a proposed change: it follows the same observer, reads the live accounts, and tracks every agent the live chat tracks, but reconciles no accounts, writes no memory scores (its prioritizer is handed a refusing writer), runs no automatic compaction, resumes no unfinished switch, opens no windows, reports no client activity to the shell (whose activity log is the live chat's), and registers nothing. Sends from it are real; a switch to another account (a handoff or a rebind, and their cancel and retry) is refused with a 400, since it would write the chat's record only into the scratch copy the live chat never reads. `CHAT_DATA_DIR` (default `data/.apps/chat`) is the chat's data directory, and every store the chat keeps (message stamps, settings, chat records, the auto-open ledger) lives under it, so a secondary chat pointed at a scratch copy keeps its writes out of the live chat's data.

The manager's tests write events through mngr's own writer into a temporary host dir and hold the observe lock to stand in for a live observer; the observe-subprocess tests are gone with the subprocess.

`app.toml` gains the chat's `[preview]` table: a preview boots `chat-app --secondary` over a scratch copy of `data/.apps/chat` (`CHAT_DATA_DIR`), probes `/api/health`, and opens on `/?chat={key}`, the chat list with the conversation the user is in selected.

The tool-call policies contract gains P8: a chat agent is asked, at the end of every turn, to tell the user it is finished, through the notification feed. It is a soft reminder delivered at stop, and the judgement of whether a given turn warrants one stays with the agent rather than being guessed from step records. Live on claude; unwired on codex pending one measurement, and `n/a` on pi and agy, whose stop channels reach no model. Documentation only.

Phase 9 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`).

- A switch that keeps the agent on a new account (a rebind) can now change the model too. Before, a rebind refused a model pick, so changing account and model meant switching and then picking from the model bar, or interrupting the first turn. Pressing the account still arms the switch at once. The strip above the composer now offers Change, and the model bar's card a Model row, for a rebind as for a handoff. Both open the switch dialog, whose rebind variant ("Switch to Anthropic 2 (Claude Code)?") starts its picker on "Keep the current model". The strip and the model bar name the pick. Reopening the dialog from Change starts from the armed pick, and picking the armed account again from the provider chooser keeps it. The dialog offers no picker for Antigravity, whose model is changed from the agent's terminal, and says so there instead of pointing at the model bar, so no switch arms a pick that cannot be applied, and a new chat started from the dialog carries none either. The server rejects such a pick at once too, and its account model options route offers nothing for Antigravity.

- `POST /api/chats/<chat-id>/handoff` accepts `model` for a rebind. The pick is applied once the agent is back on the new account and before the message it was switched with. `mngr start` does not wait for the harness the way a create does, so a switch the harness refuses is tried again for up to 30 seconds while the agent comes up. A pick outside the agent's options fails at once, except while a codex agent's daemon has not answered with the new account's options yet: the pick is then tried again too. A pick that cannot land leaves the chat in the failed phase with `failed_step: model` ("Could not set the model on Claude Code"), and the retry reruns only the pick when the restart already landed.

- Each harness now has one account-binding class (`harnesses/<harness>/account_binding.py`), registered on `HarnessSpec` as `binding_class` like the watcher, tracker, and resolver classes. It owns what differs per harness when an agent is bound to an account: the scoping variable, the files a re-auth clears, the account files seeded at sign-in, the `mngr create` arguments, the workspace's create defaults, the rebind's edit, and the move of session files during a rebind. `harnesses/account_scope.py` is gone, `harnesses/binding.py` keeps only the account resolution and the rebind set, and the rebind runner no longer checks which harness it is rebinding. Behavior is unchanged.

- The model bar no longer flickers through other models while a switch is being carried out. Before, the chip gave up the picked model the moment the backend flipped the chat's identity -- a rebind relabels the agent with the new account partway through its restart, and a handoff's successor becomes the chat's agent before it has taken the pick -- and fell back to the pushed live choice, which shows the account the chat is leaving and then whatever model the new account last ran before settling on the pick. Rebinding twice in a row walked the chip through both. Now the chip reads the picked model from the moment it is armed until the harness reports it, and a page reloaded mid-switch reads the pick off the chat rather than the live choice: `handoff.model_pick` rides the chat snapshot. A switch that failed is the exception: it never applied the pick, so the chip drops back to the model the agent is really on while the failure notice stands.

- The rebind record's `claude_sessions_config_dir` is now the harness-neutral `sessions_dir`. A record written under the old name still reads.

- The switch dialog now offers a model for a Codex account the chat has not run on. Before, a Codex account's models were read off an existing agent of that account, so switching between two Codex accounts offered no choice at all when the destination had never run one: the dialog said the agent would keep its current model and left it there, while switching from Claude to Codex, or between two Claude accounts, did offer a picker. The account is now asked for its own models instead -- a short-lived `codex app-server` bound to the account folder, one `model/list`, no agent and no conversation. That also fixes a quieter half of the same bug: two accounts of one provider can be on different subscriptions and genuinely offer different models, so an answer borrowed from another account both hid models the destination has and offered ones it cannot run, which a rebind then failed on at its model step. A successful read is kept beside the account's credential, so the picker still has a set when Codex cannot be reached at all; an account with neither offers only the default.

- `HarnessCatalog.popups` is required in the frontend, like `label`.

- The harness policy docs record P8 (a finished chat turn notifies the user) as a prose-only rule for every harness: the claude Stop hook that asked on every turn was removed because it surfaced in the chat as a chip plus a duplicated reply.

The chat manifest declares a `[pin]` at `/` with the `independent` scope, the `avatar` style, and the `floating` default mode, so every desktop holds one chat root window that is never closed and that shows each viewer the chat they selected, reached through the workspace's avatar floating in the corner of the desktop (its image says whether any agent is working). Nothing else in the chat app changes: the root page keeps reporting the selected chat as its location, and because the pinned window is independent, that report is stored for the reporting client alone.

A chat the Mind app asks to have shown, the welcome chat first of all, now lands in the pinned window: the auto-open asks the shell to `navigate` the client's view of the pinned window to the chat and to `restore` it, so the avatar's window is the one showing the conversation, and opens a root window only on a desktop that has no pinned chat window.
