Phase 6 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/plan-chat-agent-split.md`): section 6 is rewritten to the rebind as landed (the sequence, the claude session-file move, the missing cancel, the failed phase and its same-lane retry, the `REBIND_VERIFIED_HARNESSES` switch), 5.2 keys the dispatch on harness and lane rather than harness alone and says why, 4.2 and 4.6 record the `rebind` entry and the wire's `kind` and `target_label`, 5.1 and the Phase 6 entry say what the page does, and section 10 closes the per-harness question to the hand test.

Phase 7 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/plan-chat-agent-split.md`): the cleanup.

- `system/scripts/message_chat.py` posts to the chat app's `/api/chats/<chat-id>/message` route now that the `/api/agents/...` aliases are gone; its backoff to `mngr message` when the chat app cannot take the message is unchanged.

- The spec records what phase 7 landed and the decisions it settled (section 3, items 28 to 32; the Phase 7 entry; section 9's table), the workspace app model's section 7.4 and mngr-side note name the dropped aliases, and the oom_priority README names the chat-keyed presence route.

Phase 8 of the chat-agent split: the plan (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/plan-chat-agent-split.md`) records how the switch dialog (asked only for a handoff with context; a rebind is armed at once, a fresh start runs at once), the model pick, the fresh-start rule, the handoff node (none left behind by a fresh start), and the silent successor create revised sections 5.1, 5.5, and 5.8, and brings the statements elsewhere in the plan that those revisions overtook up to date: the successor's first message no longer rides `mngr create --message` (principle 16, 5.8), the `agent_switch` marker no longer renders as a chip (4.7, 6), a rebind no longer asks a confirm (6), and the snapshot's `handoff` carries `failed_step` beside `error` (4.6). The `continue-chat` reference and the `handoff-summary` skill now say the summary travels inside the successor's first message, with its path beside it, when it is 64 KB or under, and is pointed at otherwise (principle 16). The successor section of `AGENTS.md` is cut to one bullet (the trigger, the fallback commands, and the two rules), since the rest restated the `continue-chat` prompt every successor gets; principle 22 and section 7 of the plan say so. The shared notice dialog (`system/libs/workspace_ui`) takes children under its body paragraphs and a secondary action, and the modal's action row wraps.

- CI's pytest steps no longer set `PYTEST_MAX_DURATION_SECONDS`: nothing in this repo reads
  it now that the apps no longer register mngr-internal's conftest hooks. The root
  `pyproject.toml` declares the `flaky` marker beside `acceptance` and `release`.

- `AGENTS.md` no longer tells agents to set `PYTEST_MAX_DURATION_SECONDS` to their tool timeout,
  and the per-harness notes in `.mngr/settings.toml` that pointed at that line are gone: the
  variable fed the hooks' global test lock, which no longer exists here. `AGENTS.md` also stops saying pytest writes slow-test and coverage
  reports under `.test_output/`; that was the hooks' `--slow-tests-to-file` / `--coverage-to-file`,
  and those reports now print at the end of each app run.

- `system/scripts/seed_welcome_chat.py` opens the workspace's first chat on the conversation the Mind app had before the workspace existed: it posts the turns to the chat app's `POST /api/chats/seed`, retrying while the app is still coming up, and prints the chat's id. The Mind app runs it through `mngr exec` the moment a workspace is ready.

- `system/scripts/welcome_count.py` counts how many times the welcome skill has run (`data/.state/welcome/count`) so the skill can vary its greeting; `message_chat.py`'s JSON post helper is public (`post_json`) so the seed script shares it.

- `.mngr/settings.toml`: the `first` create template, stacked once per workspace, is replaced by `welcome` (sends `/welcome` to every chat that starts with no message) and `fast` (the fast-mode settings, stacked on a chat whose fast mode -- off, auto or on, a new chat's being the workspace's default -- calls for it).

- Carries the phase 7 and 8 changes of the chat-agent split (`mngr/chat-agent-refactor-8`) into this branch.

- `.mngr/settings.toml`: the codex and pi system prompts no longer inline a fixed `/welcome` reply; they point at the welcome skill, so those harnesses run the same count-varied greeting claude does.

Documents in the workspace app model contracts (section 8) that a shell client treats nothing as missing before its first non-empty `apps_updated`, alongside the system interface fix for restored tabs reading "This tab's app no longer lists it." while the app list had not arrived yet.

A hover tooltip is now a `data-hover-tooltip` attribute on the element that offers it, read at the moment the bubble goes up by one set of listeners on the document, rather than listeners and a captured string attached per element. It could previously go stale or go missing: mithril reuses an element across redraws and runs only the current vnode's hooks, so a view that stopped spreading the attrs left the old listeners and their last text in place, and attrs arriving on an element that never ran the create hook did nothing at all. Neither is expressible now -- an element stops having a tooltip exactly when the attribute goes away, whether a view passes null, stops spreading the attrs, or is patched over by a different vnode that never had them. A bubble that is already up follows the same rule, coming down when its element loses its text or leaves the page. The notice dialog's action buttons, which kept explaining themselves after the explanation went away, come right with the rest.

`hoverTooltipAttrs` takes `null` for "no tooltip". `attachHoverTooltip` (and the `HoverTooltip` handle, with its `setText`/`dispose`) is replaced by `setHoverTooltip(element, text)` for DOM built outside mithril; there is nothing to dispose, because removing the element is enough.

Says "Mind" where it named the desktop app, following the app's rename from Minds. Identifiers such as `minds-api-proxy` and the `MINDS_*` variables are unchanged.

### system/apps/chat

Periodically run context compaction on active chat agents in the background.

- **Background compaction sweeps:** Adds `ChatAutoCompactor`, which periodically sweeps active chat agents and runs `mngr autocompact run <agent_name>` to compact context before limits are exceeded.
- **Parallel agent checking:** Sweeps running agents concurrently via a worker pool, ensuring fast passes across multiple active agents.
- **Lifecycle integration:** Integrates the compactor into `ChatAgentManager` so background checks start automatically on launch and terminate cleanly on shutdown.

The "switch to another provider" link under a failed chat turn can now start the new chat on an account that is already signed in. It used to open the provider chooser with the signed-in accounts listed but not selectable, so the only ways forward were signing in to a new provider or signing in again to an existing one. When the chooser is opened to pick an account (that link, "+ Add a provider" in the composer's provider menu, or a new chat waiting for an account), clicking a signed-in account now uses it directly. The account the failed chat was running on stays listed, marked "Not working" and not pickable, and its "Sign in again" and remove buttons still work. Opened any other way, the chooser lists signed-in accounts as before.

A new chat no longer disappears from the chat list a few seconds after it is created. The observe stream reports a new agent several seconds after its create returns, and every observe event before that rebuilt the tracked agents without it, so the chat was briefly unlisted and the shell closed its tab. The chat app now keeps the agents it created until the observe stream reports them. An agent the stream never reports at all is let go after two of its full snapshots, so a create that died before the stream saw it cannot linger in the list.

Phase 3 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`): the chat app can read a chat that has run on several agents. Nothing creates such a chat yet (the handoff is the next phase), so nothing behaves differently for the user; the read side is in place and tested against hand-built records.

- The chat record store (`chat_records.py`): a record under `data/.apps/chat/chats/<chat-id>/record.json` names a chat's agents in order (the version-guarded, atomically written shape the accounts index uses); an in-memory store serves tests. A chat with no record is its one agent. The manager reads the records at build and resolves every chat-versus-agent crossing through them, so the two phase 2 bridging helpers (`chat_id_of_first_agent`, `first_agent_id_of_chat`) are gone.

- The instance list and the `chats_updated` snapshots show one chat per record, keyed by its first agent and listed from its active agent, with `agent_ids` in record order; an archived member is never listed (because the record names it, not because of an `archived_at` label). Status, stop, start, rename, and the pending-permission status come from the active agent; destroy runs one `mngr destroy --force` naming every member by id and then deletes the record; a re-auth restart skips archived members. An archived member disappearing from mngr leaves the chat standing.

- Multi-segment transcript reads: every harness's watcher is split into a `TranscriptLoader` (discovery, incremental reads, payload re-parsing; `HarnessSpec.loader_class`) and the watcher over it, so an archived agent's transcript is read with no thread and no filesystem watches. `ChatTranscript` reads across the segments: chat-global offsets and totals from the counts recorded on the record (the parsed count wins once a segment loads), tail, backfill, forward, and offset reads that cross segment boundaries, detail reads resolved by event id, and a lazily loaded, cached-with-the-chat loader per archived segment. The subagent routes resolve any member of the chat.

- Every event on the wire carries `agent_id`. A new chat-level `agent_switch` event sits between two agents' segments (id derived from the chat id and the retiring agent's sequence number, with `from_agent_id`, `to_agent_id`, `from_harness`, `to_harness`, `seq`); the chat page renders it as a "Switched from Claude to Codex" chip that opens the new agent's first section, and the subagent tab reads its key off the `/_instances` create response.

- Codex's position-derived fallback event ids (for a message, call, result, or turn marker codex gave no id of its own) are now derived from the line's content, so a re-read dedups and two codex agents of one chat cannot share an id.

Phase 4 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`): the backend of the handoff, which moves a chat to another harness. Nothing in the chat page offers it yet (the UI is the next phase), so a user sees no change until then; the API and its machinery are in place and tested against a recording `mngr`.

- `POST /api/chats/<chat-id>/handoff` (body `account_id`, `message`, `message_id`, and the client fields a send carries) moves a chat to a signed-in account on another harness. The chat app drains the current agent (the stop button's interrupt, whose returned queue text comes back in the 202 answer for the composer), asks it for a summary through the new `handoff-summary` skill unless a fresh one exists under `data/.apps/chat/chats/<chat-id>/summaries/`, then stops it, archives it under `archived-<seq>-<name>-<id>` with one `mngr rename` carrying `display_name`, `chat_id`, `chat_seq`, and `archived_at`, records its segment's length, and creates the successor under a pre-minted id with the chat's name, the account's binding, the membership labels, and a first message filled in from `.agents/shared/references/continue-chat.md` (through `--message-file`). Same-harness targets are refused until the rebind lands.

- Every step is recorded on the chat record's new `handoff` entry (`chat_records.py`: phase, target, the successor's id, the held sends, the summary's outcome, the prompt, the error) and re-checked against mngr's state, so a restart of the chat app resumes an unfinished handoff from the phase it was in (`chat_handoffs.py`). A create that fails leaves the chat in the `failed` phase with mngr's reason; `POST .../handoff/retry` with an `account_id` runs the create again with the same prompt. A half-made successor from an interrupted create is destroyed and created again.

- While a chat converges it keeps listing and reading from its retiring agent, with status `working` (or `error` once the create failed); its title and name come from the handoff entry. Stop, start, rename, interrupt, the queue actions, and the model change answer 409 with the phase (the instances API's stop, start, and rename too); destroy proceeds. A send is held: answered 202 with `{"status": "held", "phase": ...}`, persisted on the record, and delivered to the successor in order once it runs; a repeated `message_id` is not held twice. `POST .../handoff/cancel` calls the handoff off while it is still draining or summarizing, returns the confirming message for the composer, and delivers the other held sends to the agent the chat stays on.

- The transcript fan-out and the SSE streams (`/api/chats/<chat-id>/stream`, the subagent streams) are keyed by chat id rather than agent id, so an open page follows the chat through the switch and receives the `agent_switch` chip the moment the successor is active.

- The `chats_updated` snapshot's `handoff` object gains `error`; the chat app's request for a summary renders as an "Asked for a handoff summary" chip.

- A delivered send to a stopped claude or pi chat marks the agent alive at once (mngr's send starts it, and the observe stream would notice only minutes later), as a codex revive already did; a handoff of a stopped chat therefore waits for the summary the revived agent writes and stops it before archiving it, instead of reading the stale lifecycle as the agent being dead.

Phase 5 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`): a chat can be moved to another harness from its own page.

- In the composer's provider menu, pressing an account on another harness makes it the chat's pending lane: the row wears a "next" badge, the Provider row reads "Claude Code, next: OpenAI (Codex)", and pressing it again (or the account the chat runs on) takes the choice back. An account on the chat's own harness still offers to open a new chat on it, until a later phase lets a chat change account in place.

- With a lane pending, the send button reads "Switch and send" and asks a two-line confirm ("Claude wraps up what it is doing and stops." then "The conversation continues on OpenAI (Codex), starting with your message."). Confirming starts the handoff with the typed message as the new agent's first; the queued text taken off the old agent comes back to the composer.

- While the chat switches, the held messages stay on the page as bubbles captioned with the phase ("Wrapping up with Claude...", "Claude is writing a summary...", "Starting Codex..."), the strip above the composer says the same, the placeholder says a message typed now is delivered once the new harness is ready, and the Stop button becomes "Cancel switch" until the old agent is stopped. A cancel puts the confirming message back in the composer and keeps the pending lane.

- A switch whose create failed shows "Could not start Codex" with mngr's reason over the composer and a retry on any signed-in account; a refused retry says why.

- The `chats_updated` snapshot's `handoff` object gains `target_harness` and `held_sends` (the confirming message first), so a reloaded page keeps showing what is held; the 409 the app answers to stop, start, rename, interrupt, the queue actions, and the model change while a chat converges now names the harness and the phase in plain words, and the page and the shell show it as is.

- The model bar follows the new agent's harness and model; an optimistic model pick made for the old agent is forgotten when the chat moves.

Phase 6 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`): a chat can change account in place.

- Switching a chat to another account on its own harness and lane is now a rebind: the same agent is stopped, its binding repointed in its own state dir (for claude, the chat's session files move into the new account's folder first, so the transcript and `claude --resume` follow), its `account` label rewritten, and it is started again; the transcript, the tk steps, and the model settings stay. An account on another harness or lane is a handoff, as before.

- In the composer's provider menu every account but the chat's own is now a switch target (the "Launch a new chat?" prompt is gone). The confirm reads one line for a rebind ("Claude restarts on Anthropic 2 (Claude Code) and keeps this conversation.") and, for either kind of switch, offers "Start a new chat instead", which opens a new chat on that account with the typed message and leaves this chat alone.

- While the agent restarts, the held messages, the strip, and the placeholder read "Restarting Claude on Anthropic 2 (Claude Code)..."; there is no "Cancel switch" for a rebind, since the agent restarts as soon as the switch is confirmed. A restart that fails shows "Could not restart Claude" with mngr's reason, a retry on the accounts of the same harness and lane, and "Start a new chat instead".

- The `chats_updated` snapshot's `handoff` object gains `kind` (`handoff` or `rebind`), `target_label`, and the `restarting` phase; the switch route's answer gains `kind`; the 409s a converging chat answers name the account for a rebind. The chat record gains a `rebind` entry beside `handoff`.

Phase 7 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`): the cleanup.

- The older `/api/agents/...` spellings of the chat routes are gone. Every per-chat route, the create, and the subagent reads answer under `/api/chats` alone; `POST /api/chats/create` answers `chat_id` where the retired `POST /api/agents/create-chat` answered `agent_id`. `GET /api/agents` stays as the plain listing of every mngr agent.

- Every new chat is named "Chat N", whatever harness or lane it starts on: a chat can switch harness now, so a name that said "Codex 1" would be wrong the moment it moved. Chats named before this keep their names, and new numbers skip every taken name.

Phase 8 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`): the switch is chosen in a dialog, carries a model, and shows as one node.

- Pressing an account on another harness in the composer's provider menu opens the switch dialog at once ("Switch to Codex?") instead of arming a "next" lane behind the menu. The dialog takes the model the successor runs on. "Switch this chat" is the primary action and arms the switch: a strip above the composer says what the next message does, the model bar reads as the target, and "Switch and send" carries the switch out with no second confirmation. "Start a new chat" is secondary and opens a chat on that account and model with the draft moved over. The dialog's buttons wrap rather than overflow, and its backdrop covers the composer.

- The dialog appears only for a switch that will write a summary. A rebind (an account on the chat's own harness and lane) asks nothing: the press arms the switch at once, and the next message carries it out, so a turn in progress is not cut short; the strip above the composer then offers Cancel but no Change, and the model bar's card no Model row, since the agent keeps its model. A chat that has had no user turn skips the dialog too: picking another account switches it at once, with no summary and no handoff prompt, since there is nothing to hand over. The draft stays in the composer.

- The handoff renders as one node in the transcript: "Handing off to Codex..." while it runs, "Handed off from Claude Code to Codex" once done, expandable to the summary turn and the handoff prompt, "Handoff called off" for a cancelled one, which it stays once another switch is confirmed rather than re-animating as that one's progress. Once the switch has landed, a rule under the node marks where the successor's segment begins. A switch that asked for no summary and sent no handoff prompt (a fresh start) leaves no node once it has landed, rather than an empty "Handed off from Claude Code to Pi" line; the live node stands in while it runs. The `agent_switch` marker and the successor's record entry say so (`is_fresh_start`). The "Asked for a handoff summary" chip and the "Switched from" chip are gone; held messages read "Sending..." like any send.

- `POST /api/chats/<chat-id>/handoff` takes `model` (model id, effort, fast); a rebind refuses one. The successor is created silent, the pick is applied through the harness's own switch path before its first message, then the handoff prompt goes to it through the send path, then the held messages. A pick the successor cannot take fails the switch at that step (`failed_step: model` on the snapshot's `handoff`): the page reads "Could not set the model on Codex", and a retry on the same account reruns only the pick and the deliveries, adopting the successor under its pre-minted id. Once the successor is the chat's own agent only the deliveries are left, so a retry naming another account is refused rather than taking the running agent away. `POST /api/chats/create` takes `model` too, for a new chat started from the dialog.

- The page names a harness the way the backend does ("Claude Code", "Antigravity CLI"): `GET /api/harnesses` carries each harness's `label` from the one table the account labels and the handoff prompt use, and the frontend's own table of harness names is gone. The handoff node, the phase text, the switch dialog, and the failed-switch notice read from it.

- `GET /api/accounts/<account-id>/model-options` answers what a new agent on that account could run on: the catalog for a static harness, the options the account's last agent was offered for codex. A fetch that fails says so in the dialog, rather than reading as a harness with no models to pick.

- The handoff prompt the successor starts with carries the predecessor's summary in full, with the path it is kept at, rather than only the path, so the successor has its context before its first tool call. That holds for a summary of 64 KB or under (`INLINE_SUMMARY_MAX_BYTES`); a larger one is pointed at instead, and the successor is told to read it before anything else, since pi's inbox append cannot carry a message past 128 KiB and Claude Code's tmux paste was seen mangled or left unsubmitted from 384 KB. In the transcript it shows as a collapsed "Handoff prompt" chip inside the handoff node, after the summary turn, rather than as the user's own bubble at the top of the successor's segment. The message the user switched with, which rides inside that prompt, is shown as the successor's opening bubble under the rule: the `agent_switch` marker between the two segments carries it (`message` and `message_id`, kept on the successor's record entry), since no event of the successor's own holds it.

- The terminal back face of a chat whose agent is stopped by a switch reports the switch's phase under the chat's name ("Starting Codex...", "Restarting Claude Code on Anthropic 2 (Claude Code)...") instead of the retiring agent's archival name with a Start button the chat app would refuse while the chat converges.

- A step mngr refuses past a switch's point of no return (the retiring agent's archival rename, a rebind's relabel) now lands the chat in the `failed` phase with mngr's reason, so the page shows why and offers the retry, which reruns the step; before, the record kept its phase and the chat was wedged (every verb answered 409, cancel and retry were refused, sends were held) until the next restart of the chat app, as seen on a docker staging workspace.

- The app's `conftest.py` is gone: it only registered mngr-internal's shared pytest hooks
  (`imbue.imbue_common.conftest_hooks` -- a global test lock, a suite duration cap, test
  profiles keyed to a file this repo does not have), copied over when this tree was a copy
  of the monorepo. The `acceptance` / `release` / `flaky` markers those hooks declared are
  now declared in this app's `pyproject.toml`; the hook-only `--slow-tests-to-file` /
  `--coverage-to-file` options and the `resource-guards` test dependency go with it.

The onboarding conversation continues inside the workspace as its first chat, and every chat starts fast for a configurable number of turns.

- `POST /api/chats/seed` opens a chat on turns that happened before the workspace existed (`chat_seed.py`). The turns are written as the chat's first segment under `data/.apps/chat/chats/<chat-id>/seed.jsonl` and read through a `seed` pseudo-harness, the chat's record names the seed as its first member, and the chat is listed as a provisional chat in the new `awaiting_first_send` phase with its transcript on the page and a composer under it. The user's first message launches the chat's first real agent, which is named on the record as the seed's successor before its create runs (`chat_id` and `chat_seq` labels, like a handoff's), so mngr's listing of it mid-create shows the chat under the seed's id and never a second chat beside it; a create that fails takes it back off the record and destroys the agent if mngr had already made it. The provider chooser opens at that send if nothing is signed in. A later handoff's prompt lists the chat's agents as predecessors, not the seed. A restart of the app restores seeded chats still awaiting their first send from their records (and re-requests their tab if no client saw it); discarding one drops the record with it. A title with no usable characters answers 400 and one already taken 409, as a launch's requested name would.

- Every chat that starts with no message is greeted: the `welcome` create template replaces the one-time `first` template and its first-chat claim (`claim_first_chat` is gone from `accounts.py`), so `/welcome` runs each time and the skill varies what it says.

- Fast mode is a per-chat setting with three modes, off, auto and on (`chat_fast_mode.py`, `GET`/`PUT /api/chats/<chat-id>/fast-mode`, kept in the chat's folder so it survives reloads and travels with the chat across handoffs, and removed with the chat). Auto, the default, runs the chat fast for the first `fast_mode_turn_limit` of the user's turns (default 5; the seed's turns do not count) and then switches it to standard speed, once, with a one-time notice over the model bar the first time this happens in a workspace; a user who turns fast mode back on afterwards keeps it. The workspace's default for new chats and the turn limit are `GET`/`PUT /api/settings` (`chat_settings.py`, `data/.apps/chat/settings.json`). The model picker's fast row now states the chat's mode ("Auto", "Auto (off now)", "On", "Off") instead of a switch and opens a small chooser where the mode is picked, auto's turn limit edited, and the mode made the default for new chats; `/fast on` and `/fast off` in the composer choose the mode too. A chat whose mode calls for it launches through the `fast` create template, a handoff's successor included. The old fast-mode prompt modal and `POST /api/chats/<id>/fast-mode-answered` are gone.

- Carries the phase 7 and 8 changes of the chat-agent split (`mngr/chat-agent-refactor-8`) into this branch.

The model card's rows now follow the card's current state. Before, a row explaining that a read-only harness only takes a model change in its own terminal kept saying so after a fresh catalog said the model could be switched from the card, and a row that gained an explanation while the card was open showed none.

The card's rows and the image lightbox's buttons ride the workspace's new attribute-driven tooltips; the lightbox no longer tracks its buttons' tooltips in order to dispose them on close.

Says "Mind" where it named the desktop app, following the app's rename from Minds. Identifiers such as `minds-api-proxy` and the `MINDS_*` variables are unchanged.

### system/apps/system_interface

A tab no longer closes because its app briefly stopped listing the instance. Only a delete through the shell takes an instance out of the project tab sets and saved layouts now. A tab whose instance is missing from its app's list stays open with a dashed status dot and a pane that says it can't be found right now: it may come back on its own (the tab then reconnects) or it may have been removed, with a suggestion to ask an agent if that seems wrong and a Close tab button. No page is loaded while it is missing, so the tab makes no requests. Before this, a new chat's tab closed a few seconds after the chat was created whenever the chat app's list lagged behind the create.

- The app's `conftest.py` is gone: it only registered mngr-internal's shared pytest hooks
  (`imbue.imbue_common.conftest_hooks` -- a global test lock, a suite duration cap, test
  profiles keyed to a file this repo does not have), copied over when this tree was a copy
  of the monorepo. The `acceptance` / `release` / `flaky` markers those hooks declared are
  now declared in this app's `pyproject.toml`; the hook-only `--slow-tests-to-file` /
  `--coverage-to-file` options and the `resource-guards` test dependency go with it.

Fixes restored tabs reading "This tab's app no longer lists it." while the shell's app list had not arrived yet (seen on shared workspaces, where the WebSocket can take longer than the restore's wait). Until the first app list lands, no address counts as unlisted, so the tabs say they are waiting instead, and an empty first push can no longer prune them.

Hover tooltips no longer go stale when an element changes state. Before, a New Tab launcher opened before the app list loaded left the "Build a new app" tile saying "No app on this machine can start a chat" after the tile became usable, an "Open new" tile kept naming its action while greyed out for a pending create, and renaming a stopped row in the project rail left that row's "not running" explanation hanging beside the name being typed. The same could happen to the template detail dialog's actions, stopped rows in the all-apps picker and the rail, and the rail's menu rows.

A tooltip is now driven by an attribute the element carries rather than by listeners attached to it, so it cannot outlive what it was explaining. Every tooltip keeps its behaviour, and the dock's tab strip no longer has to remember to dispose a tab's tooltip when the tab closes.

Says "Mind" where it named the desktop app, following the app's rename from Minds. Identifiers such as `minds-api-proxy` and the `MINDS_*` variables are unchanged.

### system/libs/app_manifest

A manifest may declare what belongs to its app outside the app's own folder: `[[references]]` (each a literal repo-root-relative `path` plus an optional one-line `note`) and `[scope] exclude` (gitignore-style globs), backed by the `AppReference` and `ScopeRules` models and the `ReferencePath` / `ExcludeGlob` / `ReferenceNote` / `RepoRelativePath` primitives, with duplicate reference paths rejected as a cross-field rule. `load_manifest` takes a keyword-only `repo_root` and, against it (given, or derived from a `system/apps/<package>/app.toml` layout), checks that every reference exists and names neither the app's own directory nor another app's. The new `app_manifest.scope` module turns a manifest plus `system/supervisord.conf` into a creation's footprint -- its own paths, the supervisord sections it owns, its references with a `kind` derived from the prefix, the conventions for its type, the built-in plus declared excludes, and, against a diff base, the changed files that the footprint does not account for -- and reverses the link with `find_referencing_manifests`. Two CLI subcommands expose it: `app-manifest footprint <manifest> | --for-path <path>` writes the scope file, and `app-manifest references --for-path <path>` prints the apps that claim a path. Adds a `pathspec` dependency for the exclude matching, since the standard library's `PurePath.full_match` is neither available on the 3.12 CI interpreter nor gitignore-compatible. Phase 1 of app manifest scoping (`docs/system/blueprint/app-manifest-scoping/`). A `[wiring] programs` table names the supervisord programs an app owns beyond its own and its `<name>-<role>` sidecars (the browser declares `xvfb`), and the first label of every standalone program is a reserved app name.

The README names the chat-keyed presence route (`POST /api/chats/<chat_id>/presence`); the `/api/agents/...` spelling was dropped in phase 7 of the chat-agent split. Documentation only.

## [minds-v0.6.1] - 2026-09-14

### .agents

The `build-app` scaffolder writes the app's supervisord program to its own `system/supervisord.conf.d/<name>.conf` instead of appending to the shared `system/supervisord.conf`. That was the last shared file a scaffold authored, so scaffolding two apps now writes only new files and two agents can build two creations in one workspace without one editing a file the other owns. The one shared file a scaffold still writes is `uv.lock`, which `uv sync` regenerates to add the new member; it is derived rather than authored, so it stays out of a creation's footprint and is regenerated on merge rather than treated as a conflict.

The scaffolder's port pre-flight and its duplicate-name guard both scan every drop-in as well as the main config, and count only regular files: a glob is matched against whatever is on disk, so a directory named like a drop-in used to be handed to a caller that reads it, turning the pre-flight into a crash on an unrelated directory someone happened to create. Without that the pre-flight would have handed a new app port 8081, which the `browser` service holds in its own drop-in. The name guard also covers `[eventlistener:*]` declarations, since supervisord holds programs and listeners in one process-group namespace. Both, and the fact that a scaffold now authors no shared file, are pinned by a new `scaffold_flask_lib_test.py`.

`service-processes.md` states the rule without an exception: every supervisord program in this workspace is declared in exactly one file under `system/supervisord.conf.d/`, named after it.

`harden-contention.md` now records what the split does and does not buy the merge-time freshness check: no shared authored file is left in a creation's footprint, so two concurrent creations no longer collide textually, but a path-scoped diff still cannot see a change to something a creation depends on -- a shared library under `system/libs/`, a skill script an app calls, another creation's `app.toml` -- so a green check means "nothing this creation owns moved", not "this pass is still valid". It also carves generated lockfiles out of the "any merge conflict means a stale pass" rule. `uv.lock` is regenerated by every scaffold and marked `merge=binary`, so without the carve-out two concurrent creations would conflict there as a matter of course and force one into a full re-harden -- reintroducing, at the merge step, exactly the serialization this layout removes.

Every boot smoke-check now checks that the drop-ins are actually there, not just that the config parses. An `[include]` glob that matches nothing yields a config that realizes cleanly and runs no services at all, which is reachable now that the main config declares no programs of its own. So the check requires at least one realized program everywhere it is performed: `publish-template`'s assembly (exit 4), `use-template` and `update-installed-template` before they fast-forward the workspace onto a merged tree, and `update-published-template`'s re-cut. `publish-template`'s assembly additionally refuses a `--base-ref` whose tree does not name `system/supervisord.conf.d` (exit 5, alongside the existing `pyproject.toml` and `system/supervisord.conf` requirements).

`github-sync` writes its own drop-in rather than appending to the shared config; `update-self` classifies `system/supervisord.conf.d/**` as a service-class path; and `migrate-workspace` scans the drop-ins when collecting the source's and this workspace's app ports, which it needs to detect collisions before a migration.

On both sides of the migration the drop-in directory is `system/supervisord.conf.d/`, assumed rather than read out of the config's `[include]` glob: it is the template's convention, `system/test_supervisord_layout.py` pins the glob to it, and the scaffolder writes there unconditionally, so a workspace that declared another directory could not scaffold anything anyway. The source-side listing is one shell glob over the quoted path, built by a named helper rather than inlined into the SSH call so the skill's own tests run it against a local workspace; a source predating the split lists nothing and its main config is read as before. The listing costs the one extra round trip it did before.

Phase 2 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`): the skills name a chat apart from the agent it runs on.

- The skills that open or message their own chat (caretaker, manage-layout, manage-scheduled-tasks, update-self's `surface-chat-tab`, now `--chat-id`) and the ones that file a permission request with the latchkey gateway (latchkey, file-sharing, github-sync, publish-template, migrate-workspace, minds-api) use `${MINDS_CHAT_ID:-$MNGR_AGENT_ID}`: the chat's id on an agent the chat app created, the agent's own id for one that is its own chat.

- `create_worker.py launch` stamps `lead_work_dir` (the lead's `MNGR_AGENT_WORK_DIR`) beside `lead_agent`, and `worker-reporting.md` has the worker write its report straight into that checkout, falling back to the repo's main worktree when the field is absent; the `mngr rsync` delivery for a lead in a worktree of its own is gone. `lead_agent` stays the dispatching agent's id: it is what `mngr transcript` reads, and mngr knows only agents.

- The launch-task skill names the launcher by its real path, `.agents/skills/launch-task/scripts/create_worker.py`.

Workers and leads address each other by agent id, and every in-workspace message to a chat goes through the chat app (phase 1 of `docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`).

- `create_worker.py launch` stamps `lead_agent` with the lead's agent id (`MNGR_AGENT_ID`) instead of its name, reads the worker's id back from `mngr create --format jsonl` and stamps it as `worker_agent_id`, and sends the task through `system/scripts/message_chat.py` by that id. A rename of the lead's chat no longer strands the worker's report or its `mngr transcript $LEAD_AGENT`.

- New `create_worker.py reply --task-file <task> -m "..."` sends a lead's gate answer or nudge to the worker's chat through the chat app; `lead-proxy.md`, `dead-worker-recovery.md`, and the update-self, migrate-workspace, fetch-process-show, and crystallize-creation skills use it instead of `mngr message <worker>`. A task file from before the stamp takes `--name`.

- `worker-reporting.md` makes the write into the lead's workspace the primary report delivery, with the id-addressed `mngr rsync` kept for a lead in a worktree of its own; the lead's reply arrives as a message, never through `mngr message` by name.

- The update-self task-file template authors `lead_agent` as `$MNGR_AGENT_ID` (the id an older, non-stamping launcher leaves in place), not `$MNGR_AGENT_NAME`.

### system

Background programs now live one per file under `system/supervisord.conf.d/`, pulled in by an `[include]` glob. `system/supervisord.conf` declares no programs at all -- it is purely the supervisord daemon's own configuration plus the `[include]` of the drop-ins. Adding a service is writing `system/supervisord.conf.d/<name>.conf`; removing one is deleting that file.

Two agents building two independent creations in one workspace used to block each other. Every new app appended a `[program:*]` block to the single shared `system/supervisord.conf` and added entries to the root `pyproject.toml`, so one agent's in-progress work sat as uncommitted changes in the other's tree. That bites hardest at the hardening step, which refuses a dirty tree the agent cannot clean because the dirt is not its own -- so agents skipped the background pass and substituted an inline review. Removing the shared files from a creation's footprint makes the two lines of work genuinely independent. The root `pyproject.toml` now says which dependencies must stay listed and why: the built-in services supervisord starts with `uv run <name>`, whose console scripts a root-closure-scoped `uv sync` would otherwise prune. A scaffolded app is deliberately absent from that list, and what keeps the same sync from pruning it is that mngr's restore and update scripts sync with `--all-packages`.

The drop-in directory is a convention, not something readers discover: neither `configparser` nor a plain `cat` follows supervisord's `[include]`, so every reader of the config -- the OOM band checks, the scaffolder's port pre-flight and name guard, `migrate-workspace`'s port scan, and the cross-repo evals capture -- reads `system/supervisord.conf.d/*.conf` by name rather than parsing the glob out of the config. `system/test_supervisord_layout.py` is the one place that expands the declared glob, and it pins the two together: the glob reaches every drop-in on disk, and every in-repo reader sees exactly the programs the glob reaches. If the glob and the readers ever named different places, a reader would still parse a valid config, just an empty one, and assert over nothing.

One reader is cross-repo: the minds evals evidence capture reads a workspace's `system/supervisord.conf` to learn which program supervises each registered app. Against this layout the old capture finds no `[program:*]` at all and reports every app as unsupervised -- silently, since an app-free workspace gives the same answer. `system/test_supervisord_layout.py` turns that into a release gate this repo's CI can see: while any program lives in a drop-in, the mngr vendored under `system/vendor/mngr` must carry a capture that reads the drop-ins too. The gate asserts on what the capture *does*, not on how its shell is written -- it builds the capture's own shell out of the vendored source and runs it against this repo from an unrelated working directory, then checks it reached every program declared here. What the gate is coupled to is the shape of the upstream API: a builder of that name returning a shell string, and the one constant it formats in. Rename either, or read the config in Python instead of emitting shell, and the gate goes red -- deliberately, since it cannot tell that apart from the capture being dropped; its assertion names which of the two names went missing and says to re-point the test rather than drop it. It is red until that mngr change is vendored, which is the point -- provisioning is tag-pinned, so what a `minds-v<N>` template tag ships with is what binds.

Start order is unchanged: supervisord orders programs by `(priority, name)` and every program uses the default priority, so the declaring file has no bearing on startup. Verified the split is a no-op on the realized config: read both layouts through supervisord's own `ServerOptions.read_config` and diffed the resulting process configs -- the same 15 sections (14 programs plus the `oom-tag-backstop` event listener), identical order, identical commands and options, no include warnings.

The changelog gate's own tests are now hermetic. They build throwaway repos in `tmp_path` but read `CHANGELOG_BASE_REF` / `GITHUB_BASE_REF` from the process environment, so under CI they inherited the real PR's base branch -- which does not exist in a throwaway repo, and which `resolve_diff_base` deliberately refuses to resolve by falling back to `main`. It only surfaced on a stacked PR: when the base is `main` the throwaway repo has one too, so the leak resolved by coincidence and the tests passed for the wrong reason. An autouse fixture in `system/scripts/conftest.py` now clears all four Actions variables the gate reads -- the diff-base pair `CHANGELOG_BASE_REF` / `GITHUB_BASE_REF` and the branch pair `GITHUB_HEAD_REF` / `GITHUB_REF_NAME` -- for every test in that directory.

Section 12's account of how a document op treats a launcher panel is narrowed to match the dock, and the rule is per pane: a New Tab is an ordinary tab and an op docks beside it, except for one alone in the group the op fills, which stands for that pane and is dropped as the op's panel takes its place. What the other panes hold has nothing to do with it. A group showing nothing, or one launcher, is a pane to fill rather than split beside, so a direction naming it fills it and a `--new-group` for it is spent on it; a group holding several launchers is holding tabs the user asked for and is split beside like any other.

Corrected phase 1 to what the template does today (a worker's report is a file the lead polls for, never a message), stamped the lead's address by id, listed the real in-workspace message senders, and pinned the messaging script's contract: registry lookup, `mngr message` exit codes including 7 for a blocked send, 503 until the chat app knows its agents, a caller-minted message id carried on every retry (delivery is at least once; the delivered-id ledger that would make a replay a 200 is deferred to phase 4), and backoff only on a failed connection or 404.

Phase 1 of that plan. `system/scripts/message_chat.py` is the in-workspace way to message a chat: it takes the chat's id (never a name), posts to the chat app's send route, and exits with `mngr message`'s codes (0 delivered, 1 failed, 7 delivered but blocked on a dialog). It falls back to `mngr message --start` only when the chat app cannot be reached or keeps answering 404 (never on a refusal; `--start` mirrors the chat app's revive-on-send, so a stopped agent is reached either way), and retries a 503 while the chat app is still reading its agent list. `--system` marks an automated nudge so the chat renders it as a collapsed chip. A registry file that exists but does not parse is noted on stderr before the fixed-port fallback.

- Pin `ssh_bind_address = "127.0.0.1"` in the `[providers.docker]` block, so
  every local-Docker workspace container publishes its sshd on loopback only
  and is not reachable from the machine's LAN. This matches mngr's new default

  workspace's exposure does not depend on that default. Requires a vendored
  mngr that knows the field: an older `system/vendor/mngr` rejects it as an
  unknown provider setting, so this lands only after the next vendor sync.
  Existing containers keep the bind they were created with until they are

### system/apps/chat

Render Claude Code context compaction events cleanly in the chat transcript.

- **Status indicator:** Post-compaction summary messages (`isCompactSummary`) are emitted as subtle status messages ("Context was compacted") with an expandable toggle to inspect the compaction summary, rather than rendering as a large user message or intrusive chip.
- **Transcript cleanup:** Raw `/compact` invocation commands and local command output from compaction are suppressed from the chat view.
- **Turn boundary and placement:** In the frontend, "Context was compacted" renders as an inline status pill between turns, preserving previous assistant replies and progress blocks rather than absorbing or obscuring them.

Documentation only: the `[program:chat]` block now lives in `system/supervisord.conf.d/chat.conf` rather than in the shared `system/supervisord.conf`, and the README says so. The program, its command, and the app itself are unchanged -- only the file declaring it moved.

Phase 2 of the chat-agent split (`docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`): the chat app names a chat apart from the agent it runs on. Every chat still runs on exactly one agent (its id is that agent's id), so nothing behaves differently for the user; the code, the wire, and the pages are written against chats.

- `ChatId` (`primitives.py`) is distinct from an agent id in code, with the bridging rule (a chat's id is its first agent's id) named in one place and marked `CLEANUP` wherever it is assumed. Instance records, provisional chats, presence, message stamps, the auto-open ledger, and the OOM prioritizer key by chat id. `ChatState` is `ChatAppState`.

- The chat pages' socket sends `chats_updated` (a `ChatSnapshot` per chat: id, title, name, project, status, labels, the agent ids, the handoff phase carried as `null`, and the agent-level facts under `active_agent`), `provisional_chat_created`, and `provisional_chat_completed` keyed by `chat_id`, in place of `agents_updated` and the `proto_agent_*` messages.

- Routes live under `/api/chats`: `/api/chats` lists the chats, `/api/chats/create` takes `chat_id`, every per-chat route is `/api/chats/<chat-id>/...`, and a subagent view reads `/api/chats/<chat-id>/agents/<agent-id>/subagents/<session-id>/{events,stream}`. Every per-chat route, `/api/chats/create`, and the subagent reads are also served at their older `/api/agents/...` spelling, whose id is read as a chat id; `/api/agents` stays the plain listing of every mngr agent. A subagent route whose agent is not the chat's answers `Chat '<chat-id>' has no agent '<agent-id>'` (404). The chat document keeps the workspace's `system-interface-agent-id` meta tag for plugins; the page itself reads its chat id from `system-interface-chat-id`. A subagent view's instance key is `<chat-id>.<agent-id>.<session-id>`, and its page carries the chat, agent, and session ids in meta tags.

- Every agent the app creates gets `--env MINDS_CHAT_ID=<chat id>`.

- The frontend: `agentId` is `chatId` in every model and view, `models/Chats.ts` replaces `AgentManager.ts`, a `ProtoAgent` is a `ProvisionalChat`, and every agent-level read (harness, activity, model choice, queue, lifecycle state, account) comes from the chat's `active_agent`.

- The transcript read routes go through `chat_transcript.py`, a chat's transcript as its agents' segments in order (one segment today); `StoreBackedWatcher` is split into the loader that reads the resident store and the watcher that tails the files, behind a `TranscriptReader` interface.

The send route answers 503 until the chat app has read its agent list from mngr once, the same rule the instances API follows, instead of 404 for an id it has not loaded yet. In-workspace senders (`system/scripts/message_chat.py`) back off to `mngr message` on a 404, so a 404 during the app's first seconds would have routed messages around the app.

The route is now the path every in-workspace sender uses (the browser app's wake-ups, a lead's replies to a worker, the automation runner); a send that names no client posts no client-activity report, as before. A test pins the messaging script's `--system` sentinel to the tag this app's transcript classifier strips.

Codex messages and task timelines now keep their identities across the live and saved transcript.

Codex 0.154 saves user messages as `item_completed/UserMessage` with a `client_id` field. Reading the app-server spelling, `clientId`, from that file lost the correlation ID and displayed the live and saved copies twice. Both the older `user_message` format and the newer item format now preserve the live message ID.

Code-mode command results printed as JSON objects now expose their task titles and summaries just like plain stdout. The original output remains available unchanged on expansion. Task commands are recognized across code-mode batches and through `uv run`, including single-quoted arguments.

Only results paired with a recognized task command can change the timeline. Reading a helper's report or searching a transcript no longer creates phantom tasks or changes an existing task's title or status from quoted commands.

Render Claude Code context compaction events cleanly in the chat transcript.

- **Status indicator:** Post-compaction summary messages (`isCompactSummary`) are emitted as subtle status messages ("Context was compacted") with an expandable toggle to inspect the compaction summary, rather than rendering as a large user message or intrusive chip.

The update-staleness guard that pins "scaffolding an app must not raise the restart banner" now covers the file a scaffold actually writes. It listed `system/supervisord.conf`, which the `build-app` scaffolder no longer touches, and not the program's own `system/supervisord.conf.d/<name>.conf`, which it now writes -- so the guard's stated invariant (every file the scaffolder writes is listed here) had stopped holding. The banner's rules are unchanged and neither path raises it; what changes is that a future rule matching a drop-in would now fail here rather than in a user's workspace.

The New Tab page is an ordinary tab now. As many can be open as you ask for, in one pane or across panes, and one stays put until it is closed or answered -- where before exactly one could exist in the whole dock, and it folded away the moment any other tab took focus. The "+" is offered whether or not the pane already holds one.

Three things enforced the old rule and all three are gone: the focus handler that removed every launcher in the dock as soon as an instance panel was activated, the branch of the open that focused and flashed the launcher already in the target group instead of adding a second, and the "+" hiding itself while its group held one. Two helpers and a module-level flag went with them, having had no other callers.

One narrowing stays, and it is per pane: a New Tab alone in a pane stands for the pane, so the next tab docked there takes its place. That is what keeps an emptied dock tidy -- the dock is never empty, so closing the last tab mints a New Tab to stand in for it, and opening anything spends it -- and it needs nothing to recognise a stand-in by, because a New Tab you opened yourself and left alone in its pane means the same thing. What the other panes hold has no bearing on it. A New Tab sharing its pane with another tab is left alone, and so is a pane holding several. The shell applies the rule to an agent's document ops too, so `layout.py open` behaves as a click does: a pane showing nothing, or one New Tab, is filled rather than split beside, while a pane of several New Tabs is split beside like any other.

Opening something from inside a New Tab still answers that tab, and now leaves the result **where that tab stood**: the placement carries the launcher's own index within its strip and the launcher is retired after, so with three New Tabs up, opening from the middle one leaves you in the middle. Previously the panel was appended and the launcher removed afterwards, which shunted the result to the end.

The New Tab's tab glyph is a dashed squircle rather than a plus -- an unfilled outline for the one tab that is not showing anything yet. At the 14px a tab glyph renders at, the corner radius stays well under half the side (a dashed rounded rect loses its corners first and reads as a circle from about 6 up), `pathLength` restates the perimeter as 64 so the dashes fall in eighths and the path closes on a dash rather than a part-gap, and the rect sets `butt` against the file's `round` linecap, which would otherwise add half a stroke width to each dash and swallow the gaps.

The project rail gets out of the way of what it puts on screen. It expands on hover and floats over the dock, and it used to stay open until the pointer happened to leave, so opening something from it left the thing you just opened underneath it; only one case closed it, clicking a tab row that already had a tab. Now every pick that puts a tab on screen collapses it -- a shortcut row, a tab row whether or not it was already docked, an All apps row, and the two shortcut-menu entries that open or focus an instance. Picks that act on the rail itself (pin, unpin, rename, a mode flip, an app's Stop or Start) leave it open, since there is nothing new to look at, and so does switching views, which changes what the rail lists rather than opening a tab. Entering the rail again brings it back.

A collapsed rail offers nothing to aim at: no hover highlight, and no row buttons. Collapsing leaves your pointer parked over a rail that has changed shape under it, and a row's buttons sit at its right edge, which in the narrow rail is on top of the icon you just clicked -- so the three dots slid under the cursor and lit up as though you had reached for them. Hovering the rail is what opens it, so the only way to be over a collapsed row is a pick that just collapsed it.

The repair-command test follows the chat app's create command builder, which now takes the chat's id beside the agent's (phase 2 of the chat-agent split, `docs/system/blueprint/chat-agent-split/`). No behavior change in the shell.

### system/services/host_backup

Documentation only: the `[program:host-backup]` block now lives in `system/supervisord.conf.d/host-backup.conf` rather than in the shared `system/supervisord.conf`, and the README says so. The block, its program name, and the `uv run host-backup` entry point are unchanged -- the stable contract minds relies on for backup-service updates still holds, since minds addresses the service as `supervisorctl status|restart host-backup` by name and never by file. Only the file declaring it moved. The `WORKSPACE_DIR` comment in `runner.py` points at the drop-in for the `directory=` it mirrors, matching what the README already said; the value and the entry points are unchanged.

### system/services/oom_priority

The OOM band-coverage checks now read every drop-in under `system/supervisord.conf.d/` as well as the main config.

Those checks parse the config with `configparser`, which does not follow supervisord's `[include]`, so the drop-in directory is read by name (`system/test_supervisord_layout.py` pins it as the one the include glob names). Once programs moved into per-program drop-in files, a bare read of the main config returned nothing, so `test_every_service_key_in_supervisord_conf_has_a_band` and `test_every_built_in_supervisord_program_has_an_explicit_band` would have been asserting over an empty set -- and still passing, because their guards were satisfied by it. That is precisely the silent gap they were written to close, after `xvfb` and `env-converge` sat mis-banded for months. Both now see all fifteen sections -- fourteen programs plus the `oom-tag-backstop` event listener -- and both still pass.

The OOM wrapper's module docstring no longer singles out `system_interface` as declared in `system/supervisord.conf` itself: every command carrying the `oom_tag_service.py` prefix now lives under `system/supervisord.conf.d/`.

## [minds-v0.6.0] - 2026-09-12

### .agents

The update apply's cleanup of shadowing mngr installs is now shared with the workspace build rather than reimplemented alongside it.

The apply has removed stale mngr tool installs left under a second `$HOME` since minds-v0.6.0. The build needed the same sweep, for workspaces created before the tool directories were pinned, and had grown its own copy in shell. The two drifted immediately: the apply strips a shebang before splitting on whitespace and the shell copy cut at the first space, so a `#! /path` spelling resolved to nothing and the cleanup would have removed a tool environment while leaving its console script on `PATH` pointing at a dead interpreter.

That logic now lives in `tool_env.py`. Because the apply is staged and run as one self-contained unit -- so an update cannot fail on a divergence between the tree it came from and the tree it is landing -- the file is vendored byte-identically into `.agents/skills/update-self/scripts/` and imported there as a sibling rather than reached across trees. A test fails if the two copies differ.

Behaviour is unchanged: the apply still resolves which installation to keep from its own `PATH` and still sweeps both `$HOME` and the provisioner home, and its existing tests for that pass unmodified. It picks up one guard the build needed spelled out -- nothing is removed unless the installation being kept is present -- which its receipt check already implied.

The manage-scheduled-tasks skill now says which account and harness an automation agent runs on (the workspace's default, from `.mngr/settings.local.toml`) and documents `run_automation.sh`'s new `--type <harness>` option. The service-processes reference no longer claims every claude uses `~/.claude`.

The update-self apply now removes a stale second install of the mngr tool that shadows the one it refreshes. Before, a workspace that had applied an update with pre-minds-v0.4.3 scripts could carry a copy under `/home/user/.local` alongside the image's copy under `/root/.local`; every later apply refreshed only the `/root` copy (the one on the worker's PATH) while login shells, including the terminal app and the desktop app's `mngr exec`, resolved the stale one first. The first release that added a dependency to mngr then broke every command those shells ran, with the update still reporting success. Now each apply deletes any mngr tool environment and console script under `$HOME/.local` or `/root/.local` that is not the installation behind `mngr` on its own PATH.

The latchkey skill now tells agents how to ask for a connection to a domain latchkey has no service for, and when not to.

Which request to send is decided by the error text latchkey returned, not its status or exit code. `No service matches URL` means there is no service for that domain, so the agent asks for a new connection (`type: "custom-service"`); an error naming an existing service (`No credentials found for <service>`, `Request not permitted by the user`) means the service exists, so the agent asks for permissions on it as before. A second workspace whose latchkey does not know the service sends the same `custom-service` request.

A `custom-service` request names a `domain` (ASCII; punycode for anything else) and a `scheme` (`https` or `http`). By default the user pastes a token during approval, sent as a bearer `Authorization` header; a browser sign-in is a `login` object whose `url`, `flow` and `flow_params` mirror the `--login-url`, `--login-flow` and `--login-flow-params` flags of `latchkey services register`. The skill also says when not to go this route at all: a URL that needs no credentials needs no latchkey, and a service that needs a credential shape latchkey cannot attach should be handled with the user instead.

### system

The workspace build now installs the mngr tool and its plugins in one command, and pins where that install lands.

Before, `build_workspace.sh` installed the base mngr package and then registered its plugins in a second step (`mngr plugin add`). Installing the base alone rebuilds a uv tool environment from that package and drops every extra, so between the two commands the tool had no harness plugins -- and a build that stopped in that window left one that stayed that way. Such an mngr cannot resolve `[agent_types.claude]`, so `mngr create --template chat` fails on the `chat` template's `output_style`. That create is how the desktop app starts an update, so the workspace could no longer be updated from the app, while chats created by the workspace's own interface (which runs mngr from the root venv) kept working. Now both go in a single `uv tool install`, so the plugin-less state is unreachable.

The build also runs under two different `$HOME`s -- the image build's `/root`, and `/home/user` on a live create -- and uv's tool directories follow `$HOME`. Unpinned, a create installed a second copy of every tool under `/home/user/.local` that no update refreshed and that a login shell found first, which is what the desktop app's `mngr exec` and the terminal both use. `UV_TOOL_DIR` and `UV_TOOL_BIN_DIR` are now pinned to the location the build already puts on `PATH`, and a build that finds an mngr install left under another `$HOME` removes it. That removal refuses to run unless it can see the pinned install it is protecting, and resolves both directories before comparing them, so a home reached as `/root/` or through a symlink is never mistaken for a shadow of itself. Both of these run where the build does -- the image build and a create's provisioning -- so they keep new workspaces out of this state. A workspace already in it is not reached: it is never re-provisioned, and the update apply runs `setup_system.sh` rather than the build. Those remain the apply's own shadow cleanup to handle, and only once their update can start at all.

The cleanup itself is now one implementation rather than two. It already existed in the update apply, and the build had grown a second copy in shell; the two drifted immediately -- their shebang parsers disagreed on a `#! /path` spelling, which would have removed a tool environment and left its console script on `PATH` pointing at a dead interpreter. The logic now lives in `system/scripts/tool_env.py`, vendored byte-identically into the apply's own `scripts/` directory so the apply stays the self-contained, swappable unit an update needs it to be, with a test that fails if the two copies differ.

Installing mngr is now a program, `system/scripts/install_mngr.py`, rather than a line of shell in the build and a snippet in `AGENTS.md`. Every hazard the snippet had to warn about was a shell hazard -- an empty plugin list `set -e` could not see because the substitution that produced it swallowed the lister's exit status, an install landing under the wrong `$HOME`, strict mode leaking into the shell that sourced the pin -- and none of them survive being written in Python. The refusal to install a plugin-less mngr is now tested rather than documented, and `AGENTS.md`'s recovery instructions are the two commands the build itself runs: that program, and the shadow cleanup after it.

`.mngr/settings.toml` no longer defaults `commands.create.type` to `claude`: the type an unqualified `mngr create` resolves to, and the provider account it runs on, come from the git-ignored `.mngr/settings.local.toml` the chat app writes from its account store, so a create with no account signed in fails instead of launching a claude that cannot take a turn. A new `[pre_command_scripts] create` entry runs `system/scripts/require_create_account.py`, which refuses such a create with "No provider account is signed in on this machine. Sign in from a chat tab, then try again." in place of mngr's "No agent type provided" and its config-set hint; it gates on the create's project root being the work dir of the agent running it, so the create of the workspace itself -- run on the user's machine from a clone of this template that is nobody's work dir -- is never refused, and the entry's own shell test spares a plain user shell from starting `python3` at all (an mngr agent on that machine has `MNGR_AGENT_ID`, so an agent-run create there does start one). `[work_dir_extra_paths]` shares the local file into worker worktrees by symlink, so a create run from inside one resolves the same account. `system/scripts/default_account_args.py` is removed.

`system/vendor/mngr` is refreshed to the mngr branch of the same name, whose one change over the minds-v0.5.2 vendor is that a `[commands.<name>]` table in a higher-precedence settings layer adds to the parameters lower layers set instead of replacing them, which the local file depends on.

`migrate_claude_auth_test.py` isolates the create defaults the way it already isolated the host env file and the accounts store. Run from the repo root it used to leave a real `.mngr/settings.local.toml` behind, pointing at a pytest directory that no longer exists -- and that file is what the create gate reads, so a developer's checkout quietly stopped refusing creates it should have refused.

The update-self apply now removes a stale second install of the mngr tool that shadows the one it refreshes. Before, a workspace that had applied an update with pre-minds-v0.4.3 scripts could carry a copy under `/home/user/.local` alongside the image's copy under `/root/.local`; every later apply refreshed only the `/root` copy (the one on the worker's PATH) while login shells, including the terminal app and the desktop app's `mngr exec`, resolved the stale one first. The first release that added a dependency to mngr then broke every command those shells ran, with the update still reporting success. Now each apply deletes any mngr tool environment and console script under `$HOME/.local` or `/root/.local` that is not the installation behind `mngr` on its own PATH.

Bug reports now carry the agents' own diagnostics, not just the workspace services'. Before, the `--logs` half of a report collected `/var/log/supervisor/*.log` only -- and agents run under tmux, not supervisord, so no harness output reached a report at all. A report told you what a chat said and nothing about why its harness misbehaved. Under the same "include logs" consent, the archive now also holds `agent-logs/<agent>/<file>`: each agent's harness log files, which is codex's `app_server.log` and TUI tail, antigravity's `agy_cli.log`, opencode's `opencode_server.log`, and the `stderr.log` the claude and pi-coding harnesses now write.

For codex there is also the app-server's own log database, rendered to text as `agent-logs/<agent>/logs_2.sqlite.log`. `app_server.log` records what a thread did but not which request or connection asked for it; the database has carried that attribution all along -- codex writes it independently of `RUST_LOG` -- but nothing collected it, because the collector only ever looked at `*.log` files. It is also about a hundred times smaller than the text log for the same span of time, so where the text log's 256 KiB tail could cover as little as a few seconds on a busy daemon, the rendered database covers the whole session.

Only rows written by the app-server's own request layer are read. The database is the harness's entire TRACE stream, and on a live workspace it was measured carrying bearer tokens under two targets and an API key under a third, so this is an allowlist of what to include rather than a denylist of what to drop -- an allowlist can only ever miss something useful, while a denylist misses something secret.

Each running agent also contributes a capture of its tmux pane, for the harnesses whose crash output only ever reaches the screen. That one needs BOTH consents rather than the logs one alone: a TUI harness renders the conversation into its pane, so the scrollback is chat content as much as diagnostics, and a user who asks for logs while declining to send their chats has declined it too. The capture passes `--no-start`, so filing a report never wakes a stopped agent.

The harness logs, the log databases and the chats are each scanned and released or withheld on their own, so a finding in one no longer costs the report the rest. The database is deliberately its own class rather than part of the harness logs: a row the allowlist did not anticipate costs the report the database alone and still delivers `app_server.log` and every agent's `stderr.log`, which are the logs most likely to explain the bug.

Two limits changed to go with it. Each log class now fills to a total byte budget newest-first, so one busy harness cannot hand the secret scanner more plaintext than it can read inside the host's budget -- without which the report would time out rather than arrive trimmed. A class the budget could not fit whole says so, and how many files it left out, in `collection-notes.txt`: otherwise a trimmed class reads exactly like a complete one, and "the harness that broke wrote nothing" is the wrong conclusion to hand someone diagnosing that harness. A class the scan then withholds says only that, without the trimmed line: "one file was left out" reads as reassurance that the rest arrived, which is the same wrong conclusion pointed the other way. Panes get their own budget rather than competing with the log files: they are captured at collection time, so under a shared newest-first budget they would sort above every real harness log and displace the logs of the agent that actually broke. And the per-file line cap rose from 200 to 2000: the per-file read cap was already what bounded a member, so the line cap was discarding lines that had been read, and a chatty service can write 200 lines in under a second.

Workspace claude chats no longer show Claude Code's session quality survey or feedback drafts: `[agent_types.claude]` in `.mngr/settings.toml` now sets `feedbackSurveyRate = 0` and `feedbackDrafts = "off"` through `settings_overrides__extend`. Both prompt a human mid-session, which garbles an unattended chat's automated input and output. They ride the mngr-managed `--settings` overlay, like `skipDangerousModePermissionPrompt`, because in shared config-dir mode nothing else provisions the shared `settings.json`, and mngr's own unattended flags never apply to chats created inside the container.

Bump the pinned Claude Code version from 2.1.227 to 2.1.269 (the `latest` release channel at the time; `stable` still sat at 2.1.236) in both places that carry it -- the `CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION` default in `system/scripts/setup_system.sh` and the `[agent_types.claude].version` pin in `.mngr/settings.toml` -- and the pinned Codex CLI from 0.147.0 to 0.154.0 (`CODEX_VERSION` in `setup_system.sh`).

2.1.269 is the first Claude Code whose binary carries `claude-fable-5-1`, and its `fable[1m]` alias now resolves to Claude Fable 5.1, so the workspace's first chat and the `/model` picker can reach Fable 5.1. Codex 0.154.0 is the first release that knows GPT-6 Astra (`gpt-6-astra`), so a codex chat whose account is entitled to it sees it in the model bar; codex has no static catalog, so nothing else had to change for it.

Drop the vestigial `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_OPUS_4_7_FAST_MODE=1` host env entry, which its own comment scheduled for removal on the next version bump: fast mode for Opus 4.7 was removed upstream in July, so the flag gated nothing on the old pin and gates nothing on the new one.

`system/scripts/migrate_workspace_layouts.py` writes the shell's params-only layout seeds: each migrated panel's `params` carry `kind`, `address`, `tabId`, and `lastFocusedMs` (from `member_last_used.json`), and the record no longer carries a separate `tabs` block. `contracts.md` sections 6 and 7 and the workspace-app-model plan describe the layout file as dockview's document alone, with a panel's identity in its params.

`system/vendor/mngr` refreshed to the mngr commit tagged `minds-v0.6.0` (the gen-2 slice-fleet release: the workspace's vendored mngr gains the 0.6.0 version pin, the gen-2 CI fixes, and everything the gen-2 merge brought), with the root `uv.lock` relocked against it.

Integration branch for the imbue_cloud slice-fleet generation 2 program (mngr-internal `mngr/gen2-combined`: the gen-2 stack plus `main` plus mngr-internal #857, #855 and #856). The template-side changes it carries, each detailed in its own entry here:

- Remote (imbue_cloud) workspaces run their container under gVisor (`runsc`) from the bake, with a "Sandboxed runtime" section in `AGENTS.md` and the `.mngr/settings.toml` comment/rename fixes (`new-fleet-runsc-prototype.md`).

- host_backup keeps no btrfs snapshot between backup ticks and drops the `max_local_snapshots` setting (`new-fleet-phase-2.md`).

- The desktop Lima guest image pins point at imbue's artifact mirror instead of `cloud.debian.org` (`mngr-mirror-upstream-artifacts.md`, the companion of mngr-internal #856).

- The in-container owner-exec daemon pin (`system/scripts/install_owner_exec.sh`) moves from v0.2.1 to v0.2.2, which never authorizes an `authorized_keys` line carrying options (`command=`, `restrict`, `from=`, `cert-authority`); v0.2.1 stripped the options and granted such keys unrestricted exec. The monorepo's VM-install pin moves in lockstep (mngr-internal #870).

- Desktop Lima VMs now download their pinned Debian 13 (trixie) guest image from
  imbue's artifact mirror (`https://apt.imbuepackages.com/artifacts/debian-cloud-image/...`)
  instead of `cloud.debian.org`, which prunes old releases and would eventually
  break every Lima create at the pinned snapshot. Same image bytes, same release
  as the gen-2 cloud slices; mngr's `minds-admin artifacts upload` publishes a new
  release to the mirror before the pin here is bumped.

host_backup no longer keeps a btrfs snapshot between backup ticks and the `max_local_snapshots` setting is removed (mngr-internal `new-fleet-phase-2`, slice-fleet cutover phase 2); see `system/services/host_backup/changelog/new-fleet-phase-2.md`.

Remote (imbue_cloud) workspaces now run their container under gVisor (`runsc`) from the bake, with `/run` and `/tmp` on tmpfs (mngr-internal `new-fleet-runsc-prototype`, slice-fleet cutover phase 1).

- `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md`: a "Sandboxed runtime" section telling the agent what does not work inside the sandbox (ptrace tooling, eBPF, FUSE, io_uring, nested container runtimes, unusual ioctls) and that filesystem-metadata-heavy operations are several times slower.

- `.mngr/settings.toml`: the `[providers.docker]` comment no longer claims the ovh/vultr/imbue_cloud host setup applies the tmpfs mounts (it never did for slices; the slice bake's `-S` overrides do).

- `.mngr/settings.toml`: `auto_dismiss_dialogs` -> `auto_dismiss_dialogs_at_startup` for the claude, codex, pi-coding, and antigravity agent types, following the mngr harness plugins' rename (the old name fails the settings load with current mngr).

- host_backup keeps one on-host btrfs snapshot by default (`max_local_snapshots` 5 -> 1): restic reads only the newest, and each retained snapshot pins its copy-on-write delta on the slice's data disk, which now also holds docker's data-root under a single workspace quota.

### system/apps/chat

Claude Code failures now render as failures in the chat transcript.

Before, a failed turn was recognised by matching its wording for `API Error: <status>`, which most of Claude Code's failures never say. "You've hit your monthly spend limit", "You've hit your session limit", "You're out of usage credits", "Your computer went to sleep mid-response", "Can't reach the API server" and the rest arrived styled as ordinary assistant prose -- reading as if the agent had said them. Across the transcripts on one machine, 160 of 166 recorded failures rendered that way.

Now the chat reads the stamp Claude Code puts on the record itself (`isApiErrorMessage`, the HTTP status, and its own error kind), so the failure is shown in red whatever its wording. Two credential dead ends that the old prose matching also missed -- an OAuth session that expired and could not be refreshed, and `Login expired - Please run /login` -- now get the sign-in action under them. A failure Claude Code attributes to a server but that carries no 5xx status is shown without a cause: it uses that label for failures that never reached a server, so a sleeping laptop or a DNS failure is not blamed on the model provider.

The workspace's default provider account now reaches every `mngr create` that names no harness and no account, not only the chats this app creates.
