The skill keeps its name and stays the single entry point. It no longer restates the driving
commands -- `playwright-cli --help` ships with the pinned version and cannot drift -- and gains
the things `--help` cannot know about this workspace:

* the fleet owns lifecycle, so never `close` / `detach` / `close-all` / `kill-all`
* a session whose socket dropped is unrecoverable: it hangs rather than erroring
* `playwright-cli` exits 1 for everything, so on any failure run `ls` and branch on that
* a crash looks like a plain disconnect from the agent's side, and the dead name must not be
  re-attached
* **"not found" is not "not there"** on a virtualized list -- with a check that tells
  virtualized from infinite-scroll from ordinary-long, and the rule that you are at the bottom
  when rows stop advancing, not when `find` fails
* `mousewheel` fires at (0,0) unless you `hover` the pane you mean first
* snapshots are cheap and screenshots are not, with the narrow set of cases where a screenshot
  is the only thing that can answer the question

The fleet skill's idle-lease figure is corrected from 90s to 60s, which is what the code has
enforced for some time.

This is the merge of `gabriel/tactful-swift` (the inner workspace-updates work) into current `main`. It carries no changes of its own beyond resolving the merge; see that branch's `gabriel-tactful-swift.md` entry for what actually changed.

build-app now requires an icon for every new app: draw a house-style .svg in pre-flight, pass it to the scaffolder via the new required --icon-file (validated with forward_port.py, shipped as system/apps/<package>/icon.svg, registered on every start); the escape-hatch path stores the icon the same way the files app does.

### system

Every harness now launches through the OOM band wrapper, not just claude.

`[agent_types.codex]` and `[agent_types.pi-coding]` in `.mngr/settings.toml` gained the
`command` they were missing. Without it those agents ran unbanded, so under sustained
memory pressure earlyoom shed them by kernel score rather than by the user/worker tiering
-- meaning it could take a user's agent before a worker's build subprocess.

The wrapper is now `agent_oom_launch.py` and names the harness binary in the `command`
itself (`... agent_oom_launch.py codex`), so mngr splices its own flags after that base
exactly as it would after a bare binary name.

- The agy shim's test suite no longer rewrites the checkout it runs from. `test_the_kill_switch_disables_every_guard` really does execute `git rebase -i HEAD~2` (that is the point of the kill switch), and the helper that ran it inherited pytest's cwd -- so with the workspace's `GIT_EDITOR=true` the rebase ran unattended in the repo root. It passed either way, because it only asserted the exit code was not 2 and both a clean rebase (0) and a conflicted one (1) satisfy that. Observed damage: the tree was left mid-rebase and the following 93 tests failed against a half-rebased checkout. The helper now runs every command in a throwaway directory, and the test additionally asserts the guard's block reason is absent rather than inferring it from the exit code.

- `system/scripts/register_vm_exec.sh` skips cleanly on hosts without iproute2 instead of exiting 127. It resolves the gateway with `ip route`, which under `set -euo pipefail` aborted the script before its own "no default gateway; skipping" branch could run -- so supervisord logged `exited: vm-exec-register (exit status 127; not expected)` on every boot of a workspace the script is documented to no-op on. It now probes for `ip` up front and tolerates a failing `ip route`.

Bootstrap installs a permanent update-apply recovery cron entry (`/etc/cron.d/update-apply-recover`, every 5 minutes) at each boot: a plain-python3 `update_self.py recover --if-stale` that rolls back an update apply killed hard without a container restart. It is a silent no-op in every normal state -- it acts only when the apply marker exists, its recorded process is dead, and the marker has gone a grace period without an update. The drop-in carries its own `PATH` line, because cron does not inherit the image's `ENV PATH` and the recovery shells out to `mngr`, `uv` and `npm` to put the running state back, and takes a `flock`, because a tick that acts routinely outlasts the five minutes until the next one; it logs to `/var/log/supervisor/update-apply-recover.log` alongside the other scheduled jobs.

It is written at every boot rather than once by `setup_system.sh`: `/etc/cron.d` lives on the container rootfs, so an entry laid down at provision time is gone the moment the container is recreated -- and this guard is the only thing that recovers an apply whose driving agent is also gone. Writing it from bootstrap, which already knows where the recovery script lives, also stops that path being spelled out in a second place. It goes down before the entries under `data/.state/cron.d`, so a deliberate same-named entry there still overrides it.

`setup_system.sh` pins `HOME=/root` at the top and installs the pinned restic binary by decompress-then-rename, fixing the two live re-provision failures that broke real updates: the Claude installer following an agent's `HOME=/home/user` into the wrong home while the version check read `/root/.local/bin/claude`, and `bunzip2 -c > /usr/local/bin/restic` truncating a binary the running `host_backup` service was executing (ETXTBSY). `_provision_guard.sh` honors `PROVISION_FORCE=1`, which runs a guarded step even when the tree's marker matches: the update apply's rollback re-provisions from the restored tree, and that tree is exactly the one the marker was written for, so the re-run that puts the global toolchain back would otherwise be skipped. The root pytest config stops recursing into `data/`, so a staged skill copy under `data/.tasks/` (which ships its own test file) no longer breaks a bare `uv run pytest` with a basename collision.

`setup_system.sh` is now the only path that installs a global binary: the owner-exec daemon and the dufs file-viewer server, previously each its own Dockerfile layer, are chained from it like the secret scanners and agy, so an already-running workspace taking an update that ships or bumps either gets the binary from the apply's live provisioner re-run instead of a service that starts, fails to find it, and retry-loops until a rebuild. A new `system/test_provisioner_single_entry.py` holds the Dockerfile to that shape (no `RUN default-workspace-template-install-*` other than the in-repo dependency installer, and every `install*.sh` under `system/scripts/` named in `setup_system.sh`).

The Dockerfile no longer carries the toolchain version pins as `ARG`/`ENV` (Claude Code, Codex, Node, pi, opencode, the pi extensions). Nothing ever passed a build arg, and the `ENV` half persisted the image's versions into every process in the container, where a live re-run of `setup_system.sh` read them over the merged tree's `:=` defaults: an update bumping Claude Code reinstalled the image's old version, passed the script's own pin check against the same stale variable, and reported success, after which the merged `agent_types.claude.version` pin refused every new claude agent. `setup_system.sh` is the single source of truth for every pin, and `test_workspace_claude_config.py` asserts the Dockerfile stays free of them. The `@playwright/cli` pin, which only the Dockerfile's `ENV` had carried, now has its `setup_system.sh` default too, and `test_provisioner_single_entry.py` checks that every `*_VERSION` the script expands has one.

The mngr plugin set the workspace registers now lives in one place, `system/config/mngr_plugins.toml`, naming each plugin's path and which tool environments (mngr, system-interface) it goes into; `system/scripts/list_mngr_plugins.py --tool <name>` prints one tool's paths. `build_workspace.sh` reads it for the image build's `uv tool install --with-editable` and `mngr plugin add --path` calls, and the update-self apply reads the same file after a merge, so a release that adds a plugin registers it in the workspaces it updates rather than only in freshly built images.

The safe-update-apply blueprint keeps only its plan; the incident review and the review findings that used to sit beside it are folded into the mngr-internal tracker (`blueprint/inner-workspace-updates/open-threads.md`), which the plan now points at, so there is one record of what is still open across both repos.

CI runs the system interface frontend's vitest suite (`npm run test`) before building the bundle; until now only the build's type check ran there, so a failing frontend test never failed a PR. The four files prettier flagged on main are formatted so the suite's formatting check passes.

Bump the Latchkey version to 3.9.0.

# Pin @playwright/cli; vendor browser extensions; split the browser-automation guidance

**`@playwright/cli` is now installed in the image**, pinned as `ARG PLAYWRIGHT_CLI_VERSION`
in `system/Dockerfile` and installed by `setup_system.sh`, matching how Claude Code, Codex,
Pi and latchkey are pinned. It is the agent's browser-driving interface now that the browser
service no longer ships driving verbs. (Note it is `@playwright/cli`; the bare
`playwright-cli` package on npm is a deprecated stub.)

**Browser extensions moved into the Fortress env.d unit.** `browser-use` used to download
three extensions from the Chrome Web Store on a user's FIRST browser launch -- into the
browser holding their real logins, chosen by the dependency, with a network call in the
launch path. uBlock Origin Lite and "I still don't care about cookies" are now fetched once
at converge and chosen here; "Force Background Tab" is dropped, since opening links in
background tabs fought the pane's active-tab follow. Deliberately not version-pinned: the CRX
endpoint only serves the current build for an id, so a pin could only ever be a post-hoc
mismatch log. What this fixes is the timing and the ownership, not the version.

**`CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` now split browser automation by situation**, because picking the
wrong tool was the easy mistake: the fleet for anything the user should see or that needs
their real logins or their help, Playwright's Python API for headless scripting with no human
in the loop. Both run on Fortress, and the Fortress install/gVisor notes are unchanged.

**Root dependencies:** the `openai>=2.20.0` override in `pyproject.toml` is removed. It
existed only to reconcile `browser-use`'s exact `openai==2.16.0` pin with litellm, and
`browser-use` is gone -- along with 228 packages from the lockfile.

Two more harnesses can be launched from the workspace: OpenCode and Antigravity (`agy`). Both binaries are baked into the image at pinned versions, both mngr plugins are registered, and both get a New Tab tile beside Codex and Pi.

This is the launch path only. Neither harness reads its transcript yet, so a chat tab on one opens blank and its model bar is empty -- the point of this change is that `mngr create <name> --type opencode` and `--type antigravity` work at all, which they previously did not: the shared `chat` role template sets an output style, and neither plugin had anywhere to put one, so mngr rejected the create outright rather than launching an agent that would silently ignore its role.

Both harnesses also launch inside an OOM priority band, like Claude, Codex and Pi. Without one, earlyoom sheds an agent by raw kernel score rather than the user/worker tiering, so it could take a user's chat before a worker's build subprocess.

Agy chats display their conversation and a live activity indicator. Until now an Agy agent could be created and would run, but its chat tab stayed empty.

Agy chats also handle permission prompts, hide task-tracker bookkeeping, and keep the important parts of long tool output when it is shortened -- matching the other harnesses.

Refreshed `system/vendor/mngr` from the git archive of mngr `28484c1e54a71ef31a1c0e37f2a26d94c342192a` (mngr main plus the minds 0.4.3 version bump) and relocked the root `uv.lock`, as part of cutting the minds-v0.4.3 release. No `system_interface` or other consumer changes ride along; the vendor tree is verified by reproduction against the tagged mngr SHA per the release runbook.

Claude agents now deal with a dialog that is holding the TUI's input at send time, instead of failing the send.

`sensibly_deal_with_dialogs` lists the confirmations mngr may answer on the user's behalf. It is set to the model bar's own two: picking a model or an effort level sends `/model <slug>` or `/effort <level>`, and claude then asks to confirm that switching mid-session re-reads the whole history. The user already made that choice in the picker, so mngr completes it — by cycling the selector onto the named option, never by pressing Enter on whatever happens to be highlighted. Anything else that needs a real answer refuses the send with an error naming what is in the way; anything Esc closes harmlessly is dismissed regardless of the list.

`auto_dismiss_dialogs` is renamed `auto_dismiss_dialogs_at_startup` for claude, codex and pi-coding. Same behaviour; the name now says when it applies, which matters more now that a second dialog setting exists.

Claude also runs with `tui = "fullscreen"`, which pins the input bar and any dialog to the pane rather than letting them scroll out of view — so what mngr captures at send time is what is actually holding the input. tmux here runs with `alternate-screen off`, so the workspace terminal panel keeps its scrollback either way.

Claude agents now answer every dialog mngr knows a sensible answer for (`sensibly_deal_with_dialogs = ["ALL_KNOWN_DIALOGS"]`), rather than the two named model and effort switch confirmations. A dialog only becomes answerable by being given a specific option to land on, and mngr reaches it by cycling the selector onto that option rather than pressing Enter on whatever is highlighted, so opting into all of them grants no power to guess: a usage-limit prompt is answered "stop and wait for the limit to reset" and an LSP-install prompt is declined. Anything with no sensible answer still refuses to send, and anything Esc closes harmlessly is still just dismissed. The previous explicit list silently stopped covering each dialog added upstream -- a usage-limit or LSP-install prompt blocked sends outright until someone noticed.


The claude agent now opts into answering dialogs with `ALL_KNOWN_DIALOGS` rather than a wildcard: every dialog mngr can name, each answered on the option named for it, growing with the catalogue without ever becoming a guess. A dialog mngr cannot name still refuses the send rather than being guessed at, whatever the list says.

Claude agents now fall back to pressing `1` on a dialog mngr cannot name, via `sensibly_deal_with_dialogs = ["ALL_KNOWN_AND_UNKNOWN_DIALOGS"]`, instead of refusing the send. A named dialog is still answered on its own chosen option; only the unnamed case is a guess. It is chosen deliberately for a workspace: chat has no good way to show a dialog nobody has named, so refusing there strands the message until someone opens the terminal tab. The guess is bounded -- the digit is only sent to a pane actually showing a numbered selector, so it is never typed as text into whatever holds the input, and a surface that does not clear still refuses the send rather than being pressed at repeatedly. Narrowing this to `ALL_KNOWN_DIALOGS` restores refusing anything unnamed.

Fixed the model bar showing "Unrecognized model" after an agent restart. Fast mode is kept in the agent's launch settings, because Claude Code deletes the key on `/fast off` rather than writing false, so the session's own state is not recoverable from what it writes. The model is not kept there -- it is re-read from the session -- so the flag outlives the model it was chosen for. Any path that changes one without the other produces "model without fast, fast=true": a restart landing on a different model than the one you picked, or a switch onto a model that has no fast. The catalog matcher treated that pairing as an unknown model and blanked the bar, which was wrong twice over, since the model is one the catalog knows perfectly well and the flag is merely stale. Fast is no longer a matching condition; a matched model that does not support it drops the flag instead. This lives in the shared reader, so claude and codex both get it and neither carries its own repair.

A send that landed and was then blocked by a dialog now says so. mngr keeps that outcome apart from a failure -- the message was accepted, so it is recorded in `blocked_agents` rather than as a failure -- and the chat read only the failure list, so a blocked send fell through to the catch-all and reported that the agent could not be reached. That was false, and because the recovery buttons follow the failure kind, it withheld the Retry that answering the dialog makes work and offered a restart instead. The blocked outcome is now carried through in the dialog's own words, classified as a blocked input.

Taught `system/scripts/layout.py`'s service-URL recognizer the workspace-keyed share-domain shape (`<share-label>.<user-hash>.<region>.<domain>`), whose coordinate leads with a bare 32-hex share label instead of a `host-<hex>` machine label, keeping it in step with its `system_interface/layout_ops.py` mirror (see that project's entry for the full story). It also gained a first-label guard so the bare workspace-keyed origin -- whose user-hash label is also bare 32-hex -- is never misread as a service URL.

This is the merge of `gabriel/tactful-swift` (the inner workspace-updates work) into current `main`. It carries no changes of its own beyond resolving the merge; see that branch's `gabriel-tactful-swift.md` entry for what actually changed.

- Fixed agent creation on the Lima and Modal providers, which aborted with
  `setup_system.sh: PLAYWRIGHT_CLI_VERSION: unbound variable`. `@playwright/cli`
  was pinned only as a `system/Dockerfile` `ARG`, so it was defined for image
  builds and unset everywhere the script runs directly -- under `set -u`.
  `setup_system.sh` now carries its own `: "${PLAYWRIGHT_CLI_VERSION:=0.1.18}"`
  default, like every other pinned tool.

- Added `system/toolchain_pins_test.py`: fails if `setup_system.sh` expands a
  `${..._VERSION}` it does not also default. CI never runs that script, so
  nothing else catches a pin that leaves the non-docker providers broken.

# Globally unique terminal server_registered event ids

- The terminal app's `server_registered` discovery event id was derived from only the service name and URL, so every workspace (and every restart) emitted the same id -- and analytics, which collects these events fleet-wide and dedupes by event id, saw the whole fleet collapse to one event. The id now hashes in the emission timestamp, which is upgraded from hardcoded zero nanoseconds to real nanosecond precision.

The bug-report diagnostics collector's output contract is now one line: the base64 of the archive. The JSON envelope, contract version, and omissions mapping are gone -- anything withheld (a secret-scan finding, a scanner that could not run, a workspace with no conversations) is a plain-words line in the archive's own `collection-notes.txt` member, so the archive explains itself.

Collection scope widened and tightened at once: every agent's conversation is a transcript candidate (chats, background workers, and the primary services agent alike -- previously only human-opened chats), at least the five newest ride along on top of everything written to in the last two hours, and every program's log in the supervisor dir is sent (owner and stream unfiltered, supervisord's own included) so long as it was written to in the last day.

The collector's mngr calls are scoped to what can answer from inside a container: `mngr list --provider local` skips the cloud-provider probing that used to consume most of the collection budget, and each `mngr event` targets the pinned `name@host.provider` address the listing handed out.

forward_port.py now refuses a registration that would create a brand-new pickable entry without an icon, so new apps cannot fall back to the generic letter monogram; existing entries re-register untouched. Icons are registered solely via --icon-file (.svg only) -- the inline --icon markup flag is removed -- and a new --no-icon flag skips the requirement, keeping the generic letter monogram (it does not hide the entry -- that is --internal's job); the built-in system_interface/browser/terminal registrations and preview instances use it.
A bad icon file fails a new registration but only warns on an existing app's re-registration (the stored icon is kept), so a corrupted icon cannot crash-loop a running app.

Realigned the vendored mngr snapshot (`system/vendor/mngr/`) to main's current copy while merging main into this branch. The permission-state changes themselves ship from the mngr side (imbue-ai/mngr-internal#596) and reach this snapshot through the normal release sync; the dev flow overlays the live mngr checkout regardless.

# Close tab rename in the lifecycle spec

The rail-shortcuts-and-app-lifecycle spec now says "Close tab" where it said
"Hide tab", matching the renamed tab-menu verb.

Added the transcript smooth-scroll design spec (docs/system/specs/transcript-smooth-scroll.md): three layers (Visible / Physical / Virtual), two strict state machines (FOLLOW / USER_CONTROLLED scroll position, ELSEWHERE / SCROLLBAR scrollbar interaction), a custom overlay scrollbar with pixel-space physical and index-space virtual regions, and a 3-PR delivery plan.

CI's frontend step now runs the vitest unit-test suite (npm test) in addition to the typecheck and build.

CI runs the frontend test suite on Node 22 (was 20, which is past end-of-life and lacks the global `navigator` that Projects.test.ts exercises -- the suite's six failures on this branch's PR were all Node-20-only).

Added system/scripts/scroll_verification/: a standalone system-interface fixture server (serving a real session JSONL as an agent transcript) plus a Playwright driver that manually verifies the scroll engine's must-pass scenarios with content-relative measurements.

Marked the scroll portions of docs/system/specs/chat-scroll-and-selection-bugs.md as superseded by transcript-smooth-scroll.md: the machinery it diagnoses has been replaced by the transcript scroll engine (phase 3 deleted it).

The scroll verification driver (system/scripts/scroll_verification/verify_scroll.py) now gates FOLLOW pinning on sustained painted gaps (single-frame transients are bounded by the engine's list ResizeObserver) and its imports are sorted.

CI now runs the frontend test suite on Node 22 (was 20, which is past end-of-life and lacks the global `navigator` that Projects.test.ts exercises -- the suite's six failures on this branch's PRs were all Node-20-only).

The scroll verification driver waits out the engine's persistence debounce before clearing storage between phases, and polls for the restore trace record instead of assuming a fixed reload settle time, so both checks hold on transcripts that have grown past 15k events.

The scroll verification suite's A1 check is now cap-aware: it passes when the whole transcript is physical, or when a transcript larger than PHYSICAL_CAP_EVENTS converges to a cap-sized window at the live tail with no fill in flight (the engine exposes capEvents in its debug state). All 22 checks pass against a 6.8k-event fixture with a 5k cap.

### system/apps/system_interface

The OOM prioritizer resolves an agent's `*_process_started` marker filename from its
`HarnessSpec` instead of from a live activity-tracker instance.

The filename is harness identity, known as soon as the agent is. Reading it off a tracker
meant `_read_agent_process_started_at` returned `None` for any agent whose tracker had not
been registered yet -- and `_ensure_activity_tracking` skips every agent with no local
state dir -- so the prioritizer silently fell back to "no marker" and lost its aging for
exactly the agents it most needs to age. The tracker keeps its own `marker_filename`, which
it uses to bound transcript staleness; a test pins the two to the same value so they cannot
drift.

Regenerate the frontend `pnpm-lock.yaml` so it resolves `jsdom`. `package.json` already declared `jsdom: ^30.0.1` as a dev dependency (the vitest test environment), but the committed lockfile predated it and left the package unresolved, so `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` -- how CI and fresh checkouts install -- would fail the lockfile-consistency check. Relocking adds the `jsdom@30.0.1` entry and its transitive dependencies and threads `jsdom` into the `vitest` resolution. Build tooling only; no user-visible behaviour change.

The system interface hardens against update-time version skew.

Its single mngr `load_config` call site now parses with `strict=False`, so a `.mngr/settings.toml` written for a newer mngr degrades to a logged warning instead of a 500 on every agent listing and message send (the lockout that made a broken update self-locking). `mngr config set` and the CLI keep strict parsing.

The server records the tree HEAD it started from and injects a `system-interface-update-staleness` meta tag into the built app shell when the live tree has moved under it in a way that affects what this process runs (backend code, its dependency manifests, the vendored mngr, `.mngr/settings.toml` -- never ordinary agent commits, docs, or the frontend, whose bundle is rebuilt without a restart) -- `updated-not-activated`, `update-interrupted` when the update apply's marker is present, or `update-emergency` when a failed update's rollback could not restore a healthy workspace -- and a small informational banner renders the three messages, pointing the user at their agent (the meta tag is the whole surface: nothing reads a response header, so the shell does not carry one). The emergency variant outranks the other two and is the only one whose copy does not tell the user to wait: it is the one state here that will not resolve on its own, and it is invisible to both other checks (that exit clears the marker, and the rollback puts the tree content back).

The reveal machinery that lived in `reveal_system_interface.py` moved into the general update apply (`update_self.py apply`); the script keeps only the pre-merge `preview`/`unpreview` adapters, and going live is now one atomic merge-and-reveal with no agent-prose pause between landing and activation.

The frontend build now stamps its output: an npm `postbuild` step writes the git tree hash of the frontend source directory into `static/.source-tree-hash` (best-effort; absent when the build runs without a git repo). The update apply compares that stamp against the merged tree so a `--worker-bundle` built from other frontend source is never served as if it were the merged source (the apply builds live instead); a live build's stamp is checked the same way as a consistency guard.

A chat asking to have its tab surfaced (the `assist` label, or the new purpose-neutral `auto_open` label) is now shown its tab once, reliably, instead of only if a browser happened to be connected the instant it appeared. Before, the open was a broadcast to whoever was connected: a chat created from outside the workspace -- the minds app's update flow -- appeared while the user was still on their way in, so the open went to nobody and the tab never showed. The open is now held until a client has registered, and which chats have been shown is remembered on disk beside the saved layouts, so the interface that comes up after an update's own restart neither re-pops a tab the previous one surfaced nor loses one it never got to show: a recent chat found at startup that no client has seen (an update run overnight) is shown on the next connection, while older ones are left as the saved layout has them.


The bundle directory the shell routes serve from is now ordinary state configuration: `SystemInterfaceState.static_directory` defaults to the package's own `static/` and the routes read it from the state, instead of a module constant plus a `None`-means-default override that only a test ever set (and that the bundle tests patched around with `unittest.mock`).

# Drop key_available from the browser-create response

`POST /api/browsers` no longer returns `key_available`. The field reported whether an
Anthropic API key was present, which mattered only for the browser service's LLM-driven
`task` verb -- that verb is gone, and nothing in the browser needs a key any more. The
frontend never read the field; only the `createBrowser` test fixture mentioned it, and that
fixture is updated to match what the daemon actually sends.

No user-visible change to the workspace UI.

The harness registry knows about `opencode` and `antigravity`, so an agent created on either is treated as itself rather than mistaken for Claude. Both appear in the New Tab launcher.

Registering them was not optional. An unregistered harness is not neutral: `parse_harness` falls an unknown agent type back to Claude, which would have pointed Claude's transcript watcher at another harness's state directory. But a `HarnessSpec` requires a watcher, an activity tracker, a model resolver and a model catalog, and neither harness has any of those yet -- so both name a shared set of deliberately inert placeholders instead. The placeholder transcript is empty, the placeholder catalog offers nothing, and switching a model does nothing. The one live signal is the activity dot, which follows mngr's `active` marker: both plugins already maintain it, so a turn in flight shows as "Thinking…" even with no transcript behind it.

Each harness drops its own placeholder when it lands a real implementation, one harness at a time; when the last one does, the shared placeholder module goes with it.

Both harnesses launch through the shared OOM band wrapper. A test now reads `.mngr/settings.toml` and fails if any registered harness has no wrapper in its launch command -- an unbanded harness is silent (nothing errors, the agent is just disproportionately likely to be killed under memory pressure), which is how Codex and Pi went unbanded unnoticed.

OpenCode gets no New Tab tile. The harness stays registered -- so an opencode agent created from a terminal is identified as itself rather than mistaken for Claude, and its mngr plugin stays on the same launch contract as the others -- but it is not planned to get a transcript watcher, and a tile would promise a chat that always renders blank.

An Agy chat now shows its conversation. The tab was rendering blank -- the harness was registered so it could launch, but nothing read its transcript.

Agy keeps each conversation in its own SQLite database rather than a log file, so the reader tails that store directly, and it is careful about half-written rows: it only advances past a step once that step has settled, and re-reads anything still in progress until it does.

The activity indicator and its caption come with it. Agy records a tool call the moment it dispatches one, with the tool's name and arguments already filled in, so the chat can say "Running python3 showcase.py" while the command is still running rather than after it finishes. One quirk needed handling: Agy writes a short empty "deciding what to do next" step before each tool call, which would otherwise look like a finished answer and make the indicator flicker to idle between every tool.

The model bar is not part of this and still shows nothing for Agy.

Agy's tool results now go through the same handling as every other harness. Permission prompts appear as the usual approval card instead of raw text, so an Agy agent asking for access can actually be answered. Task-tracker bookkeeping commands are hidden as the structural markers they are rather than shown as work. And when a long tool result is shortened for display, the parts the chat reads out of it -- the approval request, the step-tracking lines -- are kept instead of being cut off the end.

The indicator also settles correctly after an interrupted restart. Agy picks its conversation back up where it left off, so a tool call left unfinished by the previous run was still in the store and could leave the indicator running forever; each launch now records when it started, and anything older than that is treated as finished.

Creating an Agy chat while Agy is signed out is now refused up front, with instructions, instead of producing an agent that can never take a turn -- the same preflight Codex and Pi already had. Typing `/model` or `/effort` into an Agy or OpenCode chat is declined and points at the model picker, the way it is on every other harness. `/fast` is only declined on the harnesses that actually have a fast mode -- on the others the notice would point at a control that is not shown.

Agy chats show which model they are running. The bar is display-only for Agy -- its model is changed from the agent's own terminal, not from the chat -- so it renders as a single, non-clickable name with no effort or speed controls, because Agy has neither: the tier is part of the model name itself. If Agy reports a model newer than the list the workspace ships with, the name is reconstructed from its id so the bar still reads sensibly instead of showing a shrug.

Messages sent to a busy Agy agent now show up as queued instead of being swallowed. Agy only accepts a new message once it has fully finished a turn, and it silently merges anything typed at it mid-turn into a single block -- so a second message would arrive but leave its bubble stuck on "Sending..." forever. The workspace now holds those messages itself and delivers them the moment Agy is free, so what the chat shows matches what Agy actually has.

Stop and shoulder tap work on Agy. Stop ends the current turn and puts everything that had not been sent yet back in the composer, in order, without restarting the agent. Shoulder tap ends the turn and sends the waiting messages straight away instead of waiting for Agy to finish.

The message lifecycle for Agy is covered by the same conservation test the other harnesses have: randomised rounds of sending, stopping and tapping, checking after every round that each message ended up in exactly one place -- delivered, or back in the composer -- never lost and never duplicated.

A message sent to an idle Agy no longer flashes through a queued state. It stayed "Sending…" in principle already -- the backend only marks a message queued when a turn is actually open -- but the chat drew the "Queued messages" header and the shoulder-tap button above it anyway, so a message that was on its way looked parked. The group now appears only when something genuinely is waiting. Codex gets the same fix: its shoulder-tap resend was mislabelled the same way.

A queued message also no longer briefly appears twice as it is delivered. The chip is removed before the turn it became is shown, which was already how the delivery path worked -- but the watcher reads Agy's transcript from two places at once, and the other one usually noticed the new turn first and put it on screen while the chip was still there. That path now waits for the hand-off, so the message is only ever in one state at a time.

Agy's progress timeline now renders. It never had: the code that reads Agy's transcript was guessing at the format rather than reading it, and the guess returned each command's arguments instead of its output -- for every tool call, since the harness shipped. The progress view is built entirely from lines the task tracker prints when it runs, so with the output missing there was nothing to draw and no step ever appeared. The same fix restores the output of every other Agy command too, which had been just as invisible.

Agy tool calls also read better in the activity line. Agy writes its own short description of each call ("Creating step", "Running test call 1 of 20"), which we were reading from the wrong place and always getting nothing. Seven Agy tools that previously showed their raw internal name -- background tasks, scheduling, sub-agent management, file search, and the question prompt -- now show a proper label.

Behind the scenes, the rule for recognising a task-tracker command was copy-pasted into all four harnesses and is now defined once, and the chat no longer has any harness-specific knowledge baked into it -- which is what left Agy as the only harness with no fallback when decoration was missing.

Codex agents can edit files again. A guard meant for shell commands was also inspecting Codex's file edits -- Codex delivers an edit through the same channel as a command, with the patch text where the command normally goes -- so editing any file that merely *mentioned* piping into `head` or `tail` was refused outright and the whole batch of work was abandoned. The guards now only look at actual shell commands.

Closed a hole where Codex could run commands the guards never saw: it could open a shell with one checked command and then type further commands into it, none of which were checked. That way of driving a shell is switched off; ordinary commands are unaffected.

Codex work no longer disappears from the chat. Codex can put several commands in a single tool call, and the chat was judging the whole call by the first one -- so a call that began with a task-tracking command was treated as bookkeeping and hidden, taking any real work in the same call with it. Those calls now render as ordinary work.

Antigravity agents now get the two reminders every other harness already had: the carry-over of steps left open from a previous turn, and the prompt to declare a step before doing substantive work. Neither had any way to reach Antigravity before. The step reminder covers shell work only -- Antigravity's own file-editing tools are invisible to it -- and reminders never affect whether a command succeeds.

The reminder to declare a step also got more accurate everywhere: it no longer fires on read-only commands like `ls` or `cat`, it correctly recognises a bare `ticket` command, and it no longer mistakes a word like `gtk` for a task-tracker call.

Pi's refusal messages now match the other harnesses word for word, so the same mistake gets the same explanation whichever agent you are talking to.

Removed six design documents whose work has shipped. Their durable content -- the measured shape of Antigravity's transcript and hook surface, the per-harness state of each guard, and how to re-measure both -- now lives in the harness contracts and the transcript-schema reference, which is where someone changing this code will actually look. Deleting a plan once it is built keeps the next reader from following a stale map.

Added `docs/specs/send-failure-notice.md`: a spec for showing a failed send inside the workspace instead of in a native system alert. Any send failure -- a dialog holding the agent's input, a readiness timeout, a transport error -- would open the same in-app notice the workspace already uses for declined commands, with a title, the failure text, and an OK button that Enter, Space, and Escape all dismiss. Not scoped to dialog errors, and deliberately not a harness-declared popup: those fire before a message is sent, off what the user typed, whereas this reports what the backend refused.

A send that fails now says why, inside the workspace. Previously the reason was discarded deep in the send path -- the messenger reduced mngr's result to a yes/no -- so the chat could only report "Failed to send message to agent 'Chat 2' (0 successful agents)", and it reported it through a native system alert. The harness's own words now travel to the chat, which shows them in the same notice style the workspace already uses for declined commands: a title, the reason, and an OK button that Enter, Space, Escape, and a click outside all dismiss. So a message refused because the agent is sitting on an unsubmitted shell command now says exactly that, and which keys resolve it. A failed interrupt uses the same notice. The `/welcome` resend logs the reason it failed rather than just that it did.

Specced giving that notice actions rather than only an explanation: Cancel (returns the message to the composer, prepended to any draft already there), Retry (runs the same send again), and Force (restarts the agent, then sends). Generalized deliberately -- the explanation varies per failure, the three ways out do not -- with the actions attached to the operation rather than the failure kind, so a failed interrupt, which shares this notice, still shows a single OK.

Added `docs/specs/chat-send-failure-system.md`, which maps the four layers that now decide what happens when a message does not reach an agent -- the harness-declared composer guards, mngr's send preflight and its dialog catalogue, the chat's failure notice, and the proposed recovery actions -- says which question each one can and cannot answer, and states where a given change belongs. Also records the two known rough edges: the Enter retry that can answer a picker nobody looked at, and bare `/effort` and `/model` being invisible from chat.

The failed-send notice now offers Cancel, Retry and Force instead of only an acknowledgement. Cancel returns the message to the composer, placed in front of any draft typed while the send was in flight, so neither is lost. Retry runs the ordinary send again -- useful once the user has opened the agent's terminal and dealt with whatever was in the way, which the notice now suggests. Force restarts the agent and then sends; it ends any turn in progress, so it is styled as the destructive choice and says what it does on hover. A failed interrupt, which shares this notice, still shows a single OK: the actions belong to the operation, and an interrupt has nothing to repeat.

Every notice in the chat is now one component. The overlay, the Escape key, the backdrop press and the focused first button live in one place instead of being re-typed per notice -- which they had been, and had already drifted: the agent-auth notice answered Escape not at all, and only some focused a button. A view other than the composer raises a failure through the same notice rather than a system alert, so flushing the queued messages and failing now reads exactly like failing to send, with the same Retry. Nothing in the send path opens a native dialog any more. An attachment that fails to upload also refuses the send and names the file, instead of being quietly dropped from the message.

Extended the layer map with the tmux pipeline underneath it, and with who decides which buttons a failure earns: mngr names the kind of failure, the workspace maps kinds to buttons, so a missing pane offers a restart rather than a Retry that cannot work. Also records what Retry and Force actually are, so neither drifts from the behaviour it mirrors.

A failed send now says what KIND of failure it was, and the chat offers only the recoveries that can actually work. An agent whose terminal is gone no longer offers Retry -- it would fail every time -- and says that restarting is the only way to deliver the message; a blocked input keeps Retry, because a person can clear it. mngr classifies the situation and stops there, since it has no notion of a button; the mapping from a kind to what the user is offered lives in the workspace. Anything mngr did not classify behaves exactly as before.

Force now says what it does on hover: "Restarts agent to reset it & resends message".

Fixed three ways the recovery notice could destroy what it was holding. Taking Retry or Force cleared the whole composer on success, which threw away both a draft typed while the send was failing and -- after Force -- the queued messages it had just rescued out of the agent; it now removes only the copy that was delivered. Restoring a failed message replaced the composer's attachments rather than merging, dropping anything attached while the send was in flight. And the notice component registered an Escape listener it could never remove, so every redraw left another one behind.

Force no longer leaves the message it just sent sitting in the composer. It rescues the agent's queued messages into the box before restarting, which pushed the delivered message down from the front, and the clean-up only looked at the front. A retry that fails for a different reason than the first now updates which buttons are offered, so a send that becomes unreachable mid-recovery stops offering a retry that cannot work.

Force is no longer offered while an agent is merely still starting, where restarting would discard the session it was about to finish bringing up. A retried message shows the same "sending" bubble an ordinary one does, instead of vanishing until the backend catches up. Attachments that were delivered are removed whether or not the user typed something else in the meantime -- they used to be left behind and sent again with the next message. And a failed queue flush reports the harness's own reason rather than a generic sentence.

Force no longer restarts the agent twice when it had queued messages -- rescuing those already restarts it. A failure raised from the queued-messages view now carries the same classification the composer's own failures do, so the two agree about what to offer for the same failure. An upload failure can no longer appear on a chat the user switched to while the upload was still running, and a failure raised for a chat that is never opened is dropped rather than surfacing later as a modal about something long past.

Taught the service-origin derivation the workspace-keyed share-domain shape (`<share-label>.<user-hash>.<region>.<domain>`), whose coordinate leads with a bare 32-hex share label instead of a `host-<hex>` machine label. Before this, every service panel in a workspace shared under the new domain shape derived a nested hostname (`<service-label>.<shell-label>.<share-label>...`) that the relay has no tunnel claim for, so panels died with an `SSL_ERROR_UNRECOGNIZED_NAME_ALERT` TLS error in the visitor's browser.

Updated the three copies of the rule inside this app: the canonical `frontend/src/origin.ts`, the frontend-not-built placeholder page's inline mirror in `server.py`, and the service-URL recognizer in `layout_ops.py` (which also gained a first-label guard so the bare workspace-keyed origin -- whose user-hash label is also bare 32-hex -- is never misread as a service URL).

The Claude sign-in modal's "Sign in with Imbue" deep link is now keyed by the workspace's id (its `system-services` agent id, read from the `is_primary`-labeled agent's state) instead of the machine's host id, so the link keeps working if the workspace ever changes machines. The machine's host id remains the fallback coordinate when the agent state is unreadable, and the desktop app dual-accepts both. The status field carrying it is renamed `workspace_host_id` -> `workspace_id` (internal to the system interface and its own frontend).

This is the merge of `gabriel/tactful-swift` (the inner workspace-updates work) into current `main`; see that branch's `gabriel-tactful-swift.md` entry for what actually changed.

The one conflict resolved here is in the frontend stylesheet, where `main`'s transcript custom-scrollbar rules and the update-staleness banner rules were both appended at the end of the file. Both are kept, so the transcript scrollbar and the update-staleness banner each render as their own branch intended.

Merged the workspace-id claude sign-in branch (`mngr/fix-machine-workspace-naming`, default-workspace-template PR #443) into this branch. The change itself is described in this project's `mngr-fix-machine-workspace-naming` changelog entry.

Two small workspace-UI polish fixes:

- The project picker dropdown now anchors its horizontals on the rail card itself (and the menu placement's left floor no longer pushes a menu right of its own anchor), so the picker's left border sits flush with the rail panel's border instead of 2px inside it.

- The four "Open new" tiles on the New Tab screen (Chat, File viewer, Browser, Terminal) now carry hover tooltips, reusing the rail shortcuts' copy for the same four kinds. The unbacked file viewer keeps its "coming soon" explanation, and all tooltips still drop while a create is in flight.

- The rail now sits 1px lower, so its header row's visible top edge -- the project picker bar -- lands exactly on the tab chips' top edge instead of 1px above it, and the divider under the header lines up with the pane card's top border.

# Permission cards stop showing stale or swapped verdicts

Fixed the in-chat permission cards' two ways of lying about a request's state, per the consolidated diagnosis in mngr's `specs/permission_state.md`.

Verdicts now correlate strictly by request id: the resolution notice minds sends carries the resolved request's own id, and the timeline walk pairs each verdict with the card that owns it, so out-of-order resolutions no longer swap Approved/Denied badges and a message batching several requests resolves each card independently. The old arrival-order guess -- the very mechanism that produced the swaps -- is deleted rather than kept as a fallback; a notice with no id (pre-dating id embedding) attributes nothing, and embedded pages recover such verdicts through hydration instead.

Cards also hydrate on page build: the embedding chrome pushes the workspace's recent verdicts (embed contract v3, drawn from the desktop client's durable response log) into every freshly loaded page, so a reloaded page never offers Approve and Deny for an already-decided request -- the page itself asks for nothing. The same `minds:permission-resolutions` message carries the instant flip when the user resolves a request live, replacing the v2 push type. Without an embedder, or with one predating v3, cards keep the previous transcript-driven behavior.

Permission cards no longer get stuck showing the raw scope id (e.g. `google-gmail-api`) instead of the service name: the scope-info lookup used to cache any failed fetch as a permanent null, so one transient gateway outage (a 502 during a gateway restart) pinned every card to raw ids for the life of the page. Transient failures now retry after a short delay; only a definitive 404 (no such catalog entry) or 503 (no gateway configured) keeps the raw scope.

# Share button deep link (workspace side)

Clicking Share on an app tab's menu or a sidebar app row now asks the
embedding minds chrome (via the embed contract's new
`minds:open-share-settings` type) to open its Share page focused on that app,
replacing the instructional popup that told the user where to go. The popup
(`ShareModal`) and its styles are deleted.

The deep link takes effect with the next minds release: until the vendored
contract sync lands, an older minds chrome ignores the message and the click
is a no-op, per the contract's tolerant policy. Opened directly in a browser
(no embedder), the click is likewise a no-op, matching the permission card's
"Review & respond" button.

The tab and rail object menus are reordered into an acting group (Refresh,
Share, Add to project) and a removal group in increasing severity (Close tab
-- previously labeled "Hide tab" -- Remove from project, Stop, Delete). An
app instance's service verbs now sit in those ordinary positions instead of a
trailing group. Share rows use the lucide user-plus icon, matching the minds
shell's sharing surfaces.

Phase 1 of the transcript smooth-scroll rework (docs/system/specs/transcript-smooth-scroll.md): the pure scroll engine under frontend/src/models/transcriptScroll/, not yet wired into any view.

- Strict TypeScript state machines: scroll position (FOLLOW / USER_CONTROLLED with a row-key + px-offset anchor) and scrollbar interaction (ELSEWHERE / SCROLLBAR with a frozen track mapping), as pure exhaustive reducers.

- Physical-layer geometry: exact row prefix sums, anchor resolution with an exact scrollTop round-trip, and the visible-row window computation.

- Custom-scrollbar track math: the physical region maps in pixel space, virtual end regions in event-index space; live mapping, fraction-to-target resolution, and thumb placement.

- Virtual end-spacer sizing from the measured physical average with smoothing, each update paired with its exact scrollTop compensation.

- Progressive-fill planner for the physical window (instant tail page, chunked growth toward the user, jump-window replacement, cap eviction and re-centering).

- Persistence codec for the per-agent scroll state and a ring-buffer scroll trace for the ?debug=scroll instrumentation.

- Frontend CI now runs the vitest suite (npm test) alongside the build, so these and the pre-existing frontend unit tests gate PRs.

Transcript smooth-scroll rework, phase 2 of docs/system/specs/transcript-smooth-scroll.md (phase 1 landed the pure engine; this wires ChatPanel onto it).

Phase 2 -- ChatPanel now runs on the new engine (frontend/src/views/transcript-scroll-engine.ts): the app owns anchoring end-to-end (native scroll anchoring disabled; every programmatic scrollTop write is echo-tracked and folded with any in-flight user scroll, so wheel input is never swallowed and streaming never jitters the view); the physical layer grows in the background to a 50k-event cap centered on the user, with off-window rows measured in idle-time offscreen batches; a custom auto-hiding overlay scrollbar replaces the hidden native one (track clicks and thumb drags jump by the physical/virtual mapping, which freezes while the user keeps using the scrollbar); scrolling all the way down or sending a message returns to following the tail; the per-agent scroll position persists to localStorage and restores across reload; text selections freeze row unmounting instead of the old disjoint pinned-run machinery; a dev-only ?debug=scroll trace records transitions, anchors, and every compensation write.

The old phantom-spacer estimate geometry -- the root cause of the scroll-jump bug (estimated 160px/event vs ~34px/event rendered for tool-heavy turns) -- is gone from ChatPanel; SubagentView still runs the old shared controller until phase 3 removes it.

Store changes: eviction is side/count-explicit (both ends), paging fetches take caller-specified limits, and sendMessage notifies message-sent listeners.

Manual verification tooling lives in system/scripts/scroll_verification/ (a standalone fixture server over a real session JSONL plus a Playwright driver asserting the spec's must-pass scenarios with content-relative measurements); 17/17 scenarios pass against a 6900-event real transcript. It sits outside this project so the project's code ratchets (no time.sleep / bare print / unittest.mock) keep applying to app and test code while the manual driver keeps the patterns that are its substance.

Transcript smooth-scroll rework, phase 3 of docs/system/specs/transcript-smooth-scroll.md (phases 1 and 2 landed the engine and the ChatPanel migration).

SubagentView runs on the same scroll engine with an empty virtual layer: its whole transcript is loaded, so the custom scrollbar is 100% pixel-space and the fill planner idles. One scrolling mechanism now serves all transcript viewing.

The old machinery is deleted: the shared scroll controller (transcript-scroll.ts), the virtual-window math (virtualWindow.ts), the follow-state decision (scrollFollow.ts), the mounted-row measurer (row-measurement.ts), and the disjoint pinned-run selection mechanism (selection facts consolidated in scroll-selection.ts; row estimates and the segment type live in conversation-rows.ts). The phantom-spacer estimate geometry -- the root cause of the scroll-jump bug -- is gone entirely.

A ResizeObserver on the message list catches content resizing outside any redraw (image loads, font swaps) so positioning corrects on the next frame, closing a one-frame FOLLOW gap flash during initial fill.

Live testing fixes: row geometry now measures each row's outer pitch (distance to the next element's top) rather than its margin-less border-box height -- rows carry CSS margins, so height-based geometry drifted from the DOM by the cumulative margins and deep anchors resolved to the wrong row, producing jumps on scroll and on expand/collapse (verified fixed to sub-pixel: a new expand/collapse scenario holds the top message at 0px). And the anchor is now the row CONTAINING the viewport top (offset into the row), not the next row whose top edge is visible. Holding the spanning row means its own height corrections -- a first real measurement replacing an estimate mid-scroll, or expanding/collapsing content below the fold -- shift only rows after it, so the top message on screen cannot move. This eliminates the jumps seen while wheel-scrolling up through not-yet-measured history and when expanding blocks.

Not yet manually verified: the subagent view click-through itself (the standalone fixture carries no subagent session linkage); it shares the verified engine and render path, but should be eyeballed in a real minds workspace. Possible follow-ups noted in the spec: a "jump to latest" pill and a thumb-drag position tooltip.

Further live-testing refinements: any upward wheel intent detaches from the tail immediately (the wheel event itself dispatches the transition; the 40px bottom band only governs re-attaching on the way down, and echo matching is tightened to 0.25px so a pin echo can never swallow a gesture's first small events); the FOLLOW pin only pulls the viewport down while the agent is generating or history is still filling in, never on a quiescent relayout; and positioning is event-driven -- during pure native scrolling the engine writes nothing at all, with a single compensation write only when content changes under the viewport (fill, measurement, spacer, jump, restore).

Sticky-bottom root cause (reproduced against the live workspace during real agent generation): streaming redraws run positioning every frame, and the engine's 1px classification thresholds treated a trackpad gesture's opening sub-pixel deltas as non-input, reverting each one before the next arrived -- 296px of wheel produced 1px of motion. All pending-delta classification is now exact (0.01px epsilon), so any nonzero non-clamp movement folds as user input; quiescence additionally requires fully measured geometry so the tail pin keeps following while offscreen measurements land. The verification suite gains a streaming sub-pixel-gesture scenario with frame-rate content churn (22/22).

Jumpiness under load (reproduced with 4x CPU throttling, mirroring a busy Electron app): three more root causes fixed. Row measurement now records each row's own outer size (border-box height plus its own margins) instead of the distance to the next sibling -- the message list is a flex column where margins never collapse, so the old pitch included the NEXT row's margin-top and flip-flopped as the mount boundary swept past, oscillating geometry and bouncing the anchored viewport by 18-45px per frame. The engine's per-redraw measure-and-position pass is deferred to a microtask (still pre-paint): mithril runs lifecycle hooks parent-first, so the synchronous pass measured freshly mounted rows before their own oncreate had injected content (MarkdownContent fills innerHTML in oncreate), poisoning the height table for a frame and visibly bouncing the viewport on every row mount during scrolling. And the native-input recency clock now starts at negative infinity instead of 0, which had made the initial fill's giant spacer clamp classify as recent user input during the first 150ms after page load, silently detaching a fresh chat from FOLLOW into a mid-history anchor.

The trace also records live and offscreen height measurements, and its ring holds 8000 entries so a multi-second interaction can still be reconstructed afterwards.

Live Electron testing against a real workspace surfaced one more stranding bug: scrolling to the bottom while the agent streams left the machine detached (the deciding scroll event fires while the client's fill still lags the server total, so the at-tail check fails on data grounds -- and a clamped scrollTop emits no further scroll events to retry), so the chat never re-followed new messages. A downward scroll or scrollbar drag ending in the bottom band now records a tail intent that completes the FOLLOW attach as soon as the tail is fully loaded. The ?debug=scroll handles are also attached to each engine's own scroll element (window globals are last-engine-wins when hidden dockview panels exist).

Two more live-testing fixes. A completed message that lands as a late append (after the agent already reads idle) now still pins the viewport to its bottom: the engine tracks appends the FOLLOW pin owes a scroll for, instead of gating purely on the agent's generating state -- previously the render plan windowed rows around the theoretical bottom while the pin stayed put, painting a mostly blank viewport until the next scroll. In quiescent FOLLOW the row window now tracks the actual viewport position so the mounted rows and the painted position can never disagree.

The custom scrollbar now feels like a native one: pressing ON the thumb grabs it at the pointer's offset (no teleport), pressing the empty track still jumps to that spot, and the thumb's rendered position accounts for its 24px minimum size so it spans exactly the track and never overflows the bottom on very long transcripts.

Engine-driven position changes now glide instead of snapping: the streaming follow pin advanced in discrete multi-hundred-px lurches per streamed chunk, and on a very long transcript each scrollbar pointermove teleported the content by thousands of px -- both captured live from a real session and both reading as "jumpy". Small-to-medium writes ease toward their target over a few frames (echo-tracked, so the state machines never mistake them for input, and any genuine user input cancels the glide instantly); large jumps -- track clicks, the initial pin, fill/measurement churn -- still snap, since gliding across those reads as animation or lags the fill. The debug trace can also be enabled in the embedded desktop-client pane via localStorage (no query string there).

Expanded blocks now stay expanded: which tool-call blocks, system chips, progress-step bodies, and markdown-wrapped tool outputs the user has opened is recorded in a session-scoped in-memory store keyed by stable identity (tool_call_id, event id, section + ticket id), instead of living only in the DOM or per-component state. Previously any re-render or virtualization remount silently collapsed them -- losing the user's place and snapping the row height down by the expanded content's size, which the live-session watcher captured as recurring multi-thousand-px jumps (a 7000px continuation summary and a 900px tool result flapping open/closed).

The custom scrollbar now actually fades out after its idle window in a quiescent view: hiding previously waited for the next unrelated redraw, which an idle chat or a finished subagent view never produced, so the bar stayed visible indefinitely.

A glided scroll (the eased scrollbar-drag steps) now keeps the recorded reading anchor in lockstep with the moving viewport. The anchor used to be captured at the glide's start and never updated (the glide's own writes are invisible to the state machines by design), so on a long transcript the first measurement or spacer change after a drag could teleport the viewport back by the glide distance, and a reload restored that stale position.

Dragging the scrollbar into unloaded history and stopping could leave the screen entirely blank: the SCROLLBAR interaction state froze the virtual end spacers along with the track mapping, so when the jump's fetch re-centered the loaded window the stale spacers left the viewport over an unpadded void -- outside any spacer, so even the loading overlay had nothing to key on. The freeze now covers only the track mapping and the px-per-event estimate (what stable scrubbing actually needs); the spacer sizes always track the loaded extent, so a landed jump either shows its rows or sits over a real spacer with the loading overlay.

Physical-cap regime fixes (reproduced against a 14.7k-event workspace chat with the cap temporarily lowered below the transcript length; previously the 50k cap exceeded every real chat so this regime had never run). Four fixes in the engine: a retained selection freeze range is clamped to the current rows, so a jump or eviction shrinking the window while a selection is live can no longer produce row indexes past the rows array (previously rows[i].render() threw on undefined and every subsequent redraw died, freezing the panel on "Loading messages..."); the fill planner's focus falls back to the anchor's approximate event index when the anchor row is briefly gone (a jump's window replace), instead of reading as "focus the tail" and issuing a tail window replace that discarded the jump and churned fetch/evict cycles indefinitely; planFill holds off while a landed jump awaits its re-anchor; and a landed fill that changed nothing is not refired verbatim, so the planner can never loop an identical fruitless request.

Scrollbar correctness under the cap: the frozen mapping's physical band is trusted in pixel space only while it still matches the loaded window -- once fills or evictions move the window mid-scrub it resolves in index space (new scrollbarMap helpers mappingPhysicalExtent and resolveTrackFractionToIndex, unit-tested), positioning onto the row when the target is loaded and through the jump path (loading overlay, never stale content) when it is not. A scrollbar move into a virtual region also leaves FOLLOW immediately: a near-window target fills via fetch-before, which never dispatches JUMPED_TO_INDEX, and the still-standing follow pin used to drag the viewport straight back to the bottom so the jump silently never happened.

Edge landings: dragging the scrollbar all the way down (or up) now lands exactly on the last (or first) message. Previously a drag to the track end while that edge was unloaded jumped to the edge event but anchored its row at the viewport TOP -- a tall last row left the true bottom below the fold with no scroll event ever firing to correct it -- and never re-entered FOLLOW; a chunked backfill toward the top landed wherever the height estimates put the anchor. Scrollbar and wheel gestures targeting an extreme now record explicit edge intent, and once that edge is fully loaded the engine snaps exactly onto it (the bottom also attaches FOLLOW). Two new harness scenarios (H1/H2) drag the thumb past each track end from the opposite edge and assert the exact landing; 24/24.

Edge intent is now judged by track position, not only the resolved event: a pointer released in the outermost 1% of the scrollbar track counts as "the very end/beginning". Releasing with the thumb a few px shy of the track end resolves to an event tens short of the tail (thousands of px above the bottom on a long transcript), so "scroll all the way down" previously only worked on a pixel-perfect or overshooting release. Harness scenarios H3/H4 release 3px short of each track end and assert the exact landing; 26/26.

Smooth edge convergence: the outermost 3% of the scrollbar track is an edge magnet -- a power-curve remap of the pointer fraction so the resolved position converges on the very end/beginning instead of stepping over a threshold. By 1% from the track end the remaining distance is ~4.6e-6 of the transcript (under one event below ~200k events), so approaching the end flows continuously into it; the 1% exact-pin band remains as the final catch that also re-attaches FOLLOW at the bottom. The thumb still tracks the raw pointer position, so nothing jumps visually on the track.

Scrollbar landings now reflect pointer intent exactly, with no special zones: the edge magnet and the 1% exact-pin band are removed. The scrollbar already clamps the pointer fraction, so exactly 1 (or 0) means the pointer genuinely reached the track end -- that alone triggers the exact edge landing (and FOLLOW at the bottom); every other release is an honest linear position. To make those honest positions accurate, a pending scrollbar target now re-anchors onto its exact event as soon as it is loaded, whichever fill path got there -- previously only far jumps (window replaces) re-anchored, and near-window targets landed wherever the spacer estimates put them (a 3x estimate error could land a 95% release at ~70% of the transcript) while also leaving the stale target steering the fill. Harness updated: H3 asserts a shy release lands proportionally (not snapped), H4 that finishing the drag to the end pins the exact tail.

FOLLOW now means AT the bottom, always. The quiescence rule that stopped the pin from chasing idle relayouts was over-broad: content growing under a pinned viewport with no user input (a late image load, a delayed re-measure of freshly mounted tail rows) opened a gap that nothing ever closed -- a drag to the bottom could end stranded above the tail. The pin now re-closes any gap unless the user interacted with the transcript in the last half second (so an expand click still does not fight the user mid-gesture). And the thumb no longer lies after a release: while dragging it tracks the pointer, but on pointer release it goes back to rendering the live viewport position (the frozen scrub mapping is kept), so it can no longer sit at the track end while the content is not at the bottom. New harness scenario H5 injects late growth under a pinned quiescent viewport and asserts re-pinning; 27/27.

The interacting-vs-following state machine is now explicit, replacing the 500ms recent-input timer (which bounced the view back to the bottom half a second after every interaction). FOLLOW pins the viewport to the bottom unconditionally -- streaming or idle, any late growth -- and pressing inside the transcript (a selection, an expand click, a link) detaches to USER_CONTROLLED at the current view before the press does anything, so the pin never fights an interaction and only user input ever moves an anchored view. The quiescence machinery (isFollowQuiescent, append tracking, the isStreaming config hook) is deleted; scrolling back to the bottom, dragging the scrollbar to the end, or sending a message re-enters FOLLOW as before. Harness H6 clicks tail content and injects growth, asserting the view holds to the pixel while detached; H5 keeps asserting untouched growth re-pins in FOLLOW; 28/28.

Releasing the scrollbar no longer re-syncs the thumb: it stays exactly where the pointer left it (frozen with the scrub mapping) until the user interacts by some other means -- wheel, keys, a press in the transcript -- which returns the engine to the live mapping, as originally specified. The release-time re-sync made the thumb visibly hop under a still-settling fill. With FOLLOW now pinning the bottom unconditionally, a frozen end-of-track thumb also agrees with reality after a drag to the end.

### system/libs/bootstrap

Bootstrap checks for an interrupted update apply at container start (the marker under `data/.state/update-apply/`) and rolls it back before the venv converge and before any service or agent starts, via `update_self.py recover --if-stale --no-restart`. The rollback is git restores plus plain copies of the pre-apply snapshots -- no network, no package manager and no working mngr -- with one exception: an apply that had reached its provisioner step is rolled back by re-running `setup_system.sh`, which does reach the network for the pinned toolchain (forced past the content-addressed provision guard with `PROVISION_FORCE=1`, since the restored tree is the one the guard's marker was written for and an unforced run would skip). Once the venv is converged, bootstrap wakes and messages the DRI agent the marker names, best-effort, so someone verifies state and talks to the user about retrying; the wake is held until after the converge so the woken agent's `uv run` calls cannot race it. A boot-time rollback that restored the tree but could not put a pre-apply copy back (the script's exit 3, which now records an `emergency.json` for the system interface's banner) is logged as an error rather than alongside a clean rollback, and still wakes the DRI agent: the services are booting over that mismatch, which is the state that most wants a person.

Bootstrap also owns the every-5-minutes recovery cron entry, which it lays down in `/etc/cron.d` at each boot (before installing the user-editable entries under `data/.state/cron.d`, so a deliberate same-named entry still wins). It belongs at boot rather than at provision time because `/etc/cron.d` lives on the container rootfs and does not survive the container being recreated -- which is exactly the window this guard exists to cover. Composing the entry here also means the recovery script's path is spelled out once rather than twice.

This is the merge of `gabriel/tactful-swift` (the inner workspace-updates work) into current `main`. It carries no changes of its own beyond resolving the merge; see that branch's `gabriel-tactful-swift.md` entry for what actually changed.

### system/services/host_backup

The backup's default excludes now cover the update apply's pre-apply snapshots (`data/.state/update-apply/snapshots`). Those copies are a venv, two uv tool environments and a built bundle -- exactly what the existing `**/.venv` and `**/node_modules` globs exclude everywhere else -- and they are only meaningful to an apply on this container. An apply whose rollback could not restore health keeps them indefinitely on purpose, so without this every hourly snapshot swept a full venv plus two tool environments.

This is the merge of `gabriel/tactful-swift` (the inner workspace-updates work) into current `main`. It carries no changes of its own beyond resolving the merge; see that branch's `gabriel-tactful-swift.md` entry for what actually changed.

### system/services/oom_priority

Generalized the agent launch wrapper so every harness gets an OOM band, not just claude.

`claude_oom_launch.py` is now `agent_oom_launch.py` and takes the harness binary as its
first argument, execing it in place exactly as before. `.mngr/settings.toml` gives codex
and pi-coding the `command` they were missing: without it those agents launched unbanded,
so earlyoom shed them by kernel score rather than by the user/worker tiering.

Nothing about the band logic changed -- it always resolved the band from the agent's label
rather than from which binary was running, so it was already harness-agnostic in
everything but its name and its hardcoded `execvp("claude")`.

Codex is two processes -- it uses its `command` as the prefix for both its visible
`--remote` TUI and its `app-server` daemon -- so a codex agent now registers two pids
under one agent id. Both are banded, and either being shed produces a shed-ledger record
where before there was none (an unregistered kill reads as an anonymous subprocess).

Two limits are noted in the wrapper, both strictly better than the unbanded status quo.
Shedding lands the right way only probably: killing the daemon takes the TUI with it
(`codex --remote` exits on lost connection), while killing the TUI orphans the daemon --
same band, so earlyoom picks by memory and takes the larger daemon first, which is the
outcome we want but not one we enforce. And `lookup_pid_by_agent_id` returns the first
live match, so the prioritizer's engagement re-tag reaches one of the two.

Not addressed here: the shed *notice* is claude-only (`claude_shed_notice_hook.py` is a
claude SessionStart hook), so a shed codex agent gets a ledger record but no in-session
explanation when it next starts.

The update-apply orchestrator now bands itself through this package, taking the system interface's own band (`SERVICE_BANDS["system_interface"]`) read off the tree it is being applied to. It needs no band of its own: reading the target tree's map is what lets an apply staged onto an older release band itself exactly as it does on a current one.

The scanner that checks every script's `sys.path` insert points at a real directory now pins that script's target explicitly, because the apply computes its insert from the repo root it is applied to rather than writing it as a literal the scanner could read.

The band wrapper's exec test now covers every harness binary the workspace launches (opencode and antigravity as well as claude, codex and pi), so the set it exercises matches the set wired up in `.mngr/settings.toml`.

## [minds-v0.4.2] - 2026-08-24

### .agents

Made the `update-system-interface` reveal unable to leave the workspace without an interface, which is how a failed update could previously take the UI down for good.

The reveal now takes a copy of the compiled interface before it starts. Both of its steps destroy before they produce -- the dependency install deletes the installed packages first, and the build empties the output directory first -- so a failure part-way through used to leave nothing to serve. Recovery then re-ran the very build that had just failed, which meant a broken build environment (an unreachable package registry, a build killed for memory) could not be recovered from at all. Restoring the copy needs neither the package manager nor the network, so that failure mode no longer costs you your interface. A rebuild during recovery is only attempted when there was no interface to save in the first place.

In the one case where recovery cannot get the interface back either, the copy is kept and where to find it is printed with the alarm, rather than being cleaned up along with everything else. That is the situation the copy exists for: putting it back by hand needs no package manager and no network, and by then it is the only working interface left anywhere, since the one in the workspace was erased before the build that failed. That only applies to an update that touched the interface itself, which is the only thing that erases it -- when an update to the workspace's server goes wrong the copy is identical to what is already there, so the alarm does not offer it and send you off to replace the interface with itself. An undo that cannot run its own steps raises that same alarm and keeps the copy too, instead of reporting the "nothing was changed" outcome over a half-undone workspace and cleaning the copy up on the way out. And when there is no copy at all -- there was no interface to save, or saving it failed -- the update says so the moment it skips it, so an alarm without a copy on offer is never a mystery.

The reveal now also checks that the interface actually works before declaring success, instead of only asking the backend whether it is alive. The backend answers happily while the compiled interface is missing, and the "not built" page it serves instead is itself a perfectly normal response, so nothing caught it. The check now confirms the page really is the app and that its script loads as JavaScript -- covering both the missing-interface case and the blank screen that an unserved script path produces. A rollback is held to the same standard, so it can no longer report that it restored a healthy interface when it did not.

That check is scoped to changes the update itself causes: the same probe runs before the update, and only an interface that was working beforehand has to be working after. A workspace that was already broken when the update started has the problem reported rather than the update rolled back, since undoing an unrelated change would not have fixed it.
