Restore the `X-Latchkey-Gateway-Permissions-Override` header on every git command the skills run through the latchkey gateway (`latchkey`, `publish-inspiration`, `use-inspiration`, `update-published-inspiration`, `update-installed-inspiration`), guarded with `${LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PERMISSIONS_OVERRIDE:+...}` so it is sent only when the env var exists. The `latchkey` skill's "Git operations on GitHub" section is now the canonical form of the command; the other skills mirror it.

Timeline: the skills sent both headers from the start (5cf163f5, 2026-07-07). Commit 58e2f55c (2026-07-31, "Drop LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PERMISSIONS_OVERRIDE (gone with the secondary gateway)") removed the header everywhere while retiring the remote-VPS secondary-gateway fallback -- but the override serves a second, unrelated purpose on desktop-hosted gateways (Docker/Lima/Modal workspaces): it is the per-agent authorization JWT, and the gateway evaluates requests without it against a deny-all default. That broke every gateway git push/fetch in desktop workspaces with a 403 despite approved grants. The `${VAR:+...}` guard keeps the command working on VPS gateways, which omit the env var.

Also fix `publish-inspiration` §7's permission probe: approved grants are stored under account-scoped keys (`github-git:<account>`), never bare `github-git`, so the probe's exact-key match could never see a real grant and reported "NOT permitted" forever. It now matches the `^github-git(:|$)` scope prefix.

The `latchkey` skill no longer sends users to a "Connectors" settings page to add or reconnect an account. Connections are managed from the Permissions tab of a machine's options (the key icon in the tabs along the top): "Add connection" lists services that already have an account here under "Add another account", and the rest under "Connect a new service". The skill's two references — adding a second account for a service, and reconnecting one whose credentials expired — now name that route, so an agent relaying instructions sends the user somewhere the action actually is.

`build_template.sh` now refuses to run outside a throwaway worktree.

Assembling a template resets the tree to the base version and runs `git clean
-fdxq`, which deletes untracked AND gitignored files. Pointed at a live
workspace that is `data/`, `.mngr/`, the secrets, and every scrap of runtime
state -- and the script then exits 0 and prints the next steps, so the wipe
reads as a successful publish.

What stood between that and a real mind was a sentence in the skill telling the
agent which directory to be in. That instruction cannot help on the run where
it is not followed. The script now checks two things before touching anything:
that it is not in the live workspace, and that it is in a linked worktree
rather than a main clone. Either one fails and it stops with an error naming
the fix.

`update-published-template` runs the same reset by hand rather than through the
script, so its step 4 now has the agent print `git rev-parse
--absolute-git-dir` and confirm the path is under `.git/worktrees/` before
running the reset.

Inspirations are now called templates.

The four skills are `publish-template`, `use-template`,
`update-published-template`, and `update-installed-template`, and a published
repo carries `template.md`, `template.toml`, and `template.svg`. The GitHub
topic is `minds-template` and the README's copyable line is `/use-template`.

There is no `use-inspiration` alias: the old name is gone. Anything still
pasting `/use-inspiration` -- a machine on an older workspace template, or a
README published before the rename -- needs the machine updated first.

The copyable command leads with a space -- `` /use-template <url>`` -- in both
the generated README and the minds app. A pasted string starting with `/` can
be taken as a slash command by a chat input rather than as message text.

Repos published in the older v1 format keep the filenames they already have on
disk: `inspiration-<slug>.md` and `inspiration-<slug>.svg`. The rename applies
to what gets written from now on, not to files sitting in other people's
repos, so the v1 adopt path still names them the way it will find them.

The default workspace template is unchanged and still called that -- it is
simply the default template, where a published one is not.

Reverts the template licensing change (#407).

Publishing no longer asks how you want the template licensed, writes no
`LICENSE` file, and the generated README has no License section. Adopting a
template no longer reports what the repo's license permits, and the welcome a
published template ships no longer mentions it on first boot.

This restores the previous behaviour exactly: the publish flow mentions MIT in
passing when you choose public visibility, and nothing else about licensing
happens anywhere.

Worth knowing what goes back to being true. A published template carries no
license, so by default nobody who receives it has permission to use, copy, or
modify it -- being able to clone a repo is not a grant. Adopters are not told
that, and the flow does not ask the publisher what they intended.

The assembly script's tests are kept, minus the license-specific ones. Every
assertion in that file was about license behaviour, but the harness around them
was not: it builds a real workspace, adds a linked worktree, and runs
`build_template.sh` end to end, and it is the only thing in the repo that
executes that script. It now asserts what assembly does regardless of
licensing -- that it REFUSES to run outside a throwaway worktree (the guard
that exists because this once wiped a live workspace), that the manifest trio
is written, that the README and `/welcome` are regenerated to describe this
template, and that the source workspace's version history never ships.

### system

The agentic browser fleet runs as a supervised program at slightly elevated CPU priority so agent build/test bursts cannot starve the live pixel path, and the base image now bakes the small runtime libraries (libva, x11-utils, pulseaudio) its media encoders load at import, so it works from first boot. The standalone streamed-browser prototype app has been removed: the fleet now carries its entire streaming stack (pixelflux video, pcmflux audio, XTEST input, the XFixes clipboard), so the separate service was pure duplication.

Trimmed the curl-retry comments in `system/scripts/setup_system.sh` and `system/scripts/install_secret_scanners.sh` down to the one non-obvious fact a maintainer needs -- that `--retry-all-errors` also retries a mid-transfer drop (curl exit 56) that plain `--retry` skips -- dropping the sha256 correctness argument and the cross-file references. No behavior change.

Made the provisioning scripts resilient to transient network failures when fetching pinned binaries.

`system/scripts/setup_system.sh` now retries each `curl` download of the pinned CLIs (restic, ttyd, gh, caddy, frpc, uv, Claude Code) via a shared `--retry 5 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2` flag set, so a transient GitHub-release 503 or a mid-transfer connection drop (curl exit 56) no longer aborts the whole provision under `set -e` -- the same failure mode that was intermittently failing the minds snapshot image build.

`system/scripts/install_secret_scanners.sh` now uses the same retry flag set for its scanner-tarball download (previously `--retry 3` with no `--retry-all-errors`), so the two provisioning scripts retry identically.

Every download is still sha256-verified, so a retry cannot admit a corrupt artifact.

`xvfb` and `xclip` are now baked into the base image (`setup_system.sh`) instead
of arriving via the deferred env.d browser unit. `[program:xvfb]` execs Xvfb
directly at boot, so a snapshot, restore, or fresh boot that raced the deferred
install carried a service that could not spawn (`xvfb: ERROR (spawn error)`
from `supervisorctl restart all`). The unit's xvfb step remains as an instant
no-op for rootfses built from pre-bake images, so no rollout ordering is
required.

The env.d browser unit (`system/scripts/env.d/1000-playwright-fortress.sh`) now
honors `DWT_SKIP_BROWSER_UNIT=1` in the agent environment: environments that
never use the browser stack (the minds CI snapshot producer) skip the whole
unit, including the hundreds-of-MB Fortress download. The switch is
re-evaluated every boot per the env.d contract, so clearing it converges the
browser stack on the next boot.

Two provisioning fixes left behind by earlier repo-wide migrations.

`system/scripts/setup_system.sh` now sends SIGHUP to the sshd listener after
writing the root-keys config, so the config is actually loaded on providers that
provision over SSH (Modal, Lima) rather than through a Dockerfile build step.
sshd only reads its configuration at startup. Providers that build from a
Dockerfile run this script before any sshd exists, so the file is baked into the
image and read when sshd first starts. Modal and Lima instead run it after mngr
has already started sshd, so the file landed under a listener that would never
re-read it, and every later connection resolved the authorized-keys path against
the passwd home that the preceding home move had just repointed at `/home/user`.
Since mngr writes root's key under `/root/.ssh`, authentication failed. This
previously worked only by accident, because the workspace's apt phase reinstalled
openssh-server and Debian's package scripts restart sshd on reinstall. SIGHUP is
sshd's documented reload mechanism; established sessions are unaffected, and the
signal is skipped when no sshd is running.

The `gcp` and `azure` create templates are caught up with three migrations that
skipped them. Both are byte-identical to each other and describe themselves as
mirroring the `aws` template, but neither had been touched since they were added
on 2026-07-09, leaving four references to paths and binaries that no longer
exist: the image build pointed at a Dockerfile at the repo root, `target_path`
still used the pre-cutover `/mngr/code/` layout, the outer-VM autostart unit
looked for the start script under the old `scripts/` directory, and the
first-boot seed used the pre-rename `fct-seed` binary name. They now match the
`aws` template apart from one deliberate host-environment forwarding line.

The CLAUDE.md ModuleNotFoundError workaround now gives the correct recovery. A standard workspace carries two mngr installs -- the root venv behind `uv run mngr ...`, and the uv-managed tool the bare `mngr` on PATH is, installed by `system/scripts/build_workspace.sh` -- so the entry now says which refresh fixes which: `uv sync --all-packages` for the venv, `uv tool uninstall imbue-mngr && uv tool install -e system/vendor/mngr/libs/mngr` followed by a `mngr plugin add` of the tool's plugin packages for the tool. The tool target is corrected too: it is the installable package inside the vendored monorepo, since installing the vendored root fails with a setuptools flat-layout error. The plugin re-registration is part of the recovery because reinstalling the tool rebuilds its environment from the base package alone, which would otherwise leave an `mngr` that cannot parse its own plugin config.

Added `system/scripts/refresh_workspace_view.py`, the shared motion for rebuilding the user's view of the workspace after its interface changes -- above all after `mngr start --restart system-services`, which bounces the system interface underneath whatever the user has open.

Nothing reloaded that view before. The Minds app only intervenes when a workspace looks unreachable for a sustained stretch, and a services restart that comes back quickly never crosses that bar, so the user was left reading the page the previous build had rendered.

The helper fires two channels, because neither reaches every viewer. The in-workspace `reload_system_interface` broadcast reaches every attached browser, including anyone the workspace was shared with over a Cloudflare tunnel. The Minds app's `POST /api/v1/agents/<primary>/refresh` reaches only the desktop app, but it does not go through the workspace server at all, so it still lands while that server is coming back. Both are fire-and-forget and the script always exits 0: the change has already landed on disk, so a viewer that cannot be reached is not a reason to fail a reveal.

The broadcast is explicitly best-effort. It is a live fan-out with no replay, so it reaches whoever is connected at that instant and nobody else; after a services restart that is often nobody, because browsers reconnect on exponential backoff (up to 30s). Waiting for the interface to answer before broadcasting does not fix that -- the server answering is not the same as a browser having reconnected -- so the helper does not wait, and the Minds app channel is what actually covers the common case of a user looking at the workspace in the app.

The Minds app addresses a workspace's window by its *primary* agent id, so the helper resolves that id rather than using the caller's own: a sub-agent (an `/assist` chat, a launch-task worker) has its own id, and a refresh aimed at it names no window at all -- the gateway accepts the call, the app matches it to nothing, and it reads as a success while doing nothing. The lookup selects on the `is_primary` label alone, since the `workspace` label the Minds app once set on its agents is no longer written. A lookup that names nobody skips the app channel and says so, rather than falling back to an id that would quietly do nothing. A partial listing still counts: `mngr ls` exits non-zero when any provider is unreachable, having already printed the agents it did find, and the id is taken from that output.

The system-interface shell HTML is now served `Cache-Control: no-store`. It is assembled per request and names content-hashed assets, so its freshness alone decides which bundle a reloaded page runs -- and a page cannot drop its own HTTP cache, since `location.reload(true)` is a Firefox-only extension. This matters most for tunnel viewers, where an intermediary may cache anything not marked otherwise.

- The `browser` supervisord program now tags its memory-shedding band the same way every other service does, via the `oom_tag_service.py browser` command prefix, instead of writing `oom_score_adj` 1000 inline. The program is the browser *coordinator*, not Chromium, and putting it at the top of the shedding ladder made it earlyoom's first victim in every memory-pressure episode while freeing almost none of the browser's memory -- Chromium survives the coordinator's death, and supervisord restarts it straight back into the same session. Chromium's own processes still reach the top band on their own, via the daemon's re-tagging sweep.

Point `stop_hook.base_branch` back at `main` in `.reviewer/settings.json`, and state `verify_architecture.is_enabled` explicitly.

`base_branch` had been aimed at a feature branch as a safety net: with `fetch_and_merge` on, the stop hook merged `origin/main` into the workspace's `main`-named branch and pushed it back, leaking feature commits onto the template's main. `fetch_and_merge` is off at the repo level and the whole hook is off for workspace agents (`enabled_when: false`), so the leak needs both switches flipped -- while a base branch that doesn't exist in a workspace's own remote silently made every diff look empty.

`verify_architecture` was the one gate absent from this file, so it fell through to the plugin's default of enabled -- the opposite of what the rest of the file says. Recording it as `false` makes the config say what it means: for a workspace agent, every gate is off.

Both keys are overridable per checkout via the gitignored `.reviewer/settings.local.json`, which is how a template checkout nested in a mngr checkout for active development turns the gates back on.

Reverted main to `c043d0f7a` ("Merge pull request #387 from imbue-ai/hynek/expect-auto-response"), the last commit that reached main through a real PR.

Commit `55d1e6e84` merged origin/main into a long-running agent working branch and pushed the result to main, landing roughly 90 commits of in-progress work that was not ready to ship. This revert takes that work back off main; the commits remain reachable and can be re-landed through their own PRs.

Removed from the workspace template as part of the revert: the `geopolitical_dashboard` app (a mock), the codex/pi policy-hook guards and the `POLICY_HOOKS.md` note, the claude statusline model-state recorder, the codex/pi launcher wiring in `setup_system.sh` and `supervisord.conf`, and the `harness-audit-2026-08-10`, `queue_sweep`, `shoulder_tap_atomic`, `agent-liveness-overlay`, and `live-model-state` design documents.

Kept intact: everything merged before that point, including PR #362 (browser streaming and fixes) and the `system/vendor/mngr` refresh at `029126212`, which still pins the vendored mngr to `22cd2f1839`.

`system/scripts/refresh_workspace_view.py` no longer requires `LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PERMISSIONS_OVERRIDE` to reach the Minds app. It now needs only the gateway URL and password, and forwards the override header when the variable is set.

Only a desktop-hosted gateway (a Docker, Lima, or Modal workspace) injects that variable. A VPS-hosted one -- every Vultr, imbue-cloud, AWS, GCP, or Azure workspace created since the single-gateway change -- deliberately omits it, because the extension that forwards Minds API routes back to the desktop substitutes a target JWT of its own. Requiring it therefore skipped the Minds app refresh outright on every remote workspace, reporting `latchkey gateway env not set` even though the gateway and password were both present. That left those workspaces with only the `reload_system_interface` broadcast, which a services restart has usually just disconnected -- so a reveal on a remote workspace often refreshed nothing while still reporting that it had asked for a reload.

Dropping the header entirely would break the other topology: on a desktop-hosted gateway it is the per-agent authorization JWT, and a request without it resolves against a deny-all default. Sending it only when set is the same shape the rest of the template already uses for this variable (`system/libs/bootstrap`, `system/libs/github_sync`, and the `latchkey` skill's git commands).

Bump Latchkey to the latest version.

- Fixed the pool/slice VM boot race where `minds-autostart.service` (ordered
  only `After=docker.service`) could run before the `/mngr-btrfs` data volume
  was mounted, so the workspace container failed its volume mount, the failure
  was swallowed by `|| true`, and nothing ever retried -- the workspace stayed
  down until an operator intervened (mngr-internal#266, hit on all 12 slices of
  box `9ef5ab2e` after its 2026-08-03 reboot). The service is now triggered by
  a `minds-autostart.path` unit gated on a readiness marker
  (`/mngr-btrfs/.minds-volume-ready`) that the installer creates exclusively on
  the mounted volume, behind a hard `mountpoint` check -- so the condition can
  never be satisfied by root-fs debris shadowed under the unmounted mountpoint
  (a stale snapshot-helper request replayed at boot once `mkdir`'d
  `/mngr-btrfs/snapshots` on the root fs pre-mount, which defeated an earlier
  `PathExistsGlob=/mngr-btrfs/*` condition in staging testing). The wake-up
  event is the symlink refresh lima's provision script performs right after
  mounting on every boot -- the same event-driven shape
  `scripts/minds_lima_autostart.sh` already uses for the lima direct-VM mode.
  Applied uniformly to the vultr, pool_host, aws, gcp, and azure templates
  (harmless on the loop-mount VPS modes, where the volume is up before any
  service starts and the unit simply fires at boot as before).

- Defense in depth against a premature trigger: the service sets
  `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` (previously, rapid re-triggers of a failing
  service tripped systemd's default start limit and the resulting
  `unit-start-limit-hit` permanently killed the path watcher -- observed on a
  staging box reboot), and `minds-outer-autostart.sh` now waits for
  `/mngr-btrfs` to actually be a mounted volume before touching docker
  (5s poll, 30 min hard bound, warning past 60s), so an early fire parks
  until the mount instead of burning start attempts.

- `minds-outer-autostart.sh` no longer swallows failures: a container that does
  not reach `running`, or a services-agent relaunch that fails, now fails the
  unit so the breakage is visible in `systemctl status minds-autostart`.
  `docker start` stderr now reaches the unit journal (previously discarded, so
  the real volume-mount error had to be dug out of dockerd's log).

- The installer is backfill-safe for the existing fleet: it removes the old
  direct `multi-user.target` enablement of the service, `reset-failed`s units
  a past boot may have left dead of the start limit, refuses to install when
  the volume is not mounted, and starts the path watcher immediately so
  re-running it on a live VM takes effect without a reboot.

- The gcp and azure boot units now use the same
  `/home/user/workspace/system/scripts/...` services-agent path as the other
  templates (their pre-restructure `/mngr/code/scripts/...` path had been
  silently broken by the `|| true`; upstream migrated those templates in the
  meantime and this branch adopts that path), so all five templates install
  byte-identical autostart machinery.

- Note: fleet VMs have the old unit baked in; this change only covers new
  bakes until the installer block is re-run on existing VMs (tracked as the
  rollout half of mngr-internal#266).

Sync `system/vendor/mngr` to the mngr `mngr/convert-to-iframe` branch, bringing in the minds embed contract module (`apps/minds/imbue/minds/desktop_client/static/embed_contract.js`) that the system interface now imports for all chrome<->workspace postMessage traffic, plus the forward plugin's embedding substrate (partitioned cookies, `/_bridge`, `frame-ancestors` policy, local CA).

Wire the new `share_gateway` service into the system: a supervisord program (`share-gateway`, gated on share materials in `data/.secrets/share.env`), pinned sha256-verified `caddy` 2.11.4 and `frpc` 0.70.1 binaries in `setup_system.sh`, a `share-gateway` OOM band, the Dockerfile manifest layer, and workspace-member registration in the root pyproject.

Remove the Cloudflare tunnel stack that share-gateway replaces: the `system/services/cloudflare_tunnel/` project is deleted entirely (package, tests, ratchet file, README, changelog), along with its `[program:cloudflared]` supervisord program, the `cloudflared` binary install and `CLOUDFLARED_VERSION` pin in `setup_system.sh`, its `cloudflared` OOM band, its Dockerfile manifest COPY, and the root-pyproject `cloudflare-tunnel` dependency (lockfile refreshed). Docs, skills, comments, and the system_interface share modal now describe the self-hosted sharing stack (TLS terminates inside the workspace; access is granted per email address) instead of Cloudflare tunnels.

Fixed the `owner-exec` supervisord spawn error and re-enabled the service. Root cause: `owner-exec` was a uv workspace member but not a dependency of the root project, so any root-closure-scoped `uv sync` (the backup restore flow runs one right before `supervisorctl restart all`) pruned it from the workspace venv, deleting its console script and turning the next `uv run owner-exec` into a supervisord spawn error. `owner-exec` is now a root dependency (like every other `uv run <name>` service), and the `[program:owner-exec]` block is wired back into `system/supervisord.conf`.

Web-chrome exec channel plumbing: the share gateway now allows the configured `SHARE_CHROME_ORIGIN` on state-changing cross-origin requests and lets its CORS preflights through `forward_auth` (preflights carry no credentials; the real request is still session-checked), and the owner `/_health` detail includes the service label map so the chrome can resolve service origins (most importantly owner-exec). The owner-exec service answers credentialed CORS for the configured chrome origin (including preflights on run/read-file/write-file/grants).

Service-per-origin cutover (scripts/config/docs side): the `/service/<name>/` path-prefix proxy is gone; every registered service now owns a real browser origin (`http://<name>.host-<32hex>.localhost:8421/` locally; future share hostnames nest the same way), with routing handled by the external forwarder.

`forward_port.py` now validates app names as origin hostname labels (lowercase alphanumeric/underscore runs joined by single hyphens; `localhost` and the reserved `host-`/`agent-` prefixes are rejected with a clear error on both register and `--remove`; underscores stay legal, so `system_interface` keeps its name), with a new subprocess-driven `forward_port_test.py` including a drift guard against the build-app scaffold's stricter name rule.

`layout.py` speaks service coordinates: `replace-url` expectations stay service-relative (`service:<name>[/<path>]`) and the wait-stable check compares service name + path against the panel's stored origin URL (the service name is the hostname's first label when a `host-<32hex>` label sits deeper in). The browser supervisord program drops its dead `ROOT_PATH=/service/browser` env. `docs/system/workspace-internals.md` describes the new per-origin scheme.

The in-workspace backup provisioning (`system/scripts/provision_backups.py`, run over owner-exec during a hosted web-create) now retries `restic init` through the R2 credential-propagation window. A freshly minted R2 API token is not yet valid at Cloudflare's S3 edge for a few seconds, and the web-create path runs `restic init` immediately after minting the bucket key -- so it reliably lost that race and failed the whole create's backup step with "restic init failed (exit 1): ... signature ... does not match". The init now retries for up to 60s on transient auth signals (InvalidAccessKeyId / signature-mismatch, matched against both the raw S3 codes and restic's rendered phrasings); a genuine non-auth failure still fails fast, and an already-initialized repo is still treated as success.

Merge main into the self-hosted sharing branch: the share-gateway supervisord program uses the relocated oom_tag_service.py path from the services restructure, and the browser keeps main's headful-under-Xvfb shape while serving its own origin.

Remove the last vestiges of the deleted placeholder `web` example server: its entry in oom_priority's SERVICE_BANDS (a band for a program that no longer exists).

Merge the template's main branch into the mithril-refactor stack and sync `system/vendor/mngr` to the merged mngr `mngr/mithril-merge` branch (8adbf437c6). The vendored mngr now carries both this stack's relay-based sharing / iframe / Mithril-SPA work and main's remote-service-connector modular split with pinned Modal images; main's two intervening vendor refreshes are ancestors of the synced commit, so nothing from main is lost by the wholesale re-vendor.

`system/vendor/mngr` is refreshed to the mngr commit that minds 0.3.12 ships, so a workspace's in-VM agent runs the same mngr the desktop binary does.

The agent-facing `layout.py` helper now recognizes service panels by their
unguessable per-service origin label (`<name>-<rand>`). Stored panel URLs carry
this random label as their leading hostname component, so `layout.py` maps it
back to the service name via the app registry (`data/.state/apps.toml`) when
matching `service:` refs against the live layout.

Surface real client IPs at the share gateway: frpc now stamps each spliced connection with a PROXY protocol v2 header carrying the address the relay saw, and the rendered Caddyfile consumes it via a loopback-only `proxy_protocol` listener wrapper (ahead of the tls wrapper). The gateway logs every denied or unauthenticated-non-HTML request with that real address, so scanner probes and revoked visitors are distinguishable from frpc's loopback in the share-gateway service log. Allowed requests stay unlogged.

Merge main into the mithril stack and refresh `system/vendor/mngr` to mngr `mngr/test-mithril` (b0d50fe2a6). The vendored mngr picks up the desktop client fixes from that branch: restored Electron window drag regions in the mithril SPA (all mouse input was dead on frameless Linux windows because the shell.html splash's full-window drag region was never recomputed), the SPA bundle now builds from `pnpm start`'s prestart hook, and desktop-client shutdown no longer stalls 10s in the root concurrency-group exit.

Before a template is published, the agent now shows you its README and asks
whether it describes what you built. It pastes the text into the chat, which
renders markdown, so you review a page rather than a wall of source, and if the
answer is no it rewrites and shows you again until you are happy.

The relative hero image does not resolve in a chat message, so the agent says
so rather than letting you read it as a broken README. The image itself is the
thumbnail you already approved, and the flow verifies the live GitHub page
after pushing, which is what actually catches a bad image path.

Repoints the broken `docs/system/style_guide.md` symlink. It targeted
`vendor/mngr/style_guide.md`, which resolves relative to `docs/system/` and so
pointed at a path left stale by the `system/` relayout; it now resolves to the
real file.

The repo-wide prose ratchets skip symlinks resolving into `system/vendor/`,
which is what they always intended -- until now that only worked because this
link was broken.

The vendored `system/vendor/mngr` snapshot moved with this branch's minds-side work, so the workspace builds against a mngr that knows about the per-machine Permissions screen. The snapshot is not authored here — it is refreshed from the mngr monorepo by the release sync — and the merge of main took main's copy of every file the two sides both touched, so this carries only what main had not already moved.

The changelog gate now takes a PR's base branch from the event payload instead
of the runner's `GITHUB_BASE_REF`.

On a stacked PR the two were observed to disagree -- the payload named the
parent branch while the env var said `main`. The gate could then not resolve the
base it was told to use, fell back to `origin/main`, and diffed the whole stack
rather than the one PR, failing it for changelog entries belonging to the PRs
underneath.

The failure mode was the bad kind: a green run and a red run on the same
unchanged files, which reads as flakiness rather than as a diff computed against
the wrong base.

The base now travels in `CHANGELOG_BASE_REF`, set from the event payload.
GitHub reserves the `GITHUB_` prefix, so a workflow declaring
`env: GITHUB_BASE_REF:` has it echoed in the log and then ignored -- the
runner's own value wins, and on a stacked PR that value was `main` rather than
the parent branch. Overriding it was therefore impossible under that name.

The job also places the remote-tracking ref with `git update-ref` and verifies
it, rather than trusting a `+src:dst` refspec, which was observed to succeed
while creating no ref at all. And the gate refuses an unresolvable named base
instead of falling through to `main`: falling back turned a wrong base into a
confident wrong answer, which is what made this read as a flaky check across
two runs of identical files.

Renames the inspirations feature to templates across the skills, scripts, and
docs: `build_template.sh`, `validate_template.py`, `write_template_manifest.py`,
and the published `template.md` / `template.toml` / `template.svg`.

The default workspace template keeps its name; `default-workspace-template`,
`DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_TEMPLATE`, and mngr's `create_templates` /
`apply_create_template` are untouched.

### system/apps/system_interface

Browser pane tabs now have a "Destroy browser" button, symmetric to the destroy buttons on agent and terminal tabs: it confirms, retires the browser in the fleet, and closes the tab (a plain "Close tab" still just detaches the pane). Because each browser now lives on its own service origin, the destroy request routes through a same-origin ``DELETE /api/browsers/<name>`` passthrough that forwards to the browser daemon (a direct cross-origin call would have no CORS).

Fixed the chat progress view hiding a reply the agent had already delivered.

When a Stop hook fired or a background task finished while a step was still open, the notification woke the agent back up, and the work it did next pulled the wrap-up message it had just written into that step -- where it collapsed down to a single italic caption line, or vanished entirely behind the step's expand arrow. The longer the reply, the more there was to lose.

Anything the agent had already said before such a notification now stays in the conversation as a full message, no matter what it does afterwards.

The app shell HTML is now served with `Cache-Control: no-store`, so reloading the interface always lands on the build that is currently on disk.

The shell is assembled per request and the assets it links are content-hashed, which makes its freshness the only thing deciding which bundle a reloaded page runs: a cached shell names the old bundle forever. A page cannot drop its own HTTP cache -- the `location.reload(true)` form is a Firefox-only extension -- so `reloadInterface` can only reload and trust the response to be fresh, and `no-store` is what makes that trust well-founded. This matters most for anyone viewing the workspace through a shared Cloudflare tunnel, where an intermediary is free to cache whatever is not marked otherwise.

Together with the new `system/scripts/refresh_workspace_view.py` helper, this is what makes a reveal of a changed interface actually visible to whoever is looking at it, instead of leaving them on the previous build until they navigate away and back.

- The chat OOM prioritizer now ages chats out as well as protecting them, so a chat left untouched for hours becomes more expendable under memory pressure than the worker a live chat just spawned. Previously it could only ever *protect* a chat (down from the launch band toward the protected floor) from reported UI engagement, which meant a workspace under memory pressure always shed a running worker before a chat nobody had messaged in days.

- Idle time is measured wall-clock from the most recent of: a message sent through the UI, the moment a chat's tab was switched to, either edge of a turn, or -- as a floor -- the chat's own `claude_process_started` mtime, so a freshly revived chat is never treated as stale. Switching *to* a tab counts as engagement; leaving one visible does not, so a repeated presence report never resets the clock. A chat with no evidence at all counts as fresh: it is demoted only on positive evidence of abandonment.

- Chats messaged outside the workspace UI (by `mngr message`, or by another agent) are now visible to the prioritizer. It consumes the observe stream's lifecycle states, so a chat entering a running state counts as engagement, and a chat that stays running is treated as mid-turn and exempted from aging until its turn ends. Without this an agent-driven chat would look abandoned and could be shed ahead of workers.

- Re-tagging is now event-driven plus a slow sweep (60s). The events (activity reports and lifecycle changes) still cover everything that changes a chat's engagement; the sweep exists because staleness is the one input that changes with no event to announce it -- a chat crosses a threshold by sitting still. Per-chat message times are re-seeded at startup from the durable client-activity log, so restarting the system interface no longer makes every chat look never-messaged and restart its staleness clock.

Reverted the system interface to its state at `c043d0f7a`, as part of taking the accidentally-merged agent branch back off main.

This removes the in-progress harness work that landed via `55d1e6e84`: the per-harness shoulder tap (atomic interrupt-and-flush for codex and pi), the message queue mirror and stop-button retract machinery, the live model-state bar and its pickers, the codex/pi launcher labels and sign-in copy, the Powered-by credit, and the e2e suite's move onto Fortress.

The reverted work is still reachable in git and can be re-landed through its own PRs.

The latchkey scope-catalog endpoint no longer sends
`X-Latchkey-Gateway-Permissions-Override`: the header (and its
`LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PERMISSIONS_OVERRIDE` env var) went away with the secondary
gateway, so `resolve_scope_info` takes just the gateway password and
`/api/latchkey/scopes/<scope>` only 503s when the gateway URL or password is
missing.

Adopt the minds embed contract for all chrome<->workspace messaging.

The system interface now imports the embed contract module from the vendored mngr tree (`@minds/embed-contract`, a vite alias to `system/vendor/mngr/apps/minds/imbue/minds/desktop_client/static/embed_contract.js`) and routes every postMessage exchange with the embedding minds chrome through one workspace-side endpoint (`frontend/src/embed.ts`). This replaces the ad-hoc `window.parent.postMessage` / relay-window messages that grew alongside the old Electron content-relay design; the minds chrome now embeds this UI as a cross-origin iframe in both the desktop app and plain-browser mode.

Concrete changes:

- Permission-request cards send `minds:open-request-modal` through the contract endpoint (same wire format as before, so older minds chromes keep working).

- The Claude sign-in modal's "Sign in with Imbue" handshake sends `minds:open-ai-keys-page` to the embedding chrome and waits for the contract ack; the ack now means "a minds chrome is present" (plain-browser chrome acks too), not "the desktop app is present", and the fallback alert wording changed accordingly.

- The dockview workspace now actually handles `minds:close-active-tab` (the chrome's Cmd/Ctrl+W forward): it closes the active tab. Previously the message was posted by the Electron relay but nothing listened.

- A new allowlist-by-file ratchet (`test_embed_ratchets.py`) forbids raw `postMessage` / `message`-listener usage outside the embed boundary, so the whole message surface stays auditable in `embed.ts` + the vendored contract (see minds' `docs/embed-contract.md`).

Service-per-origin cutover: the system interface no longer proxies services. `proxy.py` and `service_dispatcher.py` (the `/service/<name>/` forwarding layer with its service-worker bootstrap, fetch-prefixing service worker, HTML rewriting, WebSocket shim, and cookie-Path scoping) are deleted; every registered service is reached on its own browser origin via the external forwarder, derived by one rule: `serviceOrigin(name) = protocol//name.location.host/` (the shell always runs at the bare workspace origin `host-<32hex>.localhost:8421` locally; future share hostnames nest the same way).

Frontend: a new `frontend/src/origin.ts` (`deriveServiceOrigin`) owns the derivation; all panel-URL builders (`serviceRefUrl`, `getTerminalUrl`, `buildAgentTerminalUrl`, `buildSessionTerminalUrl`, `resolveReplaceUrl`, the "+" menu) emit absolute service origins. On layout restore, persisted URLs are treated as stale hints: service panel URLs are re-derived from `serviceName` (preserving any `?query`, e.g. a browser pane's `session=<name>`) and agent-terminal URLs are rebuilt from their ttyd dispatch args, so saved layouts stay portable across hosts. Service panels are cross-origin iframes now; `IframePanel`'s src-reassignment refresh is the normal path.

Backend: a new same-origin `GET`/`POST /api/browsers` passthrough forwards the browser fleet API to the registered `browser` service's local backend (503 JSON error when unregistered or unreachable), so the shell UI keeps a same-origin endpoint for listing and creating browsers (`CreateBrowserModal` drops its `browserServiceUrl` attr). Layout ref resolution (`layout_ops.py`) parses service iframes by origin -- the service name is the URL host's first label when a `host-<32hex>` label sits deeper in the hostname -- instead of the removed `/service/<name>/` path prefix.

The workspace UI supports being driven cross-origin by the hosted minds web chrome: restored tabs reopen against the shared workspace's labeled service origin (the routable entry origin) rather than the deliberately-unrouted bare share domain, and the workspace accepts cross-origin navigation/drive requests from the hosted chrome.

The workspace "+" menu no longer hides a service named `web`. That filter targeted the deleted placeholder example server, and would have hidden a legitimate user-built service that happened to use the name.

Workspace service panels now open at an unguessable per-service origin. Each
registered service is assigned a persistent random hostname label
(`<name>-<rand>`, e.g. `terminal-x7k9q2w1`), and the system interface builds
every panel's iframe origin from that label instead of the bare service name --
locally `http://<label>.host-<hex>.localhost:8421/` and `https://<label>.<domain>`
when shared. Saved layouts stay portable: they still persist the service name and
re-derive the URL from that name's current label at render time.

Fix a runaway iframe-nesting bug: deriveServiceOrigin now prefixes a service's label onto the workspace host COORDINATE (the ``host-<hex>`` label and everything after it) rather than onto ``window.location.host`` verbatim. Because the shell runs at its own label origin (the bare origin redirects there locally; only ``*.<domain>`` is served on a share), deriving relative to the current host verbatim nested every service under the shell's label -- routing it back to the shell (a dockview inside a dockview). Stripping to the coordinate first keeps every service origin a single label deep.

Every service now owns a full browser origin derived from the workspace host coordinate (origin.ts; the /service/ path-prefix proxy and service dispatcher are deleted), and the frontend adopts the shared embed contract: embed.ts is the single sanctioned postMessage boundary with the embedding minds shell (sourced from the vendored mngr tree so both sides stay in lockstep, enforced by ratchet tests), with dockview workspace, iframe panel, and Claude-login modal updated to match.

The latchkey scope-catalog endpoint sends the `X-Latchkey-Gateway-Permissions-Override` header again when `LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PERMISSIONS_OVERRIDE` is set, fixing 403s from desktop-hosted gateways (which evaluate override-less requests against a deny-all default). The header is optional: VPS gateways omit the env var and keep working with the password header alone. The override had been sent until commit 58e2f55c (2026-07-31) removed it along with the retired VPS secondary-gateway fallback, not realizing desktop gateways still require it for authorization.

- Restyled the in-chat permission-request card: a muted "Permission request" eyebrow now tops the card, followed by a lock badge beside a short title ("Local files", "Other machines", "Device accounts", or the resolved service name) with the agent's rationale directly beneath it. The pending card pairs a solid green "Review & respond" button with a plain-text "Show raw request" toggle, and resolved requests render as a compact one-line receipt ("Approved" in green, "Denied" in neutral, "Couldn't complete" in amber).

- The card no longer lists the specific requested permissions inline (the old "Requesting" line and its hover tooltips); those details live in the review modal and the raw-request disclosure.

- The card flips to Approved/Denied the moment the request is resolved in the Minds app's review popup, rather than waiting for the resolution to come back through the agent transcript. The verdict arrives over the minds embed contract (the same postMessage path in the desktop app and in a plain browser), which admits it only from this page's own embedder and only with a well-formed payload; the transcript's own resolution still wins once it lands.

- All messaging with the embedding Minds app now goes through that shared contract module rather than hand-rolled postMessage calls, so both ends of the boundary ship from one source of truth.

- The in-chat permission card no longer loses a still-pending request to output truncation. A latchkey permission-request response is often longer than the transcript's per-result output limit — the gateway pretty-prints the created request and echoes its target and precomputed effect, and curl's progress meter is printed ahead of it — so the response was being cut mid-object and the card fell back to an apologetic "couldn't read this request" line for a request that still needed an answer. The parser now finds and parses the request before truncating, carries it on the tool-result event as structured data, and keeps the object whole in the raw output, so the card shows the request's name and its "Review & respond" button every time.

- A card whose transcript predates that fix now recovers what survived the cut rather than giving up on the whole request: the request's name, the agent's rationale, and a working "Review & respond" button all come back from a truncated response, and any field that did not survive is simply left off instead of guessed at. When nothing at all can be read the card says so in one short line rather than a paragraph, and the "Show raw request" disclosure stays available in every state.

- The in-chat permission card now leads with a key rather than a padlock, and its badge shows the app being asked about — Slack's own mark on a Slack request, Gmail's on a Gmail request. A service we ship no artwork for, and a request that names no app at all (local files, other machines, device accounts), fall back to a neutral cube. The marks are the same artwork the Minds app's Permissions screen uses, read from the vendored mngr tree at build time rather than copied in, so the two surfaces cannot drift and the card looks the same embedded in the Minds app and opened directly in a browser.

The permission-request scan over tool output is now bounded: a probe cap and a RecursionError guard keep a pathological response (kilobytes of braces, or absurdly nested JSON) from stalling transcript parsing or killing the session watcher outright — measured, a 100KB brace wall dropped from ~3s to ~3ms. The chat card's recovery-scan comments now also give the scan's real trigger (a response past the backend's preservation ceiling, since an agent's rationale has no length limit), and a test pins that case end to end.

The vendored mngr snapshot is back to exactly main's copy: this PR no longer carries an early vendor delta. The in-chat card's instant Approved/Denied flip rides the PERMISSION_REQUEST_RESOLVED embed-contract message, which only exists on the mngr side's own PR, so until the next release sync delivers it the card simply keeps the transcript-driven flip it always had, and the four tests that assert the instant flip skip themselves — gated on a probe of the vendored contract, so they come back on their own when the sync lands.

### system/libs/bootstrap

Reverted bootstrap to its state at `c043d0f7a`, as part of taking the accidentally-merged agent branch back off main.

The initial chat agent is created with `--transfer none` again rather than `--type claude`, and the boot-time `uv sync --all-packages --frozen` venv converge is removed. Both landed via `55d1e6e84` as part of in-progress harness work and can be re-landed through their own PRs.

Stop sending `X-Latchkey-Gateway-Permissions-Override` on the boot-time
timezone fetch: the header (and its `LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PERMISSIONS_OVERRIDE` env
var) went away with the secondary gateway, so the gateway password header is
the only auth the minds-api-proxy call needs. The fetch no longer treats a
missing override as "gateway env not set" and skips.

The bootstrap now converges the workspace venv (`uv sync --all-packages`) at boot, before it starts supervisord, so background services that depend on newly-vendored workspace packages (in particular the `owner-exec` service) start cleanly on first boot rather than failing with a spawn error.

The boot-time timezone fetch through the latchkey gateway sends the `X-Latchkey-Gateway-Permissions-Override` header again when `LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PERMISSIONS_OVERRIDE` is set, fixing the fetch on desktop-hosted gateways (which deny override-less requests via a deny-all default and left containers on UTC). The header is optional so VPS gateways, which omit the env var, keep working. The override had been sent until commit 58e2f55c (2026-07-31) removed it along with the retired VPS secondary-gateway fallback.

The workspace venv is converged to the committed lockfile once at boot, before
supervisord starts anything, instead of being reconciled lazily by whichever
`uv run` happens to need it first. Removes the intermittent `ModuleNotFoundError`
that hit services importing during that rewrite window.

### system/libs/github_sync

Remove the secondary-gateway fallback: gateway provisioning now gives every
workspace exactly one (primary) Latchkey gateway.

`LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_SECONDARY` is gone from the config module, the visibility
check is a single `latchkey curl` attempt (an unreachable gateway is simply
`unknown`, retried on the next tick), and the post-commit hook no longer pushes
a proxied URL through the secondary gateway when the normal push fails -- the
failure lands in `/tmp/post-commit-push.log` and is retried on the next commit.

`LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PERMISSIONS_OVERRIDE` went away with it: the git wiring
writes only the `X-Latchkey-Gateway-Password` extra header (a re-wire replaces
the old two-header entry), and it no longer refuses to wire when the override
is unset.

Restore the `X-Latchkey-Gateway-Permissions-Override` header in the global git wiring, now optional: when `LATCHKEY_GATEWAY_PERMISSIONS_OVERRIDE` is set (desktop-hosted gateways -- Docker/Lima/Modal workspaces) it is written as a second `extraHeader` entry alongside the password; when unset (remote-VPS gateways) only the password header is written, so both topologies work.

Timeline: the wiring sent both headers until commit 58e2f55c (2026-07-31) dropped the override while retiring the VPS secondary-gateway fallback. On desktop gateways the override is the per-agent authorization JWT and requests without it hit a deny-all default, so github-sync pushes in desktop workspaces failed with 403 despite approved grants. Unlike the pre-58e2f55c wiring, the override is no longer required -- its absence just means a VPS-style gateway.

### system/services/env_converge

Adds the template-manifest schema: a pydantic model for `template.toml`
covering a template's identity, its derivation recipe, the activation
prerequisites an adopter must satisfy, the environment it declares (apt package
names, npm globals, uv tools, cargo crates, and carried `env.d` units), and the
lineage of templates it was built on.

The declaration shape deliberately mirrors the environment record: apt is a
bare name list, because versions are a function of the pinned snapshot
timestamp and so replaying names at the adopter's timestamp yields versions
consistent with the rest of their environment; the other sources are not
snapshot-pinned, so for them the recorded version is the pin. Cargo is included
because `~/.cargo/bin` binaries ride the backup as files, which makes the cargo
record matter precisely for templates and genuinely fresh homes.

The module imports only pydantic and the standard library, so the publish flow
can validate against the same schema from a worktree that has no virtualenv.

A declared `env.d` unit is now checked against the assembled tree, not just
against its own name. The name rules prove a unit would ship if it existed; a
typo in its path satisfies every one of them and then simply never runs on the
adopter's machine, which is precisely the surprise the manifest is there to
remove.

Parsing is strict, and the `format` field is a wall rather than a hint. The
only thing that parses a manifest is the publish gate, and everything it reads
it is about to write back out, so an unrecognised key is a typo worth failing
on -- `apt_packages` for `apt` would otherwise mean quietly installing nothing.
A manifest declaring a format this workspace does not write is refused with a
plain message naming both versions, instead of a validation dump.

That refusal is what stops an older workspace from re-publishing a newer
template: it would either stamp its own format on tables it never understood,
leaving a file the next reader cannot parse, or drop them and delete what the
template's author declared. Adopting is unaffected -- nothing on that path
parses a manifest, so an agent reads the TOML and makes what it can of it.

`inspiration_manifest.py` becomes `template_manifest.py`, and its models rename
to match (`TemplateManifest`, `TemplateIdentity`, and the rest). The manifest's
`[inspiration]` table is now `[template]`.

Reverts the manifest validator's license check (#407).

`check_unfinished_placeholders` no longer flags a README still carrying the
`MINDS_TEMPLATE_LICENSE` token, because the publish flow no longer writes that
placeholder. Its other checks -- the unreplaced FILL-IN block and the
un-replaced placeholder thumbnail -- are unchanged.

### system/services/oom_priority

- Chat agents can now be shed *before* worker agents once they have gone stale. Previously a chat's memory-shedding band was capped below the worker band, so under memory pressure earlyoom always took a running worker before any chat -- even a chat nobody had messaged in days. That is backwards in the common case: shedding an idle chat costs almost nothing (its transcript stays on disk and readable, and the next message transparently revives it, so the only cost is a slower next message), whereas shedding a running worker destroys in-flight work. The chat band range now straddles the worker band: `CHAT_AGENT_FLOOR` (300, a chat being engaged with right now) through `CHAT_AGENT_BASE` (560, idle but recently used, and still the launch band) up to the new `CHAT_AGENT_STALE_CEILING` (800, untouched long enough to count as abandoned). The ceiling stays below `AGENT_SUBPROCESS` (900), so an agent's own build/test/browser subprocesses are still shed before any agent.

- Engagement and staleness are now combined through a single freshness factor that decays with idle time -- full for the first hour, reaching zero at 24 hours. Engagement bonuses (open tab, visible tab, message recency) are scaled by it, and the remainder lifts the score toward the stale ceiling. The practical effect: a chat with no engagement at all becomes more expendable than a worker after roughly five hours, while an actively-used tab takes most of a day; but presence only *delays* the climb, so a tab left open and untouched for a day still ends at the ceiling. A chat that is mid-turn is exempt entirely -- it is doing work a shed would destroy rather than defer -- and starts aging from when its turn ended.

- The whole schedule is a table of `(idle_seconds, freshness)` points in `bands`, linearly interpolated, so the curve can be reshaped (or made non-linear by adding points) without touching any logic.

- The browser band now holds only the processes that actually hold a browser's memory. The `browser` supervisord program is the *coordinator* -- the daemon that launches and drives Chromium -- and it was being tagged at `SHARED_BROWSER` (1000), the absolute ceiling, which made it the highest-scoring process in the whole workspace and therefore earlyoom's first victim in every memory-pressure episode. Shedding it frees almost nothing (measured: a 125 MB coordinator next to a 1069 MB Chromium tree, none of which was released when it died), and supervisord restarts it straight back into the same session, so it acted as a lightning rod that absorbed sheds without relieving pressure. It now gets an ordinary `SERVICE_BANDS` entry (70, the most expendable built-in service) and `supervisord_program_band("browser")` resolves to that rather than to the browser band.

- `shared_browser_oom_score_adj` now scales Chrome's self-assigned gradation against its real range (0-300, `CHROMIUM_SELF_ASSIGNED_MAX`) instead of 0-1000, so a renderer lands at the ceiling rather than at 937. Under the old scaling every Chromium process was squeezed into the bottom third of the band and the top was left to processes that had merely *inherited* a high value -- which is never a renderer, since a renderer always self-writes.

- The shared `xvfb` display now has a real band (65). Its supervisord command passed `xvfb` to the tagging wrapper, but there was no such key in `SERVICE_BANDS`, so it silently took the unknown-key fallback to `USER_SERVICE` (200) -- which sits *above every built-in service*, making the X display the first service earlyoom would shed. The only signal was a warning on its own stderr, repeated on every restart (21 of them in one workspace, alongside 20 sheds). A new test parses `supervisord.conf` and fails if any key it passes to the wrapper is missing a band, so the next service to hit this is caught in CI rather than months later in a log nobody reads.

- The coverage check now enumerates the programs `supervisord.conf` actually defines (every built-in one, that is -- a program that declares itself user-created by passing the `user` key is exempt, since for it the fallback band is the intended one), rather than the keys passed to the tagging wrapper, and it found three more gaps. Programs that skip the wrapper are not untagged -- the backstop listener tags them from their *program name* instead, and because that path only ever *raises*, a built-in missing from the band maps is not left alone but actively pushed to `USER_SERVICE` (200), above every other built-in. `env-converge` was in exactly that state: the one-shot first-boot provisioner, which runs with `autorestart=false` and whose loss mid-run leaves the rootfs half-provisioned with nothing to finish it, is the program `bands` explicitly documents as needing to stay `PROTECTED` -- but it was being raised to 200 on every boot, because the map still named `deferred-install`, the program it replaced and which no longer exists. `env-converge` and `eval-worker` (also a one-shot, and whose memory lives in the agent and browser processes it spawns rather than in itself) are now `PROTECTED`, and `cron` gets a real service band (55): a shed defers its scheduled jobs rather than losing them, since the every-minute checkers fire at the due hour or the first minute the container is back up.

- `owner-exec` now has a band too (5), and it is the *least* expendable service in the workspace. It was the first service caught by the new test above -- it had shipped with the same silent fallback to `USER_SERVICE` (200) that `xvfb` had, which would have made the owner's SSH-equivalent authority path the first thing shed under memory pressure. A web-only workspace has no desktop and no SSH client, so `owner-exec` is the only way its owner can act on it at all, including to repair whatever else broke; it is also the single writer of the sharing grants for the desktop client, and a small HTTP server whose death frees almost nothing. That puts it below even the terminal.

Remove the `web` entry from SERVICE_BANDS: it steered OOM shedding for the placeholder example server that the browser fleet replaced, so it banded a program that no longer exists. A user service named `web` now gets the ordinary user-service band like any other.

Update the OOM shed bands for the sharing redesign: the cloudflared band is replaced by the share-gateway stack (gateway + caddy + frpc children inherit its band).

### system/services/share_gateway

New `share_gateway` service: the in-workspace half of the self-hosted sharing redesign.

While share materials (`data/.secrets/share.env`, written by the minds app) are present, the runner keeps the whole share stack up: caddy terminating the workspace's real TLS certificate locally (the relay never sees plaintext), an frpc tunnel to the region's relay authenticated by the per-share relay token, and a forward_auth gateway that checks the `imbue_machine_session` cookie, re-reads the owner's grants file on every request (instant revocation; malformed grants fail closed), enforces the WebSocket/non-GET Origin policy, and strips the session cookie before requests reach services.

Visitors without a session are redirected to the accounts broker; the login callback verifies the broker's 60-second audience-bound handoff token (JWKS, nonce, single-use jti) and sets a 24-hour workspace-domain cookie.

The TLS private key is generated in the workspace and never leaves it; the connector signs CSRs via ACME DNS-01, and a daily check renews certificates within 30 days of expiry.

Shared workspaces now hand every backend a trustworthy identity for the request:

- The share gateway sets `X-Share-Owner` (`true`/`false`) on every request, plus `X-Share-Email` carrying the visitor's verified email whenever they are not the owner. caddy strips any client-supplied copy of these headers before authorization and re-injects only the values verified by `/_auth/verify`, so a request can never spoof ownership or an email.

- The owner's email is never sent per-request. Services that need it read `data/.state/share/owner_email`, a file the minds app writes while the workspace is shared and removes when unshared (so its presence also signals that sharing is active).

Embeddable cross-origin workspace sharing for the hosted web client. The share gateway now supports the hosted minds chrome embedding a workspace in a cross-site iframe: an owner fast path, cross-origin session cookies (`SameSite=None; Secure; Partitioned`) so the workspace session is readable inside the iframe, an origin policy that admits the configured chrome origin, health endpoints the chrome can probe, and the injected share materials (including `SHARE_CHROME_ORIGIN`) needed for the workspace's frpc to dial the relay and terminate TLS in-workspace.

Merge main into the self-hosted sharing branch (the share_gateway service lands as described in this PR's sibling entries; its supervisord program follows the relocated oom_tag_service.py path).

Fix WebSocket connections through shared workspaces: caddy's forward_auth copies the client's Connection/Upgrade headers into the auth subrequest, making the gateway's WSGI server reject it with a 400 and deny every WebSocket at the auth step (the terminal panel showed "press enter to reconnect" on shares). The rendered Caddyfile now strips the Upgrade header from the auth subrequest (`header_up -Upgrade`) after capturing it in X-Forwarded-Upgrade for the gateway's WebSocket Origin rule, which stays enforced.

Stop advertising HTTP/3 (Alt-Svc) on shared-workspace responses: h3 is UDP, which the SNI-passthrough relay can never carry, so browsers probed a dead path before falling back. The rendered Caddyfile now restricts the server to h1/h2.

Give every service an unguessable ``<name>-<rand>`` origin label (minted once by forward_port.py and persisted in apps.toml, stable across re-share). On a share the workspace's frpc now claims those explicit labels plus a dedicated ``auth-<rand>`` label instead of the wildcard, so the relay drops any SNI it was not told about -- a scanner that learns the bare workspace domain from Certificate Transparency now reaches nothing. The ``auth-<rand>`` label is the sole origin serving the public ``/_auth/*`` login callback, so every app label owns its full path space; caddy routes each service by its label, adds ``Referrer-Policy: same-origin``, and frpc hot-reloads when a service is registered while shared.

New service: the in-workspace half of the self-hosted sharing redesign, replacing the cloudflared tunnel stack. Idles on data/.secrets/share.env; while sharing is enabled it runs an in-workspace caddy TLS terminator (the key never leaves the workspace; certs come from the connector via CSR + ACME DNS-01), an frpc tunnel to the region relay, and a forward-auth gateway enforcing data/.secrets/share_grants.toml per request (grant edits need no restart or token rotation).

## [minds-v0.3.11] - 2026-08-01

### system

- Bump the Latchkey CLI installed inside workspaces (`LATCHKEY_VERSION` in
  `system/scripts/setup_system.sh`) to 3.3.0, matching the version Minds
  bundles and installs on remote hosts.

setup_system.sh now reloads a running sshd after writing the `60-workspace-root-keys.conf` drop-in. The script moves root's passwd home to /home/user and compensates by pointing sshd at the absolute /root/.ssh/authorized_keys -- but a running sshd listener hands its boot-time config to every future session, so without a reload the stale relative AuthorizedKeysFile resolved against the new home (which has no authorized_keys) and every root login was silently refused from that moment on. In lima mode, where the script runs against a live sshd at first boot, this made every locally-created machine permanently unreachable to mngr ("waiting for system interface to be ready" forever) while perfectly healthy inside; docker image builds run with no sshd up, where the reload is a no-op.

`system/vendor/mngr` is refreshed to the mngr commit that minds 0.3.11 ships, so a workspace's in-VM agent runs the same mngr the desktop binary does.

### system/apps/system_interface

A chat created from the workspace UI could be left permanently stuck on "No conversation data", even though the agent finished being created a second later and was perfectly healthy. The panel now recovers on its own -- no page reload, no tab switch.

`create-chat` returns as soon as the background `mngr create` starts, and the agent is only registered when that finishes, so the new panel's first transcript fetch races ahead of it and gets a 404. That miss was latched and only ever cleared by the next transcript fetch, which the panel never made again for an agent it had already loaded. The panel now retries that fetch when the agent-state broadcast names the agent -- the same registry the transcript endpoint resolves against, so the retry is guaranteed to land rather than being a blind timer.

The creation build log, which is supposed to cover that window, is not a reliable backstop: the frontend holds the proto-agent only between the `proto_agent_created` and `proto_agent_completed` broadcasts, so any delivery lag longer than the creation itself leaves no render in which the cover is up, and the panel drops straight onto the 404.

Two further fixes on the same path:

The "No conversation data" view captured the agent's terminal once per redraw and redrew on every capture, so the loop only stopped if a capture came back with content. For an agent that has one it settles after a handful of requests; for one with no pane to capture it never stops, and was measured at roughly 170 requests per second, each shelling out to tmux. It now captures once per agent.

A `proto_agent_created` that arrives after its agent is already registered no longer strands the panel on a false "Agent creation failed" screen. The build log is now only shown while the agent is not yet a real agent; asking for a finished creation's log gets a "Proto-agent not found" reply, which the panel used to read as a failed creation and keep on screen indefinitely.

Fix two chat-transcript desynchronization bugs (both reproduced live against an imbue cloud workspace), plus diagnostic logging for the investigation:

- A failed snapshot refetch during an SSE reconnect is no longer terminal: it retries with backoff until it succeeds. Previously one failed refetch (typical while the transport was still flapping) left a permanent hole in the transcript -- events emitted during the outage never appeared even though the reconnected stream kept delivering new ones, so the chat silently disagreed with the TUI.

- The transcript window can no longer freeze permanently after such a hole poisoned its offset arithmetic. A forward page that comes back empty now snaps the window's believed start to the tail (the server's authoritative "you are at the end"), so hasMoreAfter cannot stick true forever -- the state that made the client silently discard every incoming live event, spam the events endpoint with the same cursor, and show a stuck "Loading messages..." overlay until a manual page reload. Backfill/forward pages that land after the window changed are discarded (staleness fence), a non-abutting older page is rejected instead of corrupting the window (contiguity guard), and all transcript fetches carry a 30s timeout so a hung request can never pin the panel's single-fetch guard.

- Diagnostic logging: the backend logs every /api/ws connection open/close with a disconnect reason, client_state registrations and layout switches, and SSE stream open/close with a close reason; the 412 layout-op rejection logs and reports the connected-client registry. The frontend logs ([si-ws] / [si-sse] / [si-transcript] console prefixes) WebSocket open/close/reconnect, client_state sends, SSE stream lifecycle, snapshot retries, and discarded stale pages.

## [minds-v0.3.10] - 2026-07-30

### .agents

The `agentic-browser-fleet` skill now notes that, on resume after a human held the browser, the live view may have been resized and the page reflowed -- so every cached element number should be treated as stale and `state` re-run before acting.

The `agentic-browser-fleet` and `manage-layout` skills now tell agents the browser pane is surfaced automatically when the user is watching that chat, so they shouldn't manage it by hand: never open a bare `service:browser` (rejected -- no browser bound); if a user explicitly asks to open one, use `service:browser?session=<name>`; otherwise point them at the "+ -> browser" menu.

- `update-self` now runs the *target* version's own copy of the skill instead of the local one. Once the target ref is resolved, a new `bootstrap-skill` step (`update_self.py`) `git archive`s that ref's skill dir to a fixed staged path (`data/.tasks/update-self/skill-at-target/...`) and the rest of the pass -- lead and worker -- runs from there, so fixes to the update flow itself ship on the way in. The staged path is addressed by literal rather than a shell env var (which didn't survive Claude's fresh-shell-per-command Bash tool and silently fell back to the stale local copy); a ref that predates the skill stages the local copy instead.

- The reveal step for a `service` / `system/supervisord.conf` / `bootstrap` change now prescribes a full services-agent restart (`mngr start --restart system-services`) and forbids the surgical `supervisorctl reread && update`, which doesn't re-run `bootstrap` and so misses `system/libs/bootstrap` changes.

- Fixed the "what's new" collector (`update_self.py changelog-entries`): it scanned only the top-level `changelog/` dir, so it missed every entry under the current bucketed layout (`.agents/changelog/`, `system/changelog/`, `libs/*/changelog/`, ...). It now gathers newly-added entries from every project bucket (excluding the vendored subtree).

The `manage-layout` skill now states up front where its script actually lives: `layout.py` sits at the repo root (`system/scripts/layout.py`, i.e. `/mngr/code/scripts/layout.py`), not inside the skill's own folder. Agents were reading the relative `python3 system/scripts/layout.py ...` commands as skill-relative and looking for a nonexistent `.agents/skills/manage-layout/scripts/layout.py`.

Added a `migrate-workspace` skill: bring everything from another (older, broken, or replaced) workspace into this one -- apps, skills, documents, data, scheduled automations, and every past chat. An old workspace cannot update itself across the tree reorganization and the Debian 12 -> 13 base-image change, so the guidance becomes "create a fresh workspace and have its agent pull the old one in"; this skill is that pull. It is reached by description match alone, worded for how users actually phrase the request, and it has an escape hatch for being asked from the *old* side (it creates the new workspace, then hands off to that workspace's agent).

The flow runs over a live SSH session brokered through the minds API, so the old workspace has to be startable; a source that will not start is handled in prose via a backup export instead. The lead agent gets access with one batched permission request, takes a fresh backup on both sides, checks that this workspace is genuinely fresh, and resolves what the user actually authored by diffing the source against *its own* template base -- which excludes template-version drift by construction. It then surfaces the whole inventory and every question it can up front (collisions, unmerged branches, billing-relevant AI decisions) before dispatching a worker for the transfer, path rewriting, app/job re-registration, and chat recreation.

Everything under the source's data tree comes over, including `anthropic.env` so migrated integrations keep working; only the app-minted `restic.env` and `cloudflare_tunnel.env` are excluded, since each points at the *old* workspace's own resources. Every old agent except the source's primary is recreated dormant via `mngr create --template chat --adopt <session.jsonl>`, keeping its old name and its original creation label, so its full history renders in a tab and a message revives it. Agent-name collisions auto-suffix and are reported; app, skill, and port collisions stop and ask, because that wiring collides for real.

Both sides' pre-flight backups now run in the background, so the lead keeps detecting the layout and building the inventory while they run instead of blocking on them; they are collected just before the worker is dispatched, which is the first step that writes anything.

Supporting material: `references/pre-declutter-layout.md` (the old->new path map for `minds-v0.3.9` and earlier, the substrate deltas, the per-old-skill replacement table, a tour of the capabilities that did not exist then, and the `host-backup-now` hang described below), `references/agent-recreation.md` (the session-adoption mechanics), and `scripts/migrate_workspace.py` (layout detection, baseline diff, agent/branch/port/job enumeration, the latchkey and AI-integration audits, path mapping and reference rewriting, and agent recreation -- each reporting what it could *not* settle, so a partial result never reads as "nothing there").

Documented a pre-declutter source's `host-backup-now`, which can appear to hang for half an hour despite the backup tick having finished. That version ends its wait only on a restic outcome, so a tick that never reaches restic -- most likely one skipped for a missing `restic.env`, which is exactly the "backups were never configured" case Step 3 anticipates -- leaves it polling to its 30-minute default and exiting 2 with no output. The skill now bounds both invocations with an explicit `--timeout`, and the reference explains how to read the tick's real outcome off the service's events log, including where that log lives on a source too old to publish its events-dir pointer.

The `minds-api` skill's headline workflow now points at this skill instead of carrying a thinner version of the same flow, and its description no longer claims migration as its own job.

The `update-self` skill's pre-flight backup step now reads `host-backup-now`'s exit code instead of relying on the printed event: exit 0 is a captured restore point, exit 3 means backups are not configured (so there is no restore point and the user has to be asked before proceeding), exit 1 is a failed backup attempt, and exit 2 means the outcome could not be observed at all. Previously the step could also stall for the command's full 30-minute timeout when backups were not configured; `host-backup-now` now returns as soon as the tick resolves.

`update-self` no longer updates a workspace past the version of the Minds app running it.

The workspace template ships the code the app talks to (the system interface, the vendored `mngr`), so a workspace that pulled a template newer than its app would be speaking a protocol the app doesn't know. The update flow now reads the app's own version (`GET /api/v1/app/version`, allowed for every workspace by default -- no permission prompt) and caps the default target at the newest release at or below it. When the app is running a dev branch rather than a release, there is nothing to compare against and nothing is capped.

If the app can't be reached at all -- it's closed, the gateway is down, or it's too old to report its version -- the update stops with a plain-language reason instead of proceeding uncapped, since an app that can't answer is often exactly the app a newer template would outrun.

An explicit `--override` still works, but one naming a version newer than the app (or a branch/commit whose version can't be compared) now surfaces for confirmation before anything is merged, and the approval message says when a newer release was held back so you know that updating the app unlocks it.

Asking for an update when your workspace is already on the newest version it may take now tells you so, instead of running a whole update pass -- backup, isolated copy, validation -- that merges nothing. Which of the two things it means is spelled out: either you are simply current, or a newer release exists and your Minds app is what is holding it back, in which case updating the app is what gets it for you. A workspace that is *behind* the version its app supports still updates to it as before -- being capped is not the same as having nothing to gain.

A changelog entry arriving in an update is now treated as documentation wherever it lives. Previously only a top-level one was: an entry under a service or skill directory inherited that directory's go-live action, so a release's own release notes could restart a service or be run through a dependency analysis. Every release ships such entries, so this happened on nearly every update.

A ceiling is now parsed as a full semantic version rather than only as a stable release, so an app running a release candidate (`minds-v0.4.0-rc1`) caps its workspaces like any other -- previously such a ceiling parsed as "not a stable tag" and was treated as *no ceiling at all*, letting a workspace update arbitrarily far past that app. Prereleases order below the release they precede, so an rc1 ceiling admits the prior release but not the final one. Capping by a prerelease does not make prereleases selectable: the default target is still only ever a stable release.

Update the wording of the Latchkey skill to reflect changes related to per-account permissions.

The `use-ai-integration` skill's keyed (litellm/direct-HTTP) path now resolves credentials from the shared Claude `settings.json` env block at call time (`read_workspace_ai_credentials()` in `claude_p.py`) instead of `os.environ`, so services pick up workspace auth changes without restarts. The skill docs and `references/billing-and-credentialing.md` describe the settings-env credential contract.

Keyed integrations now pin their key at setup: the skill instructs snapshotting `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (+ `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, never the subscription oauth token) into `data/.secrets/anthropic.env` via the new `write_anthropic_env_snapshot()` helper, and `read_workspace_ai_credentials()` resolves that snapshot first (then the settings env, then the process env). A built service therefore keeps billing against the key it was set up with when the user later switches the workspace's sign-in; the user asks the agent to rewrite or delete the snapshot to re-key or retire integrations.
